      Start

      How this guide works

      What the guide covers, how each module is laid out, how to use the practice problems and tools, and a few suggested routes through the material.

      This guide teaches digital hardware from the bottom up. It starts with how a voltage on a wire comes to stand for a 0 or a 1, builds through logic gates, arithmetic circuits, memory elements and state machines, and arrives at processors, memory systems, microcontrollers and GPUs. Along the way it covers the electrical layer (circuits, transistors, CMOS, interfacing between chips) and the implementation layer (Verilog, power, heat and the chip design flow). No prior hardware knowledge is assumed, but the explanations are written to be precise rather than casual: every term is defined, every formula is derived or justified, and worked examples show each method step by step.

      Part I: Foundations: information as bits

      The digital abstraction

      Why hardware represents information with two voltage bands, the four thresholds that make that reliable, how switches compute logic functions, how much information n bits can hold, and how time enters through gate delay and the clock.

      Practice15 problems

      Every digital system rests on one decision: a continuously varying physical quantity, almost always a voltage, is interpreted as one of only two symbols, 0 and 1. That decision throws away most of the information a voltage could carry, and in exchange makes computation reliable, composable and cheap to build at enormous scale. This module covers the rules that make the decision work: the voltage thresholds that define a valid 0 and 1, the noise margins between them, the way each gate restores a degraded signal, how networks of switches compute logic functions, and how propagation delay and the clock bring time into the picture.

      Analog and digital signals

      A signal is a physical quantity whose value carries information. In electronics it is usually the voltage of a circuit node measured relative to a shared reference node called ground (0 V). How the value is interpreted is what separates analog from digital.

      Analog signal

      A signal whose information is carried by its exact value. Every voltage in the allowed range has a distinct meaning, so any disturbance of the voltage changes the information it carries.

      Digital signal

      A signal whose range is divided into a small number of bands, each mapped to one symbol. A binary digital signal has two bands, read as 0 and 1, separated by a band of voltages that no valid signal may occupy. Small disturbances that keep the voltage inside its band do not change the information.

      A microphone output, a thermistor divider and an audio line are analog: 0.731 V and 0.734 V mean different things. The output of a logic gate is digital: on a 3.3 V system, 3.1 V and 3.3 V both mean 1. The price is that each wire carries far less information (one bit instead of a precise value), so a digital system needs many wires or many time steps to move the same information. The benefit is that information survives noise, copying and long chains of processing without degrading, as long as no disturbance pushes a voltage across into another band.

      Two bands are used rather than three or ten because, for a fixed supply voltage, two bands give the widest possible separation between symbols, and because the circuit that decides between them can be as simple as one transistor that is either on or off. Some systems do use more levels where density matters more than margin: multi-level-cell flash stores 2 to 4 bits per cell as 4 to 16 charge levels, and fast serial links use PAM4 signaling (4 voltage levels, 2 bits per symbol). Both pay for the density with smaller margins and more complex receivers.

      The four thresholds and noise margins

      To make "a high voltage means 1" precise, every logic family specifies four voltages. Two are promises made by an output (the driver) and two are promises made by an input (the receiver).

      SymbolBelongs toMeaning
      VOHdriver outputthe lowest voltage the output is guaranteed to produce when it drives a 1
      VOLdriver outputthe highest voltage the output is guaranteed to produce when it drives a 0
      VIHreceiver inputthe lowest input voltage guaranteed to be read as 1
      VILreceiver inputthe highest input voltage guaranteed to be read as 0

      An input voltage between VIL and VIH is in the forbidden (undefined) region: the receiver may read it as 0, as 1, or inconsistently, and a CMOS input held there draws extra current because both of its transistors are partly on. The exact switching point inside that band varies with temperature, supply voltage and manufacturing, which is why datasheets only guarantee behavior outside it.

      The noise margins follow directly from the four thresholds:

      NMH = VOH − VIH (margin for a 1) NML = VIL − VOL (margin for a 0)

      For the levels above, NMH = 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 V and NML = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 V. If both margins are positive, the driver's output is always inside what the receiver accepts. If either is negative, the two parts are not compatible without something between them, such as a level shifter or a pull-up resistor (Module 13).

      Worked example

      Checking two parts from different families

      Device A has VOH = 3.4 V, VOL = 0.5 V, VIH = 3.3 V, VIL = 1.0 V. Device B has VOH = 3.2 V, VOL = 0.6 V, VIH = 3.0 V, VIL = 0.7 V. Can A drive B, and can B drive A?

      A drives B. Compare A's output guarantees with B's input requirements: NMH = 3.4 − 3.0 = 0.4 V and NML = 0.7 − 0.5 = 0.2 V. Both positive, so this direction works, with the low state the weaker one.

      B drives A. NMH = 3.2 − 3.3 = −0.1 V. A valid 1 from B can be as low as 3.2 V, which is below the 3.3 V that A needs to be sure it sees a 1. This direction fails even with zero noise. (NML = 1.0 − 0.6 = 0.4 V is fine, but one failing margin is enough.)

      Compatibility is directional: always compare the driver's VOH and VOL with the receiver's VIH and VIL.

      Common mistake

      Pairing the four numbers from the same device. VOH − VIH of a single chip says nothing about a link; a noise margin always pairs one device's output thresholds with another device's input thresholds. A second common slip is reversing the inequality for the low state: the driver's VOL must be below the receiver's VIL.

      Restoration: why noise does not accumulate

      Noise margins explain why a single link is reliable. The deeper reason digital systems scale to billions of gates is restoration: the output of a logic gate is not a copy of its input. The input only controls whether the output is connected to the supply rail or to ground, and the output voltage comes from that rail. A degraded input such as 2.6 V on a 5 V system (a valid but weak 1) therefore produces a full-strength output near 5 V, and the next gate receives a fresh, clean signal.

      Compare a chain of analog amplifiers. Each stage adds a little noise of its own, and nothing removes the noise from earlier stages; with independent noise of 1 mV rms per stage, a 1000-stage chain ends with about √1000 × 1 mV ≈ 32 mV rms of accumulated noise. A chain of 1000 logic gates with 0.4 V margins makes an error only if a single stage sees a disturbance larger than 0.4 V, which for 1 mV rms noise is a 400-standard-deviation event. This is the property that lets a processor push data through thousands of gate levels every nanosecond without losing it.

      Where V_IL and V_IH come from going deeper

      Plot a gate's output voltage against its input voltage and you get its voltage transfer characteristic (VTC). A useful logic gate has a VTC that is flat near both rails and steep in the middle: small input changes near 0 or VDD barely move the output, while in the transition region the gain magnitude exceeds 1.

      The requirement that the gain magnitude exceed 1 somewhere is what makes restoration possible: a gate with gain below 1 everywhere would shrink every signal it passed. Module 12 derives the VTC of the CMOS inverter, the circuit that sets these thresholds in nearly every digital chip today.

      Computing with switches

      The simplest device that turns logic into hardware is a controlled switch: closed (conducting) when its control input is 1, open when it is 0. Connect switches between a voltage source and a lamp and the lamp computes a function of the controls.

      Series: AND

      ABlamp
      000
      010
      100
      111

      Parallel: OR

      ABlamp
      000
      011
      101
      111

      Series and parallel combinations nest: A in series with (B in parallel with C) conducts when A·(B + C) = 1. Given switches controlled by each variable and by its complement, a series-parallel network can implement any logic function. Claude Shannon showed this correspondence between relay circuits and Boolean algebra in 1937, and it is still the organizing idea of transistor-level design.

      In a chip, the switches are MOSFETs. An NMOS transistor conducts when its gate voltage is high; a PMOS transistor conducts when its gate voltage is low. One difference from the lamp circuit matters: a logic gate must actively drive its output to both values, so every CMOS gate has a network of switches that connects the output to the supply when the function is 1 and a complementary network that connects it to ground when the function is 0. Module 12 builds every gate this way.

      Combinational logic

      Logic whose outputs depend only on the present values of its inputs. Given the same inputs it always produces the same outputs, after a short delay.

      Sequential logic

      Logic whose outputs depend on its present inputs and on stored state, which summarizes past inputs. It contains memory elements such as latches and flip-flops.

      Bits and the size of information

      One binary digit, a bit, has 2 possible values. Two bits have 4 combinations (00, 01, 10, 11), three bits have 8, and in general each added bit doubles the count.

      Key idea

      n bits can represent 2n distinct patterns. To give a distinct code to each of N different things you need at least ⌈log2 N⌉ bits, where ⌈ ⌉ means round up to the next integer.

      Examples: 26 letters need ⌈log2 26⌉ = 5 bits (24 = 16 is too few, 25 = 32 is enough). One million items need 20 bits, since 220 = 1,048,576. A memory with 65,536 locations needs 16 address bits. Note that the bits only give each item a distinct pattern; what the pattern means is a separate decision, covered in Module 2.

      GroupSizePatterns
      bit12
      nibble4 bits (one hex digit)16
      byte8 bits256
      wordthe natural width of a processor's registers: 8 bits on an AVR microcontroller, 32 or 64 on most CPUs232 ≈ 4.29 × 109, 264 ≈ 1.84 × 1019

      Bits within a group are numbered from the right starting at 0. Bit 0 is the least significant bit (LSB) and bit n − 1 is the most significant bit (MSB). Memory capacities usually use binary multiples: 1 KiB = 210 = 1024 bytes, 1 MiB = 220 bytes, 1 GiB = 230 bytes. Storage vendors and communication rates use decimal multiples instead: 1 GB = 109 bytes, 1 Gb/s = 109 bits per second. The gap grows with size, which is why a "500 GB" drive appears as about 466 GiB.

      Time: propagation delay and levels of logic

      A gate's output does not change the instant its input does. The transistors must charge or discharge the capacitance of the wire and of every gate input connected to the output, and that takes time (Module 10 shows the RC behavior behind it).

      Propagation delay

      tpd: the maximum time from an input change to the moment the output has settled at its new valid value. Its companion, the contamination delay tcd, is the minimum time from an input change until the output first starts to change.

      Delays add along a path. If a signal passes through a NAND gate (15 ps), then a NOR gate (20 ps), then an inverter (8 ps), the path delay is 43 ps. The levels of logic of a circuit is the largest number of gates on any path from an input to an output; the path with the largest total delay is the critical path, and it determines how soon the circuit's outputs can be trusted after its inputs change. Reducing levels of logic, at the cost of more gates or larger gates, is one of the basic trade-offs in digital design (Module 6 and Module 9 show examples).

      Clocks and synchronous design

      Most digital systems coordinate their storage elements with a clock, a square wave that alternates between 0 and 1 at a fixed rate. Registers sample their inputs only at clock edges, so all stored state changes at (nearly) the same instant, and between edges the combinational logic has time to settle.

      • The period T is the time for one full cycle; the frequency is f = 1/T, measured in hertz (cycles per second).
      • The rising edge is the 0 → 1 transition and the falling edge is 1 → 0. Most designs capture data on rising edges.
      • The duty cycle is the fraction of each period that the signal is high: a signal high for 2 ns of every 8 ns has a 25% duty cycle.
      FrequencyPeriod
      1 kHz1 ms
      1 MHz1 µs
      16 MHz62.5 ns
      100 MHz10 ns
      1 GHz1 ns
      2.5 GHz400 ps

      Key idea

      A synchronous circuit works only if every signal launched at one clock edge has settled before the next edge arrives. The clock period must therefore be longer than the slowest register-to-register path. Module 17 turns this into exact setup and hold equations.

      At high frequencies the physical size of a chip matters too. Light travels about 12 cm in 400 ps in vacuum, and on-chip wires carry signals far more slowly than that because of their resistance and capacitance, so a long wire can consume a large part of a clock period. This is one reason fast designs keep critical logic physically close together and why the clock itself is distributed through a carefully balanced tree of buffers.

      Levels of abstraction

      No one designs a chip with tens of billions of transistors by thinking about transistors. Hardware is designed as a stack of layers, each of which hides the details of the one below behind a simpler contract. The digital abstraction in this module is one such contract: above it, a wire carries a 0 or a 1 and nothing else.

      LayerUnit of designCovered in
      Devicestransistors, wires, capacitanceModule 12, Module 10
      CircuitsCMOS gates, latches, memory cellsModule 12, Module 21
      Logicgates, Boolean functionsModule 5 to Module 7
      Register-transfer leveladders, muxes, registers, state machinesModule 8 to Module 16, Module 27
      Microarchitecturedatapaths, pipelines, cachesModule 18 to Module 20
      Instruction setinstructions, registers, memory modelModule 18
      System and softwareprograms, interrupts, driversModule 23 to Module 26

      Abstractions leak. A noise margin violated by a long cable, a gate delay that breaks a timing constraint, or a hot chip that slows down are all lower layers showing through. Much of hardware engineering consists of knowing when an abstraction can be trusted and when it cannot.

      Summary

      • A binary digital signal maps two voltage bands to 0 and 1 with a forbidden band between them.
      • VOH and VOL are output guarantees; VIH and VIL are input requirements. NMH = VOH − VIH and NML = VIL − VOL, always pairing a driver with a receiver.
      • Gates restore signals to full swing, so noise does not accumulate through long chains of logic.
      • Switches in series compute AND and in parallel compute OR; transistors are voltage-controlled switches.
      • n bits give 2n patterns; N items need ⌈log2 N⌉ bits.
      • Gate delays add along a path; the critical path sets how long a circuit takes to settle, and the clock period must exceed it.

      Practice problems

      Which of these are digital signals? (a) the voltage across a thermistor in a thermostat, (b) the output of a logic gate, (c) the sound-pressure signal from a microphone, (d) the voltage on one data line of a memory bus.

      Solution

      (b) and (d). A gate output and a bus data line are interpreted only as 0 or 1. The thermistor voltage and the microphone signal carry information in their exact values, so they are analog. (The thermostat may later convert its analog voltage to a digital number with an ADC.)

      Which two of VOH, VOL, VIH, VIL are guarantees made by a driver, and which two are requirements of a receiver? For each, say whether it is a minimum or a maximum.

      Solution

      Driver guarantees: VOH is the minimum voltage of a driven 1, and VOL is the maximum voltage of a driven 0. Receiver requirements: VIH is the minimum input voltage read as 1, and VIL is the maximum input voltage read as 0.

      How many distinct patterns do 12 bits have? How many bits are needed to give each of 1000 items its own code?

      Solution

      212 = 4096 patterns. For 1000 items: 29 = 512 is too few and 210 = 1024 is enough, so 10 bits.

      A logic family has VOH = 2.7 V, VOL = 0.5 V, VIH = 2.0 V and VIL = 0.8 V. Compute both noise margins for one gate of this family driving another. Which logic state is more vulnerable to noise?

      Solution

      NMH = 2.7 − 2.0 = 0.7 V; NML = 0.8 − 0.5 = 0.3 V. The low state is more vulnerable: a disturbance of just over 0.3 V can push a driven 0 into the undefined band.

      A 5 V CMOS receiver needs VIH = 3.5 V and VIL = 1.5 V. It is driven by a TTL output with VOH = 2.4 V and VOL = 0.4 V. Is the connection reliable? If not, which state fails?

      Solution

      NML = 1.5 − 0.4 = 1.1 V, fine. NMH = 2.4 − 3.5 = −1.1 V: a valid TTL high can be far below what the CMOS input needs, so the high state fails. Common fixes are a pull-up resistor to 5 V on the line (which raises the high level when the TTL output stops pulling up), or a receiver from a TTL-compatible CMOS family (such as 74HCT) whose VIH is 2.0 V.

      Using the two devices from the worked example (A: VOH 3.4, VOL 0.5, VIH 3.3, VIL 1.0; B: VOH 3.2, VOL 0.6, VIH 3.0, VIL 0.7, all in volts), can device B drive another device B? Give both margins.

      Solution

      Pair B's outputs with B's inputs: NMH = 3.2 − 3.0 = 0.2 V, NML = 0.7 − 0.6 = 0.1 V. Both positive, so yes, but with small margins; 0.1 V of noise on a low is enough to cause trouble.

      A switch controlled by A is in series with a parallel pair of switches controlled by B and C, all between a source and a lamp. Write the Boolean expression for "the lamp is on" and list the input combinations that light it.

      Solution

      Lamp = A·(B + C). It is on when A = 1 and at least one of B, C is 1: ABC = 101, 110, 111.

      A clock runs at 1.6 GHz. What is its period? A second signal is high for 2 ns and low for 6 ns, repeating. What are its frequency and duty cycle?

      Solution

      T = 1 / 1.6 × 109 = 625 ps. The second signal has period 8 ns, so f = 1 / 8 ns = 125 MHz, and it is high 2 of every 8 ns: a 25% duty cycle.

      A drive is sold as 500 GB (decimal gigabytes). How large is it in GiB? A memory is 16 GiB; how many address bits does it need if every byte has its own address?

      Solution

      500 × 109 / 230 = 500 × 109 / 1,073,741,824 ≈ 465.7 GiB. 16 GiB = 24 × 230 = 234 bytes, so 34 address bits.

      Circuit Y = NOT(NOR(NAND(A, B), C)) uses gates with tpd of 15 ps (NAND), 20 ps (NOR) and 8 ps (inverter). How many levels of logic does it have, what is the delay of each input-to-output path, and what is the critical path?

      Solution

      Three levels (NAND, NOR, inverter). Paths from A and from B pass through all three gates: 15 + 20 + 8 = 43 ps. The path from C skips the NAND: 20 + 8 = 28 ps. The critical paths are A → Y and B → Y at 43 ps; the output cannot be trusted until 43 ps after any input changes.

      A gate input that is not connected to anything measures 1.6 V on a system with VIL = 0.8 V and VIH = 2.0 V. What is the gate's output, and what else goes wrong? How is this prevented?

      Hint

      Think about what both transistors of a CMOS input stage do when the gate voltage is midway between the rails.

      Solution

      The output is undefined: 1.6 V is in the forbidden band, so the gate may read 0 or 1 and can change its mind as the floating node drifts with nearby noise. In a CMOS input, a mid-level voltage turns both the pull-up PMOS and the pull-down NMOS partly on, so current flows straight from supply to ground and the gate wastes power and heats up. The fix is never to leave an input floating: tie unused inputs to a rail, and give any input that can be disconnected (a button, a connector) a pull-up or pull-down resistor that sets a defined default level.

      Using only switches, each controlled by one of A, A′, B or B′, draw (or describe) a network that conducts exactly when A ⊕ B = 1.

      Solution

      A ⊕ B = A·B′ + A′·B. Build each product as a series pair and put the two pairs in parallel: (switch A in series with switch B′) in parallel with (switch A′ in series with switch B). The first branch conducts for A = 1, B = 0 and the second for A = 0, B = 1. That is four switches, the same count as the pull-down network of a CMOS XOR built from complemented inputs.

      A register-to-register path contains 12 gates of 25 ps each, and the registers add 60 ps of their own overhead per cycle. What is the highest clock frequency at which this path works?

      Solution

      The signal needs 12 × 25 + 60 = 360 ps per cycle, so T ≥ 360 ps and fmax = 1 / 360 ps ≈ 2.78 GHz. Shortening the path to 8 gates would allow T = 260 ps, about 3.85 GHz.

      A signal crosses a cable on which up to 0.35 V of noise can couple, in either direction. The driver has VOH = 2.9 V and VOL = 0.45 V; the receiver has VIH = 2.3 V and VIL = 0.8 V. Is the link reliable? If not, give two different ways to fix it and say what each changes.

      Solution

      NMH = 2.9 − 2.3 = 0.6 V, which covers 0.35 V of noise. NML = 0.8 − 0.45 = 0.35 V, exactly equal to the worst-case noise: zero remaining margin, so the link is not reliable (any extra disturbance, a supply droop or ground offset between the two ends causes errors). Fixes: (1) a driver with a lower VOL, for example one that sinks more current or is less loaded, which increases NML directly; (2) a receiver with hysteresis (a Schmitt-trigger input), whose effective VIL for a falling input is lower but which will not chatter on noise; (3) reduce the noise itself with shielding, a shorter cable or differential signaling, where the receiver looks at the difference between two wires and common noise cancels.

      Explain quantitatively why a chain of 1000 inverters reproduces its input faithfully while a chain of 1000 unity-gain analog amplifiers does not, assuming each stage adds independent noise of 2 mV rms and the logic family has 0.3 V noise margins.

      Solution

      Analog chain: nothing removes noise once added, and independent noise adds in power, so after 1000 stages the noise is √1000 × 2 mV ≈ 63 mV rms, and the signal's exact value, which is the information, is corrupted. Digital chain: each inverter re-derives its output from the supply rails, so the noise seen at each input is only the noise added since the previous stage, about 2 mV rms. An error needs a single-stage excursion of 0.3 V, i.e. 150 standard deviations, an event with essentially zero probability. The digital chain therefore has a practically zero error rate; it still delays the signal, by 1000 × tpd.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Module02of 28

      Part I: Foundations: information as bits

      Number systems and codes

      Positional notation in any base, exact conversion methods for integers and fractions, hex and octal shorthand, how many bits a quantity needs, and the codes hardware uses besides plain binary: BCD, ASCII, Gray, one-hot and parity.

      Builds onDigital abstractionToolsNumber converterPractice16 problems

      A group of bits has no meaning by itself. The pattern 01000001 is the number 65 to an adder, the letter A to a terminal, the two decimal digits 41 to a BCD display driver, and a set of eight independent on/off flags to a peripheral register. This module covers the most important way of giving bits meaning, positional binary numbers, and the conversions between binary, decimal, octal and hexadecimal that every hardware engineer does constantly. It then covers the other codes digital systems use and why each exists.

      Bits plus context

      Key idea

      Information = bits + context. Hardware stores and moves patterns; the interpretation of a pattern is a convention shared by whoever writes it and whoever reads it. The same adder adds unsigned and signed numbers, and the same memory stores text and machine instructions. Most bugs at the hardware–software boundary are two parties disagreeing about context: signed versus unsigned, byte order, or units.

      Positional number systems

      In a positional system with radix (base) r, each digit position has a weight that is a power of r, and a number's value is the sum of each digit times its weight. Digits range from 0 to r − 1. Positions to the left of the radix point have weights r0, r1, r2, …; positions to the right have weights r−1, r−2, ….

      value = dn−1·rn−1 + … + d1·r1 + d0·r0 + d−1·r−1 + d−2·r−2 + …
      SystemRadixDigitsWritten in this guideIn C, C++ and Verilog
      Binary20, 110112 or 0b10110b1011 (C23, C++14, GCC), 4'b1011 (Verilog)
      Octal80 to 761580615 (a leading zero), 9'o615
      Decimal100 to 9397397, 10'd397
      Hexadecimal160 to 9, A to F0x18D or 18D160x18D, 12'h18D

      Hexadecimal needs sixteen digit symbols, so A through F stand for 10 through 15. Each binary position doubles in weight moving left (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …) and halves moving right (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, …).

      Common mistake

      In C and C++, an integer literal that starts with 0 is octal. int x = 010; sets x to 8, and int y = 09; does not compile because 9 is not an octal digit. Never pad decimal constants with leading zeros in C.

      Converting to decimal

      Multiply each digit by its weight and add. This works for any base and for fractional parts.

      Worked example

      Binary, octal and hex to decimal

      1110.012 = 8 + 4 + 2 + 0 + 0·½ + 1·¼ = 14.25.

      6158 = 6·64 + 1·8 + 5·1 = 384 + 8 + 5 = 397.

      0x2C = 2·16 + 12·1 = 44. 0x1F4 = 1·256 + 15·16 + 4 = 256 + 240 + 4 = 500.

      For binary, it is faster to add only the weights of the 1 bits. With practice you read 8-bit patterns directly: 1100 1000 is 128 + 64 + 8 = 200.

      Converting from decimal

      Integer part: repeated division (or subtracting powers)

      Divide by the target radix repeatedly. Each remainder is the next digit, starting with the least significant, and you stop when the quotient reaches 0. Reading the remainders from last to first gives the number.

      Worked example

      397 to base 8 and 156 to binary

      397 ÷ 8 = 49 remainder 5; 49 ÷ 8 = 6 remainder 1; 6 ÷ 8 = 0 remainder 6. Reading upward: 6158.

      156 ÷ 2 = 78 r 0, 78 ÷ 2 = 39 r 0, 39 ÷ 2 = 19 r 1, 19 ÷ 2 = 9 r 1, 9 ÷ 2 = 4 r 1, 4 ÷ 2 = 2 r 0, 2 ÷ 2 = 1 r 0, 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Reading upward: 1001 11002 = 0x9C.

      For binary there is an equivalent method that many people find faster, sometimes called "making change": subtract the largest power of two that fits, write a 1 in that position, and repeat with the remainder. 156 = 128 + 28 = 128 + 16 + 12 = 128 + 16 + 8 + 4, so bits 7, 4, 3 and 2 are 1: 1001 1100. The division method is the one that works for any radix.

      Fractional part: repeated multiplication

      Multiply the fraction by the radix. The integer part of the product is the next digit (most significant first); keep the fractional part and repeat. Stop when the fraction becomes 0 or you have enough digits.

      Worked example

      4.375 and 0.1 to binary

      Integer part: 4 = 1002. Fraction 0.375: 0.375 × 2 = 0.75; 0.75 × 2 = 1.5; 0.5 × 2 = 1.0, done. Reading downward: .011, so 4.375 = 100.0112. Check: 4 + ¼ + ⅛ = 4.375.

      0.1: 0.2 → 0, 0.4 → 0, 0.8 → 0, 1.6 → 1, 1.2 → 1, 0.4 → 0, 0.8 → 0, 1.6 → 1, 1.2 → 1, … The pattern 0011 repeats forever: 0.110 = 0.0 0011 0011 0011…2.

      Key idea

      A fraction has a finite binary expansion only if its denominator, in lowest terms, is a power of two. 0.375 = 3/8 terminates; 0.1 = 1/10 does not, because 10 has a factor of 5. That is why 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in any binary floating-point format (Module 4).

      Hexadecimal and octal: shorthand for binary

      Because 16 = 24 and 8 = 23, each hex digit corresponds to exactly 4 bits and each octal digit to exactly 3 bits. Conversion is therefore a matter of grouping, with no arithmetic. Group outward from the radix point: to the left for the integer part and to the right for the fraction, padding the outermost groups with zeros.

      Hex0123456789ABCDEF
      Binary0000000100100011010001010110011110001001101010111100110111101111

      Worked example

      One number in three bases

      101001110.112.

      Hex, groups of 4 from the point: integer 1 0100 1110 → 0001 0100 1110 = 1 4 E; fraction .11 → .1100 = .C. Result: 14E.C16.

      Octal, groups of 3: integer 101 001 110 = 5 1 6; fraction .110 = .6. Result: 516.68.

      Check in decimal: 0x14E = 256 + 64 + 14 = 334 and 0.C16 = 12/16 = 0.75, so 334.75; 5168 = 320 + 8 + 6 = 334 and 0.68 = 6/8 = 0.75. All three agree.

      To convert between octal and hex, go through binary: 6158 → 110 001 101 → regroup by 4 from the right → 1 1000 1101 → 0x18D.

      Common mistake

      Grouping from the wrong end. In 1 0100 1110 the lone 1 on the left is the most significant group; grouping from the left instead (1010 0111 0) shifts every bit and gives a wrong value. Always start at the radix point.

      Powers of two and estimation

      n2nname
      8256values in a byte
      101,024Ki (about a thousand)
      124,096a common page size in bytes
      1665,536values in 16 bits
      201,048,576Mi (about a million)
      2416,777,216colors in 24-bit RGB
      301,073,741,824Gi (about a billion)
      324,294,967,296values in 32 bits
      641.8 × 1019values in 64 bits

      The approximation 210 ≈ 103 makes mental estimates easy: split the exponent into tens and a remainder. 237 = 27 × 230 ≈ 128 × 109, so a 37-bit address reaches about 128 billion bytes (exactly 128 GiB). In the other direction, log2(106) ≈ 20 and log2(109) ≈ 30.

      How many values, how many bits

      With n digits in radix r there are rn distinct combinations: 3 hex digits give 163 = 4096 combinations and 4 decimal digits give 104 = 10,000. For binary, n bits give 2n combinations, so an unsigned n-bit number ranges from 0 to 2n − 1.

      Worked example

      Minimum number of bits

      A sensor reports one of 384 distinct values. 28 = 256 is too few and 29 = 512 is enough, so it needs 9 bits. Note that the answer depends on the number of distinct values, not on the largest value: if the readings were the 384 even numbers from 0 to 766, they would still need only 9 bits with the right encoding (store the reading divided by 2).

      Other codes

      Binary-coded decimal (BCD)

      BCD stores each decimal digit in its own 4-bit group, using only the patterns 0000 to 1001. 439 in BCD is 0100 0011 1001, while 439 in binary is 1 1011 0111. BCD uses more bits (12 instead of 9 here) and needs special arithmetic: when a digit sum exceeds 9, the adder adds 6 to skip the six unused patterns. Its advantage is that each digit can drive a display or be printed without division. Clocks, calculators, real-time-clock chips and some financial software use it.

      ASCII and Unicode

      ASCII assigns 7-bit codes (stored in a byte) to 128 characters: control codes, digits, upper and lower case letters and punctuation. The layout is designed so that common operations are cheap:

      CharacterHexDecimalNote
      '\0' (NUL)0x000terminates C strings
      '\n' (LF)0x0A10line feed
      '\r' (CR)0x0D13carriage return
      ' ' (space)0x2032first printable character
      '0' … '9'0x30 … 0x3948 … 57digit value = code − 0x30
      'A' … 'Z'0x41 … 0x5A65 … 90
      'a' … 'z'0x61 … 0x7A97 … 122differs from upper case only in bit 5 (0x20)

      Converting a digit character to its value is c - '0'; the reverse is v + '0'. Upper and lower case differ in bit 5 only, so c | 0x20 lowercases a letter, c & ~0x20 uppercases it, and c ^ 0x20 toggles case. A character in C is just a small integer: 'H' + 1 == 'I', and char c = 72; stores the letter H. These facts matter whenever you print numbers to a display that only accepts characters (Module 26).

      Unicode extends the idea to more than a million code points covering every writing system. Its usual encoding, UTF-8, uses 1 to 4 bytes per character and is backward compatible with ASCII: every ASCII byte means the same thing in UTF-8.

      Gray code

      In a Gray code, consecutive values differ in exactly one bit. The standard (reflected) Gray code is built by taking the n−1-bit sequence, writing it forward with a 0 prefix, then backward with a 1 prefix. For 3 bits: 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100.

      Decimal01234567
      Binary000001010011100101110111
      Gray000001011010110111101100

      Conversion: binary to Gray is g = b ^ (b >> 1) (each Gray bit is the XOR of two adjacent binary bits). Gray to binary goes from the MSB down: the binary MSB equals the Gray MSB, and each next binary bit is the previous binary bit XOR the current Gray bit. Gray codes are used where a value is read while it changes, so that a reading taken mid-transition is wrong by at most one step: rotary and shaft encoders, counters passed between clock domains (Module 17), and the row and column labels of Karnaugh maps (Module 7).

      One-hot and thermometer codes

      A one-hot code uses n bits for n values, with exactly one bit set: 0001, 0010, 0100, 1000. It wastes bits but makes decoding trivial (each bit is its own "is it value k?" signal), which is why decoder outputs and fast state machines use it (Module 16). A thermometer code sets the lowest k bits to represent k (0000, 0001, 0011, 0111, 1111) and appears in flash ADCs.

      Parity

      A parity bit is one extra bit chosen so that the total number of 1s is even (even parity) or odd (odd parity). For even parity the parity bit is the XOR of all data bits. If any single bit flips in storage or transmission, the count changes from even to odd and the receiver detects the error, though it cannot tell which bit flipped. More generally, a code whose valid words all differ in at least d bit positions (its minimum Hamming distance) can detect d − 1 errors and correct ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋. Parity has distance 2; the ECC used in server memory has distance 4 (correct 1, detect 2).

      Integers in C and C++

      Hardware fixes the width of every register, and C code that touches hardware should say exactly how wide each variable is. The plain types do not: int is 16 bits on an 8-bit AVR microcontroller and 32 bits on a desktop, and whether char is signed depends on the compiler. The fixed-width types from <stdint.h> (<cstdint> in C++) remove the ambiguity:

      TypeWidthRange
      uint8_t80 to 255
      int8_t8−128 to 127
      uint16_t160 to 65,535
      int16_t16−32,768 to 32,767
      uint32_t320 to 4,294,967,295
      int32_t32−2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647
      uint8_t  reg  = 0x41;        // exactly 8 bits: fits an 8-bit peripheral register
char     c    = reg;         // the same bits, now read as the character 'A'
uint16_t big  = 0x18D;       // 397
uint32_t mask = 1u << 31;    // 'u' makes the constant unsigned so bit 31 is well defined

      In practice

      Datasheets give register addresses and bit masks in hex, and debuggers display memory in hex, because each hex digit maps to 4 bits you can read off directly. Fluency in hex ↔ binary is the single most used skill in embedded and hardware debugging; aim to convert any byte in your head.

      Summary

      • Value = Σ digit × radixposition, with negative positions after the radix point.
      • Decimal to radix r: divide repeatedly for the integer part (remainders, least significant first) and multiply repeatedly for the fraction (integer parts, most significant first).
      • Hex = 4 bits per digit, octal = 3; group outward from the radix point.
      • n digits of radix r give rn combinations; N values need ⌈log2 N⌉ bits.
      • BCD, ASCII, Gray, one-hot and parity each trade bits for a property: easy display, text, single-bit changes, trivial decoding, error detection.

      Practice problems

      Convert 1011 01102 to decimal and to hex.

      Solution

      128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182. Groups: 1011 = B, 0110 = 6, so 0xB6. Check: 11 × 16 + 6 = 182.

      What decimal value does each represent: 0xFF, 0x100, 7778?

      Solution

      0xFF = 15 × 16 + 15 = 255. 0x100 = 162 = 256. 7778 = 7 × 64 + 7 × 8 + 7 = 511 (= 29 − 1, nine 1 bits).

      How many distinct values can 3 hexadecimal digits represent? How many bits is that?

      Solution

      163 = 4096 values, the same as 12 bits (each hex digit is 4 bits).

      Convert 397 to binary, then to octal and hex by grouping.

      Solution

      397 = 256 + 128 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 1 1000 11012. Octal: 110 001 101 = 6158. Hex: 1 1000 1101 = 0x18D.

      Convert 6158 directly to hexadecimal without going through decimal.

      Hint

      Expand each octal digit into 3 bits, then regroup by 4 starting from the right.

      Solution

      6 1 5 → 110 001 101 → regroup: 1 1000 1101 → 0x18D.

      Convert 13.625 to binary.

      Solution

      13 = 1101. Fraction: 0.625 × 2 = 1.25 → 1; 0.25 × 2 = 0.5 → 0; 0.5 × 2 = 1.0 → 1. So 13.625 = 1101.1012. Check: 8 + 4 + 1 + ½ + ⅛ = 13.625.

      Convert 110101.01112 to hex and octal.

      Solution

      Hex: 0011 0101 . 0111 → 35.716. Octal: 110 101 . 011 100 → 65.348. Both equal 53.4375 in decimal.

      Encode 2025 in BCD and in binary. How many bits does each need?

      Solution

      BCD: 0010 0000 0010 0101 (16 bits). Binary: 2025 = 1024 + 512 + 256 + 128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 1 = 111 1110 1001 (11 bits, 0x7E9).

      In C, a variable char d holds one of the characters '0' to '9'. Write an expression for its numeric value. Then write an expression that turns an int v between 0 and 9 into its digit character.

      Solution

      d - '0' and v + '0'. The digits are consecutive codes 0x30 to 0x39, so subtracting or adding 0x30 converts between character and value.

      Convert the binary value 0110 to Gray code, and the Gray code 1011 back to binary.

      Solution

      Binary → Gray: g = b ⊕ (b ≫ 1) = 0110 ⊕ 0011 = 0101. Gray → binary from the MSB: b3 = 1; b2 = b3 ⊕ g2 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1; b1 = b2 ⊕ g1 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0; b0 = b1 ⊕ g0 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. Result 1101 (13). Check: 1101 ⊕ 0110 = 1011.

      A data logger must record any one of 384 distinct sensor states. What is the minimum number of bits per record? If it stores 10,000 records per second, how many bytes per hour does it need if each record is padded to a whole number of bytes?

      Solution

      28 = 256 < 384 ≤ 512 = 29, so 9 bits. Padded to 2 bytes per record: 10,000 × 3600 × 2 = 72,000,000 bytes (72 MB, about 68.7 MiB) per hour. Packing records at 9 bits each would need 40.5 MB, which is why loggers sometimes pack bits.

      Without a calculator, estimate how many address bits a byte-addressed memory of 48 GiB needs, and what a 40-bit address can reach.

      Solution

      48 GiB = 48 × 230 bytes. 32 < 48 ≤ 64, so it needs 26 × 230 = 236 addresses: 36 bits (35 bits only reach 32 GiB). 240 = 210 × 230 = 1024 GiB = 1 TiB.

      Write C expressions that (a) uppercase a lowercase ASCII letter c, (b) test whether c is a decimal digit, (c) convert a hex digit character ('0'–'9', 'a'–'f') to its value.

      Solution

      (a) c & ~0x20 (equivalently c - 32). (b) c >= '0' && c <= '9'. (c) (c <= '9') ? c - '0' : c - 'a' + 10. For mixed case, lowercase first with c | 0x20, which leaves digits unchanged because digits already have bit 5 set (0x30 to 0x39).

      Compute the even parity bit for the byte 0x5B. A receiver gets 0x5B with parity bit 0. Is an error detected? Can a parity check detect two flipped bits?

      Solution

      0x5B = 0101 1011 has five 1 bits, so the even-parity bit is 1 (making six). Receiving parity 0 with that data gives an odd total, so an error is detected (either a data bit or the parity bit itself flipped). Two flipped bits change the count by an even number, so parity cannot detect them.

      A colleague writes uint16_t limits[] = { 0100, 0250, 1000 }; intending one hundred, two hundred fifty and one thousand. What values does the array actually hold, and how would a code review catch this?

      Solution

      Leading zeros make C octal literals: 01008 = 64, 02508 = 2·64 + 5·8 = 168, and 1000 is decimal 1000. The code compiles without warnings by default. Catch it by banning leading zeros on decimal constants in the style guide (compilers and linters such as clang-tidy can flag octal literals), or by writing values in the base that matches their meaning.

      Show that a 4-bit Gray-coded counter changes exactly one bit per step, including the wrap from 15 back to 0, and explain why that property matters when another circuit samples the counter at an arbitrary moment.

      Solution

      Gray(15) = 1111 ⊕ 0111 = 1000 and Gray(0) = 0000, which differ only in the MSB; the reflected construction guarantees one-bit differences between all other neighbors too (each half is a Gray sequence, and the middle and wrap boundaries differ only in the prefix bit). If a sampler catches the counter mid-change, only one bit is uncertain, so it reads either the old value or the new value, both of which are correct to within one count. With plain binary, 0111 → 1000 changes four bits; bits that have and have not switched yet can combine into any of 16 patterns, for example 1111, which is wrong by eight counts.

      Module03of 28

      Part I: Foundations: information as bits

      Signed integers and binary arithmetic

      The four ways hardware represents negative numbers, why two's complement won, extension and truncation, addition and subtraction with one adder, the exact rules for detecting overflow, shifts as multiplication and division, and the integer rules of C and C++ that follow from all of this.

      Builds onNumber systemsTools4-bit adder and subtractorPractice16 problems

      A binary number with n bits has 2n patterns. Unsigned arithmetic assigns them the values 0 to 2n − 1. To represent negative numbers, some of those patterns must be reassigned, and the choice of which patterns mean which negative values determines how complicated the arithmetic hardware becomes. This module compares the candidate systems, explains why nearly every processor uses two's complement, and then covers the arithmetic itself: addition, subtraction, overflow detection, extension, truncation and shifting. It ends with the integer rules of C and C++, which are a direct consequence of the hardware.

      Four representations of signed numbers

      Sign-magnitude

      The MSB is a sign bit (0 for +, 1 for −) and the remaining n − 1 bits hold the magnitude, just as people write −19. The range is −(2n−1 − 1) to +(2n−1 − 1), and there are two zeros, 0000 0000 (+0) and 1000 0000 (−0). Addition is awkward: to add numbers with different signs, the hardware must compare magnitudes, subtract the smaller from the larger and pick the sign, which needs a comparator and a subtractor as well as an adder. Sign-magnitude survives where it is natural, most importantly in the significand of floating-point numbers (Module 4).

      One's complement

      A negative number is formed by inverting every bit of the positive number: +19 = 0001 0011, −19 = 1110 1100. The range is the same as sign-magnitude, and there are still two zeros (0000 0000 and 1111 1111). Addition almost works with a plain adder, except that a carry out of the MSB must be added back into the LSB ("end-around carry"). One's complement arithmetic survives in the Internet checksum used by IP, TCP and UDP.

      Two's complement

      Two's complement

      A signed binary representation in which the MSB has weight −2n−1 instead of +2n−1, and all other bits keep their usual positive weights. An n-bit two's complement number ranges from −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1 and has exactly one zero.

      Bit76543210
      Weight−1286432168421

      So 1110 1101 = −128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = −19, and 0001 0011 = +19. A number is negative exactly when its MSB is 1. The range is asymmetric: 8 bits run from −128 to +127, because the pattern 1000 0000 that would have been −0 is used for −128 instead.

      Excess (biased) representation

      In excess-B (also called offset binary or biased) notation, a pattern whose unsigned value is u represents u − B. With 8 bits and B = 128, 0000 0000 means −128, 1000 0000 means 0 and 1111 1111 means +127. Its useful property is that the ordering of the bit patterns, read as unsigned numbers, matches the ordering of the values, so an unsigned comparator compares biased numbers correctly. The exponent field of IEEE floating point uses a bias for exactly this reason, and many ADCs output offset binary.

      One pattern, five values

      Since the bits carry no record of the system, the same pattern takes different values under each convention:

      8-bit patternUnsignedSign-magnitudeOne's complementTwo's complementExcess-128
      0000 00000+0+00−128
      0111 1111127+127+127+127−1
      1000 0000128−0−127−1280
      1001 0011147−19−108−109+19
      1111 1110254−126−1−2+126
      1111 1111255−127−0−1+127

      Four two's complement patterns are worth memorizing: all zeros is 0, all ones is −1, a 1 followed by zeros is the most negative value, and a 0 followed by ones is the most positive. Use the number converter in the previous module to check any pattern under all five readings.

      Why two's complement won

      Two's complement arithmetic is ordinary binary arithmetic modulo 2n. An n-bit adder computes the sum of two patterns and discards any carry out of the MSB, which is exactly addition modulo 2n. In two's complement, −x is represented by the pattern 2n − x, and modulo 2n the values x and x − 2n are the same residue. So adding the patterns for a and −b gives the pattern for a − b with no special cases: the same adder circuit adds unsigned numbers and two's complement numbers, and the result bits are correct for both interpretations whenever the true result fits.

      Negation: invert and add 1

      For any n-bit pattern x, x + x′ (x plus its bitwise complement) is all ones, which is 2n − 1. Therefore x′ + 1 = 2n − x, which is the two's complement pattern of −x. That gives the standard recipe:

      −x = x′ + 1 (invert every bit, then add 1)

      Worked example

      Negating 18 in 8 bits

      +18 = 0001 0010. Invert: 1110 1101. Add 1: 1110 1110 = 0xEE. Check with weights: −128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 2 = −18.

      A shortcut that avoids the addition: scanning from the right, copy every bit up to and including the first 1, then invert all bits to its left. 0001 0010 → keep "10", invert "000100" → 1110 11 + 10 = 1110 1110.

      The recipe works in both directions: inverting 1110 1110 gives 0001 0001, and adding 1 gives 0001 0010 = 18. This is how you read the magnitude of a negative two's complement number.

      Common mistake

      Two different things are both called "two's complement". The two's complement system is the representation: a way of reading bit patterns. Taking the two's complement is an operation: invert and add 1, which negates a number. A negative number in the system is not "a positive number with the two's complement taken" unless you are computing it from its magnitude. Also, negating the most negative value overflows: in 8 bits, −(−128) gives 1000 0000 again, because +128 is not representable.

      Extension and truncation

      Moving a value to a wider register requires filling the new upper bits. To preserve the value:

      • Zero extension (for unsigned values) fills the new bits with 0.
      • Sign extension (for two's complement values) fills the new bits with copies of the old MSB.

      Why sign extension works: adding a 1 above the old MSB changes the MSB weight from −2k to −2k+1, and turning the old MSB into an ordinary bit of weight +2k compensates exactly: −2k+1 + 2k = −2k. Repeating the argument covers any number of new bits.

      Truncation drops upper bits. It preserves an unsigned value only if all dropped bits are 0, and it preserves a two's complement value only if all dropped bits are equal to the new MSB, i.e. the value already fits. Truncating 0000 0101 (+5) to 4 bits gives 0101 (+5); truncating 0001 0101 (+21) to 4 bits gives 0101 (+5), which is wrong; truncating 1111 1011 (−5) gives 1011 (−5), which is right.

      Addition and subtraction

      Binary addition works column by column like decimal addition, with a carry of 1 whenever a column sum reaches 2. In each column the possible sums are 0, 1, 2 (= 102, write 0 carry 1) and 3 (= 112, write 1 carry 1).

      carries   1 1 1 1
          0 1 1 0 1     (13)
        + 0 0 1 1 1     ( 7)
          ---------
          1 0 1 0 0     (20)

      Subtraction reuses the adder: A − B = A + (−B) = A + B′ + 1. A circuit computes it by inverting B through XOR gates and setting the carry into the least significant column to 1, as Module 9 shows at gate level.

      Hexadecimal addition works the same way with a carry whenever a column reaches 16: 0x3A + 0x2C: A + C = 22 = 16 + 6, write 6 carry 1; 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. The sum is 0x66 (58 + 44 = 102). For hex subtraction, borrow 16: 0x50 − 0x1F: 0 − F needs a borrow, 16 − 15 = 1; then 5 − 1 − 1 = 3. The result is 0x31 (80 − 31 = 49).

      Overflow

      An n-bit result can only hold n bits. Overflow means the true mathematical result does not fit in the representation being used, so the stored bits represent a different value. Whether a given addition overflowed depends on the interpretation, so the hardware reports two separate flags, and software chooses which to check.

      Carry flag (C)

      The carry out of the most significant column of an addition. For unsigned addition, C = 1 means the result overflowed. For subtraction computed as A + B′ + 1, C = 0 means a borrow occurred (A < B as unsigned numbers), so the unsigned result is wrong.

      Overflow flag (V)

      Signed (two's complement) overflow. It occurs exactly when two operands with the same sign produce a result with the opposite sign. In hardware, V = (carry into the MSB) ⊕ (carry out of the MSB).

      Adding numbers of opposite signs can never overflow, because the result lies between the two operands. Overflow needs both operands to be large in the same direction. The carry-based formula follows from looking at the MSB column: if both operands are positive (MSBs 0) and a carry comes into the MSB, the sum's MSB becomes 1 (negative) and there is no carry out, so the two carries differ; if both are negative (MSBs 1) and no carry comes in, the MSB becomes 0 with a carry out, and again they differ. In every non-overflow case the two carries agree.

      4-bit additionResultCUnsigned readingVSigned reading
      0110 + 0101101106 + 5 = 11, correct16 + 5 gave −5: overflow
      1100 + 01010001112 + 5 gave 1: overflow0−4 + 5 = 1, correct
      1001 + 1010001119 + 10 gave 3: overflow1−7 + −6 gave +3: overflow
      0011 + 0100011103 + 4 = 7, correct03 + 4 = 7, correct

      Worked example

      Subtraction and the meaning of C

      7 − 5 in 4 bits: 0111 + 1010 + 1 = 1 0010. Result 0010 = 2, C = 1: no borrow, correct for both interpretations.

      5 − 7: 0101 + 1000 + 1 = 0 1110. Result 1110: as a signed number it is −2, which is correct (V = 0). As an unsigned number it reads 14, which is wrong; C = 0 signals the borrow, because 5 < 7.

      In practice

      Processors record these flags in a status register (on AVR microcontrollers, SREG holds C, Z, N, V and others) and conditional branches test them. "Branch if lower" for unsigned comparison tests C after a subtraction; "branch if less than" for signed comparison tests N ⊕ V. Compilers pick the instruction from the declared type, which is one reason signed and unsigned types must be declared correctly.

      Shifts as multiplication and division

      Shifting a binary number left by k positions multiplies it by 2k, just as appending zeros multiplies a decimal number by powers of ten. Shifting right divides by 2k, but what fills the vacated upper bits matters.

      The arithmetic right shift rounds toward −∞: −7 = 1001 shifted right once is 1100 = −4, because −3.5 rounds down to −4. Integer division in C and C++ rounds toward zero instead (−7 / 2 = −3), which is why compilers cannot replace a signed division by a single arithmetic shift; they add a correction for negative operands first. A left shift overflows when any bit shifted out, or the new sign bit, differs from what the true product needs: 0100 0000 (64) shifted left is 1000 0000, which is −128 as a signed byte.

      How many bits a result needs

      • The sum of two n-bit unsigned numbers needs at most n + 1 bits. The sum of k such numbers needs n + ⌈log2 k⌉ bits: three 4-bit numbers have a maximum sum of 3 × 15 = 45, which needs 6 bits.
      • The product of an m-bit and an n-bit unsigned number needs m + n bits: 255 × 255 = 65,025 fits in 16 bits. The same holds for two's complement: (−128) × (−128) = 16,384 needs 16 signed bits.

      Integers in C and C++

      C and C++ map their integer operations straight onto the hardware above, with a few rules every embedded or systems programmer has to know.

      • Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2n, by definition. uint8_t x = 255; x++; leaves x = 0.
      • Signed overflow is undefined behavior. The compiler may assume it never happens and optimize accordingly, so if (x + 1 < x) can be deleted as always false. The hardware wraps, but the language makes no promise.
      • Integer promotion: operands narrower than int (char, short, uint8_t) are converted to int before any arithmetic. Results are computed in int and only truncated when stored.
      • Usual arithmetic conversions: if one operand is unsigned and the other signed of the same rank, the signed one is converted to unsigned, so −1 becomes the maximum unsigned value.
      • Shifts: shifting by the type's width or more is undefined, left-shifting a 1 into or past the sign bit of a signed type is undefined in C, and right-shifting a negative signed value was implementation-defined until C++20 (in practice, arithmetic). Use unsigned types for bit manipulation.
      uint8_t a = 200, b = 100;
int     s = a + b;      // 300: a and b are promoted to int before the addition
uint8_t t = a + b;      // 44: 300 is truncated to its low 8 bits when stored (300 - 256)

if (-1 < 0u) { }        // never taken: -1 is converted to unsigned (all ones), which is huge

int16_t p = 300 * 300;  // with 16-bit int (AVR), 300 * 300 overflows int: undefined behavior
int32_t q = 300L * 300; // the long operand forces a 32-bit multiplication: 90000

uint32_t m = 1u << 31;  // fine. 1 << 31 with 32-bit int shifts into the sign bit: undefined in C

      Common mistake

      Mixing signed and unsigned in comparisons and loop bounds. for (unsigned i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) never terminates, because an unsigned value is always ≥ 0 and wraps from 0 to the maximum. Compilers warn about this with -Wall -Wextra; build with warnings on and treat them as errors in embedded code.

      Summary

      • Two's complement gives the MSB weight −2n−1; range −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1; one zero; negate by inverting and adding 1.
      • One adder serves unsigned and signed numbers because both are arithmetic modulo 2n.
      • Zero-extend unsigned values, sign-extend signed values; truncation is safe only if the value fits.
      • Unsigned overflow: C = 1 after addition, C = 0 after subtraction. Signed overflow: same-sign operands give an opposite-sign result; V = cin,MSB ⊕ cout,MSB.
      • Left shift multiplies by 2k; logical right shift divides unsigned values; arithmetic right shift divides signed values, rounding toward −∞.
      • In C, narrow types promote to int, unsigned wraps, signed overflow is undefined, and signed operands convert to unsigned in mixed comparisons.

      Practice problems

      Give the range of an 8-bit number in unsigned, sign-magnitude and two's complement form. How many zeros does each have?

      Solution

      Unsigned 0 to 255 (one zero). Sign-magnitude −127 to +127 (two zeros, +0 and −0). Two's complement −128 to +127 (one zero).

      What decimal value does the 8-bit two's complement pattern 0xF6 represent?

      Solution

      0xF6 = 1111 0110. The MSB is 1, so it is negative. Invert: 0000 1001; add 1: 0000 1010 = 10. The value is −10. (Or: 246 − 256 = −10.)

      Sign-extend the 6-bit two's complement number 101101 to 8 bits and give its value.

      Solution

      Copy the MSB (1) into the two new bits: 1110 1101. Value: −128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = −19, the same as the 6-bit value −32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = −19.

      Write −37 in 8-bit two's complement, in binary and hex.

      Solution

      +37 = 0010 0101. Invert: 1101 1010. Add 1: 1101 1011 = 0xDB. Check: −128 + 64 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = −37.

      Give the value of the 8-bit pattern 1100 1000 as unsigned, sign-magnitude, one's complement, two's complement and excess-128.

      Solution

      Unsigned 128 + 64 + 8 = 200. Sign-magnitude: sign 1, magnitude 100 1000 = 72 → −72. One's complement: invert to 0011 0111 = 55 → −55. Two's complement: 200 − 256 = −56. Excess-128: 200 − 128 = +72.

      Add the 8-bit numbers 0x5C + 0x4A. Give the result in hex and state whether it overflows as unsigned and as signed.

      Solution

      C + A = 12 + 10 = 22 = 0x16: write 6, carry 1. 5 + 4 + 1 = 10 = A. Result 0xA6, no carry out. Unsigned: 92 + 74 = 166, fits (C = 0). Signed: both operands positive (MSB 0) but 0xA6 has MSB 1 (−90), so signed overflow (V = 1): the true sum 166 exceeds +127.

      Compute 0x40 − 0x5B in 8 bits the way the hardware does. What are the result and the C flag, and what does C tell you?

      Solution

      0x5B = 0101 1011, inverted 1010 0100. 0x40 + 0xA4 + 1 = 0xE5 with no carry out, so result 0xE5, C = 0. C = 0 means a borrow: as unsigned numbers 64 < 91, so the unsigned result is wrong. As signed numbers 64 − 91 = −27, and 0xE5 = 229 − 256 = −27 is correct (V = 0).

      Truncate each 8-bit two's complement value to 4 bits and say whether the value is preserved: 0000 0110, 1111 1010, 0001 1010, 1110 0101.

      Solution

      0110: +6 → +6, preserved (dropped bits 0000 equal the new MSB 0). 1010: −6 → −6, preserved (dropped 1111 equal new MSB 1). 1010 from 0001 1010 (+26): becomes −6, not preserved. 0101 from 1110 0101 (−27): becomes +5, not preserved.

      Using 4-bit two's complement, compute −3 − 5 and −8 − 1 the way an adder would. Show the carries into and out of the MSB and use them to decide overflow.

      Solution

      −3 − 5 = 1101 + (0101)′ + 1 = 1101 + 1010 + 1. Adding: 1101 + 1011 = 1 1000. Carry into bit 3: bits 0–2 are 101 + 011 = 1000, so carry in = 1; carry out = 1. V = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0: result 1000 = −8, correct. −8 − 1 = 1000 + 1110 + 1 = 1000 + 1111 = 1 0111. Carry into bit 3: 000 + 111 = 111, carry in = 0; carry out = 1. V = 1: the result 0111 (+7) is wrong because −9 is below the range.

      Explain, using x + x′ = 2n − 1, why inverting and adding 1 negates a two's complement number. Then explain why the same steps applied to −128 in 8 bits give −128.

      Solution

      x + x′ is all ones, which is 2n − 1, so x′ + 1 = 2n − x. Modulo 2n, the pattern 2n − x is congruent to −x, so it is the two's complement encoding of −x. For x = −128 = 1000 0000: x′ = 0111 1111, and adding 1 gives 1000 0000 again. The mathematically correct +128 is congruent to −128 modulo 256, and +128 is outside the 8-bit range, so the negation overflows.

      Three 4-bit unsigned numbers are added. How many bits must the sum have to never overflow? What about sixteen 4-bit numbers, and the product of a 4-bit and a 6-bit number?

      Solution

      Three: max 45, which needs 6 bits (n + ⌈log2 3⌉ = 4 + 2). Sixteen: max 16 × 15 = 240, which needs 8 bits (4 + log2 16). Product: max 15 × 63 = 945 < 1024, so 10 bits (4 + 6).

      What do these C expressions evaluate to on a system with 32-bit int? (a) (uint8_t)(250 + 10), (b) -7 >> 1 (assume arithmetic shift), (c) -7 / 2, (d) (int8_t)0x9C.

      Solution

      (a) 260 truncated to 8 bits: 4. (b) Arithmetic shift rounds toward −∞: −4. (c) Division truncates toward zero: −3. (d) 0x9C = 156, read as a signed byte: 156 − 256 = −100.

      An 8-bit microcontroller compares two unsigned bytes by computing A − B and branching on the carry flag. For A = 0x30, B = 0x50, what are C, Z and N? Which branch, "lower" (C = 0) or "same or higher" (C = 1), is taken?

      Solution

      0x30 + 0xAF + 1 = 0xE0, no carry out. C = 0, Z = 0 (result not zero), N = 1 (MSB of 0xE0). C = 0 means a borrow, so A < B: the "lower" branch is taken, which is correct since 48 < 80.

      Prove that V = cn−1 ⊕ cn (carry into the MSB XOR carry out of the MSB) detects two's complement overflow, by considering the four combinations of operand signs.

      Hint

      Let a and b be the operand MSBs and cn−1 the carry into the MSB column. The result MSB is s = a ⊕ b ⊕ cn−1 and the carry out is cn = majority(a, b, cn−1).

      Solution

      a = 0, b = 0 (both non-negative): cn = 0 and s = cn−1. Overflow means s = 1, which happens exactly when cn−1 = 1 ≠ cn. a = 1, b = 1 (both negative): cn = 1 and s = cn−1. Overflow means a non-negative result, s = 0, exactly when cn−1 = 0 ≠ cn. a ≠ b (opposite signs): overflow is impossible, and indeed cn = majority(0, 1, cn−1) = cn−1, so V = 0. In all cases V = 1 exactly when overflow occurs.

      The function below is meant to detect signed overflow. Explain why it can fail after compiler optimization, and rewrite it so it is correct.

      bool add_overflows(int a, int b) {
    int s = a + b;
    return (a > 0 && b > 0 && s < 0) || (a < 0 && b < 0 && s >= 0);
}
      Solution

      If a + b overflows, the program has already executed undefined behavior, so the compiler may assume a + b never overflows and simplify the test (for example, conclude that a > 0 and b > 0 imply s > 0, and delete the check). The test must not perform the overflowing addition. Either compare against the limits first, or use a compiler builtin:

      bool add_overflows(int a, int b) {
    return (b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b) || (b < 0 && a < INT_MIN - b);
}
// GCC/Clang: int s; bool ovf = __builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &s);

      Another correct approach is to add in unsigned arithmetic, which wraps by definition, and examine the sign bits.

      An interviewer asks: "Implement x / 8 for a signed 32-bit int using shifts, matching C's rounding toward zero." Write the expression and explain the correction term.

      Solution

      An arithmetic shift rounds toward −∞, so negative values that are not multiples of 8 come out one too low. Adding 7 (that is, 23 − 1) to negative values before shifting turns floor into truncation:

      int div8(int x) {
    int bias = (x >> 31) & 7;    // 7 if x is negative, 0 otherwise (x >> 31 is all ones or zero)
    return (x + bias) >> 3;
}

      Check: x = −9 gives (−9 + 7) >> 3 = −2 >> 3 = −1, and −9 / 8 = −1.125 truncates to −1. Without the bias, −9 >> 3 = −2. Compilers emit exactly this sequence for signed division by a power of two.
