      Part II: Combinational logic

      Decoders, encoders, multiplexers and buses

      The standard combinational building blocks that larger designs are assembled from: decoders with enables and how to build big ones from small ones, encoders and priority encoders, multiplexers and mux trees, implementing any function with a decoder or a mux, and sharing a wire between several drivers with tri-state buffers.

      Builds onCanonical formsPractice15 problems

      Designing every function gate by gate does not scale. Real designs are built hierarchically from a small set of well-understood blocks, each with a clear interface, and the blocks in this module appear in nearly every digital system: decoders select one of many things by number, encoders do the reverse, multiplexers choose which of several signals passes through, and tri-state drivers let several sources share one wire. Each is also a general-purpose way to implement logic functions.

      Buses and hierarchical notation

      A bus is a group of wires carrying one multi-bit value. In diagrams a bus is drawn as one thick line with a slash and a width (/8), and its bits are named with a range: D[7:0] has D[7] as the MSB and D[0] as the LSB. A block that operates on whole buses, such as an 8-bit 2-to-1 multiplexer, is internally eight identical 1-bit blocks sharing their control signals. That regularity is what makes wide datapaths easy to design and to lay out.

      Decoders

      Decoder

      A block with n inputs and 2n outputs that asserts exactly one output: the one whose index equals the binary value of the input. Equivalently, output Yi is the minterm mi of the inputs. The output pattern is one-hot.

      Most decoders have an enable input: when it is inactive, all outputs are inactive regardless of the address. Enable is simply an extra input to every AND gate, so an enabled decoder computes Yi = EN·mi. Many standard parts (the classic 74x138 3-to-8 decoder, for example) have active-low outputs: the selected output is 0 and all others are 1. On a schematic, active-low signals are marked with a bubble or a name ending in _L, _N or a prime.

      Building larger decoders from smaller ones

      A large decoder is built as a tree: a first-level decoder on the most significant address bits drives the enables of second-level decoders, each of which decodes the remaining bits.

      Decoders are how memories select a location. A memory with 220 words cannot use a single decoder with a million AND gates driving one long line each; instead the address is split into a row part and a column part, a row decoder selects one row of the cell array, and a column multiplexer selects a word within it (Module 21).

      A decoder implements any function

      Because the outputs of a decoder are the minterms of its inputs, ORing the right outputs gives any function in canonical SOP form. A 3-to-8 decoder plus two OR gates is a full adder: S = Y1 + Y2 + Y4 + Y7 and Cout = Y3 + Y5 + Y6 + Y7. With active-low outputs, use NAND gates instead of OR, by De Morgan: Y1 + Y2 + Y4 + Y7 = (Y1′·Y2′·Y4′·Y7′)′. This approach is efficient when one decoder serves many functions of the same inputs.

      Encoders and priority encoders

      An encoder is the inverse of a decoder: it takes a one-hot input of 2n lines and outputs the n-bit index of the active one. A 4-to-2 encoder is Y1 = I2 + I3, Y0 = I1 + I3. If more than one input is active, a plain encoder produces a meaningless OR of codes, and if none is active it outputs 0, indistinguishable from "input 0 active".

      A priority encoder fixes both problems: it reports the index of the highest-priority active input and adds a valid output that is 1 when any input is active. With inputs A (highest priority), B, C, D (lowest) mapped to codes 3, 2, 1, 0:

      ABCDG1G0V
      1XXX111
      01XX101
      001X011
      0001001
      0000000

      The X entries in the input columns mean "any value" (each row stands for several truth-table rows). Reading the table: G1 = A + A′B = A + B; G0 = A + A′B′C = A + B′C (simplification theorem); V = A + B + C + D. Interrupt controllers use priority encoders to pick which pending request to service first, and floating-point hardware uses them as leading-one detectors for normalization.

      Multiplexers

      Multiplexer (mux)

      A block with 2n data inputs, n select inputs and one output, which passes the data input whose index equals the select value. A 2-to-1 mux computes Y = S′·I0 + S·I1.

      Written out, a 4-to-1 mux is Y = S1′S0′·I0 + S1′S0·I1 + S1S0′·I2 + S1S0·I3: each select combination enables one minterm, which is ANDed with its data input. Internally that is a 2-to-4 decoder on the select lines, four AND gates and an OR gate. An N-to-1 mux needs ⌈log2 N⌉ select bits.

      Mux trees

      Large muxes are built as trees of small ones. In a tree of 2-to-1 muxes, all muxes in one stage share a select bit. With the least significant select bit on the first stage, the data inputs appear in natural order.

      The stages can use the select bits in any order, but the data inputs must then be relabeled. If S1 controls the first stage instead, the first-stage muxes must pair inputs that differ only in S1: (I0, I2) and (I1, I3). For an 8-to-1 tree with S2 on the first stage, the first stage takes the pairs (I0, I4), (I2, I6), (I1, I5), (I3, I7). A useful check: inputs paired by a mux must have select codes that differ only in that mux's select bit.

      Wide muxes repeat the 1-bit design: choosing between two 32-bit buses takes thirty-two 2-to-1 muxes sharing one select line, and its delay is that of a single mux. Building a 16-to-1 mux can use five 4-to-1 muxes in two stages, or one 8-to-1 and two 2-to-1 stages; the choice depends on which sizes the technology offers and on delay.

      A mux implements any function

      Connect the function's inputs to the select lines and put the truth table's output column on the data inputs as constants: a 2n-to-1 mux is then a lookup table (LUT) for any n-input function. This is exactly how FPGAs implement logic (Module 21).

      A smaller mux suffices with one variable left over. Shannon's expansion splits any function on one variable: F = S′·F(S = 0) + S·F(S = 1), which is a 2-to-1 mux whose data inputs are the two cofactors. Applied to n − 1 variables, a 2n−1-to-1 mux implements any n-variable function if each data input may be 0, 1, the remaining variable or its complement.

      Worked example

      F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 2, 6, 7) on a 4-to-1 mux

      Put A on S1 and B on S0. For each AB combination, look at the two rows (C = 0 and C = 1) and express F as a function of C:

      A BrowsF for C = 0, 1data input
      0 00, 10, 1I0 = C
      0 12, 31, 0I1 = C′
      1 04, 50, 0I2 = 0
      1 16, 71, 1I3 = 1

      One 4-to-1 mux and an inverter replace a two-level circuit. With only a 2-to-1 mux and A on its select line, the same procedure needs F(A = 0) = B ⊕ C and F(A = 1) = B as data inputs.

      Since a 2-to-1 mux with constants available can produce NOT (I0 = 1, I1 = 0), AND (S = A, I0 = 0, I1 = B) and OR (S = A, I0 = B, I1 = 1), the 2-to-1 mux is functionally complete on its own.

      Demultiplexers

      A demultiplexer routes one data input to one of 2n outputs selected by n bits, with all other outputs 0. It is the same circuit as a decoder with its enable used as the data input.

      Tri-state buffers and shared buses

      Muxes combine signals with logic. The alternative for a shared wire is to let several drivers connect to it directly, with only one allowed to drive at a time. A tri-state buffer has a data input, an enable, and an output that is either the data value (enabled) or Z, high impedance (disabled), meaning the output transistors are both off and the buffer is effectively disconnected.

      Common mistake

      Bus contention occurs when two enabled drivers try to drive the same wire to different values. The two output stages form a low-resistance path from supply to ground: two drivers with 25 Ω output resistance on a 3.3 V bus pass about 3.3 / 50 = 66 mA, enough to overheat or damage them, and the bus sits at an undefined middle voltage. The opposite fault, no driver enabled, leaves the bus floating; buses that can be idle need a pull-up or pull-down resistor or a "bus keeper" to hold a valid level.

      Inside chips, tri-state buses have largely been replaced by multiplexers, which have no contention risk and are easier for timing tools to analyze. Tri-state outputs remain essential on chip pins (bidirectional data pins, memory buses) and in the form of open-drain outputs used by I2C and interrupt lines (Module 13).

      In practice

      In Verilog, a mux is a conditional expression assign y = s ? b : a; or a case statement, and a tri-state driver is assign pin = en ? data : 1'bz;. Synthesis tools map wide case statements to mux trees or to AND-OR logic, whichever is smaller or faster (Module 27).

      Summary

      • A decoder outputs all minterms of its inputs; with OR gates it builds any function. Trees of small decoders build large ones through their enables.
      • A priority encoder reports the highest-priority active input plus a valid bit.
      • An N-to-1 mux needs ⌈log2 N⌉ select bits; a tree of 2-to-1 muxes needs N − 1 of them.
      • A 2n-to-1 mux is a lookup table for any n-variable function; with residues, a 2n−1-to-1 mux suffices.
      • Tri-state outputs allow shared wires; exactly one driver must be enabled at a time.

      Practice problems

      How many outputs does a 5-to-32 decoder have, and how many are active at once (when enabled)? How many select lines does a 32-to-1 mux need?

      Solution

      32 outputs, exactly one active. A 32-to-1 mux needs log2 32 = 5 select lines.

      A 3-to-8 decoder with active-high outputs and an active-high enable receives A2A1A0 = 110 and EN = 1. Which output is active? What if EN = 0?

      Solution

      110 = 6, so Y6 = 1 and all others 0. With EN = 0, all outputs are 0.

      Write the equation of a 2-to-1 mux and use it to explain why a mux with S = A, I0 = 0, I1 = B computes A·B.

      Solution

      Y = S′·I0 + S·I1. Substituting: Y = A′·0 + A·B = A·B.

      Implement a full adder with a 3-to-8 decoder (active-high outputs) and OR gates. Then redo it for a decoder with active-low outputs.

      Solution

      Active high: S = Y1 + Y2 + Y4 + Y7, Cout = Y3 + Y5 + Y6 + Y7. Active low (outputs Yi′): use NAND gates: S = NAND(Y1′, Y2′, Y4′, Y7′) and Cout = NAND(Y3′, Y5′, Y6′, Y7′), since (a′·b′·c′·d′)′ = a + b + c + d.

      How many 2-to-4 decoders are needed to build a 4-to-16 decoder as a tree, and how are they connected?

      Solution

      Five: one first-level decoder on A3A2 whose four outputs drive the enables of four second-level decoders, each decoding A1A0 into four of the sixteen outputs. The first-level decoder's own enable is the overall enable.

      A priority encoder has inputs I3 (highest priority) to I0 and outputs Y1Y0 and V. What are the outputs for I3I2I1I0 = 0110, 0001 and 0000?

      Solution

      0110: highest active is I2 → Y = 10, V = 1. 0001: only I0 → Y = 00, V = 1. 0000: none → Y = 00 (don't care), V = 0. The valid bit is what distinguishes the last two cases.

      Build a 3-to-1 mux (select 00 → I0, 01 → I1, 1X → I2) from 2-to-1 muxes.

      Solution

      Two 2-to-1 muxes: the first, with select S0, chooses between I0 and I1; the second, with select S1, chooses between the first mux's output (S1 = 0) and I2 (S1 = 1). When S1 = 1, S0 is ignored, which matches the 1X code.

      A 4-to-1 tree of 2-to-1 muxes must use S1 on its first stage and S0 on its second. Which data inputs go into each first-stage mux?

      Solution

      First-stage muxes pair inputs whose codes differ only in S1: (I0, I2) with select S1, and (I1, I3) with select S1. The second stage chooses between those results with S0: S0 = 0 picks the (I0, I2) mux, S0 = 1 picks the (I1, I3) mux.

      Implement F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12, 15) with an 8-to-1 mux using A, B, C as the select lines.

      Hint

      For each ABC combination, compare F in the D = 0 and D = 1 rows.

      Solution

      Rows in pairs (D = 0, 1): ABC = 000 → m0, m1 = 1, 0 → D′; 001 → m2, m3 = 0, 1 → D; 010 → m4, m5 = 0, 1 → D; 011 → m6, m7 = 1, 0 → D′; 100 → m8, m9 = 0, 1 → D; 101 → m10, m11 = 1, 0 → D′; 110 → m12, m13 = 1, 0 → D′; 111 → m14, m15 = 0, 1 → D. (F is the 4-input even parity function, which is why every residue is D or D′.)

      Implement F(A, B, C) = A·B + B′·C with a single 2-to-1 mux, using B as the select line and any of 0, 1, A, A′, C, C′ as data inputs.

      Solution

      Shannon expansion on B: F(B = 0) = C and F(B = 1) = A. So S = B, I0 = C, I1 = A: Y = B′·C + B·A, exactly F. A single mux replaces two ANDs, an OR and an inverter.

      Show that a 2-to-1 mux is functionally complete by building NOT, AND and OR from it, given constants 0 and 1.

      Solution

      NOT A: S = A, I0 = 1, I1 = 0 (Y = A′). AND: S = A, I0 = 0, I1 = B (Y = AB). OR: S = A, I0 = B, I1 = 1 (Y = A′B + A = A + B). Since {AND, OR, NOT} is complete, so is the 2-to-1 mux.

      A 6-to-1 multiplexer must select by S2S1S0 as follows: I0 for 000, I1 for 001, I2 for 01X, I3 for 10X, I4 for 110 and I5 for 111. Build it from 2-to-1 muxes with the fewest muxes possible.

      Solution

      Six inputs need at least 5 two-input muxes (each mux reduces the number of candidates by one). A 5-mux solution splitting on S2 last: for S2 = 0, mux A (select S0) picks I0/I1, then mux B (select S1) picks A's output (S1 = 0) or I2 (S1 = 1). For S2 = 1, mux C (select S0) picks I4/I5, then mux D (select S1) picks I3 (S1 = 0) or C's output (S1 = 1). Mux E (select S2) picks B (0) or D (1). 5 muxes. The X codes are what let I2 and I3 skip the S0 stage.

      Four devices share an 8-bit tri-state bus. Each device's output enable comes from a 2-to-4 decoder driven by a 2-bit "owner" register. What goes wrong if the decoder's enable input is wired permanently active, and what goes wrong if the owner register is not reset at power-up?

      Solution

      With the decoder always enabled, some device always drives the bus, which is fine for contention (exactly one) but means the bus can never be released, for example to let an external tester or a bidirectional device drive it. If the owner register is not reset, it powers up with a random value, so a random device drives the bus at startup; that is safe electrically, because the decoder still guarantees only one enable, but it may drive garbage to the others until software sets the register. The dangerous case would be enables generated by independent logic instead of a decoder, where two could be active at once.

      Design a 16-to-1 multiplexer in three ways: from 2-to-1 muxes, from 4-to-1 muxes, and from one 8-to-1 plus 2-to-1 muxes. Give the mux count and the number of mux levels (delay) for each.

      Solution

      2-to-1 only: a binary tree of 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 muxes, 4 levels. 4-to-1 only: four on the first stage (selects S1S0) and one on the second (S3S2): 5 muxes, 2 levels. 8-to-1 plus 2-to-1: two 8-to-1 muxes on S2S1S0 and one 2-to-1 on S3: 3 muxes, 2 levels (or, with a single 8-to-1, eight 2-to-1 muxes in front of it on S0 and the 8-to-1 on S3S2S1: 9 muxes, 2 levels). Delay depends on each mux's internal delay, which grows with its size, so fewer levels of larger muxes is not automatically faster.

      An 8-to-3 priority encoder (I7 highest) is often built from two 4-to-2 priority encoders. Describe the structure and give the equations that combine them.

      Solution

      Encoder H handles I7–I4 and outputs h1h0 and valid Vh; encoder L handles I3–I0 and outputs l1l0 and VL. If any upper input is active, the upper encoder wins: Y2 = Vh; Y1 = Vh ? h1 : l1; Y0 = Vh ? h0 : l0 (two 2-to-1 muxes with select Vh); V = Vh + VL. This scales recursively, which is how wide leading-one detectors are built with logarithmic delay.

      Part II: Combinational logic

      Adders, comparators and the ALU

      Arithmetic in gates: half and full adders, the ripple-carry adder and its delay, one circuit for addition and subtraction, comparators, carry-lookahead for speed, adding many bits at once, multipliers, shifters, and an ALU that shares one adder among several operations.

      Builds onSigned arithmetic, Decoders and muxesPractice14 problems

      Module 3 showed that two's complement lets one adder serve both signed and unsigned numbers and both addition and subtraction. This module builds that adder from gates, then the circuits around it: comparators, faster adders, multi-operand adders, multipliers, shifters, and finally an arithmetic logic unit (ALU) of the kind found at the center of every processor's datapath.

      Half adder and full adder

      Adding two bits A and B produces a 2-bit result: a sum bit S and a carry C. That circuit is a half adder:

      ABCS
      0000
      0101
      1001
      1110
      S = A ⊕ B C = A·B

      A column of a multi-bit addition has three inputs, the two operand bits and the carry from the column to its right, so the basic cell is the full adder. Its outputs, read as a 2-bit number CoutS, count how many of its three inputs are 1, which is why a full adder is also called a 3:2 counter or compressor.

      ABCinCoutS
      00000
      00101
      01001
      01110
      10001
      10110
      11010
      11111

      S is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1, so S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, which no SOP simplifies (its four minterms are mutually non-adjacent). Cout is the majority function, with minimal SOP A·B + A·Cin + B·Cin, or equivalently A·B + Cin·(A ⊕ B), which reuses the XOR already needed for the sum.

      S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin Cout = A·B + Cin·(A ⊕ B)

      The terms in the carry equation have names that matter for fast adders: generate g = A·B (this column produces a carry no matter what comes in) and propagate p = A ⊕ B (this column passes an incoming carry through). Cout = g + p·Cin.

      The ripple-carry adder

      Chaining n full adders, each carry out driving the next carry in, adds two n-bit numbers. Bit 0's carry in is the adder's C0 input (0 for plain addition) and the last carry out is Cn, the unsigned overflow.

      Its weakness is delay. In the worst case a carry generated in bit 0 must travel through every stage, for example 0111…1 + 0000…1. If each full adder's carry path is two gate levels (AND then OR), an n-bit ripple adder needs about 2n gate delays for the carry plus the final XOR for the sum. A 64-bit ripple adder therefore takes around 130 gate delays, far too slow for a processor that wants an addition every cycle at several gigahertz.

      Subtraction, overflow and the adder/subtractor

      Subtraction is A + B′ + 1. Inverting B under control of a signal SUB is a job for XOR gates (B ⊕ SUB is B when SUB = 0 and B′ when SUB = 1), and the "+ 1" comes from feeding SUB into the carry input C0.

      The flags fall out of the same circuit: C = Cn; V = Cn−1 ⊕ Cn; N = Sn−1; Z = (Sn−1 + … + S0)′, a NOR of all result bits. The interpretation rules from Module 3 apply: after a subtraction, C = 0 signals a borrow. You can explore all four flags in the 4-bit adder tool.

      Comparators

      Equality. A = B when every bit pair matches. Each XNOR gives 1 for a matching pair, and an AND of all XNORs gives EQ. Equivalently, EQ = (A ⊕ B) is all zeros: XOR each pair and NOR the results. A 32-bit equality comparator is 32 XOR gates and a 32-input NOR tree, about log2 32 + 1 = 6 levels deep.

      Magnitude. Rather than build a dedicated circuit, subtract and inspect the flags:

      Question (after computing A − B)UnsignedSigned (two's complement)
      A = BZ = 1Z = 1
      A < BC = 0 (a borrow occurred)N ⊕ V = 1
      A ≥ BC = 1N ⊕ V = 0
      A > BC = 1 and Z = 0N ⊕ V = 0 and Z = 0

      The signed rule needs V because overflow flips the sign: for 4-bit −8 − 1, the result 0111 has N = 0, which alone would suggest −8 ≥ 1; V = 1 corrects it. Processors expose exactly these conditions as branch instructions.

      Carry-lookahead: computing carries in parallel

      The recurrence Ci+1 = gi + pi·Ci can be expanded so that every carry depends only on the g's, p's and C0, which are all available after one gate delay:

      C1 = g0 + p0·C0 C2 = g1 + p1·g0 + p1·p0·C0 C3 = g2 + p2·g1 + p2·p1·g0 + p2·p1·p0·C0 C4 = g3 + p3·g2 + p3·p2·g1 + p3·p2·p1·g0 + p3·p2·p1·p0·C0

      Each line reads naturally: a carry enters column i + 1 if some column j ≤ i generates one and every column between j and i propagates it. Each equation is a two-level AND-OR, so all four carries are ready after three gate delays (g/p, AND, OR), and the sums one XOR later, regardless of position.

      For wider adders the idea is applied hierarchically. Each 4-bit block computes a group generate G = g3 + p3·g2 + p3·p2·g1 + p3·p2·p1·g0 and a group propagate P = p3·p2·p1·p0, and a second-level lookahead unit computes the block carries from the G's and P's exactly as the first level computed bit carries from g's and p's. Each level multiplies the reach by 4, so the delay grows with log4 n rather than n: a 64-bit adder needs three levels. Parallel-prefix adders (Kogge-Stone, Brent-Kung, Han-Carlson) are the general form of this idea and are what fast processors use.

      Other speedups trade area for time differently. A carry-select adder computes the upper half twice, once assuming a carry in of 0 and once assuming 1, and uses the real carry from the lower half to select the right result with a mux. A carry-skip adder lets a carry bypass a block whose propagate signals are all 1.

      Arithmetic with constants and resource sharing

      An incrementer (X + 1) is an adder with B = 0 and C0 = 1, which reduces each full adder to a half adder: Si = Xi ⊕ Ci, Ci+1 = Xi·Ci. Program counters and counters use it. Adding any constant similarly simplifies the full adders whose B input is fixed.

      Worked example

      Mapping if/else onto hardware

      Compute if (s) y = x + 5; else y = x - 1; for 8-bit x.

      Mapping 1: build both results with two adders (x + 0000 0101 and x + 1111 1111) and select with an 8-bit 2-to-1 mux controlled by s. Delay: one adder plus one mux.

      Mapping 2: select the constant first, y = x + (s ? 0000 0101 : 1111 1111), with a single adder. That uses one adder instead of two; the mux on the constant is just wiring and inverters, since each constant bit is either s or 1.

      The general rule: hardware computes every branch of a conditional in parallel unless you deliberately share resources. Sharing saves area, can add delay (a mux in the path), and is one of the main decisions in datapath design.

      Adding many numbers and many bits

      The sum of k numbers of n bits each needs n + ⌈log2 k⌉ bits. When many bits of the same weight must be added, as in counting the 1s in a word (population count) or summing the partial products of a multiplier, full adders are used as 3:2 compressors: each takes three bits of weight 2ʲ and produces one bit of weight 2ʲ and one of weight 2ʲ+1.

      Worked example

      Counting the 1s in 7 bits

      Seven 1-bit inputs have a count from 0 to 7, which needs 3 bits. Two full adders compress six inputs into two sum bits (weight 1) and two carries (weight 2). A third full adder adds the two sum bits and the seventh input: its sum is bit 0 of the count and its carry is one more weight-2 bit. A fourth full adder adds the three weight-2 bits: its sum is bit 1 and its carry is bit 2. Four full adders in total.

      A carry-save adder applies the same idea to whole numbers: a row of independent full adders turns three n-bit numbers into two (a sum word and a carry word) with no carry propagation at all, in one full-adder delay. Reducing many operands with carry-save layers and doing one carry-propagate addition at the end is how multipliers and multiply-accumulate units are built (Wallace and Dadda trees).

      Multiplication

      Binary multiplication is long multiplication with digits 0 and 1: each bit of the multiplier selects either 0 or a shifted copy of the multiplicand (a partial product, formed by AND gates), and the partial products are added.

           1011      (11)
   × 1101      (13)
   ------
     1011      bit 0 = 1
    0000       bit 1 = 0
   1011        bit 2 = 1
+ 1011         bit 3 = 1
---------
 10001111      (143)

      An m-bit by n-bit unsigned product needs m + n bits. An array multiplier computes all m·n partial-product bits at once with AND gates and adds them in a grid of adders; a sequential multiplier reuses one adder over n cycles (shift and add), trading time for area. Signed multiplication uses the same hardware with a correction for the sign bits (Booth recoding is the common method).

      Shifters

      Shifting by a constant is free: it is wiring. Shifting by a variable amount needs a barrel shifter, built from log2 n stages of 2-to-1 muxes. Stage k shifts by 2ᵏ or passes the value through, controlled by bit k of the shift amount, so any shift from 0 to n − 1 takes the same time.

      The arithmetic logic unit

      An ALU computes one of several operations on two operands X and Y, chosen by a function code. The obvious design builds every operation separately and selects one result with a mux. A better design notices that the arithmetic operations differ only in what is fed to a single adder:

      F2 F1 F0Operationadder A inputadder B inputCin
      000X + YXY0
      001X − YXY′1
      010X (pass)X00
      011Y − XX′Y1
      1xxlogic: AND, OR, XOR …(adder unused)

      The control signals are combinational functions of the function code. Reading the table, with the logic operations as don't cares for the adder controls:

      S0 (invert X) = F1·F0 S1 (zero Y) = F1·F0′ S2 (invert Y) = F1′·F0 Cin = F0 S3 (logic result) = F2

      The opcode assignment matters: here F0 = 1 exactly for the subtractions, so the carry input is a single wire. A careless assignment would need extra gates for every control signal. Choosing encodings so that control logic is simple is a recurring theme in processor design (Module 18).

      Key idea

      Arithmetic hardware is built from one cell, the full adder, arranged differently for different goals: in a chain for small adders, with lookahead for fast ones, in carry-save trees for multi-operand sums and multipliers, and behind steering muxes for an ALU.

      Summary

      • Full adder: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B); generate g = AB, propagate p = A ⊕ B.
      • Ripple-carry delay grows linearly with width; carry lookahead makes it logarithmic at the cost of fan-in and area.
      • Subtract with XOR-inverted B and C0 = 1; compare with the flags of A − B (unsigned: C; signed: N ⊕ V).
      • k operands of n bits need n + ⌈log2 k⌉ result bits; an m × n product needs m + n bits.
      • Barrel shifters use log2 n mux stages; ALUs share one adder by steering its inputs.

      Practice problems

      Give the half-adder outputs for A = B = 1, and the full-adder outputs for A = 1, B = 0, Cin = 1.

      Solution

      Half adder: 1 + 1 = 102 → C = 1, S = 0. Full adder: 1 + 0 + 1 = 102 → Cout = 1, S = 0.

      Define generate and propagate for a column of an adder, and write Ci+1 in terms of them.

      Solution

      Generate gi = Ai·Bi: the column produces a carry by itself. Propagate pi = Ai ⊕ Bi: the column passes an incoming carry on. Ci+1 = gi + pi·Ci.

      In a ripple-carry adder whose full adders have a carry delay of 40 ps (Cin to Cout) and a sum delay of 60 ps (Cin to S), what is the worst-case delay of a 16-bit addition?

      Solution

      The carry ripples through bits 0 to 14 (15 × 40 = 600 ps) to reach bit 15's carry input, and bit 15's sum takes another 60 ps: about 660 ps (assuming the g/p inputs settle in time, which they do since they depend only on A and B).

      For A = 1011 and B = 0110, compute gi and pi for each bit, then C1 to C4 with C0 = 0 using the lookahead equations.

      Solution

      Bits 3 to 0: A = 1 0 1 1, B = 0 1 1 0, so g = A·B = 0 0 1 0 (only g1 = 1) and p = A ⊕ B = 1 1 0 1 (p3 = p2 = p0 = 1, p1 = 0).

      C1 = g0 + p0·C0 = 0 + 1·0 = 0. C2 = g1 + p1·g0 + p1·p0·C0 = 1. C3 = g2 + p2·g1 + p2·p1·g0 + p2·p1·p0·C0 = 0 + 1·1 + 0 + 0 = 1. C4 = g3 + p3·g2 + p3·p2·g1 + p3·p2·p1·g0 + p3·p2·p1·p0·C0 = 0 + 0 + 1·1·1 + 0 + 0 = 1.

      Each sum bit pairs pi with the carry into the same column, Si = pi ⊕ Ci: S3 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0, S2 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0, S1 = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0, S0 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. Result C4 S = 1 0001 = 17 = 11 + 6.

      How many bits are needed to hold (a) the sum of five 8-bit unsigned numbers, (b) the product of a 12-bit and a 5-bit unsigned number, (c) the count of 1s in a 32-bit word?

      Solution

      (a) 8 + ⌈log2 5⌉ = 11 bits (max 5 × 255 = 1275 < 2048). (b) 12 + 5 = 17 bits. (c) The count ranges over 0 to 32, which is 33 values: 6 bits.

      Write the logic for a 4-bit equality comparator using XOR gates and one NOR gate. How would you also get A ≠ B?

      Solution

      EQ = NOR(A3 ⊕ B3, A2 ⊕ B2, A1 ⊕ B1, A0 ⊕ B0): any mismatching pair makes its XOR 1 and the NOR 0. A ≠ B is the OR of the same four XORs (or EQ inverted).

      Multiply 1101 × 0110 (unsigned) by listing the partial products, and check in decimal.

      Solution

      Multiplier bits from bit 0: 0, 1, 1, 0. Partial products: 0000, 1101 (shifted 1), 1101 (shifted 2), 0000 (shifted 3). Sum: 11010 + 110100 = 1001110 = 78. Check: 13 × 6 = 78.

      After computing A − B in 8 bits, the flags are C = 1, Z = 0, N = 0, V = 1. Interpret the result as an unsigned comparison and as a signed comparison, and give an example pair of operands that produces these flags.

      Solution

      Unsigned: C = 1 means no borrow, so A ≥ B, and Z = 0 rules out equality: A > B. Signed: N ⊕ V = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1: A < B. The two readings disagree, which is exactly why processors have separate unsigned and signed branch conditions.

      Example: A = 0x9C, B = 0x64. Unsigned these are 156 and 100; signed they are −100 and +100. 156 + (B′ = 155) + 1 = 312 = 256 + 56, so the result is 0x38 = 56 with C = 1, N = 0, Z = 0. The true signed difference −200 does not fit in 8 bits, so V = 1 (a negative minus a positive produced a positive).

      Using the ALU table in the text, derive the control equations for S0 (invert X), S1 (zero Y), S2 (invert Y) and Cin from F2F1F0, treating the logic operations (F2 = 1) as don't cares for these signals.

      Solution

      S0 = 1 only for 011 (Y − X); with F2 = 1 rows as don't cares, the map gives S0 = F1·F0. S1 = 1 only for 010: S1 = F1·F0′. S2 = 1 only for 001: S2 = F1′·F0. Cin = 1 for 001 and 011: Cin = F0. And S3 = F2 selects the logic result.

      Design a circuit that adds four 1-bit values A, B, C, D and outputs their count as a binary number. How many output bits does it need, and how many full and half adders?

      Solution

      The count is 0 to 4: 3 output bits. One full adder on A, B, C gives s1 (weight 1) and c1 (weight 2). A half adder adds s1 and D: its sum is bit 0, its carry c2 has weight 2. A second half adder adds c1 and c2: its sum is bit 1 and its carry is bit 2. Total: 1 full adder and 2 half adders. (c1 and c2 are both 1 only when the count is 4.)

      For the statement if (s) y = x + 5; else y = x - 1; on 8-bit values, give the 8-bit constant fed to the adder in each case for the one-adder implementation, and express each bit of that constant as a function of s.

      Solution

      x + 5 adds 0000 0101; x − 1 adds 1111 1111 (−1 in two's complement, carry in 0). Bit by bit (bit 7 down to bit 0): bits 7..3 are 0 when s = 1 and 1 when s = 0, so they equal s′; bit 2 is 1 in both cases (1); bit 1 is 0 or 1, so s′; bit 0 is 1 in both (1). The "mux" is just six inverted copies of s and two constant 1s feeding one adder.

      A 32-bit barrel shifter is built from 2-to-1 muxes. How many stages and how many muxes does it need, and what is its delay in mux delays? Compare with shifting one position per clock cycle.

      Solution

      log2 32 = 5 stages of 32 muxes: 160 muxes, with a delay of 5 mux delays for any shift amount. A one-bit-per-cycle shift register needs only one mux per bit (32), but a shift by 31 takes 31 cycles. The barrel shifter trades area for constant, short latency.

      Write the group generate G and group propagate P for a 4-bit lookahead block, and use them to design a 16-bit adder with two levels of lookahead. Estimate its carry delay in gate levels and compare with a 16-bit ripple adder.

      Solution

      G = g3 + p3·g2 + p3·p2·g1 + p3·p2·p1·g0 and P = p3·p2·p1·p0, so the block's carry out is G + P·Cin. For 16 bits: four 4-bit blocks produce (Gk, Pk); a second-level unit computes block carries C4 = G0 + P0·C0, C8 = G1 + P1·G0 + P1·P0·C0, and so on, with the same equations as the first level. Delay: g/p (1 level), block G/P (2 levels), second-level carries (2 levels), carries inside each block from its block carry (2 levels), sum XOR (1): roughly 8 gate levels. A 16-bit ripple adder needs about 2 × 16 = 32 levels for the carry chain plus the XOR.

      Design a one-digit BCD adder: two BCD digits plus a carry in produce a BCD digit and a carry out. Use a 4-bit binary adder and a correction step, and give the condition for correction.

      Hint

      The binary sum ranges from 0 to 19. Which sums are not valid BCD digits, and what must be added to fix them?

      Solution

      Add the digits in binary: the 5-bit result K Z3 Z2 Z1 Z0 (K is the binary carry) ranges from 0 to 9 + 9 + 1 = 19. If it is 10 or more, the BCD result must be (sum − 10) with a decimal carry. Adding 6 (0110) to the low 4 bits does exactly that, because 16 − 10 = 6 skips the six unused codes. Correction is needed when the sum exceeds 9: Cout = K + Z3·Z2 + Z3·Z1 (K covers 16–19; Z3·Z2 and Z3·Z1 cover 10–15). A second 4-bit adder adds 0 Cout Cout 0 to Z3..Z0, ignoring its carry. Example: 8 + 7 = 15 = 0 1111 → correction (Z3·Z2 = 1) → 1111 + 0110 = 1 0101 → digit 5 with Cout = 1, i.e. 15.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      The electrical reality under the logic: circuit laws, RC behavior and filters, analog building blocks, transistors and CMOS gates, and what it takes for two chips to talk.

      Part III: Circuits and the physical layer

      Circuits: voltage, current and RC behavior

      The circuit laws every hardware engineer uses daily: Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws, dividers and Thevenin equivalents, capacitors and the RC time constant that sets gate delay, inductors, impedance, and first-order filters.

      Builds onDigital abstractionToolsRC filter explorerPractice16 problems

      Logic diagrams hide the electrical reality that makes them work or fail. A gate output is a transistor connecting a wire to the supply or to ground through some resistance; the wire and every gate input attached to it form a capacitance; the time to charge that capacitance is the gate's delay, and the energy spent doing so is most of the chip's power. This module builds the circuit analysis needed to reason about those effects, and about the analog parts that surround every digital system: dividers, filters, sensors and loads.

      Charge, current, voltage and power

      Current

      The rate at which charge flows past a point, I = dQ/dt, measured in amperes (1 A = 1 coulomb per second). By convention current flows from higher to lower potential through a load, opposite to the direction electrons actually move.

      Voltage

      The potential difference between two points: the energy per unit charge gained or lost moving between them, measured in volts (1 V = 1 joule per coulomb). A voltage is always between two nodes; "the voltage at a node" means relative to a chosen reference node called ground.

      Power is the rate of energy transfer, P = V·I, in watts. An element that has current entering its more positive terminal absorbs power (a resistor, a charging battery); one with current leaving its positive terminal delivers it. Energy is power integrated over time, E = P·t for constant power. Two numbers to keep in mind: a microcontroller pin at 5 V delivering 20 mA supplies 0.1 W, far too little to drive a loudspeaker or motor directly, while a modern GPU at about 1 V can draw several hundred amperes.

      Resistance and Ohm's law

      For a resistor the current is proportional to the voltage across it:

      V = I · R

      Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω). Substituting Ohm's law into P = VI gives the power a resistor dissipates as heat: P = I2R = V2/R. Resistors have power ratings (1/8 W and 1/4 W are typical for small parts) that must exceed this. A conductor of resistivity ρ, length L and cross-sectional area A has R = ρL/A, which is why on-chip wires, with cross sections measured in tens of nanometers, have significant resistance: it grows with length and shrinks with width.

      Common mistake

      Ohm's law describes resistors, not every element. A diode, LED or transistor has a non-linear current-voltage relationship. Treating an LED as a resistor (or forgetting the series resistor it needs) is a classic interfacing mistake, covered in Module 13.

      Kirchhoff's laws

      Two conservation laws let you analyze any circuit:

      • Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): the currents entering a node sum to zero (what flows in flows out), because charge cannot accumulate at a junction of wires.
      • Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL): the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero, because returning to the starting node returns to the starting potential.

      Systematic circuit analysis (nodal analysis) assigns an unknown voltage to each node except ground, writes KCL at each node with every current expressed through Ohm's law, and solves the resulting linear equations. Most circuits in digital design are simple enough to reduce by inspection instead, using the series and parallel rules below.

      Series and parallel resistors

      Elements in series carry the same current, so their voltages add: Req = R1 + R2 + …. Elements in parallel share the same voltage, so their currents add: 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …. For two resistors, R1 ∥ R2 = R1R2/(R1 + R2); n equal resistors in parallel give R/n; and a parallel combination is always smaller than its smallest member.

      To analyze a series-parallel network, collapse it step by step into one equivalent resistance, find the total current, then expand back out, applying Ohm's law to each piece.

      Voltage and current dividers

      Two resistors in series across a source form a voltage divider. The same current I = VS/(R1 + R2) flows through both, so each resistor's share of the voltage is proportional to its resistance:

      Vout = VS · R2 / (R1 + R2)

      The loaded case is the one that matters in practice. With VS = 10 V and R1 = R2 = 10 kΩ the unloaded output is 5 V; a 10 kΩ load makes the bottom half 5 kΩ, and the output falls to 10 × 5/15 = 3.33 V. A useful rule is that the load should be at least ten times R1 ∥ R2 (the divider's Thevenin resistance, introduced next) for the output to stay within about 10% of the formula; when that is impossible, buffer the output with an op-amp follower (Module 11). Dividers appear everywhere: scaling a battery voltage into an ADC's input range, biasing, potentiometers (a divider with a movable tap), and resistive sensors such as thermistors or photoresistors paired with a fixed resistor.

      The dual result is the current divider: a current I entering two parallel resistors splits in inverse proportion to resistance, I1 = I · R2/(R1 + R2). More current takes the easier path.

      Thevenin equivalents: what a load sees

      Any linear network of sources and resistors, viewed from two terminals, is indistinguishable from a single voltage source VTH in series with a single resistance RTH. This is the most useful idea in interfacing because it answers the question "how much will the voltage sag when I connect a load?"

      To find the equivalent: VTH is the open-circuit voltage at the terminals; RTH is the resistance seen looking into the terminals with every independent voltage source replaced by a short and every current source by an open. For the divider above, VTH = VSR2/(R1 + R2) and RTH = R1 ∥ R2. With a load attached, Vload = VTH · RL/(RTH + RL): the source resistance and the load form a divider.

      Every real source has a Thevenin resistance: a battery's internal resistance, a logic output's transistor on-resistance (tens of ohms), a sensor's output impedance. A digital output that reads 1.8 V instead of 5 V while driving an LED is this effect, worked through in Module 13. A related result: a load draws maximum power from a source when RL = RTH, at 50% efficiency, which matters for RF and audio matching but not for logic, where you want RL ≫ RTH so the voltage holds.

      Capacitors

      Capacitor

      Two conductors separated by an insulator. It stores charge Q = C·V on its plates; capacitance C is measured in farads. Because current is the rate of change of charge, i = C·dv/dt: a capacitor's voltage cannot change instantly, and it passes no DC current once charged.

      A capacitor charged to V stores energy ½CV2. Capacitors combine opposite to resistors: in parallel their capacitances add (more plate area), in series 1/Ceq = 1/C1 + 1/C2. Typical values span many orders of magnitude: a CMOS gate input is about a femtofarad (10−15 F) in a modern process, a millimeter of on-chip wire a fraction of a picofarad, a ceramic decoupling capacitor 100 nF, and an electrolytic bulk capacitor hundreds of microfarads.

      In digital systems capacitance is both a nuisance and a tool. Every wire and gate input is a parasitic capacitor that must be charged and discharged on every transition, which costs time and energy. Deliberate capacitors placed next to each chip's supply pins (decoupling or bypass capacitors) act as local charge reservoirs: when thousands of transistors switch at once, the charge comes from the nearby capacitor rather than through the long, inductive supply path.

      RC circuits: the time constant

      Connect a source VS through a resistor R to an uncharged capacitor C at t = 0. KVL gives VS = iR + vC, and i = C·dvC/dt, so

      RC · dvC/dt + vC = VS ⇒ vC(t) = VS (1 − e−t/RC)

      The product τ = RC is the time constant (ohms × farads = seconds). The capacitor starts charging at the rate VS/τ, as if it would reach VS in one time constant, but the current falls as the capacitor voltage approaches the source, so the approach is exponential.

      Elapsed timeFraction of the final value reachedFraction remaining
      1τ63.2%36.8%
      2τ86.5%13.5%
      3τ95.0%5.0%
      5τ99.3%0.7%

      Three derived numbers are used constantly:

      • The time to cross a threshold Vth while charging toward VS: solve Vth = VS(1 − e−t/τ) to get t = τ · ln(VS/(VS − Vth)).
      • The 50% point is at t = τ ln 2 ≈ 0.69 RC, the usual estimate for a gate's propagation delay.
      • The 10%-to-90% rise time is τ(ln 0.9 − ln 0.1) ≈ 2.2 RC.

      Why the time constant is gate delay

      When a CMOS gate's output switches, one transistor connects the output wire to the supply or to ground through its on-resistance Ron, and that resistance charges or discharges the total load capacitance: the input capacitance of every gate it drives (its fanout), the wire, and the gate's own output capacitance. To first order the propagation delay is therefore tpd ≈ 0.69·Ron·Cload. This single model explains a long list of design facts:

      • Delay grows linearly with fanout, because each extra input adds capacitance.
      • Wider transistors switch faster (lower Ron) but present more input capacitance to whatever drives them, so speeding up one gate slows its predecessor.
      • Long wires are slow. A wire's resistance and capacitance both grow with length L, so its own delay grows with L2; long on-chip wires are broken into segments with repeaters (buffers) to make the delay grow linearly instead.
      • Every transition moves charge C·VDD through a resistance, which is where dynamic power comes from (Module 12).

      Inductors

      An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field, ½LI2, and resists changes in current: v = L·di/dt (L in henries). Its current cannot change instantly, the dual of a capacitor's voltage. If you try to interrupt the current abruptly, for example by switching off a transistor driving a relay coil or motor, di/dt becomes very large and so does the voltage: interrupting 100 mA in 1 μs through 10 mH produces about 1000 V, enough to destroy the transistor. The cure is a flyback diode that gives the current a path to decay through (Module 13).

      Inductance also appears where nobody put an inductor: every wire, package pin and bond wire has a few nanohenries. When many outputs switch at once, the supply and ground currents change quickly, and L·di/dt across the package inductance makes the chip's internal ground bounce relative to the board's ground. This is ground bounce (or simultaneous switching noise), and it is another reason for decoupling capacitors and many supply pins.

      Sinusoids and impedance

      Signals can be analyzed as sums of sinusoids v(t) = A·sin(2πft + φ), with frequency f in hertz, angular frequency ω = 2πf and period T = 1/f. For sinusoids, capacitors and inductors behave like frequency-dependent resistors described by an impedance Z, a complex number whose magnitude scales amplitude and whose angle shifts phase:

      ElementImpedanceMagnitudeBehavior
      ResistorZ = RRsame at all frequencies
      CapacitorZ = 1/(jωC)1/(2πfC)open circuit at DC, short circuit at high frequency
      InductorZ = jωL2πfLshort circuit at DC, open circuit at high frequency

      With impedances, every divider and series-parallel rule above works for sinusoids at a given frequency. That is all that is needed to analyze filters.

      First-order RC filters

      Swap one resistor of a divider for a capacitor and the divider ratio becomes frequency dependent. In the low-pass version the capacitor sits across the output; at low frequency its impedance is huge and the output follows the input, while at high frequency it shorts the output toward ground:

      H(f) = vout/vin = 1 / (1 + j·f/fc), fc = 1/(2πRC)

      Filter gains are usually quoted in decibels: for voltage ratios, gain in dB = 20·log10(|vout/vin|). A ratio of 1/√2 = 0.707 is −3 dB (half the power, hence "half-power point"), 0.5 is −6 dB, 0.1 is −20 dB and 0.01 is −40 dB. A first-order filter falls by 20 dB per decade (6 dB per octave) beyond fc; cascading n sections makes an n-th order filter that falls 20n dB per decade. The phase shift of the low-pass is −45° at fc, approaching −90° far above it.

      The cutoff frequency and the time constant are the same fact seen in two domains: fc = 1/(2πτ). A low-pass filter is slow to respond to steps for exactly the reason it attenuates high frequencies.

      In practice

      Where first-order filters show up in digital systems:

      • Anti-aliasing before an ADC: remove frequencies above half the sampling rate (Module 11).
      • PWM to analog: a low-pass with fc far below the PWM frequency turns a pulse train into its average voltage.
      • Debouncing: an RC on a switch input smooths the bounces into one slow edge, which a Schmitt-trigger input then cleans up.
      • AC coupling: a series capacitor (a high-pass) removes a DC offset, as in audio inputs.
      • Supply filtering: a series resistor or inductor followed by a capacitor keeps digital switching noise out of an analog supply.
      Second-order circuits and resonance going deeper

      A circuit with both an inductor and a capacitor is second order. A series RLC circuit has a resonant frequency f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), where the inductor's and capacitor's impedances cancel. Depending on the damping, set by R, its step response either approaches the final value smoothly (overdamped), as fast as possible without overshoot (critically damped), or overshoots and rings (underdamped). Ringing on a fast digital edge, caused by trace inductance and pin capacitance, is an underdamped RLC response; series termination resistors add the damping that removes it.

      Summary

      • V = IR; P = VI = I2R = V2/R. KCL: currents into a node sum to zero. KVL: voltages around a loop sum to zero.
      • Series resistances add; parallel conductances add. Divider: Vout = VSR2/(R1 + R2), valid only for light loads.
      • Any linear two-terminal network is a Thevenin source VTH with series RTH; the load and RTH form a divider.
      • i = C dv/dt; τ = RC; 63% after 1τ, 99% after 5τ; t50% ≈ 0.69RC; t10–90% ≈ 2.2RC; t to threshold = τ ln(VS/(VS − Vth)).
      • Gate delay ≈ 0.69 RonCload; wire delay grows with length squared.
      • v = L di/dt: interrupting inductive current creates large voltage spikes.
      • |ZC| = 1/(2πfC); RC filter cutoff fc = 1/(2πRC), −3 dB there, −20 dB/decade beyond.

      Practice problems

      A 4.7 kΩ resistor has 12 V across it. Find the current and the power it dissipates.

      Solution

      I = 12/4700 = 2.55 mA. P = V2/R = 144/4700 = 30.6 mW, well within a 1/4 W rating.

      Find the equivalent resistance of (a) two 1 kΩ resistors in parallel, (b) three 3 kΩ resistors in parallel, (c) a 2 kΩ resistor in series with the combination in (b).

      Solution

      (a) 1k·1k/2k = 500 Ω. (b) 3 kΩ/3 = 1 kΩ. (c) 2 + 1 = 3 kΩ.

      Currents of 3 mA and 2 mA flow into a node. One wire carries 1 mA out of it. What is the current in the fourth wire, and in which direction?

      Solution

      KCL: in = out, so 3 + 2 = 1 + I, I = 4 mA flowing out of the node.

      A divider has R1 = 10 kΩ on top and R2 = 20 kΩ on the bottom, fed from 5 V. Find the output voltage unloaded and with a 20 kΩ load.

      Solution

      Unloaded: 5 × 20/30 = 3.33 V. Loaded: R2 ∥ RL = 10 kΩ, so 5 × 10/20 = 2.50 V. The load equal to R2 pulled the output down by 25%.

      An LED with a forward voltage of 2.0 V should carry 10 mA from a 5 V supply. What series resistor is needed, and how much power do the resistor and the LED each dissipate?

      Solution

      The resistor drops 5 − 2 = 3 V at 10 mA: R = 3/0.01 = 300 Ω (use the next standard value, 330 Ω, for slightly less current). PR = 3 V × 10 mA = 30 mW; PLED = 2 V × 10 mA = 20 mW.

      R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF are charged from 0 V by a 5 V step. What is the time constant, and what is the capacitor voltage after 2 ms and after 5 ms?

      Solution

      τ = 104 × 10−7 = 1 ms. At 2 ms: 5(1 − e−2) = 5 × 0.865 = 4.32 V. At 5 ms: 5 × 0.993 = 4.97 V.

      Convert to decibels: a voltage gain of 0.5, a voltage gain of 0.707, a voltage gain of 1000, and a power ratio of 0.5.

      Solution

      20 log10 0.5 = −6.02 dB; 20 log10 0.707 = −3.01 dB; 20 log10 1000 = 60 dB; for power use 10 log10: 10 log10 0.5 = −3.01 dB. Halving the power and multiplying the voltage by 0.707 are the same event.

      Find the Thevenin equivalent of a divider with VS = 9 V, R1 = 6 kΩ (top) and R2 = 3 kΩ (bottom), then the output voltage with a 2 kΩ load.

      Solution

      VTH = 9 × 3/9 = 3 V; RTH = 6k ∥ 3k = 2 kΩ. With RL = 2 kΩ: 3 × 2/(2 + 2) = 1.5 V. Check directly: R2 ∥ RL = 1.2 kΩ, 9 × 1.2/7.2 = 1.5 V.

      A 10 kΩ pull-up resistor charges a wire with 100 pF of capacitance from 0 V toward 5 V. A receiving input reads 1 once the voltage passes 3.0 V. How long after release does the input read 1?

      Solution

      τ = 104 × 10−10 = 1 μs. t = τ ln(5/(5 − 3)) = 1 μs × ln 2.5 = 0.92 μs. This is why pull-up resistors limit the speed of open-drain buses: halve R to halve the delay, at the cost of more current when the line is low.

      An RC low-pass has R = 1.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Find fc, and the gain in dB at 10 kHz and at 100 kHz.

      Solution

      fc = 1/(2π × 1600 × 10−7) = 995 Hz ≈ 1 kHz. At 10 kHz, |H| = 1/√(1 + 102) = 0.0995 → −20 dB. At 100 kHz, |H| ≈ 0.01 → −40 dB: one decade further, 20 dB lower.

      A 1 μF capacitor charged to 5 V is discharged through 1 kΩ. How much energy was stored, how long until the voltage falls below 0.5 V, and where does the energy go?

      Solution

      E = ½CV2 = ½ × 10−6 × 25 = 12.5 μJ. τ = 1 ms; 5e−t/τ = 0.5 → t = τ ln 10 = 2.3 ms. All of the energy is dissipated as heat in the resistor.

      A transistor switches off 100 mA flowing through a 10 mH relay coil in 1 μs. Estimate the voltage the coil produces, and explain what a flyback diode does about it.

      Solution

      v = L di/dt = 0.01 × 0.1/10−6 = 1000 V. The coil keeps its current flowing by raising the voltage at the transistor's drain until something breaks down. A diode across the coil, cathode to the supply, gives the current a loop to circulate in; the drain then rises only one diode drop above the supply while the current decays through the coil's resistance.

      A logic gate with 2 kΩ output resistance drives four gate inputs of 5 fF each and a wire of 20 fF. Estimate the propagation delay. What happens if the fanout doubles?

      Solution

      Cload = 4 × 5 + 20 = 40 fF. tpd ≈ 0.69 × 2000 × 40 × 10−15 = 55 ps. With eight inputs Cload = 60 fF and tpd ≈ 83 ps: delay grows linearly with fanout, offset by the fixed wire load.

      A chip's supply current steps by 1 A for 2 ns whenever a block wakes up, and the supply inductance prevents the regulator from responding that fast. What decoupling capacitance keeps the supply droop under 50 mV during the step?

      Solution

      The capacitor must supply Q = I·Δt = 1 A × 2 ns = 2 nC while its voltage drops at most ΔV = 0.05 V: C = Q/ΔV = 2 × 10−9/0.05 = 40 nF. In practice several smaller capacitors are used in parallel, because a capacitor's own series inductance limits how fast it can deliver charge.

      A PWM output at 62.5 kHz with 50% duty cycle and 5 V amplitude is smoothed by an RC low-pass. Choose fc so the ripple's fundamental component is about 1% of its unfiltered amplitude, then estimate the ripple and how long the output takes to settle after the duty cycle changes.

      Hint

      A 50% square wave of amplitude V has a fundamental sinusoid of amplitude (2/π)V. Far above fc a first-order low-pass attenuates by about fc/f.

      Solution

      Attenuation of 1/100 at 62.5 kHz needs fc ≈ 625 Hz (for example R = 2.5 kΩ, C = 100 nF). The fundamental has amplitude (2/π) × 5 ≈ 3.2 V, so the remaining ripple is about 32 mV amplitude. τ = 1/(2πfc) ≈ 255 μs, so settling to within 1% takes about 5τ ≈ 1.3 ms. Lower fc means less ripple and slower response; a second-order filter improves the trade-off.

      A button is connected through a 10 kΩ pull-up with a 1 μF capacitor from the input to ground. Pressing the button shorts the capacitor to ground through 100 Ω. The input is a Schmitt trigger with thresholds 3.0 V (rising) and 1.5 V (falling) at 5 V. How long after a press does the input read 0, and how long after release does it read 1? Can 5 ms of contact bounce after release cause a false reading?

      Solution

      Press: discharge through 100 Ω (the 10 kΩ path is negligible), τ = 100 μs. Falling below 1.5 V: t = τ ln(5/1.5) ≈ 0.12 ms. Release: charge through 10 kΩ, τ = 10 ms. Rising past 3.0 V: t = 10 ms × ln(5/2) ≈ 9.2 ms. Bounce during release briefly reconnects the capacitor to ground, which can reset the charging, but no edge reaches the input until the contacts have been open long enough for the voltage to climb from below 1.5 V past 3.0 V (about 6 ms of uninterrupted charging), and the hysteresis prevents chatter near the threshold. The input sees one clean edge.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Part III: Circuits and the physical layer

      Diodes, op-amps and data conversion

      The analog parts that sit at the edges of every digital system: diodes and LEDs, operational amplifiers and comparators, hysteresis, sampling and aliasing, analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters, and PWM as a cheap DAC.

      Builds onCircuits and RCPractice15 problems

      Digital logic interprets voltages as 0 and 1, but the world it measures and controls is continuous: temperatures, audio, light levels, motor speeds. The interface consists of a small set of analog building blocks. This module explains how each works and what limits it, at the depth needed to choose and use them correctly and to answer the analog questions that appear in hardware interviews.

      Diodes

      Diode

      A two-terminal device, usually a p-n junction, that conducts current easily in one direction (anode to cathode, forward bias) and blocks it in the other (reverse bias). The symbol's bar marks the cathode.

      A diode's current rises exponentially with forward voltage, I ≈ IS·eV/(nVT), where VT = kT/q ≈ 26 mV at room temperature and n is between 1 and 2. Exponential means that every additional 60 to 120 mV multiplies the current by ten, so over the range of currents a circuit actually uses, the voltage across a conducting diode is nearly constant: about 0.6 to 0.7 V for silicon. That constant drop is the basis of the simple model "off below VF, a fixed VF drop when on."

      Uses that appear in digital hardware:

      • LEDs emit light when forward biased; VF is roughly 1.8 to 2.2 V for red, yellow and green and 2.8 to 3.4 V for blue and white. Because the voltage is nearly fixed while the current is not, an LED must have its current set by something else, normally a series resistor: R = (Vsupply − VF)/I.
      • Protection: every chip's I/O pin has clamp diodes to VDD and to ground that conduct if the pin is driven beyond the supply rails, steering electrostatic discharge and overvoltage into the supply.
      • Flyback diodes across inductive loads (Module 13), reverse-polarity protection in a supply input, and rectifiers that convert AC to DC.
      • Zener diodes are designed to break down at a specified reverse voltage and hold it, which makes them simple voltage references and clamps.

      Common mistake

      With a low supply, the LED resistor has little voltage to work with and the current becomes sensitive to VF. A blue LED (VF ≈ 3.0 V) on a 3.3 V supply leaves 0.3 V across the resistor; a ±0.1 V variation in VF changes the current by a third.

      The operational amplifier

      Operational amplifier

      A differential amplifier with very high voltage gain (typically 105 or more), very high input impedance and low output impedance. Its output is A·(V+ − V−), limited to the range between its supply rails.

      On its own an op-amp is nearly useless as an amplifier: with a gain of 100,000, a 50 μV difference already drives the output to a rail. Its power comes from negative feedback, which connects the output back to the inverting input through a network that sets the gain. With negative feedback in place, two rules describe an ideal op-amp circuit:

      1. The output does whatever is necessary to make V− equal to V+ (the inputs form a "virtual short").
      2. No current flows into either input.

      Every standard configuration follows from those rules and a line of algebra.

      • Voltage follower. The output is wired directly to V−, so rule 1 gives vout = vin. A gain of 1 sounds pointless, but the input draws no current and the output can supply milliamps: a follower isolates a high-impedance source (a divider, a sensor) from the load that would otherwise drag it down.
      • Non-inverting amplifier. Rf and Rg divide the output, so V− = vout·Rg/(Rf + Rg). Setting this equal to vin gives vout/vin = 1 + Rf/Rg. The input impedance is essentially infinite.
      • Inverting amplifier. V+ is grounded, so V− is held at 0 V (a virtual ground). The input current vin/Rin cannot enter the op-amp, so it all flows through Rf, and vout = −(vin/Rin)·Rf: gain −Rf/Rin. The input impedance is Rin.
      • Summing amplifier. Several input resistors into the same virtual ground add their currents: vout = −Rf(v1/R1 + v2/R2 + …). With binary-weighted resistors this is a simple DAC; it is also an audio mixer.
      • Integrator. Replace Rf with a capacitor and the output is −(1/RC)∫vindt: the basis of active filters, ramp generators and integrating ADCs.

      Real op-amps add limits that matter in practice. The gain-bandwidth product (GBW) is roughly constant, so a circuit with gain G has a bandwidth of about GBW/G: a 1 MHz op-amp set for a gain of 100 is useful only to about 10 kHz. The slew rate caps how fast the output can change (V/μs), which limits large, fast signals. The output cannot reach the supply rails unless the part is specified "rail-to-rail", and small offset voltages (microvolts to millivolts) appear as errors after high gain.

      Comparators and hysteresis

      Without feedback, an op-amp or a dedicated comparator outputs high when vin > Vref and low otherwise: a one-bit ADC. Comparators are built for this job, with fast recovery from saturation and outputs that match logic levels (often open-drain).

      A comparator alone has a problem with slow, noisy signals. Near the threshold, noise pushes the input back and forth across it, and the output chatters between 0 and 1, producing many edges where there should be one. The fix is hysteresis: two thresholds, a higher one (VT+) that the input must cross while rising and a lower one (VT−) for falling. Once the output switches, the threshold moves away from the input, and noise smaller than the gap VT+ − VT− cannot switch it back. A comparator with hysteresis, built with a little positive feedback, is a Schmitt trigger.

      Schmitt-trigger inputs are everywhere in digital hardware: logic gates such as the 74HC14, reset and clock inputs, and the digital input buffers of many microcontrollers, including AVR parts. Combined with an RC filter they are the standard hardware debouncer for mechanical switches.

      Sampling and aliasing

      Before a continuous signal can be processed digitally it is sampled at a fixed rate fs and each sample is quantized. Sampling alone loses no information under one condition, the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem: a signal containing no frequencies at or above fs/2 (the Nyquist frequency) is completely determined by its samples. Audio is sampled at 44.1 or 48 kHz because human hearing extends to about 20 kHz.

      A component above fs/2 does not disappear: it produces exactly the same samples as a lower frequency and is indistinguishable from it. This is aliasing. A frequency f appears at |f − k·fs| for whichever integer k brings the result into the range 0 to fs/2.

      Because aliasing cannot be undone after sampling, an analog anti-aliasing filter, a low-pass, must remove content above fs/2 before the ADC. Practical systems sample somewhat faster than twice the highest frequency of interest so the filter has room to roll off. The same effect explains why wagon wheels appear to turn backwards in film, and why sampling a slowly varying sensor at a rate synchronized to mains interference (50 or 60 Hz) can produce a phantom slow drift.

      Analog-to-digital conversion

      An n-bit ADC with reference voltage Vref divides its input range into 2n steps of width 1 LSB = Vref/2n and outputs the step number. An ideal converter that rounds has a quantization error of at most ±½ LSB; one that truncates has an error between 0 and 1 LSB. For a 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference, 1 LSB is 4.88 mV, and an input of V gives a code of about V/Vref × 1024.

      Quantization error behaves like noise with an RMS value of LSB/√12. For a full-scale sine wave this gives a best-case signal-to-quantization-noise ratio of about 6.02n + 1.76 dB: each extra bit buys 6 dB. Real converters add other noise and distortion, so their performance is summarized by an effective number of bits, ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02, where SINAD is the measured signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio in dB.

      ArchitectureHow it worksTypical use
      Flash2n − 1 comparators against a resistor ladder compare the input with every threshold at once; a priority encoder produces the codeFastest (GHz), but comparator count doubles per bit, so usually ≤ 8 bits
      Successive approximation (SAR)One comparator and an internal DAC run a binary search, deciding one bit per step from the MSB down8–18 bits, kHz to MHz; the ADC in most microcontrollers
      Sigma-delta (ΔΣ)A 1-bit modulator runs far faster than needed; digital filtering trades that speed for resolution and pushes noise out of band16–24 bits at audio and lower rates
      PipelinedA chain of low-resolution stages, each resolving a few bits and passing the residue on10–16 bits at tens to hundreds of MS/s

      Worked example

      One SAR conversion

      A 4-bit SAR ADC with Vref = 3.2 V (1 LSB = 0.2 V) converts Vin = 2.05 V. Each step sets the next bit to 1, converts the trial code with the internal DAC, and keeps the bit only if Vin is at least the DAC voltage:

      StepTrial codeDAC voltageV_in ≥ DAC?Result so far
      110001.6 Vyes1000
      211002.4 Vno1000
      310102.0 Vyes1010
      410112.2 Vno1010

      The result 1010 (code 10, 2.0 V) is reached in n = 4 comparisons, one per bit, which is why SAR converters are compact and moderately fast.

      On the ATmega328P the ADC is a 10-bit SAR converter with an 8-input multiplexer. ADMUX selects the reference (REFS1:0; 01 = AVCC) and the channel (MUX3:0), and ADLAR left-adjusts the result so that ADCH alone holds the top 8 bits. ADCSRA enables the converter (ADEN), starts a conversion (ADSC, which reads 1 until the conversion finishes) and sets the ADC clock prescaler (ADPS2:0). Full 10-bit accuracy needs an ADC clock of 50 to 200 kHz, so a 16 MHz system clock is divided by 128 to give 125 kHz; a conversion takes 13 ADC clocks, about 104 μs.

      void adc_init(void)
{
    ADMUX  = (1 << REFS0) | (1 << ADLAR);      // AVCC reference, left-adjusted result
    ADCSRA = (1 << ADEN) | (7 << ADPS0);       // enable; prescaler 128 -> 125 kHz
}

uint8_t adc_sample(uint8_t channel)
{
    ADMUX = (ADMUX & 0xF0) | (channel & 0x0F);  // change channel, keep REFS and ADLAR
    ADCSRA |= (1 << ADSC);                      // start one conversion
    while (ADCSRA & (1 << ADSC)) { }            // ADSC clears when the result is ready
    return ADCH;                                // top 8 of the 10 bits
}

      In practice

      One ADC pin can read several buttons. Each button connects a different point of a resistor ladder to the pin, so each produces a different voltage, and the software compares the reading against thresholds halfway between the expected values. LCD shields commonly read five buttons this way through a single analog input. The thresholds must leave margin for resistor tolerance and supply variation.

      Digital-to-analog conversion

      The inverse problem, producing a voltage proportional to a binary number, has three common solutions.

      Binary-weighted resistors feeding a summing amplifier (R, 2R, 4R, 8R, …) are simple in principle but need resistor values spanning a ratio of 2n−1, all matched to better than 1 LSB, which is impractical beyond a few bits.

      The R-2R ladder uses only two resistor values. Analyze it one bit at a time (superposition), with the other bit inputs at 0 V. Looking toward the LSB end from any node, the ladder presents exactly 2R, because the termination 2R in parallel with a 2R leg is R, plus the next series R makes 2R again, and so on. The MSB's leg therefore forms a divider with the 2R behind it and contributes Vref/2 to the output; each step further from the output passes through one more halving divider, so the next bit contributes Vref/4, then Vref/8. The result is an exact binary weighting from two matched values.

      Pulse-width modulation (PWM) needs no DAC hardware at all: a digital output switches between 0 and VDD at a fixed frequency, and the fraction of each period spent high, the duty cycle D, sets the average voltage D·VDD. A low-pass filter with a cutoff far below the PWM frequency extracts the average. For many loads no filter is needed: LEDs, heaters and motors respond to average power, and the eye or the load's own inertia does the filtering.

      PWM resolution and frequency trade against each other: a counter clocked at fclk with N steps per period gives fPWM = fclk/N. With a 16 MHz clock, 8-bit PWM runs at 62.5 kHz, while 10-bit PWM runs at only 15.6 kHz. Timer configuration for PWM is in Module 25.

      Summary

      • A conducting diode drops about 0.7 V (silicon) or 2 to 3 V (LEDs); set LED current with a series resistor R = (VS − VF)/I.
      • Op-amp with negative feedback: V+ = V−, no input current. Follower gain 1, non-inverting 1 + Rf/Rg, inverting −Rf/Rin. Bandwidth ≈ GBW/gain.
      • Comparators make 1-bit decisions; hysteresis (Schmitt trigger) prevents chatter on noisy, slow inputs.
      • Sample above twice the highest frequency present; content above fs/2 aliases to |f − kfs| and must be filtered out first.
      • n-bit ADC: LSB = Vref/2n; SQNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB. Flash is fastest, SAR is the microcontroller workhorse, sigma-delta gives the most bits.
      • R-2R ladders and PWM with a low-pass filter are the common cheap DACs.

      Practice problems

      An 8-bit ADC has a 5 V reference. What is 1 LSB, and what code (truncating) does a 2.0 V input produce?

      Solution

      1 LSB = 5/256 = 19.5 mV. Code = ⌊2.0/5 × 256⌋ = ⌊102.4⌋ = 102 (0x66).

      What is the gain of a non-inverting amplifier with Rf = 9 kΩ and Rg = 1 kΩ? Of an inverting amplifier with Rf = 47 kΩ and Rin = 10 kΩ?

      Solution

      Non-inverting: 1 + 9/1 = 10. Inverting: −47/10 = −4.7 (a 0.5 V input gives −2.35 V, if the supplies allow negative outputs).

      What minimum sampling rate does the sampling theorem require for audio up to 20 kHz? Why do real systems use 44.1 or 48 kHz rather than exactly that?

      Solution

      More than 40 kHz. The extra margin lets a practical anti-aliasing filter pass 20 kHz while attenuating everything above 22 to 24 kHz; an ideal brick-wall filter at exactly fs/2 cannot be built.

      A 4-bit R-2R DAC with Vref = 3.3 V is given the code 1011. What is its output voltage?

      Solution

      Vout = 3.3 × 11/16 = 2.27 V.

      An ATmega328P reads 614 from its 10-bit ADC with AVCC = 5.0 V as the reference. What is the input voltage? What would the 8-bit left-adjusted ADCH value be?

      Solution

      V = 614 × 5/1024 = 3.00 V. ADCH holds the top 8 of 10 bits: 614 >> 2 = 153.

      A 30 kHz tone is sampled at 44.1 kHz with no anti-aliasing filter. At what frequency does it appear in the samples?

      Solution

      |30 − 44.1| = 14.1 kHz, which is inside the audible band and indistinguishable from a real 14.1 kHz tone.

      How many comparators does an 8-bit flash ADC need? How many comparison steps does an 8-bit SAR ADC take?

      Solution

      Flash: 28 − 1 = 255 comparators, one conversion per clock. SAR: 8 steps with a single comparator. Each extra bit doubles the flash converter but adds one step to the SAR.

      Trace a 4-bit SAR conversion of 1.35 V with Vref = 3.2 V. Give each trial code and decision.

      Solution

      LSB = 0.2 V. Trial 1000 (1.6 V): 1.35 < 1.6 → 0. Trial 0100 (0.8 V): yes → 1. Trial 0110 (1.2 V): yes → 1. Trial 0111 (1.4 V): no → 0. Result 0110 = 6, representing 1.2 V (truncation error 0.15 V, less than 1 LSB).

      What is the ideal SQNR of a 12-bit ADC? A 12-bit converter is measured with a SINAD of 62 dB. What is its ENOB?

      Solution

      SQNR = 6.02 × 12 + 1.76 ≈ 74 dB. ENOB = (62 − 1.76)/6.02 ≈ 10.0 bits: the bottom two bits are effectively noise.

      An op-amp has a gain-bandwidth product of 1 MHz. You need a gain of 100 for a signal with content up to 50 kHz. Does one stage work? What about two cascaded stages?

      Solution

      One stage: bandwidth ≈ 1 MHz/100 = 10 kHz, too low. Two stages of gain 10 each give 100 overall, each with bandwidth 1 MHz/10 = 100 kHz. Cascading two identical poles narrows the bandwidth to about 64% of one stage, roughly 64 kHz, which works.

      An inverting summing amplifier has Rf = 10 kΩ and four inputs through 10 kΩ, 20 kΩ, 40 kΩ and 80 kΩ, each driven by a logic output at 0 V or 5 V. What is the output for the input pattern 1111? For 1010 (the 10 kΩ input first)? What property must the resistors have for this DAC to be accurate?

      Solution

      vout = −10k(v3/10k + v2/20k + v1/40k + v0/80k). For 1111: −(5 + 2.5 + 1.25 + 0.625) = −9.375 V. For 1010: −(5 + 1.25) = −6.25 V. The resistors must be matched to a fraction of the smallest weight: the 10 kΩ resistor's error must be well under 1/8 of its value relative to the 80 kΩ one, and the spread grows as 2n−1, which is why R-2R ladders replace this design beyond a few bits.

      A slowly varying sensor signal has ±0.3 V of noise. A Schmitt trigger has thresholds VT+ = 2.0 V and VT− = 1.0 V. Can the noise cause extra transitions? What is the minimum hysteresis for this noise level?

      Solution

      Noise of ±0.3 V spans 0.6 V peak to peak, less than the 1.0 V hysteresis: once the output switches high at 2.0 V, the input would have to fall below 1.0 V, which noise around a level near 2.0 V cannot do. No extra transitions. The hysteresis must exceed the noise's peak-to-peak amplitude, 0.6 V, with margin.

      Five buttons share one ADC input. A 2 kΩ resistor pulls the input to 5 V; each button grounds a different point of a series ladder of 330 Ω, 620 Ω, 1 kΩ and 3.3 kΩ, so the buttons connect the input to ground through 0, 330, 950, 1950 and 5250 Ω. Compute the voltage and 10-bit ADC reading for each button and for no button, and choose decision thresholds.

      Solution

      V = 5 × Rb/(2000 + Rb):

      ButtonR to groundVoltageADC (×1024/5)
      10 Ω0 V0
      2330 Ω0.71 V145
      3950 Ω1.61 V330
      41950 Ω2.47 V506
      55250 Ω3.62 V741
      noneopen5 V1023

      Thresholds halfway between neighbors: 72, 237, 418, 623, 882. A reading below 72 is button 1, between 72 and 237 button 2, and so on. The midpoints maximize the tolerance to resistor and supply variation. Pressing two buttons at once registers as the one closest to the input on the ladder.

      A blue LED with VF = 3.0 V ± 0.1 V is driven from 3.3 V through a resistor chosen for 5 mA. What is the resistor, and what range of current results? How would you drive it more consistently?

      Solution

      R = (3.3 − 3.0)/0.005 = 60 Ω. With VF = 2.9 V the current is 0.4/60 = 6.7 mA; with 3.1 V it is 0.2/60 = 3.3 mA: a ±33% spread. Use a higher supply (5 V gives (2.0 ± 0.1)/400 Ω = 5 mA ± 5%), or a constant-current driver, which servos the current directly instead of relying on the headroom.

      With a 16 MHz timer clock, what PWM frequency results from 8-bit and from 10-bit fast PWM? You need a filtered DAC output with less than 1% ripple and want to settle within 1 ms. Which resolution can meet both with a first-order filter?

      Solution

      8-bit: 16 MHz/256 = 62.5 kHz. 10-bit: 16 MHz/1024 = 15.6 kHz. Settling within 1 ms needs 5τ ≤ 1 ms, so τ ≤ 200 μs and fc ≥ 800 Hz. With fc = 800 Hz, a first-order filter attenuates the PWM fundamental by about fc/fPWM: 800/62,500 ≈ 1.3% at 8 bits but 800/15,600 ≈ 5% at 10 bits. Since the fundamental is at most about 64% of the 5 V swing, the 8-bit case gives roughly 0.8% ripple and meets both requirements; the 10-bit case cannot without a higher-order filter. Resolution, update rate and ripple trade against each other.

      No problems here match the current filter.
