      Part III: Circuits and the physical layer

      Transistors and CMOS logic

      How a MOSFET works, why NMOS pulls down and PMOS pulls up, how CMOS gates are built from dual networks, why inverting gates are natural and NAND beats NOR, and where the delay and power of a chip come from.

      Builds onBoolean algebra, Circuits and RCToolsCMOS switch-level explorerPractice15 problems

      Every gate in the previous modules is, physically, a handful of transistors. Knowing how those transistors behave explains facts that otherwise look arbitrary: why the basic gates are NAND and NOR rather than AND and OR, why fan-in is limited, why a chip's power depends on the square of its supply voltage, and why clock frequencies stopped rising around 2005 while transistor counts kept growing.

      From vacuum tubes to tens of billions of transistors

      Early electronic computers used vacuum tubes as switches; ENIAC (1945) had about 18,000 of them and consumed around 150 kW. The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, replaced the tube with a smaller, cooler, more reliable solid-state switch, and the integrated circuit (Kilby and Noyce, 1958–59) put many transistors and their wiring on one piece of silicon. In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that the number of components per chip was doubling at a regular rate, later settled at about every two years; this Moore's law held for five decades through steady shrinking of transistor dimensions.

      The Intel 4004 (1971) had about 2,300 transistors with 10 μm features and ran at 740 kHz. Large chips today have tens of billions: NVIDIA's GA100 GPU has 54 billion, and a recent laptop processor such as Apple's M4 about 28 billion. The transistor itself has changed shape to keep control of the channel as it shrank: from the planar MOSFET to the FinFET (a vertical fin wrapped by the gate on three sides, in production from 2011) to gate-all-around nanosheet transistors, in which the gate surrounds stacked horizontal channels. Process "node" names such as 5 nm or 3 nm are now marketing labels rather than any physical dimension. Growth now also comes from stacking dies vertically (3D integration, high-bandwidth memory) and combining several dies in one package (chiplets).

      Semiconductors and the MOSFET

      Pure silicon is a poor conductor. Doping it with a small amount of an element with five valence electrons (phosphorus, arsenic) adds free electrons and makes n-type silicon; doping with an element with three (boron) creates holes, missing electrons that move like positive charges, and makes p-type silicon.

      MOSFET

      Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor. A voltage on the gate, insulated from the silicon by a thin oxide, creates or removes a conducting channel between the source and drain. The gate draws no DC current: it controls the channel through the electric field across the oxide, like the plate of a capacitor.

      In an NMOS transistor, a positive gate-to-source voltage VGS pushes holes away from the surface under the gate and attracts electrons. Once VGS exceeds the threshold voltage VT (a few hundred millivolts in modern processes), enough electrons gather to form a thin n-type inversion layer, the channel, connecting source and drain. The transistor's strength is set by its geometry: current scales with the channel width W divided by its length L, and the minimum L is the process's defining dimension.

      A PMOS transistor is the complement: p-type source and drain in an n-type region (an n-well), conducting when the gate is pulled sufficiently below its source, that is, when the gate is low and the source is at VDD. Its carriers are holes, which move about two to three times more slowly than electrons, so a PMOS needs roughly twice the width of an NMOS for the same current.

      The switch model, and strong and weak levels

      For logic, a MOSFET is a voltage-controlled switch: an NMOS is on when its gate is 1 and off when it is 0; a PMOS is on when its gate is 0. The bubble on the PMOS gate in the symbol is a reminder.

      The model has one important refinement. An NMOS conducts only while its gate is at least VT above its source. When it pulls a node down, the source is at ground and VGS = VDD throughout, so it pulls the node all the way to 0 V: NMOS passes a strong 0. When it tries to pull a node up, its source is the node itself; as the node rises, VGS shrinks, and the transistor turns off when the node reaches VDD − VT: NMOS passes a weak 1. The PMOS behaves symmetrically, passing a strong 1 and a weak 0. This is why CMOS gates always use NMOS transistors to connect the output to ground and PMOS transistors to connect it to VDD.

      Beyond the switch: current and voltage

      Delay and power calculations need a little more than on and off. An NMOS operates in one of three regions:

      • Cutoff (VGS < VT): no channel; only a small leakage current flows.
      • Linear or triode (VDS < VGS − VT): the channel extends from source to drain and the transistor behaves like a resistor controlled by VGS: ID = k[(VGS − VT)VDS − VDS2/2], with k = μCoxW/L.
      • Saturation (VDS ≥ VGS − VT): the channel pinches off near the drain and the current stops growing with VDS: ID ≈ (k/2)(VGS − VT)2, the classic square law.

      Two consequences matter for digital design. First, the current a transistor can deliver, and hence how fast it charges a load, grows with W/L and with the gate overdrive VGS − VT; lowering VDD toward VT makes circuits dramatically slower. Second, below threshold the current does not drop to zero but decreases exponentially, roughly tenfold for every 60 to 100 mV of VGS reduction. That subthreshold leakage is why lowering VT to gain speed costs static power.

      Resistor-load logic, and why CMOS replaced it

      The simplest transistor inverter uses one NMOS to pull the output down and a resistor to pull it up. Series NMOS transistors make a NAND (the output falls only if all are on); parallel ones make a NOR.

      When the output is low, the resistor and the on transistor form a divider: VOL = VDD·Ron/(Ron + R), so R must be much larger than Ron. That divider also conducts continuously: every gate with a low output burns VDD2/(R + Ron). And the rising edge is slow, because the large resistor must charge the load. A million such gates at a few milliwatts each would dissipate kilowatts. CMOS removes both problems by replacing the resistor with a network of PMOS transistors that is on exactly when the NMOS network is off.

      The CMOS inverter

      A PMOS from VDD to the output and an NMOS from the output to ground, with their gates tied together, form the complementary-MOS (CMOS) inverter. Input 0 turns the PMOS on and the NMOS off, pulling the output to VDD; input 1 does the opposite. In either steady state one transistor is off, so no current flows from supply to ground, and the outputs reach the rails exactly.

      The point where Vout = Vin is the switching threshold VM; sizing the PMOS about twice as wide as the NMOS puts it near VDD/2 and balances the rise and fall times. The steep transition is what makes digital logic robust (Module 1): the region where |gain| > 1 defines VIL and VIH, and every gate restores degraded levels to clean rails, so noise does not accumulate through a chain of gates.

      Static CMOS gates: dual networks

      Every static CMOS gate generalizes the inverter: a pull-down network (PDN) of NMOS transistors between the output and ground, and a pull-up network (PUN) of PMOS transistors between VDD and the output. The PDN conducts exactly for the input combinations where the output should be 0, and the PUN is its dual, conducting for exactly the other combinations, so for every input one network drives the output and the other is off.

      The construction rule follows from the switch model: transistors in series conduct when all are on, an AND of their gate conditions; transistors in parallel conduct when any is on, an OR. The PDN therefore implements F′ with NMOS (series for AND, parallel for OR), and the PUN is obtained by swapping series and parallel and using PMOS. The PUN's PMOS transistors conduct on complemented inputs, which by De Morgan's theorem is exactly the dual structure.

      Two facts follow directly. A single CMOS stage is always inverting: raising an input can only turn NMOS on and PMOS off, so it can only pull the output down. That is why NAND and NOR are the native gates and AND costs an extra inverter (6 transistors instead of 4). And an n-input NAND or NOR uses 2n transistors.

      Worked example

      Designing a complex gate

      Build F = ((A + B)·C)′, an OR-AND-INVERT gate (OAI21), as one CMOS stage.

      PDN (implements the expression inside the inversion): A and B in parallel (A + B), in series with C. The output is pulled low when (A or B) and C.

      PUN (the dual): A and B in series, the pair in parallel with C, all PMOS. The output is pulled high when C = 0 or when A = B = 0, which is exactly F = C′ + A′B′ = ((A + B)C)′.

      Total: 6 transistors, one gate delay. Building the same function from a 2-input OR (NOR + inverter, 6 transistors) followed by a NAND (4) would use 10 transistors and three stages. Complex AOI and OAI gates are standard cells in every library for this reason.

      Sizing, fan-in, and why NAND beats NOR

      Transistors in series add their resistances. To give a gate the same worst-case drive as a reference inverter, a series stack of n transistors must each be about n times wider. In a NAND the series stack is NMOS, the faster type; in a NOR it is PMOS, which is already about twice as weak. A NOR2 sized for equal strength therefore needs PMOS transistors four times the NMOS reference width, presenting more input capacitance per input than a NAND2: by the standard "logical effort" measure, a NAND2 input is 4/3 as hard to drive as an inverter input and a NOR2 input 5/3. Designs favor NAND, and NOR gates with more than about three inputs are avoided.

      The same effect limits fan-in. Adding inputs makes the series stack longer (more resistance) and adds capacitance on internal nodes and the output, so the delay of a gate grows roughly with the square of its fan-in: tpd ≈ a1·FI + a2·FI2 + a3·FO, where FO is the fanout. In practice gates rarely exceed four or five inputs; a wide AND is built as a tree of NAND and NOR gates, which by De Morgan alternate cleanly.

      Driving a large load: tapered buffers going deeper

      Suppose a small gate must drive a load 64 times its own input capacitance, such as a long bus or a clock net. The delay of each stage is roughly proportional to its electrical effort h, the ratio of load to input capacitance, plus a fixed parasitic term p ≈ 1. Driving 64× directly costs about 64 + 1 = 65 units. Inserting a chain of inverters that each grow 4× (1, 4, 16, driving 64) costs three stages of 4 + 1 = 5 units each, 15 in total. The optimum stage effort is about 4, which is why the delay of an inverter driving four copies of itself, the FO4 delay, is the standard unit for comparing circuit speed across processes. A pipeline stage in a high-frequency processor is on the order of 10 to 20 FO4 delays.

      Transmission gates and tristate outputs

      Because an NMOS passes a strong 0 but a weak 1, and a PMOS the reverse, putting one of each in parallel, driven by complementary enable signals, gives a switch that passes both levels fully: a transmission gate (TG). Unlike a logic gate, it does not restore levels; it simply connects two nodes when enabled.

      A tristate output adds a third state to 0 and 1: high impedance (Z), in which both the pull-up and pull-down are off and the output is effectively disconnected. A tristate inverter puts an extra PMOS in series with the pull-up and an extra NMOS in series with the pull-down, both controlled by an enable. Tristate drivers let several devices share a bus, provided exactly one is enabled at a time (Module 8).

      Where delay comes from

      A switching gate charges or discharges its load through a transistor's on-resistance, so its delay is approximately 0.69·Ron·Cload (Module 10). Cload includes the input capacitance of each driven gate (proportional to their transistor widths), the wire, and the gate's own drain capacitance. Making a gate wider lowers Ron but raises the load on whatever drives it, which is why circuit speed is a chain-wide optimization rather than a property of single gates, and why designers reason in FO4 delays.

      Where power goes

      CMOS draws no current while idle, apart from leakage, but every output transition moves charge. Charging a load capacitance CL from 0 to VDD draws CLVDD of charge from the supply at voltage VDD, an energy of CLVDD2: half ends up stored on the capacitor and half is dissipated in the PMOS. Discharging dumps the stored half into the NMOS.

      If a fraction α of the chip's total switched capacitance C makes a 0 → 1 transition each clock cycle (the activity factor), the dynamic power is

      Pdynamic = α · C · VDD2 · f

      Two smaller contributions complete the picture. During each transition both networks conduct briefly, causing short-circuit current. And transistors that are off still leak: subthreshold leakage grows exponentially as VT is lowered, plus tunneling through the very thin gate oxide. In modern processes static (leakage) power can be a substantial fraction of the total, especially in large, mostly idle structures such as caches.

      Key idea

      Power scales with VDD2 and with frequency, and achievable frequency itself scales roughly with VDD (more overdrive, faster switching). Running slower at a lower voltage therefore saves energy per operation, not just power: this is dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), used by every modern processor.

      For decades, Dennard scaling made each process generation better on every axis: shrinking dimensions and voltage by a factor κ kept power density constant while transistors became faster and more numerous. Around 2005 the supply voltage stopped scaling, because VT cannot be lowered further without unacceptable leakage, and power density began to rise with each generation. Clock frequencies plateaued at a few gigahertz, and performance growth shifted to parallelism (multicore CPUs, GPUs) and specialization (Module 22). Power, not transistor count, became the limiting resource. The standard techniques for managing it:

      • Clock gating: stop the clock to registers whose values will not change, cutting their α to zero (Module 15).
      • Power gating: disconnect idle blocks from the supply with large "sleep" transistors, eliminating their leakage, at the cost of losing state and a wake-up delay.
      • DVFS: lower voltage and frequency when full speed is not needed.
      • Multi-VT design: use fast, leaky low-threshold transistors only on critical paths and slower, low-leakage ones everywhere else.

      Summary

      • NMOS: on when gate = 1, passes strong 0 and weak 1. PMOS: on when gate = 0, passes strong 1. Hence NMOS pull-down, PMOS pull-up.
      • Cutoff, triode (resistor-like) and saturation (current ≈ (k/2)(VGS − VT)2); k ∝ W/L; holes are 2–3× slower than electrons.
      • Static CMOS: the PDN implements F′ (series = AND, parallel = OR); the PUN is its dual. Stages are inverting; n-input NAND/NOR use 2n transistors.
      • Series stacks are slow; NAND beats NOR because its series stack is NMOS. Delay grows about quadratically with fan-in.
      • Transmission gates pass both levels; tristate outputs add a high-impedance state for shared buses.
      • Pdynamic = αCVDD2f, plus short-circuit and leakage power. Voltage scaling stalled around 2005, ending frequency growth and making power the central constraint.

      Practice problems

      For each transistor type, state whether it conducts when its gate is 1 and when it is 0, and which logic level it passes well.

      Solution

      NMOS: conducts with gate 1, off with gate 0; passes a strong 0. PMOS: conducts with gate 0, off with gate 1; passes a strong 1.

      How many transistors are in a static CMOS 3-input NAND? A 3-input AND? A 4-input NOR?

      Solution

      NAND3: 6. AND3 = NAND3 + inverter: 8. NOR4: 8 (though its four series PMOS make it slow; a designer would rather build it as two NOR2s feeding a NAND2 through inverters, or restructure the logic).

      A CMOS gate output drives 10 fF from 0 to 1 V and back. How much energy does the supply deliver during the rising edge, and how much is dissipated over the full cycle?

      Solution

      Rising edge: the supply delivers C·V2 = 10 fF × 1 V2 = 10 fJ; 5 fJ is stored on the capacitance and 5 fJ dissipated in the PMOS. On the falling edge the stored 5 fJ is dissipated in the NMOS. Total dissipated per full cycle: 10 fJ.

      A resistor-load NMOS inverter uses R = 10 kΩ and VDD = 5 V; the transistor's on-resistance is 500 Ω. Find VOL and the static power while the output is low. What would a million such gates, half of them low, dissipate?

      Solution

      VOL = 5 × 500/10,500 = 0.24 V. P = 52/10,500 = 2.4 mW. Half a million low gates: about 1.2 kW, impossible for one chip. A CMOS gate dissipates essentially nothing while static.

      Design the transistor networks for F = ((A + B)·C)′ and for F = (A·(B + C))′. Give the transistor count for each.

      Solution

      ((A + B)C)′: PDN = (A ∥ B) in series with C; PUN = (A series B) ∥ C. (A(B + C))′: PDN = A in series with (B ∥ C); PUN = A ∥ (B series C). 6 transistors each.

      A chip has 20 nF of total switched capacitance with an activity factor of 0.1, runs at 2 GHz and 1.0 V. Estimate its dynamic power.

      Solution

      P = αCV2f = 0.1 × 20 × 10−9 × 12 × 2 × 109 = 4 W.

      The chip in the previous problem lowers its voltage to 0.8 V and its frequency to 1.6 GHz. By what factor does dynamic power change? Energy per clock cycle? Performance?

      Solution

      Power ∝ V2f: 0.64 × 0.8 = 0.51 (about 2 W). Energy per cycle ∝ V2: 0.64. Performance ∝ f: 0.8. The work gets done more slowly but with 36% less energy, the core argument for DVFS.

      A single NMOS transistor with VT = 0.3 V is used as a switch to pass a 1 from a 1.0 V signal to a capacitive node, with its gate at 1.0 V. What voltage does the node reach? Why is this a problem for a gate driven by that node, and what fixes it?

      Solution

      The NMOS turns off once its source (the node) reaches VG − VT = 0.7 V. A degraded 1 reduces noise margin, and in the gate it drives the PMOS is not fully off (its VGS is −0.3 V, at threshold), causing static leakage current. A transmission gate (adding a parallel PMOS) passes the full 1.0 V; alternatively, a restoring gate (inverter) follows the pass transistor.

      An NMOS has k = 200 μA/V2 and VT = 0.4 V. What is its saturation current at VGS = 1.0 V (square law)? What if W is doubled? What if VGS drops to 0.7 V?

      Solution

      I = (k/2)(VGS − VT)2 = 100 μA × 0.36 = 36 μA. Doubling W doubles k: 72 μA. At 0.7 V: 100 μA × 0.09 = 9 μA, a quarter, showing how strongly speed depends on gate overdrive.

      With holes half as mobile as electrons, size a NAND2 and a NOR2 so each has the drive of an inverter with a 1-unit NMOS and 2-unit PMOS. Compare the input capacitance per input (proportional to total gate width on that input).

      Solution

      NAND2: two series NMOS each 2 units; two parallel PMOS each 2 units (one alone must match the inverter). Per input: 2 + 2 = 4 units. NOR2: two parallel NMOS each 1 unit; two series PMOS each 4 units. Per input: 1 + 4 = 5 units. Relative to the inverter's 3 units, the logical efforts are 4/3 and 5/3: the NOR is harder to drive and larger.

      The Intel 4004 (1971) had about 2,300 transistors. If transistor counts doubled exactly every two years, how many would a chip have in 2021? Compare with real chips of that year.

      Solution

      50 years = 25 doublings: 2,300 × 225 ≈ 2,300 × 3.36 × 107 ≈ 7.7 × 1010, about 77 billion. The largest chips around 2021–2022 had roughly 50 to 80 billion transistors, so the trend held remarkably well for half a century.

      An inverter has VOL = 0.05 V, VOH = 0.95 V, VIL = 0.42 V and VIH = 0.58 V at VDD = 1 V. What are its noise margins? Why does a steeper transfer curve improve them?

      Solution

      NML = 0.42 − 0.05 = 0.37 V; NMH = 0.95 − 0.58 = 0.37 V. VIL and VIH are where the gain magnitude is 1; a steeper curve (higher gain) squeezes them together toward VM, widening both margins toward VDD/2.

      A gate with input capacitance C must drive a load of 64C. Compare the delay of driving it directly with driving it through a chain of inverters whose sizes grow by 4× per stage, assuming each stage's delay is (load/input capacitance) + 1 in units of τ.

      Solution

      Direct: 64 + 1 = 65τ. Chain: the original gate drives an inverter of 4C, which drives 16C, which drives the 64C load: three stages with effort 4, each costing 4 + 1 = 5τ, total 15τ, over 4× faster. Adding stages helps until the per-stage effort falls to about 4; beyond that the fixed parasitic delay of extra stages dominates.

      Implement F = A·B + C (not inverted) in static CMOS with the fewest transistors. Explain why the obvious approach from earlier modules (an AND gate feeding an OR gate) is worse.

      Solution

      Build the inverting complex gate AOI21, (AB + C)′, with 6 transistors (PDN: A series B, in parallel with C; PUN: (A ∥ B) in series with C), then invert: 8 transistors, two stages. AND (6 transistors: NAND + INV) followed by OR (6: NOR + INV) uses 12 transistors in four stages. Since every CMOS stage inverts, efficient designs absorb inversions into complex gates rather than building AND and OR literally.

      A processor at 0.8 V draws 40 W of dynamic power and 6 A of leakage current. What is its total power? If half the chip is idle and clock-gated, how does power change? What if the idle half is power-gated instead?

      Solution

      Leakage power = 0.8 V × 6 A = 4.8 W; total 44.8 W. Clock gating the idle half removes its dynamic power (assuming it is uniformly half): 20 + 4.8 = 24.8 W; the leakage remains because the transistors are still powered. Power gating removes both its dynamic power and its leakage: 20 + 2.4 = 22.4 W, but the gated half loses its state and needs time to wake up.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Module13of 28

      Part III: Circuits and the physical layer

      Interfacing: logic levels, drive and loads

      What it takes for chips and devices to work together electrically: logic-level compatibility and noise margins, output current and fanout, driving LEDs, reading buttons, open-drain buses, level shifting, switching motors and relays, and the basics of signal integrity.

      Builds onCircuits and RC, CMOSPractice15 problems

      Inside one chip, every gate was designed to drive the gates around it. At the boundary, nothing is guaranteed: a microcontroller pin may drive an LED, another chip built in a different process, a long cable, or a motor. Two classic surprises motivate this module. An LED connected straight to an output pin lights, but measuring the pin shows 1.8 V instead of 5 V. And an enable signal passed from one chip to another is never recognized as a 1, even though both "use logic levels". Both failures are electrical, and both follow from the circuit ideas in Module 10 and Module 12.

      Logic levels and noise margins

      A datasheet specifies four voltages that define a logic family's interface. Two are promises made by outputs and two are requirements of inputs:

      ParameterMeaning
      VOH (min)An output driving 1 is guaranteed to be at least this high (at its rated current)
      VOL (max)An output driving 0 is guaranteed to be at most this low
      VIH (min)An input is guaranteed to read 1 for any voltage at or above this
      VIL (max)An input is guaranteed to read 0 for any voltage at or below this

      Between VIL and VIH an input's interpretation is undefined; it may read either value, oscillate, or draw extra current. A driver and receiver are compatible when VOH > VIH and VOL < VIL, and the differences are the noise margins: NMH = VOH − VIH and NML = VIL − VOL. Noise margins are the amount of interference (coupled noise, ground bounce, supply variation) the link can absorb without error.

      Worked example

      Checking compatibility in both directions

      Two devices have these specifications (output currents are negative when flowing out of a pin, the usual datasheet convention):

      DeviceV_OHV_IHV_ILV_OLI_OHI_IHI_OLI_IL
      A3.4 V3.3 V1.0 V0.5 V−4 mA−1 mA10 mA2 mA
      B3.2 V3.0 V0.7 V0.6 V−2 mA−1 mA6 mA2 mA

      A driving B: NMH = 3.4 − 3.0 = 0.4 V and NML = 0.7 − 0.5 = 0.2 V, both positive: compatible.

      B driving A: NMH = 3.2 − 3.3 = −0.1 V. B's weakest 1 can fall in A's undefined region, so the link fails, even though NML = 1.0 − 0.6 = 0.4 V is fine. Compatibility must be checked in each direction separately.

      Common families make the problem concrete. Classic 5 V TTL uses VIH = 2.0 V and VIL = 0.8 V, with outputs guaranteeing only 2.4 V and 0.4 V. 5 V CMOS inputs typically need 70% of VDD (3.5 V) for a 1 and accept 30% (1.5 V) as a 0; the ATmega328P at 5 V needs 0.6·VCC = 3.0 V and accepts 0.3·VCC = 1.5 V. 3.3 V parts (LVCMOS/LVTTL) output close to 3.3 V and accept TTL-like thresholds, and 1.8 V and lower families scale thresholds with their supply. A 3.3 V output driving a 5 V CMOS input therefore fails (3.3 < 3.5), works only marginally into the ATmega at 5 V, and works comfortably into a TTL-threshold input such as the 74HCT family. Mismatched families need a level shifter, covered below.

      Output current, input current and fanout

      Voltages are only half of the interface. Each input draws some current, IIH when high and IIL when low, and each output can supply at most IOH while holding VOH and sink at most IOL while holding VOL. The number of inputs one output can drive, its fanout, is limited in each state by the ratio of the output's capability to each input's demand:

      fanout = min( |IOH| / |IIH| , IOL / IIL )

      For A driving copies of B in the example above: high, 4 mA/1 mA = 4; low, 10 mA/2 mA = 5; so A can drive 4 B inputs. Exceed that and the output voltage moves out of its guaranteed band, eroding the noise margin. If one signal must reach more inputs, split the load among buffers.

      CMOS inputs draw almost no static current (microamps of leakage), so their DC fanout is in the thousands. What limits CMOS fanout is capacitance: every input adds a few picofarads on a board (femtofarads on chip), and the output must charge all of it through its resistance, so delay grows linearly with fanout. A design that "works" with a large fanout may simply be slow.

      The output pin as a source with resistance

      A CMOS output is a PMOS to VDD and an NMOS to ground. When it drives 1, the PMOS on-resistance, typically tens of ohms for a microcontroller pin, sits between the supply and the pin: a Thevenin source with RTH = RP. The pin voltage is whatever the divider formed by RP and the load produces.

      This explains the 1.8 V LED. An LED connected directly to the pin with no resistor draws as much current as the PMOS can supply, and its own forward voltage, about 1.8 to 2 V for red, pins the voltage there; the PMOS drops the remaining 3 V while carrying a current far beyond its rating. The pin reads 1.8 V because that is the only voltage consistent with both devices, and the chip is being damaged in the process. For the ATmega328P the recommended maximum is 20 mA per pin, with an absolute maximum of 40 mA and additional limits on the total current through each port and the package.

      Driving LEDs

      An LED needs its current set by a series resistor. It can be wired so that the pin sources current (active-high) or sinks it (active-low):

      The resistor value follows from KVL around the loop: R = (VDD − VF − Vdrop)/I, where Vdrop is the pin's own voltage loss at that current (often neglected; a few tenths of a volt at 10 to 20 mA). For a red LED (VF ≈ 2 V) at 10 mA from 5 V, R ≈ 300 Ω; 330 Ω is the nearest standard value. Software must match the wiring: with an active-low LED, writing 0 turns it on.

      Reading buttons and switches

      A CMOS input has extremely high impedance: it neither defines its own voltage nor draws current. An unconnected (floating) input therefore drifts with leakage and picks up noise, reading random values and possibly sitting mid-supply, where both input transistors conduct and waste current. Every input must be driven by something, including inputs connected to switches when the switch is open.

      A pull-up resistor ties the input to VDD; the button connects it to ground when pressed. The button wins because it is a near-zero resistance compared with the pull-up, and only VDD/R flows while it is held (0.5 mA for 10 kΩ at 5 V). A pull-down with the button to VDD works too, giving an active-high button. Most microcontrollers include optional internal pull-ups (20 to 50 kΩ on the ATmega328P), enabled on the AVR by making the pin an input (DDR bit 0) and writing 1 to its PORT bit:

      DDRD  &= ~(1 << PD2);           // PD2 is an input
PORTD |=  (1 << PD2);           // enable its internal pull-up
if ((PIND & (1 << PD2)) == 0) { // button pressed (active-low)
    /* ... */
}

      The pull-up value is a compromise: lower values resist noise better and charge the line's capacitance faster, while higher values waste less current when the button is pressed. Mechanical contacts also bounce, making and breaking contact for several milliseconds; software debouncing is in Module 23, and the hardware alternative (RC filter plus Schmitt trigger) in Module 11.

      Open-drain outputs and shared lines

      An ordinary (push-pull) output actively drives both levels. If two push-pull outputs share a wire and disagree, one PMOS and one NMOS form a low-resistance path from VDD to ground: bus contention, which wastes tens of milliamps, produces an undefined voltage, and can damage the drivers. An open-drain (open-collector in bipolar logic) output has only the pull-down transistor: it can drive 0 or let go, and a single external pull-up resistor provides the 1.

      The line computes the AND of all devices' "release" signals, a wired-AND, with no possibility of contention. This is how I2C shares its SDA and SCL lines, how several chips share one interrupt request line, and how devices running at different supply voltages can share a signal (each sees the pull-up voltage). The cost is the rising edge: it is driven only by the pull-up resistor charging the line capacitance, with time constant Rpull-up·Cline. The resistor must be small enough for the required rise time and large enough that a driver can pull the line below VOL: R ≥ (VDD − VOL)/IOL.

      Tristate outputs are the other way to share a wire (Module 8): every device has a full push-pull driver with an enable, and the protocol guarantees that exactly one is enabled at a time.

      Level shifting

      When two families' levels are incompatible, or when a higher voltage would exceed an input's absolute maximum rating, a level shifter sits between them.

      • A resistor divider safely drops a 5 V output to a 3.3 V input, one direction only, and adds an RC delay with the input's capacitance.
      • A single MOSFET with its gate at the low supply translates a bidirectional open-drain line such as I2C: when the low side pulls down, the transistor turns on and pulls the high side down too; when the high side pulls down, the transistor's body diode and then the channel pull the low side down; when both release, each side's pull-up raises it to its own supply.
      • Translator ICs (and logic families with TTL-compatible inputs, such as 74HCT, or 5 V-tolerant inputs) handle push-pull signals and high speeds.

      Common mistake

      Driving a 5 V signal into a 3.3 V input that is not 5 V-tolerant forward-biases the input's clamp diode into the 3.3 V supply. With no series resistance, the current can damage the pin or even raise the 3.3 V rail. Check the input's absolute maximum rating, usually VDD + 0.3 V or 0.5 V.

      Driving loads larger than a pin

      Motors, relays, solenoids, high-power LEDs and speakers need more current, and often more voltage, than a logic pin can provide. A speaker is a good illustration: a pin delivering 5 V at 20 mA supplies 0.1 W, and connecting an 8 Ω speaker directly would ask for over 600 mA. The pin should provide only the control signal; a transistor switch or amplifier, powered from a suitable supply, provides the power.

      • Choose a logic-level MOSFET, whose on-resistance RDS(on) is specified at a gate voltage the pin can supply (4.5 V or 2.5 V). Its conduction loss is I2RDS(on): 2 A through 20 mΩ dissipates 80 mW.
      • The gate resistor (tens to hundreds of ohms) limits the current spike into the gate capacitance and damps ringing; the pull-down keeps the MOSFET off while the microcontroller is in reset and its pins are floating inputs.
      • An inductive load needs a flyback diode across it. Without one, interrupting the coil current produces a voltage spike (v = L di/dt) that can destroy the transistor (Module 10).
      • Bidirectional motor control uses an H-bridge of four switches; speed is controlled with PWM.
      • A hobby servo separates the two roles in its three wires: power and ground from a supply that can deliver the motor current, and a signal wire that carries only a logic-level PWM pulse whose width sets the angle.

      Signal integrity in brief

      At high edge rates, wires stop behaving like ideal connections:

      • Ground bounce and supply droop. When many outputs switch together, the surge of current through the package's supply and ground inductance (L·di/dt) shifts the chip's internal ground, eroding noise margins. Decoupling capacitors placed close to every supply pin (100 nF ceramic is typical, plus larger bulk capacitors per board) supply the transient current locally.
      • Transmission lines. A signal travels along a circuit-board trace at about half the speed of light, roughly 15 cm/ns. When a trace is longer than about one-sixth of the distance an edge travels during its rise time, the trace must be treated as a transmission line with characteristic impedance Z0 (often 50 Ω). A mismatch between Z0 and the driver or receiver impedance reflects part of the edge, causing overshoot and ringing. A series termination resistor at the driver, chosen so that driver impedance plus resistor equals Z0, absorbs the reflection.
      • Crosstalk. Capacitive and inductive coupling between neighboring traces injects noise. Spacing, ground planes and slower edges reduce it.
      • Differential signaling. High-speed links (LVDS, USB, PCIe, HDMI, Ethernet) send each bit on a pair of wires driven in opposite directions and read the difference, which rejects noise common to both wires and allows small swings and very high data rates.

      Summary

      • Compatibility: VOH > VIH and VOL < VIL, checked in each direction. NMH = VOH − VIH; NML = VIL − VOL.
      • Fanout = min(|IOH/IIH|, IOL/IIL); for CMOS, capacitance limits fanout through delay.
      • An output is a Thevenin source: the load sets the pin voltage. Respect per-pin and per-package current limits (20 mA recommended, 40 mA absolute maximum per ATmega328P pin).
      • LEDs need series resistors; inputs must never float; buttons use pull-ups (internal or external) and read active-low.
      • Open-drain outputs with a pull-up share lines safely (wired-AND, I2C); push-pull outputs on one wire cause contention.
      • Level-shift between families; switch large loads with logic-level MOSFETs, gate pull-downs and flyback diodes.
      • Fast edges bring ground bounce, reflections and crosstalk; decouple supplies, terminate long lines, and use differential pairs for the fastest links.

      Practice problems

      A 5 V TTL family has VOH = 2.4 V, VIH = 2.0 V, VIL = 0.8 V and VOL = 0.4 V. What are its noise margins?

      Solution

      NMH = 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 V; NML = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 V.

      Write the two AVR statements that make PB3 an input with its internal pull-up enabled, and an expression that is true when a button from PB3 to ground is pressed.

      Solution

      DDRB &= ~(1 << PB3); and PORTB |= (1 << PB3);. Pressed: (PINB & (1 << PB3)) == 0.

      Using devices A and B from the worked example, how many B inputs can one A output drive? How many A inputs can one B output drive (ignoring the voltage problem)?

      Solution

      A → B: high 4/1 = 4, low 10/2 = 5, fanout 4. B → A: high |−2|/|−1| = 2, low 6/2 = 3, fanout 2.

      A red LED (VF = 2.1 V) is wired active-low to a 5 V pin and should carry 15 mA. At 15 mA the pin's VOL is 0.5 V. What resistor is needed, and what does the code write to turn the LED on?

      Solution

      R = (5 − 2.1 − 0.5)/0.015 = 160 Ω (use 160 or 180 Ω). Active-low: write 0 to the pin to turn it on.

      Why should an unused CMOS input never be left unconnected? Name two acceptable ways to terminate it.

      Solution

      A floating input picks up noise and leakage, may read random values, and may sit mid-supply where both input transistors conduct, wasting current and possibly oscillating. Tie it to VDD or ground (directly or through a resistor), or on a microcontroller enable the internal pull-up or configure the pin as an output.

      A 3.3 V device's output (VOH = 3.1 V at its load) drives three possible 5 V receivers: a 5 V CMOS gate with VIH = 3.5 V, an ATmega328P at 5 V (VIH = 3.0 V), and a 74HCT gate (VIH = 2.0 V). Which links work, and with what high-level margin?

      Solution

      5 V CMOS: 3.1 − 3.5 = −0.4 V, fails. ATmega: 3.1 − 3.0 = +0.1 V, marginal: it may work on the bench but has almost no noise immunity. 74HCT: 3.1 − 2.0 = +1.1 V, robust. The low levels are fine in all three cases.

      Size the pull-up resistors for an I2C bus at 3.3 V with 200 pF of bus capacitance. Drivers must hold VOL ≤ 0.4 V while sinking at most 3 mA, and the 30%–70% rise time must not exceed 1 μs (tr ≈ 0.85RC).

      Solution

      Minimum: R ≥ (3.3 − 0.4)/0.003 = 967 Ω. Maximum: 0.85 × R × 200 pF ≤ 1 μs → R ≤ 5.9 kΩ. Any standard value between, typically 2.2 kΩ to 4.7 kΩ, works; lower values give faster edges and more power while the line is held low.

      Two push-pull outputs, each with 25 Ω pull-up and pull-down resistance, are accidentally connected and drive opposite values at 3.3 V. What current flows and what is the wire's voltage? Why is the same mistake harmless with open-drain outputs?

      Solution

      The path VDD → 25 Ω → wire → 25 Ω → ground carries 3.3/50 = 66 mA, above typical pin ratings, and the wire sits near 1.65 V, in the undefined region. Open-drain outputs can only pull low; there is no pull-up transistor to fight, so the line is simply low.

      A 12 V, 2 A motor is switched by a MOSFET with RDS(on) = 20 mΩ at VGS = 4.5 V. How much power does the MOSFET dissipate when on? What changes if the gate is driven from a 3.3 V pin and the datasheet gives RDS(on) only at 4.5 V and 10 V?

      Solution

      P = I2R = 4 × 0.02 = 80 mW. At VGS = 3.3 V the transistor may be only partly on, with much higher and unspecified resistance: it could dissipate watts and overheat. Choose a MOSFET specified at 2.5 V or lower, or add a gate driver.

      Four outputs of a chip switch at the same time, each driving 15 pF through a 3.3 V swing with the current flowing for about 1 ns. The ground pin and bond wire have 5 nH of inductance. Estimate the ground bounce.

      Solution

      Charge per output = 15 pF × 3.3 V ≈ 50 pC; over 1 ns that is about 50 mA each, 200 mA total. If that current ramps up in roughly 1 ns, di/dt ≈ 0.2 A/ns and V = L·di/dt ≈ 5 nH × 0.2 A/ns = about 1 V, a large fraction of the noise margin. Remedies: more ground pins, slower edges where speed is not needed, and decoupling capacitors close to the pins.

      A signal with a 1 ns rise time travels on a board trace at 15 cm/ns. Beyond roughly what trace length should it be treated as a transmission line? A driver has 15 Ω output impedance and the trace has Z0 = 50 Ω. What series termination resistor is appropriate?

      Solution

      The edge spans 15 cm; one-sixth of that is about 2.5 cm. Series termination makes the source impedance match the line: R = 50 − 15 = 35 Ω (33 Ω is the nearest standard value).

      A CMOS output has 50 Ω output resistance and its inputs draw 1 μA leakage, while the output can supply 4 mA. Each driven input adds 5 pF (including wiring). If the 10%–90% rise time must stay under 10 ns, what fanout is allowed? Compare with the DC fanout.

      Solution

      DC fanout: 4 mA/1 μA = 4000. Rise time 2.2RC ≤ 10 ns → C ≤ 10/(2.2 × 50) ns/Ω ≈ 91 pF → at most 18 inputs. Capacitance, not DC current, limits CMOS fanout.

      A 5 V output must drive a 3.3 V input that is not 5 V-tolerant. Its clamp diode to the 3.3 V supply drops 0.6 V. Estimate the clamp current through a 1 kΩ series resistor, then design a resistor divider instead and give its output voltage.

      Solution

      The input is clamped at about 3.3 + 0.6 = 3.9 V, so the resistor carries (5 − 3.9)/1000 ≈ 1.1 mA into the 3.3 V supply through the diode: survivable but poor practice, and it can lift a lightly loaded supply. A divider of 1.8 kΩ over 3.3 kΩ gives 5 × 3.3/5.1 ≈ 3.24 V, within range and drawing 1 mA from the 5 V output.

      Explain how the single-MOSFET bidirectional level shifter works in each of three cases: the 3.3 V side pulls low; the 5 V side pulls low; neither side pulls low. Why does it only work with open-drain signals?

      Solution

      The gate is tied to 3.3 V and the source to the 3.3 V side. (1) Low side pulls low: VGS = 3.3 V, the MOSFET turns on and pulls the 5 V side low too. (2) High side pulls low: the MOSFET's body diode (anode on the 3.3 V side, cathode on the 5 V side) conducts and drags the low side down to about 0.6 V; then VGS exceeds threshold and the channel pulls it fully low. (3) Neither: both sides float up through their pull-ups; with the source at 3.3 V, VGS = 0 and the MOSFET is off, so each side sits at its own supply. It needs open-drain drivers because the 1 is always provided by a pull-up resistor; a push-pull driver on one side would fight the shifter.

      Why can a microcontroller pin drive a hobby servo's control input directly but not a small 8 Ω speaker? Quantify the speaker case at 5 V.

      Solution

      The servo's signal wire only carries a logic-level PWM pulse into a high-impedance input; the motor current comes from the servo's separate power wire. The speaker is the load itself: 5 V across 8 Ω would demand 625 mA, more than 15 times the pin's 40 mA absolute maximum. Even at the 20 mA limit the pin delivers only 0.1 W. Use an audio amplifier (or at least a transistor) powered from the supply, with the pin providing only the signal.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Part IV: Sequential logic

      Latches and flip-flops

      How a circuit remembers: bistable feedback, the SR and D latches, the edge-triggered flip-flop built from two latches, its setup, hold and clock-to-Q times, resets, and the T and JK variants.

      Builds onDecoders and muxes, CMOSToolsLatch vs flip-flop labPractice15 problems

      Every circuit so far has been combinational: its outputs are a function of its present inputs only. A counter, a processor register or a state machine must also depend on the past. Circuits with memory are sequential, and they are built from one new kind of element: a cell that stores a bit and changes it only when told to.

      Sequential circuit

      A circuit whose outputs depend on the history of its inputs as well as their present values. The history is summarized by the circuit's state, stored in memory elements (latches or flip-flops) and fed back into its logic.

      Why feedback through logic is not enough

      Consider the most obvious way to build a counter: feed an adder's output back to its own input, so that the value computes value + 1 forever. Two things go wrong. First, the adder's output bits settle at different times (the low bit after a gate or two, the high bits after the carry ripples), so the input sees a mixture of old and new bits and computes nonsense from them; the circuit races around the loop as fast as the gates allow, with no meaningful sequence of values. Second, nothing sets the starting value.

      The fix is to break the loop with an element that answers three questions: how to hold a bit indefinitely, when to accept a new value (all bits at the same instant, after the logic has settled), and how to initialize it at power-up. The rest of this module builds that element.

      Storing a bit: the bistable element

      A wire that is left unconnected after being charged does hold its voltage for a while, but the charge leaks away through junctions and gate oxides in milliseconds or less. (DRAM is built exactly this way and must be refreshed for that reason; see Module 21.) A permanent store must actively restore its own value, and the simplest circuit that does so is a pair of inverters connected in a loop.

      Plotting both inverters' transfer curves on the same axes shows why the loop holds a value. A consistent state must lie on both curves, and they cross three times. At the two outer crossings, small disturbances are corrected: noise that moves Q slightly is amplified back to the rail. Those points are stable and store 0 or 1. The middle crossing, where both nodes sit near VDD/2, is also a consistent state, but any disturbance grows: it is metastable, like a ball balanced on a hilltop. A circuit can be pushed into that point by an input that changes at exactly the wrong moment, and it then takes an unpredictable time to fall to one side. This becomes important in Module 17.

      The loop has no input, so it can only hold whatever value it happened to start with. Writing a new value needs either drivers strong enough to overpower the inverters (the approach of an SRAM cell) or a switch that opens the loop while the new value is applied (the approach of a latch).

      The SR latch

      Replacing each inverter with a NOR gate adds an input to each side of the loop. A NOR with one input at 0 behaves as an inverter, so with both new inputs at 0 the circuit is the bistable loop. Raising S (set) forces Q′ to 0 and therefore Q to 1; raising R (reset) forces Q to 0.

      SRQ*
      00Q
      010
      101
      11x

      Here Q* denotes the next value of Q and the row 0 0 | Q means "unchanged". The combination S = R = 1 is excluded: it forces both outputs to 0, so Q′ is no longer the complement of Q, and if both inputs return to 0 at the same moment the two gates race to set the loop, possibly entering the metastable state. Circuits that use an SR latch must guarantee S and R are never 1 together.

      In practice

      An SR latch is the classic hardware debouncer for a single-pole, double-throw switch. The switch's common terminal grounds either the S′ or the R′ input of a NAND latch. When the contact bounces, it only touches and leaves the same terminal, which re-asserts the same input; the latch changes state on the first touch and ignores the rest. It never sees both inputs active, because the switch cannot touch both terminals at once.

      The D latch

      The SR latch's two inputs and forbidden combination are awkward. A D latch has a data input D and an enable C (also called G, gate, or clock). While C = 1 the latch is transparent: Q follows D. When C falls to 0 the latch becomes opaque and holds the value D had at that moment.

      CDQ*
      00Q
      01Q
      100
      111

      Functionally a D latch is a 2-to-1 multiplexer whose output is fed back to one of its own inputs: with C = 1 it selects D, and with C = 0 it selects its own output, which then circulates and holds.

      Built from an SR latch, the gating is S = D·C and R = D′·C: when C = 1 exactly one of S and R is 1, setting or resetting according to D, and when C = 0 both are 0 and the latch holds. Because R is derived from D′, the forbidden combination can never occur.

      Why a latch is not enough

      Try to build the counter again with a register of D latches between the adder's output and its input. While the latches are transparent, the loop is closed again: the new value passes through, round the adder, and back to the latch inputs, and if C stays high long enough it races around repeatedly. The circuit works only if the enable pulse is shorter than the loop delay yet long enough for the latches to capture data, a window that varies with temperature and voltage and is impossible to guarantee. The same thing happens in a shift register made of latches: during the transparent phase a bit races through every stage at once instead of moving one position.

      What is needed is an element that takes a snapshot of its input at one instant and never lets its input and output be connected at the same time.

      The edge-triggered D flip-flop

      Two D latches in series, enabled on opposite phases of the clock, have exactly that property. While the clock is low, the first (leader or master) latch is transparent and follows D, while the second (follower or slave) is opaque and holds Q. When the clock rises, the leader closes, capturing D as it was just before the edge, and the follower opens, passing that captured value to Q. While the clock stays high, D can change freely: the leader is closed. There is never a transparent path from D to Q.

      Q* = D (sampled at each rising clock edge; Q holds between edges)

      With flip-flops, a shift register works: at each clock edge every flip-flop samples its neighbor's output as it was before the edge, because each flip-flop's output only changes a short time (the clock-to-Q delay) after the edge, too late to be seen by its neighbor at the same edge. Each bit therefore moves exactly one position per clock. The counter works too: the adder sees a stable input for a whole clock period, has time to settle, and its result is captured all at once at the next edge.

      Flip-flop timing parameters

      A flip-flop's edge is not infinitely sharp in practice. Three parameters describe its timing:

      • Setup time tsetup: D must be stable this long before the clock edge, so the leader latch's loop has settled to the new value before it closes.
      • Hold time thold: D must remain stable this long after the edge, because the leader takes a moment to close fully (the clock reaches its transmission gates through internal inverters).
      • Clock-to-Q delay tclk→Q: after the edge, Q takes this long to show the new value. Datasheets give a maximum (for speed calculations) and a minimum or contamination value (for hold calculations).

      These three numbers, together with the delays of the logic between flip-flops, determine the maximum clock frequency of a synchronous design and whether it works at any frequency at all (hold violations). Module 17, Timing: setup, hold, clocks and metastability develops the constraints.

      Initialization: set, reset and clear

      At power-up each flip-flop's loop settles to an arbitrary value, so every sequential system needs a way to force a known starting state. Flip-flops offer two kinds of reset:

      • An asynchronous clear (or preset) input acts immediately, without waiting for a clock edge, and overrides D and the clock. It works even if the clock is not running yet, which is why it is common for power-on reset.
      • A synchronous reset is just logic in front of D, for example an AND gate that forces D to 0 when RESET = 1. It takes effect at the next clock edge, like any other data.

      Common mistake

      An asynchronous reset is asynchronous on its way out too. If it is released close to a clock edge, some flip-flops may leave reset one cycle earlier than others, or go metastable. The standard practice is to assert reset asynchronously but release it synchronously, using a reset synchronizer (Module 17).

      Other flip-flop types

      The D flip-flop is universal: every other type is a D flip-flop with logic in front of D. Two variants still appear in textbooks, interview questions and some older parts:

      TypeBehaviorCharacteristic equationBuilt from a D flip-flop
      Dload DQ* = D—
      T (toggle)T = 1 inverts Q, T = 0 holdsQ* = T ⊕ QD = T ⊕ Q
      JKJ sets, K resets, J = K = 1 togglesQ* = J·Q′ + K′·QD = J·Q′ + K′·Q

      A T flip-flop with T = 1 toggles on every edge, dividing the clock frequency by two with a 50% duty cycle, the basis of ripple counters (Module 15). The JK flip-flop removes the SR latch's forbidden case by defining J = K = 1 as toggle. When designing state machines with these types, the excitation table gives the inputs needed for each transition; for a JK flip-flop: 0 → 0 needs J = 0, K = x; 0 → 1 needs J = 1, K = x; 1 → 0 needs J = x, K = 1; 1 → 1 needs J = x, K = 0.

      Analyzing a sequential circuit

      Given a circuit of flip-flops and gates, its behavior follows from a mechanical procedure. Because Q holds for a whole cycle, everything combinational can be evaluated once per cycle:

      1. Write the Boolean equation for every flip-flop's D input and every output, in terms of the current Q values and the inputs.
      2. For each clock cycle, evaluate those equations with the current Q values and that cycle's inputs.
      3. At the clock edge, each Q takes the D value just computed. Repeat.

      Worked example

      Tracing a two-flip-flop circuit

      A circuit has D1 = X + Q1·Q0, D0 = X·Q1 and output F = Q1·Q0. It starts at Q1Q0 = 00 and receives X = 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0 in successive cycles.

      CycleQ1 Q0XD1 = X + Q1Q0D0 = X·Q1F = Q1Q0
      00 01100
      11 01110
      21 10101
      31 01110
      41 10101
      51 00000

      Each row's D values become the next row's Q values. The output depends only on the state, so it is valid for the whole cycle: a Moore-style output (Module 16).

      Summary

      • Cross-coupled inverters store a bit with two stable states and one metastable state.
      • SR latch: S sets, R resets, S = R = 1 forbidden. D latch: transparent while C = 1, holds while C = 0.
      • Latches in a feedback loop race while transparent; an edge-triggered flip-flop (two latches on opposite clock phases) samples D only at the clock edge: Q* = D.
      • Setup and hold times define a window around the edge where D must be stable; clock-to-Q is the output delay.
      • Asynchronous resets act immediately; synchronous resets act at the next edge. Release resets synchronously.
      • T: Q* = T ⊕ Q. JK: Q* = JQ′ + K′Q. Both are D flip-flops with logic in front.

      Practice problems

      Complete the sentence for each element: "While the clock or enable is 1, its output ___; it changes only ___."

      (a) a D latch with active-high enable (b) a rising-edge D flip-flop

      Solution

      (a) The latch's output follows D while C = 1 and holds while C = 0; it can change any time C is 1. (b) The flip-flop's output holds while the clock is 1 (and while it is 0); it changes only just after a rising edge, to the value D had at the edge.

      A NOR SR latch has Q = 0. The inputs then go S R = 10, 00, 01, 00, 10, 10. What is Q after each step?

      Solution

      10 sets: 1; 00 holds: 1; 01 resets: 0; 00 holds: 0; 10 sets: 1; 10 again: 1.

      How do you make a T flip-flop from a D flip-flop? What does a T flip-flop with T = 1 do to a 100 MHz clock?

      Solution

      Feed D = T ⊕ Q (an XOR of T with the flip-flop's own output). With T = 1, D = Q′ and the output toggles at every rising edge, producing a 50 MHz square wave with a 50% duty cycle.

      A clock has rising edges at t = 10, 30, 50 ns and is high for 10 ns after each. D is 0 until t = 14, 1 from 14 to 23, 0 from 23 to 27, and 1 after 27. Ignoring delays, what are the outputs of an active-high D latch and a rising-edge flip-flop at t = 25 and at t = 45?

      Solution

      The latch is transparent during 10–20, 30–40 and 50–60. At t = 25 it is opaque, holding the value D had when C fell at t = 20: 1. At t = 45 it holds the value from t = 40, when D was 1: 1. The flip-flop samples at 10 (D = 0) and 30 (D = 1): at t = 25 it shows 0, at t = 45 it shows 1. The 4 ns low pulse on D (23–27) is seen by neither, because it occurs while the latch is opaque and away from the edges.

      Give the gating logic that turns an SR latch into a D latch with enable C, and explain why the forbidden input combination cannot occur.

      Solution

      S = D·C, R = D′·C. S and R both 1 would require D and D′ both 1, which is impossible. When C = 0 both are 0 and the latch holds.

      Write the excitation table of a T flip-flop: for each transition Q → Q*, what must T be?

      Solution

      0 → 0: T = 0. 0 → 1: T = 1. 1 → 0: T = 1. 1 → 1: T = 0. In short, T = Q ⊕ Q*: toggle exactly when the bit must change.

      A two-bit circuit has D0 = Q0 ⊕ E and D1 = Q1 ⊕ (E·Q0). Starting from Q1Q0 = 00, find the state after each of five edges with E = 1, 1, 0, 1, 1. What is the circuit?

      Solution

      00 → (E=1) 01 → (E=1) 10 → (E=0) 10 → (E=1) 11 → (E=1) 00. It is a 2-bit counter with count enable E: bit 0 toggles when enabled, and bit 1 toggles when enabled and bit 0 is 1, exactly the carry of an incrementer.

      Implement a JK flip-flop with a D flip-flop and gates, and verify all four input combinations.

      Solution

      D = J·Q′ + K′·Q. J K = 00: D = Q (hold). 01: D = 0 (reset). 10: D = Q′ + Q = 1 (set). 11: D = Q′ (toggle).

      Explain what happens in a NOR SR latch when S = R = 1 and then both inputs return to 0 at exactly the same time.

      Solution

      With S = R = 1 both NOR outputs are 0, so Q = Q′ = 0. When both inputs drop together, each NOR sees inputs 0 and 0 and starts to drive its output to 1; whichever gate is slightly faster wins and forces the other back to 0. If they are evenly matched the loop can sit at the metastable point and oscillate or hover before resolving. The final state is unpredictable, which is why the combination is forbidden.

      Four D latches, all enabled by the same clock, are chained in series as a would-be shift register. What happens to a value applied at the input during one high phase of the clock? What changes if they are replaced with flip-flops?

      Solution

      While the clock is high all four latches are transparent, so the input propagates through every stage within a few gate delays: after one high phase all four outputs hold (roughly) the same value. The register does not shift. With flip-flops each stage samples its predecessor's old output at the edge, since the predecessor's new output appears only after tclk→Q, and the data moves exactly one stage per edge. (Latch-based designs can shift by alternating two non-overlapping clock phases between neighboring latches.)

      A counter built from a register, an incrementer and a mux has tclk→Q = 80 ps, incrementer delay 300 ps, mux delay 40 ps and tsetup = 50 ps. What is its maximum clock frequency?

      Solution

      T ≥ 80 + 300 + 40 + 50 = 470 ps, so fmax = 1/470 ps ≈ 2.13 GHz.

      A flip-flop has an asynchronous active-high CLR input and D = 1, clocked at rising edges every 20 ns starting at 10 ns. CLR is high from t = 24 to t = 33 ns. When is Q 0? What if the clear were synchronous instead?

      Solution

      Asynchronous: Q falls at t = 24 (plus a small delay) and stays 0 until the first edge after CLR is released, at t = 50. (At t = 30 the edge occurs while CLR is still active, so the clear wins.) Synchronous: Q falls at the edge at t = 30 (CLR is 1 then) and returns to 1 at the edge at t = 50.

      Design a circuit that outputs a one-cycle pulse whenever a synchronous input X changes from 0 to 1. Then modify it to detect any change of X.

      Solution

      Store X in a flip-flop so that Q holds X's value from the previous cycle. A rising edge of X is "now 1, previously 0": P = X·Q′, which is 1 for exactly the one cycle in which X has risen but the flip-flop has not yet captured it. Any change: P = X ⊕ Q. (If X is asynchronous, synchronize it first with two flip-flops and apply the detector to the synchronized signal.)

      In a positive-edge master-slave flip-flop, the master latch is transparent while the clock is low. Suppose D changes from 0 to 1 at a time when the clock is high and changes back to 0 before the clock falls. Does Q change? What if the pulse on D occurs while the clock is low and ends before the rising edge?

      Solution

      Clock high: the master is opaque, so the pulse never enters the flip-flop; Q does not change. Clock low: the master follows the pulse but, since D is back to 0 before the edge, the master holds 0 when it closes; the slave passes 0, so Q does not change either. Only the value of D in the setup-and-hold window around the rising edge matters.

      Three T flip-flops with T = 1 are chained so that each is clocked by the previous one's Q′ (the first by a 64 MHz clock). What frequencies appear at the three outputs, and what sequence do they count? What is the drawback compared with a synchronous counter?

      Solution

      Each stage halves the frequency: 32 MHz, 16 MHz, 8 MHz, and Q2Q1Q0 counts up 0, 1, 2, …, 7. Because each stage is clocked by the previous one, the delays accumulate: after the edge that takes 011 to 100, the outputs pass through 010 and 000 before settling. Any logic decoding the count sees those glitches, and the settling time grows with the number of bits. A synchronous counter changes all bits together, one tclk→Q after the common edge (Module 15).

      Part IV: Sequential logic

      Registers, counters and shift registers

      Flip-flops in groups: registers with load enables and the right way to gate a clock, shift registers and LFSRs, synchronous counters with reset, load and enable, ring and Johnson counters, and frequency dividers.

      Builds onLatches and flip-flops, Adders and ALUsPractice14 problems

      A single flip-flop stores one bit. Real designs store words, and the standard sequential components are all groups of flip-flops sharing a clock, with a little combinational logic in front of their D inputs that decides what each one loads at the next edge. That logic is what distinguishes a register from a counter from a shift register.

      Registers and load enables

      A register is n flip-flops sharing a clock (and usually a reset), storing an n-bit word. A plain register loads its input at every clock edge. Most registers must instead hold their value until told to load, which needs an enable: when EN = 0, Q* = Q.

      The enable belongs on the data path, not on the clock. It is tempting to AND the clock with the enable so that the register simply sees no edge, but logic on a clock path delays that register's clock relative to every other register (skew), and if the enable changes while the clock is high, the AND gate passes a truncated pulse or an extra edge.

      Clock gating is nevertheless one of the most effective power-saving techniques, because an idle register that receives no clock edges consumes no dynamic power in its flip-flops or its clock wiring (Module 12). It is done with a dedicated integrated clock-gating (ICG) cell: a latch that is transparent while the clock is low captures the enable, and an AND gate combines the latched enable with the clock. Because the latch output can only change while the clock is low, the AND gate's enable input is stable whenever the clock is high. Synthesis tools insert ICG cells automatically when they recognize the enable-mux pattern on a group of flip-flops.

      Shift registers

      Connecting each flip-flop's output to the next one's input makes a shift register: at each edge every bit moves one position, the first flip-flop loads a serial input, and the last one's old value falls off the end.

      Variants are named by how data enters and leaves: serial-in serial-out (a delay line of n cycles), serial-in parallel-out (deserializer, as in a receiver), and parallel-in serial-out (serializer: a mux in front of each flip-flop selects between parallel load and shift). Serial interfaces such as SPI and UARTs are built around shift registers (Module 26).

      A universal shift register puts a 4-to-1 mux in front of each bit, controlled by a 2-bit mode S1S0. For bit i of an n-bit register:

      S1 S0OperationD_i comes from
      0 0holdQ_i
      0 1shift rightQ_(i+1); the top bit takes the serial input DSR
      1 0shift leftQ_(i−1); bit 0 takes the serial input DSL
      1 1parallel loadinput bit IN_i

      Shifting left by one position multiplies an unsigned value by 2; shifting right divides by 2 (arithmetic right shift, which copies the sign bit into the top position, does the same for two's complement values).

      Linear-feedback shift registers

      Feed the XOR of a few chosen bits (the taps) back into the input of a shift register, and it steps through a long, scrambled-looking sequence of states. With the right taps, an n-bit LFSR visits all 2n − 1 nonzero states before repeating, a maximal-length sequence. The all-zeros state is excluded because it maps to itself (XOR of zeros is zero), so an LFSR must be seeded with a nonzero value.

      Starting from s3s2s1s0 = 1000, it produces 0001, 0010, 0100, 1001, 0011, 0110, 1101, 1010, 0101, 1011, 0111, 1111, 1110, 1100, and returns to 1000 after 15 steps. The taps correspond to a primitive polynomial over GF(2), here x4 + x3 + 1; tables of such polynomials exist for every width. LFSRs cost one flip-flop per bit plus a few XOR gates and are used as pseudo-random sequence generators in built-in self-test, as scramblers in serial links, and in the closely related form of CRC (cyclic redundancy check) circuits, which divide a message by a polynomial to compute a checksum.

      Synchronous counters

      A counter is a register whose next value is computed from its current value. The general-purpose design is a register, an incrementer and a few muxes that implement priority among control inputs: a synchronous reset (RST), a parallel load (LD) and a count enable (CE).

      Looking at one bit at a time gives a compact gate-level form. In binary counting, bit i toggles exactly when all lower bits are 1 (that is when the carry reaches it), so with T flip-flops or the equivalent XOR in front of D flip-flops:

      T0 = EN, T1 = EN·Q0, T2 = EN·Q0·Q1, Ti = EN·Q0·Q1···Qi−1

      The AND chain is the incrementer's carry chain, and for wide counters it is computed with lookahead, exactly as in an adder (Module 9). The AND of all bits and EN is the terminal count (TC) or ripple-carry-out signal, which can enable the next counter in a cascade.

      • Modulo-N counters count 0 to N − 1 and wrap. Detect the last state and force a synchronous reset: a decade (mod-10) counter clears when it reaches 9 and is enabled. Only the bits that are 1 in N − 1 need checking, if the states above N − 1 can never occur.
      • Up/down counters add +1 or −1 (all ones) according to a direction input.
      • Down counters with load are the heart of programmable timers: load a value, count down, and signal when zero is reached. Microcontroller timers are exactly this, with a programmable clock prescaler in front (Module 25).

      Ripple counters

      A counter can also be built without an incrementer: chain toggle flip-flops so that each stage is clocked by the previous stage's output. Stage i toggles when stage i − 1 falls from 1 to 0, which is exactly binary counting.

      Because each flip-flop has a different clock, the outputs are not synchronous with each other or with anything else in the design, and logic that decodes them sees glitches. Synchronous design, in which every flip-flop shares one clock, avoids this whole class of problems and is assumed by every timing tool; ripple counters are confined to frequency dividers whose outputs are used only as clocks or only after settling.

      Ring, Johnson and Gray counters

      Other state sequences trade flip-flops for simpler decoding:

      • A ring counter is a shift register whose output feeds its input, initialized with a single 1 (one-hot). With n flip-flops it cycles through n states, and each state is decoded by a single flip-flop output, with no logic at all.
      • A Johnson counter (twisted ring) feeds back the inverted last bit. With n flip-flops it cycles through 2n states, for example 000, 001, 011, 111, 110, 100 for n = 3, and every state is decoded by one 2-input gate looking at the boundary between the 1s and 0s. Only one bit changes per step, so decoding is glitch-free.
      • A Gray-code counter also changes exactly one bit per step but uses all 2n codes. It can be built as a binary counter whose output is converted with G = B ⊕ (B >> 1). Gray counters are essential for pointers that cross between clock domains (Module 17).

      Frequency division

      Bit i of a binary counter driven by clock f toggles at f/2i+1, a square wave with 50% duty cycle. Division by an arbitrary N uses a modulo-N counter: its terminal-count output is a one-cycle pulse at f/N, which is usually what a synchronous design wants (an enable for slower logic, rather than a new clock). A 50% duty cycle at f/N for even N comes from toggling a flip-flop every N/2 input cycles; for odd N it needs both clock edges, for example ORing a signal with a copy of itself delayed by half a cycle through a falling-edge flip-flop.

      Key idea

      In synchronous design, slow events are created with enables, not with new clocks. A counter that produces a one-cycle "tick" every millisecond lets every flip-flop in the design stay on the main clock, so timing analysis remains a single, well-defined problem.

      Summary

      • A register is n flip-flops on one clock; a load enable is a feedback mux on D, never a gate on the clock. Clock gating for power uses latch-based ICG cells.
      • Shift registers move data one position per edge (SIPO, PISO, SISO, universal with a 4-to-1 mux per bit).
      • An n-bit maximal LFSR cycles through 2n − 1 nonzero states; the all-zero state locks up.
      • Synchronous counter: register + incrementer + priority muxes (RST > LD > CE); Ti = EN·Q0···Qi−1.
      • Ripple counters chain clocks and produce transient wrong values; avoid them except as dividers.
      • Ring: n states from n flip-flops; Johnson: 2n states; Gray: one bit changes per count.

      Practice problems

      How many flip-flops are needed for a counter that counts 0 to 9? For one that counts 0 to 999?

      Solution

      10 states need ⌈log2 10⌉ = 4. 1000 states need ⌈log2 1000⌉ = 10 (as a binary counter; three cascaded decade counters in BCD would use 12).

      How many distinct states does a 4-bit ring counter cycle through? A 4-bit Johnson counter? A 4-bit binary counter?

      Solution

      Ring: 4. Johnson: 8. Binary: 16.

      A 4-bit SIPO shift register (serial input into Q0, shifting toward Q3) starts at Q3Q2Q1Q0 = 0000. What does it hold after shifting in 1, 0, 1, 1 (in that order)?

      Solution

      0001 → 0010 → 0101 → 1011. The first bit in has reached Q3.

      Write the toggle conditions T0 to T3 for a 4-bit synchronous up counter with enable EN, and the terminal-count signal.

      Solution

      T0 = EN, T1 = EN·Q0, T2 = EN·Q0Q1, T3 = EN·Q0Q1Q2. TC = EN·Q0Q1Q2Q3, which is 1 in the cycle before the counter wraps from 15 to 0.

      Why is assign gclk = clk & en; a poor way to implement a register enable? Give two reasons.

      Solution

      (1) If en changes while clk is high, gclk gets a truncated pulse or an extra edge, which may or may not clock the register (a glitch on a clock). (2) The AND gate delays the register's clock relative to the rest of the design, creating skew that can cause hold or setup violations. Use an enable mux on D, or an integrated clock-gating cell if the goal is power.

      Design the clear condition for a synchronous modulo-6 counter (0 to 5) built from a 3-bit counter with enable EN. Why is a 2-input AND gate enough to detect the last state?

      Solution

      The counter must go from 5 (101) to 0 instead of 6: clear when EN·Q2·Q0. Among the reachable states 0 to 5, only 101 has Q2 = Q0 = 1 (111 would also match, but it is never reached), so Q1 need not be checked. A robust design also clears from the unreachable states 6 and 7 in case a glitch or power-up ever lands there.

      For a 4-bit universal shift register, write the four mux inputs feeding bit 0 and bit 3, for modes hold, shift right, shift left and load.

      Solution

      Bit 0: hold Q0; shift right Q1; shift left DSL; load IN0. Bit 3: hold Q3; shift right DSR; shift left Q2; load IN3. The serial inputs appear only at the end that data enters from.

      The LFSR in the text is seeded with 0001 (s3s2s1s0). List the next five states. What happens if it is ever loaded with 0000?

      Solution

      New s0 = s3 ⊕ s2, then shift: 0001 → 0010 → 0100 → 1001 → 0011 → 0110. From 0000 the feedback is 0 ⊕ 0 = 0, so it stays at 0000 forever; real designs either guarantee a nonzero seed or add logic to escape the all-zero state.

      A 3-bit Johnson counter shifts left (Q0 → Q1 → Q2) and loads Q0 with Q2′. List its states from 000. Which 2-input gate decodes state 011 (Q2Q1Q0)?

      Solution

      000 → 001 → 011 → 111 → 110 → 100 → 000. State 011 is the only one with Q2 = 0 and Q1 = 1 (the boundary between 0s and 1s), so it is decoded by Q2′·Q1. Every Johnson state is decoded by one such 2-input AND of adjacent bits.

      A system clock is 16 MHz. You need a one-cycle tick every 1 ms to enable slower logic. What modulus and how many bits does the counter need?

      Solution

      1 ms × 16 MHz = 16,000 cycles: a modulo-16,000 counter (count 0 to 15,999, tick on 15,999). 214 = 16,384 ≥ 16,000, so 14 bits.

      A block of 2,048 flip-flops consumes 3 fJ per flip-flop per clock edge including its share of the clock tree, at 1 GHz. The block is idle 75% of the time. How much power does clock gating save?

      Solution

      Ungated: 2048 × 3 fJ × 109 /s = 6.1 mW. Gated during the idle 75%: savings ≈ 0.75 × 6.1 = 4.6 mW (minus a little for the ICG cells), leaving about 1.5 mW.

      A 3-bit ripple counter is decoded by an AND gate for the value 4 (Q2·Q1′·Q0′). Show that the decoder output pulses briefly when the counter goes from 7 to 0, and explain why this is harmful.

      Solution

      From 111, Q0 falls first (110), then Q1 falls (100), then Q2 falls (000). For one stage delay the outputs read 100 = 4, so the decoder emits a glitch that has nothing to do with the real count. If that signal drives a clock, an asynchronous reset or anything outside a synchronous sampling point, the glitch acts as a real event. A synchronous counter sampled by flip-flops on the same clock never exposes these states.

      Design a divide-by-3 clock with a 50% duty cycle from a clock CLK.

      Hint

      A mod-3 counter on rising edges gives a signal that is high for one cycle out of three. How can you stretch it by half a cycle?

      Solution

      Build a mod-3 counter on rising edges and decode one state, giving Y high for 1 of every 3 cycles. Sample Y with a falling-edge flip-flop to get Yn, the same pulse delayed by half a cycle. Then OUT = Y + Yn is high for 1.5 cycles out of 3: a 50% duty cycle at f/3. Because the result combines both clock edges, it depends on the input clock's own duty cycle, and the OR output should be treated carefully as a clock (glitch-free by construction here, since Y and Yn overlap).

      Give the logic that converts a 4-bit binary count B to Gray code G, and the inverse conversion. Why does a counter that crosses clock domains use Gray code?

      Solution

      Binary to Gray: G3 = B3, Gi = Bi+1 ⊕ Bi, i.e. G = B ⊕ (B >> 1). Gray to binary: B3 = G3, Bi = Bi+1 ⊕ Gi (a prefix XOR from the top bit down). When a multi-bit value is sampled asynchronously while it changes, each bit may be caught old or new. With binary counting, 0111 → 1000 changes four bits and could be read as any of 16 values; with Gray code only one bit changes, so the sampled value is either the old count or the new one, never something else.

      No problems here match the current filter.
