      Part IV: Sequential logic

      State machines in hardware

      Datapath and control, the formal model of a finite state machine, Moore and Mealy outputs, a complete design by K-map and by one-hot inspection, sequence detectors, correct specifications, and state minimization.

      Builds onRegisters and counters, K-mapsToolsSequence detector generatorPractice13 problems

      Registers and counters follow fixed patterns. Most digital systems need control that depends on what has happened so far: a protocol handler waits for a start bit, a cache controller walks through a miss, a divider repeats until done. That control is a finite state machine (FSM), and implementing one in hardware is a direct application of everything in the last two modules.

      Datapath and control

      Larger designs separate into two parts. The datapath holds and transforms data: registers, adders, comparators, multiplexers, counters and memories. The control unit is an FSM that decides, cycle by cycle, what the datapath does: which register loads, which mux input is selected, whether a counter counts. It issues control signals to the datapath and reads back status signals from it, such as "result is zero" or "A < B".

      Worked example

      Dividing 13 by 4

      INIT loads REM = 13, DIVISOR = 4 and clears QUO. Then the controller alternates between TEST, which examines the subtractor's borrow output, and SUB, which writes the difference back into REM and increments QUO:

      StateREMQUOREM − DIVISORborrowaction
      TEST13090go to SUB
      SUB13090REM ← 9, QUO ← 1; go to TEST
      TEST9150go to SUB
      SUB9150REM ← 5, QUO ← 2; go to TEST
      TEST5210go to SUB
      SUB5210REM ← 1, QUO ← 3; go to TEST
      TEST13−31go to DONE

      Each row shows the register values during that cycle; the loads requested in a SUB cycle take effect at the clock edge that ends it. The result is quotient 3, remainder 1. The number of cycles grows with the quotient, which is why real dividers use shift-and-subtract (one quotient bit per cycle) instead, but the structure, a datapath steered by a state machine, is the same.

      What a state machine is

      The state of a system is exactly what it must remember about the past in order to respond correctly to future inputs. A play/pause button needs one bit of state (playing or paused); a detector looking for the pattern 101 must remember how much of the pattern it has seen so far.

      Finite state machine

      A model of sequential behavior consisting of a finite set of states, an initial state, a set of inputs and outputs, a next-state function that maps (current state, input) to the next state, and an output function. In a Moore machine the outputs depend only on the current state; in a Mealy machine they depend on the current state and the current inputs.

      State diagrams draw states as circles and transitions as arrows labeled with the input condition that causes them. Moore outputs are written inside the states; Mealy outputs are written on the arrows after a slash (input/output).

      The hardware structure

      Every synchronous FSM has the same three parts: a state register of flip-flops holding the current state's code, next-state logic that computes the next code from the current state and inputs, and output logic.

      Key idea

      Because a D flip-flop simply loads D at the edge (Q* = D), designing the next-state logic means one thing: for each state S and input combination, make the D inputs equal to the code of the state the machine should be in next cycle.

      Moore and Mealy outputs

      The same behavior can usually be described either way. A detector for the pattern 101 (allowing overlaps, so that 10101 contains two matches) needs four Moore states but only three Mealy states, because the Mealy machine can announce the match on the transition instead of entering a dedicated "found" state.

      The trade-offs:

      • Mealy machines often need fewer states and respond a cycle earlier.
      • A Mealy output has a combinational path from input to output, so it can glitch when inputs glitch, and connecting Mealy machines in a loop can create combinational cycles.
      • Moore outputs change only after clock edges, which makes timing easier to reason about. Many designs go further and register their outputs (compute the output for the next state and store it in a flip-flop), making outputs glitch-free at the cost of one cycle of latency.

      Specifying transitions correctly

      A hardware FSM must be told what to do in every state for every input combination. Two rules make a specification complete and consistent:

      1. The conditions on the arrows leaving a state must be mutually exclusive: no input combination may satisfy two of them.
      2. They must be all-inclusive: every input combination must satisfy one of them. In particular, "stay in this state" must be drawn as an explicit self-loop with its condition.

      For example, if a state has arrows labeled A and B to two different states, the combination A = B = 1 is ambiguous and A = B = 0 is missing. Fix it by assigning priority (A; A′·B; A′·B′ for the self-loop). An arrow with no label means "always" (condition 1). With k inputs a state has up to 2ᵏ input combinations, but conditions are usually written as simplified expressions.

      Design by state encoding and K-maps

      Consider a Moore machine with input X and output F that is 1 when the last two or more inputs were 1. It needs three states: S0 (last input 0, or start), S1 (one 1), S2 (two or more consecutive 1s, F = 1).

      The design procedure:

      1. State table: for each state and input, the next state and the output.
      2. Encoding: assign each state a binary code. Three states need ⌈log2 3⌉ = 2 flip-flops: S0 = 00, S1 = 01, S2 = 10, with 11 unused.
      3. Transition table: substitute the codes.
      4. K-maps: one per flip-flop D input and per output, treating unused codes as don't cares.
      Q1 Q0 (state)XD1 D0 (next)F
      00 (S0)000 (S0)0
      00 (S0)101 (S1)0
      01 (S1)000 (S0)0
      01 (S1)110 (S2)0
      10 (S2)000 (S0)1
      10 (S2)110 (S2)1
      11 (unused)xxxx

      From the maps: D1 = X·Q1 + X·Q0 (the next state is S2 when X = 1 in S1 or S2), D0 = X·Q1′·Q0′ (next state S1 only from S0 with X = 1), and F = Q1. Two flip-flops, a handful of gates. The reset input must force the flip-flops to 00.

      Common mistake

      Treating unused codes as don't cares minimizes logic, but the machine's behavior in those states is then whatever the logic happens to produce. If a glitch or radiation upset ever lands the machine in 11, it might stay there. Safety-critical designs instead specify a recovery transition from every unused code back to a known state.

      One-hot encoding: design by inspection

      Instead of packing states into the minimum number of bits, a one-hot encoding uses one flip-flop per state, exactly one of which is 1. Next-state logic can then be read directly off the diagram: the flip-flop for state S must be 1 next cycle if the machine is in some state with an arrow into S and that arrow's condition is true.

      DS = Σ over arrows into S of (Qsource · condition)

      For the consecutive-1s detector: DS1 = QS0·X; DS2 = QS1·X + QS2·X; DS0 = X′·(QS0 + QS1 + QS2) = X′, since exactly one of the three is always 1. Each output is the OR of the state bits in which it is 1: F = QS2. Reset presets the initial state's flip-flop and clears the rest.

      EncodingFlip-flops for n statesNext-state logicTypical use
      Binary⌈log2 n⌉larger, derived with K-maps or toolsASICs with many states, where flip-flops are costly
      One-hotnsimple: one term per incoming arrowFPGAs (plentiful flip-flops), fast control logic
      Gray⌈log2 n⌉moderatesequential state sequences with minimal toggling (power)

      Because the encoding is invisible from outside the machine, it is a free design choice, and synthesis tools pick one automatically unless told otherwise.

      A machine with hysteresis

      A water tank has two level sensors: L = 1 when the water is above the low mark, H = 1 when it is above the high mark. The pump should start when the water drops below the low mark and keep running until it reaches the high mark. Between the marks the correct action depends on history (filling or draining), so a combinational function of L and H cannot do it: the controller needs one bit of state.

      Reading the arrows into ON: D = Q′·L′ + Q·H′ (turn on from OFF when the water is below the low mark; stay on until it reaches the high mark), and the output is simply Q. This is the same idea as the Schmitt trigger's hysteresis (Module 11), implemented with a flip-flop.

      Sequence detectors

      Detecting a fixed bit pattern is the classic FSM exercise and a common interview question. A Moore detector for an n-bit pattern has n + 1 states (Sk = "the last k inputs match the first k pattern bits"), and a Mealy detector has n. The only subtle part is where to go on a mismatch: to the state for the longest suffix of what has been seen that is also a prefix of the pattern. For 1011 with overlapping matches, after seeing 101 and then 0, the input ends in 10, which is a prefix of 1011, so the machine goes to the "seen 10" state rather than back to the start. The sequence-detector tool above computes these transitions for any pattern.

      State minimization

      Two states are equivalent if, for every possible future input sequence, the machine produces the same outputs starting from either. Equivalent states can be merged. The standard algorithm refines a partition: start by grouping states with identical outputs; then repeatedly split any group whose members, for some input, go to states in different groups; stop when no group splits. The remaining groups are the states of the minimal machine. Designs written by hand often contain redundant states; synthesis tools merge them.

      Summary

      • Datapath + controller: the FSM issues control signals and reads status signals.
      • An FSM is a state register, next-state logic and output logic; to reach state S next cycle, set D to S's code now.
      • Moore outputs depend on state only (one cycle later, glitch-free); Mealy outputs also depend on inputs (earlier, fewer states, combinational paths).
      • Transitions out of every state must be mutually exclusive and all-inclusive.
      • Binary encoding: fewest flip-flops, K-maps with unused codes as don't cares. One-hot: one flip-flop per state, DS = OR of (source · condition).
      • Sequence detectors: n + 1 Moore states for an n-bit pattern; on mismatch go to the longest suffix that is a prefix.
      • Minimize by partition refinement: split groups until members agree on outputs and next-state groups.

      Practice problems

      What is the minimum number of flip-flops for a machine with 5 states using binary encoding? Using one-hot encoding?

      Solution

      Binary: ⌈log2 5⌉ = 3. One-hot: 5.

      In one sentence each, define a Moore output and a Mealy output.

      Solution

      A Moore output is a function of the current state only. A Mealy output is a function of the current state and the current inputs.

      Write the one-hot next-state equations for the overlapping 101 Moore detector (states S0 to S3, input X) and its output.

      Solution

      Arrows into each state: S0 from S0 and S2 on 0: DS0 = X′(QS0 + QS2). S1 on 1 from S0, S1 and S3: DS1 = X(QS0 + QS1 + QS3). S2 on 0 from S1 and S3: DS2 = X′(QS1 + QS3). S3 on 1 from S2: DS3 = X·QS2. Output = QS3.

      A state has two outgoing arrows labeled A and B (to different states) and no self-loop. What is wrong with the specification, and how would you fix it if A should have priority?

      Solution

      The conditions overlap when A = B = 1 (not mutually exclusive) and nothing covers A = B = 0 (not all-inclusive). Fix: label the arrows A and A′·B, and add a self-loop labeled A′·B′.

      Using the divider of the worked example, how many cycles does dividing 20 by 6 take from INIT to DONE, and what are the results?

      Solution

      Quotient 3, remainder 2. Cycles: INIT, then (TEST, SUB) three times, then a final TEST that sees the borrow, then DONE: 1 + 6 + 1 = 8 cycles before entering DONE.

      Design a Moore machine whose output is 1 when the input X has been 1 for three or more consecutive cycles. Use four states encoded 00 (no 1s), 01, 10, 11 (three or more) and derive D1, D0 and the output.

      Solution

      On X = 0 every state goes to 00; on X = 1 the count advances and saturates at 11. Transition table rows (Q1Q0, X → next): 00,1 → 01; 01,1 → 10; 10,1 → 11; 11,1 → 11; any,0 → 00. K-maps give D1 = X·(Q1 + Q0), D0 = X·(Q1 + Q0′), and the output F = Q1·Q0. Check 01,1: D1 = 1, D0 = 1·(0 + 0) = 0 → 10 ✓.

      Draw (in words) the Moore state machine for the overlapping pattern 1011: give each state's meaning and its transitions on 0 and 1.

      Solution

      Sinit (nothing): 1 → S1, 0 → Sinit. S1 (seen 1): 0 → S10, 1 → S1. S10: 1 → S101, 0 → Sinit. S101: 1 → S1011, 0 → S10 (the input ends in 10). S1011 (output 1): 1 → S1 (ends in 1; 11 is not a prefix), 0 → S10 (ends in 10). Five states.

      Feed the input sequence 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1 (one bit per cycle) into the Moore and Mealy 101 detectors. In which cycles is each output 1?

      Solution

      Matches end at the inputs in positions 4 and 6 (1-based: the bits 1 0 1 at 2–4 and the overlapping 1 0 1 at 4–6). The Mealy output is 1 during cycles 4 and 6, while the final 1 is present. The Moore output is 1 during cycles 5 and 7, the cycles after those inputs are clocked in.

      Minimize this Moore machine (output in parentheses; next states for X = 0, X = 1): A(0): A, B. B(0): C, B. C(0): A, D. D(1): E, B. E(0): A, D.

      Solution

      Group by output: {A, B, C, E} and {D}. Split by next-state groups: C and E both go to (group 1, D) while A and B go to (group 1, group 1), giving {A, B}, {C, E}, {D}. A goes to (A, B) and B to (C, B): different groups for X = 0, so split: {A}, {B}, {C, E}, {D}. C and E agree, so C ≡ E. The minimal machine has 4 states; it is the 101 detector.

      The pump controller gets an extra input KILL that forces the pump off immediately and keeps it off while KILL = 1. Modify the next-state equation and say whether the output should be Moore or Mealy.

      Solution

      D = KILL′·(Q′·L′ + Q·H′). If the output stays Moore (pump = Q), the pump stops at the next clock edge after KILL rises. If it must stop immediately, use a Mealy output pump = Q·KILL′. With a fast clock the difference is negligible, and the Moore form avoids glitches on the motor drive.

      Design a two-requester arbiter with alternating priority. Inputs R1, R0; outputs G1, G0 (at most one grant, combinational from the current state and requests). When both request, grant the one that did not receive the most recent grant. Give the state, the grant equations and the next-state equation.

      Solution

      One state bit P records who has priority (P = 0: requester 0). Grants: G0 = R0·(R1′ + P′), G1 = R1·(R0′ + P): a lone request is always granted, and a tie goes to the priority holder. After a grant, priority passes to the other side: P* = G0 + G1′·P (set when 0 is granted, clear when 1 is granted, hold when nobody is). The grant outputs are Mealy outputs of a one-bit FSM. This is a two-input round-robin arbiter.

      A controller has 12 states. Compare a binary and a one-hot implementation in flip-flops and in the complexity of each next-state equation, and say which you would choose for an FPGA and why.

      Solution

      Binary: 4 flip-flops, but each D input is a function of 4 state bits plus the inputs, often needing several logic levels. One-hot: 12 flip-flops, and each DS is an OR of a few (state bit · condition) terms, one per incoming arrow. On an FPGA, flip-flops are plentiful (one per logic cell) and each LUT has a limited number of inputs, so one-hot usually gives fewer logic levels and a faster clock; it is the default for FPGA synthesis tools.

      A traffic controller has states MG (main road green), MY, SG (side road green), SY. A side-road sensor S and a timer signal T (1 when the current state's minimum time has elapsed; the timer restarts on every state change) are inputs. Main stays green until a car waits and the minimum time has passed; yellows last one timer interval; side green ends when the timer expires or no car is waiting. Write the transition conditions and the one-hot next-state equations.

      Solution

      Transitions: MG → MY on S·T, else stay. MY → SG on T, else stay. SG → SY on T + S′, else stay. SY → MG on T, else stay. One-hot: DMG = QMG·(S·T)′ + QSY·T; DMY = QMG·S·T + QMY·T′; DSG = QMY·T + QSG·S·T′; DSY = QSG·(T + S′) + QSY·T′. The timer is a datapath counter that the controller restarts whenever the state changes: an FSM and a counter working together.

      Part IV: Sequential logic

      Timing: setup, hold, clocks and metastability

      The rules every synchronous design must satisfy: setup and hold constraints, critical paths and maximum frequency, clock skew and jitter, how violations are fixed, and how signals cross safely between clock domains despite metastability.

      Builds onLatches and flip-flops, Registers and countersToolsSetup and hold slack calculatorPractice14 problems

      Synchronous design makes a promise: if every flip-flop shares one clock, and every path between flip-flops settles within a clock period without changing too soon after an edge, then the circuit behaves exactly as its logic equations say, regardless of the detailed delays. This module states that promise precisely. The two inequalities it produces, the setup and hold constraints, are checked on every path of every chip by static timing analysis (STA) tools, and are among the most frequently asked topics in hardware interviews.

      Delays of a path

      A combinational block has two delays of interest. Its propagation delay tpd is the longest time from any input change until all outputs are stable at their new values. Its contamination delay tcd is the shortest time from an input change until any output starts to change. Both come from the gates along the slowest and fastest paths through the block. Flip-flops likewise have a maximum and a minimum clock-to-Q delay.

      The setup constraint: how fast can the clock run?

      At a clock edge, FF1 launches a new value: it appears at Q after tclk→Q, then propagates through the logic, arriving at FF2's D input after at most tclk→Q + tpd. FF2 needs it to be stable tsetup before the next edge, one period T later:

      T ≥ tclk→Q + tpd + tsetup

      The setup slack is the difference between the two sides; negative slack is a violation. The path with the least slack is the critical path, and it sets the maximum frequency fmax = 1/Tmin. A violation means FF2 may capture the old value, or a mixture, or go metastable, so the circuit fails at that frequency. But it can always be fixed by slowing the clock, which is why parts are "speed binned" and why overclocking eventually fails.

      Worked example

      Finding the maximum frequency

      A design's flip-flops have tclk→Q = 60 ps and tsetup = 40 ps. Three register-to-register paths have logic delays of 520, 610 and 380 ps. The critical path is the 610 ps one: Tmin = 60 + 610 + 40 = 710 ps, so fmax ≈ 1.41 GHz. At a 750 ps clock (1.33 GHz) its slack is 750 − 710 = 40 ps, and the other two paths have 130 ps and 270 ps.

      The hold constraint: does the circuit work at all?

      The second constraint concerns the same edge, not the next one. At an edge, FF2 is capturing the value launched one cycle earlier, and it needs that value to stay stable for thold after the edge. But the same edge also causes FF1 to launch a new value, which can arrive as soon as tclk→Q,min + tcd later. If the new value arrives too soon, it corrupts the capture:

      tclk→Q,min + tcd ≥ thold

      Key idea

      The clock period does not appear in the hold constraint. A hold violation cannot be fixed by slowing the clock: the chip fails at every frequency. Hold must be fixed in the design, typically by inserting delay buffers on the too-short path.

      The paths at risk are short ones: a shift register (one flip-flop's output wired directly to the next one's input, tcd ≈ 0) relies entirely on tclk→Q,min exceeding thold, which flip-flop designers guarantee for flip-flops in the same library, as long as the clock arrives at both at the same time. That proviso leads to skew.

      Clock skew and jitter

      The clock is distributed across a chip by a large network of buffers and wires (an H-tree, a mesh, or a tuned tree), and it does not arrive everywhere at the same instant. The skew between two flip-flops is the difference in their clock arrival times; define δ = (capture clock arrival) − (launch clock arrival). Including skew:

      setup: T + δ ≥ tclk→Q + tpd + tsetup hold: tclk→Q,min + tcd ≥ thold + δ

      A late capture clock (positive δ) gives the data more time, helping setup, but extends the window during which the old value must be held, hurting hold by exactly the same amount. Skew can therefore be used deliberately ("useful skew") to borrow time for a critical path, but uncontrolled skew is dangerous mainly because of hold, which no clock-frequency change can repair.

      Jitter is variation in the clock period itself from cycle to cycle, caused by noise in the clock generator (a PLL) and the distribution network. In the setup check it reduces the usable period: if consecutive edges can be up to tjitter closer together than nominal, the constraint becomes T − tjitter ≥ tclk→Q + tpd + tsetup. Real STA adds further margins for on-chip variation in voltage, temperature and manufacturing.

      Fixing timing violations

      ViolationRemedies
      Setup (path too slow)Reduce logic levels (restructure, carry-lookahead instead of ripple); use faster (larger, lower-VT) cells; shorten long wires or add repeaters; pipeline by adding a register in the middle of the path (Module 19); retime by moving existing registers to balance stage delays; or lower the clock frequency.
      Hold (path too fast)Add delay buffers on the short path; reduce skew between the launch and capture clocks. Never fixable by the clock frequency.

      STA also needs to be told about paths that should not be checked normally. A multicycle path is one the design deliberately allows two or more cycles to complete (for example, a result read only every other cycle); a false path is a structural path that can never actually be exercised, or one between unrelated clock domains, which are handled by the synchronization techniques below rather than by timing.

      Metastability

      Setup and hold can be guaranteed for signals launched by the same clock. They cannot be guaranteed for a signal that comes from outside (a button, a sensor, a serial line) or from a different clock domain: such a signal can change at any moment, and sooner or later it will change inside some flip-flop's setup-and-hold window.

      When that happens, the flip-flop's internal loop can be left near its balance point, the metastable state of the cross-coupled inverters (Module 14). Its output hovers at an intermediate voltage, or oscillates, and only resolves to 0 or 1 after an unbounded, random time. The resolution is exponential: the probability that the flip-flop is still unresolved t after the edge is proportional to e−t/τ, where τ, the regeneration time constant of the loop, is a few tens of picoseconds in modern processes.

      The failure rate of a synchronizer is expressed as a mean time between failures:

      MTBF = etr/τ / (T0 · fclk · fdata)

      where tr is the time allowed for resolution before the value is used, fclk is the sampling clock frequency, fdata is the rate at which the asynchronous input changes, and T0 is a device constant related to the width of the vulnerable window. Because tr appears in an exponent, a little more resolution time makes an enormous difference. With τ = 20 ps, T0 = 50 ps, fclk = 1 GHz and fdata = 10 MHz, allowing tr = 0.45 ns gives an MTBF of about 3 hours, while allowing tr = 0.9 ns gives about 2 million years.

      Synchronizers

      The standard defense is the two-flip-flop synchronizer: the asynchronous signal goes into one flip-flop clocked by the destination clock, whose output goes straight into a second flip-flop. The first may go metastable, but it has almost a full clock period to resolve before the second samples it, so the second flip-flop's output is clean with an extremely high MTBF. Very fast clocks or high-reliability designs use three stages.

      Rules for using synchronizers correctly:

      • Put no logic between the two flip-flops; it would eat resolution time. The input must come directly from a flip-flop in the source domain, not from combinational logic, whose glitches could be sampled.
      • Synchronize a signal in one place. Two separate synchronizers on the same input can resolve differently in the same cycle, so different parts of the design disagree about its value.
      • Never synchronize a multi-bit value bit by bit. If several bits change together, each synchronizer may resolve its bit to the old or new value independently, producing a value that never existed. A binary counter going from 0111 to 1000 could be read as 1111 or 0000.

      Multi-bit data crosses clock domains in one of three ways:

      • Gray code for counters and pointers: only one bit changes per increment, so the sampled value is always either the old or the new count.
      • Handshaking: the source holds the data stable and raises a single request signal, which is synchronized into the destination; the destination then reads the data (now known to be stable) and returns a synchronized acknowledgment.
      • An asynchronous FIFO: a dual-port memory written with the source clock and read with the destination clock. The write and read pointers are kept in Gray code and each is synchronized into the other domain to compute the full and empty flags. Synchronization delay makes the flags conservative (the FIFO may look full or empty a little longer than it is), which is safe.

      A single-cycle pulse is a special problem: when it goes from a fast clock domain to a slower one, it may be shorter than a destination clock period and fall between edges entirely. A pulse synchronizer converts each pulse into a change of level (a toggle flip-flop in the source domain), synchronizes the level, and recovers a pulse by detecting edges of the synchronized level with an XOR against its delayed copy.

      Synchronizing resets

      An asynchronous reset is convenient because it works without a clock, but its release is an asynchronous event: if it is released near a clock edge, flip-flops may leave reset in different cycles or go metastable, and a state machine can start in an illegal state. The standard reset synchronizer asserts reset asynchronously and releases it synchronously.

      Summary

      • Setup: T + δ ≥ tclk→Q + tpd + tsetup. The worst path is the critical path; fmax = 1/Tmin.
      • Hold: tclk→Q,min + tcd ≥ thold + δ. Independent of frequency; fix with delay on short paths.
      • Positive skew (capture later) helps setup and hurts hold equally; jitter subtracts from the period.
      • Fix setup with fewer logic levels, faster cells, pipelining or retiming; fix hold with buffers.
      • Asynchronous inputs cause metastability; MTBF grows exponentially with resolution time.
      • Use two-flip-flop synchronizers for single bits, Gray code, handshakes or async FIFOs for multi-bit data, toggle synchronizers for pulses, and assert-async/deassert-sync for resets.

      Practice problems

      Define setup time and hold time in one sentence each, and state which one limits the maximum clock frequency.

      Solution

      Setup time: how long before the clock edge D must be stable. Hold time: how long after the edge D must remain stable. The setup constraint limits the clock frequency; the hold constraint does not involve the period.

      tclk→Q = 50 ps, tsetup = 30 ps, and the critical path's logic delay is 400 ps. What is fmax? What is the slack at 2 GHz?

      Solution

      Tmin = 50 + 400 + 30 = 480 ps → fmax ≈ 2.08 GHz. At 2 GHz (T = 500 ps) the slack is +20 ps.

      A path has tclk→Q,min = 40 ps, tcd = 20 ps, and the capture flip-flop's hold time is 70 ps. Is there a hold violation? Would halving the clock frequency help? What would?

      Solution

      40 + 20 = 60 ps < 70 ps: a 10 ps hold violation. Halving the frequency does not help, since the period is not in the hold check. Add at least 10 ps of delay (buffers) on that path, or reduce skew if the capture clock is late.

      Why must a two-flip-flop synchronizer have no logic between its two flip-flops?

      Solution

      The time between the first flip-flop's output settling and the second flip-flop sampling it is the metastability resolution time. Logic in between consumes part of that time and reduces the MTBF exponentially; it could also let a metastable intermediate voltage propagate into several gates that interpret it differently.

      A path has tclk→Q = 50 ps (max) and 40 ps (min), logic delay 400 ps (max) and 20 ps (min), setup time 30 ps and hold time 40 ps. The capture clock arrives 30 ps after the launch clock. Compute Tmin and the hold slack, and compare both with the zero-skew case.

      Solution

      Setup: T + 30 ≥ 50 + 400 + 30 = 480 → Tmin = 450 ps (2.22 GHz), versus 480 ps without skew: the late capture clock gives the path 30 ps more. Hold: 40 + 20 ≥ 40 + 30? 60 ≥ 70 is false: −10 ps hold slack. Without skew it would have been +20 ps; the skew moved 30 ps from hold to setup.

      A path consists of a NAND (35 ps), XOR (60 ps), NOR (40 ps) and inverter (15 ps) in series; a parallel path from the same launch flip-flop goes through just one inverter (15 ps) to the same capture flip-flop. With tclk→Q = 45/35 ps (max/min), tsetup = 25 ps and thold = 30 ps, find fmax and check hold.

      Solution

      tpd = 35 + 60 + 40 + 15 = 150 ps; Tmin = 45 + 150 + 25 = 220 ps → fmax ≈ 4.5 GHz. Hold uses the shortest path: tcd = 15 ps (taking each gate's delay as its contamination delay too); 35 + 15 = 50 ≥ 30: met, with 20 ps slack.

      Using MTBF = etr/τ/(T0fclkfdata) with τ = 20 ps, T0 = 50 ps, fclk = 1 GHz and fdata = 10 MHz, compute the MTBF for resolution times of 0.45 ns and 0.9 ns.

      Solution

      Denominator: 50 × 10−12 × 109 × 107 = 5 × 105 /s. tr = 0.45 ns: e22.5 ≈ 5.9 × 109 → MTBF ≈ 1.2 × 104 s ≈ 3.3 hours. tr = 0.9 ns: e45 ≈ 3.5 × 1019 → MTBF ≈ 7 × 1013 s ≈ 2.2 million years. Doubling the resolution time squared the exponential factor.

      A 4-bit binary counter in clock domain A is read in domain B by synchronizing each bit with its own two-flip-flop synchronizer. The counter changes from 0111 to 1000 just as domain B samples. Which values could B see? How does Gray code fix this?

      Solution

      Each of the four bits may independently be captured old or new, so B could see any of the 16 values formed by mixing 0111 and 1000 bit by bit (0000, 1111, 0101, and so on). In Gray code consecutive counts differ in exactly one bit (0100 → 1100 for 7 → 8), so only that bit is uncertain and B sees either 7 or 8, both of which are legitimate values.

      A 1 GHz clock has a cycle-to-cycle jitter of up to 30 ps. A path has tclk→Q = 50 ps, tsetup = 30 ps. What is the longest logic delay it can tolerate?

      Solution

      The shortest period that can occur is 1000 − 30 = 970 ps, so tpd ≤ 970 − 50 − 30 = 890 ps.

      Explain why a reset synchronizer asserts its output asynchronously but deasserts it synchronously. What could go wrong with a fully asynchronous release?

      Solution

      Asynchronous assertion lets reset take effect immediately, even without a running clock (at power-up). Releasing reset is an asynchronous event relative to the clock: if it happens near an edge, some flip-flops may see it before the edge and others after, or go metastable, so a state machine can leave reset with some bits updated and others not, landing in an illegal state. Synchronizing the release makes every flip-flop leave reset on the same, well-defined edge.

      A path has two pipeline stages with combinational delays of 600 ps and 200 ps (tclk→Q = 50 ps, tsetup = 30 ps). What is fmax? If the register between the stages can be moved so that the logic splits 400/400 (retiming), what is the new fmax?

      Solution

      Before: T ≥ 50 + 600 + 30 = 680 ps → 1.47 GHz. After retiming: T ≥ 50 + 400 + 30 = 480 ps → 2.08 GHz. The latency in cycles is unchanged (still two stages), and the function is unchanged because only the register's position moved.

      A one-cycle pulse in a 500 MHz domain must be delivered as a one-cycle pulse in a 100 MHz domain. Why does a plain two-flip-flop synchronizer fail, and what circuit works?

      Solution

      A 2 ns pulse can fall entirely between two 10 ns destination edges and never be sampled. A toggle (pulse) synchronizer works: in the source domain each pulse toggles a flip-flop, turning the pulse into a level change that persists; a two-flip-flop synchronizer brings the level into the destination; a third flip-flop holds the previous synchronized value, and their XOR produces a one-cycle pulse per toggle. Pulses must be spaced far enough apart (a few destination cycles) for each toggle to be seen.

      An asynchronous FIFO has 8 entries and uses 4-bit pointers. Explain why the pointers have 4 bits instead of 3, and how full and empty are detected (in binary terms, before Gray coding).

      Solution

      With 3-bit pointers, "write pointer equals read pointer" happens both when the FIFO is empty and when the writer has lapped the reader (full). The extra bit counts wraps: empty when all 4 bits are equal; full when the low 3 bits are equal and the top bits differ (the writer is exactly one lap ahead). In Gray code the same tests become: empty when the Gray pointers are equal; full when the top two bits of the two Gray pointers are both different and all remaining bits are equal. Each flag is computed in its own domain from a synchronized (slightly stale) copy of the other pointer, which can only make the flag pessimistic, never wrong.

      A designer fixes a setup violation by delaying the capture flip-flop's clock by 100 ps (useful skew). What new risks must be checked?

      Solution

      (1) Hold on every path into that flip-flop now has 100 ps less margin, and short paths into it may fail. (2) Setup on every path that starts at that flip-flop loses 100 ps, because it now launches later; the violation may simply move one stage downstream. (3) The added delay is subject to process and voltage variation, so the margin must hold across corners. Useful skew borrows time; it does not create it.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Part V: Computer organization and architecture

      Inside a processor: datapath and control

      How the building blocks become a computer: buses and memory-mapped I/O, instruction sets and encodings, why registers exist, the register file, a single-cycle datapath and its control signals, and how C statements turn into instructions.

      Builds onState machines, Adders and ALUs, Registers and countersPractice12 problems

      A processor is the datapath-plus-controller pattern of Module 16 taken to its logical end: a datapath general enough to perform any computation, and a controller that takes its instructions from memory instead of having them wired in. This module assembles one from the parts already built: registers, an ALU, multiplexers, decoders and memory.

      Processor, memory and I/O

      A computer has three kinds of component. The processor (CPU) executes instructions. Memory holds both the program and its data as numbered locations, each identified by an address. I/O devices (ports, displays, timers, network interfaces) connect it to the outside world. They communicate over buses: an address bus carries the location being accessed, a data bus carries the value, and control signals say whether the access is a read or a write and when it is valid.

      Most processors use memory-mapped I/O: each device's control and data registers are assigned addresses, and the processor reads and writes them with ordinary load and store instructions. On the ATmega328P, for example, the GPIO register PORTB sits at data-space address 0x25, so the C statement PORTB = 0x20; compiles to a store of the value 0x20 to that address. Writing to it does not change a memory cell; it changes the voltages on eight pins (Module 23).

      It helps to know where things live while a program runs: the compiled program and its global variables are in memory (loaded from storage when the program starts), local variables are in registers or on the stack in memory, the processor's working values are in its registers, and a display's pixels are in video memory that the display hardware reads continuously.

      Instruction sets

      Instruction set architecture

      The contract between hardware and software: the registers a program can see, the instructions and their binary encodings, the data types, how memory is addressed, and how exceptions behave. Any processor implementing the ISA runs the same programs; ARM, x86-64 and RISC-V are ISAs.

      Modern ISAs are mostly load-store (RISC) designs: arithmetic instructions operate only on registers, and separate load and store instructions move data between registers and memory. This keeps each instruction simple and regular, which makes it fast to decode and easy to pipeline. Older CISC designs such as x86 allow arithmetic directly on memory operands; modern x86 processors translate those instructions internally into RISC-like micro-operations.

      Registers exist because memory is slow and far away compared with the ALU. Consider F = (X + Y) − (X·Y) with X, Y and F in memory. A machine that can only operate memory-to-memory reads two operands and writes one result for each of its three operations: 9 memory accesses, with the intermediate results stored and reloaded. A load-store machine loads X and Y once (2 accesses), computes everything in registers, and stores F (1 access): 3 accesses. Compilers work hard to keep values in registers for exactly this reason.

      Encoding instructions

      An instruction is a binary word divided into fields: an opcode saying what to do, and operand fields naming registers or holding constants (immediates). Decoding means slicing the word into fields, which is free in hardware (just wires), and then decoding the opcode into control signals.

      Fixed field positions are a deliberate design choice: in RISC-V the source register fields are in the same place in every format that has them, so the register file can be read in parallel with decoding the opcode, before the processor even knows what the instruction is.

      The register file

      A register file is an array of registers with read and write ports. A typical integer register file has 32 registers of 32 or 64 bits, two read ports (for the two source operands) and one write port (for the result).

      • A write port is a decoder on the write address, ANDed with a global write enable (RegWrite), producing the load enable of exactly one register. The write data goes to every register's D inputs; only the enabled one loads it.
      • A read port is an n-to-1 multiplexer whose select is the read address. An m-bit-wide n-to-1 mux is simply m separate n-to-1 muxes sharing the same select lines: a 32-bit read port on a 32-register file is 32 copies of a 32-to-1 mux.
      • Adding a port adds another mux (read) or decoder plus data path (write). Register files with many ports, as needed by processors that issue several instructions per cycle, grow quickly in area and delay.

      A single-cycle datapath

      The datapath below executes one instruction per clock cycle for a small RISC-V-like instruction set: register arithmetic (add), arithmetic with an immediate (addi), load word (lw), store word (sw) and branch if equal (beq).

      Follow each instruction through it:

      • add rd, rs1, rs2: read rs1 and rs2, the ALU adds them (ALUSrc selects the register), and the ALU result is written to rd (MemtoReg selects the ALU).
      • lw rd, offset(rs1): the ALU adds rs1 and the sign-extended immediate to form the address, the data memory is read, and the loaded value is written to rd. This is the longest path: instruction memory, register read, ALU, data memory, register write.
      • sw rs2, offset(rs1): the address is computed the same way, and rs2 is written to the data memory. Nothing is written to the register file.
      • beq rs1, rs2, offset: the ALU subtracts and checks for zero; if equal, the next-PC logic loads PC + offset instead of PC + 4.
      InstructionRegWriteALUSrcALU opMemReadMemWriteMemtoRegBranch
      add10 (reg)add000 (ALU)0
      addi11 (imm)add000 (ALU)0
      lw11 (imm)add101 (mem)0
      sw01 (imm)add01x0
      beq00 (reg)subtract00x1

      The control unit is a combinational decoder from opcode bits to these signals: a truth table like any other, minimized with the techniques of Module 7. The ALU's own function code comes from the instruction's function fields, as in the ALU of Module 9. The don't-care entries (MemtoReg for instructions that do not write a register) are what make the logic small.

      In a single-cycle design the clock period must accommodate the slowest instruction (lw), so every instruction takes that long, and the instruction and data memories must be separate because both are accessed in the same cycle. Two alternatives fix these problems. A multi-cycle design breaks each instruction into steps (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back), one per short clock cycle, sequenced by a state machine; simple instructions finish in fewer cycles and hardware such as the ALU and memory can be reused across steps. A pipelined design overlaps the steps of successive instructions, the subject of Module 19.

      The instruction cycle

      Whatever the implementation, the processor repeats the same loop:

      1. Fetch: send the PC to memory, read the instruction, and advance the PC (to PC + 4 for 32-bit instructions).
      2. Decode: split the instruction into fields, read the source registers, and generate control signals.
      3. Execute: perform the ALU operation, compute an address, or evaluate a branch condition.
      4. Memory access (loads and stores only).
      5. Write back the result to a register.
      6. Check for pending interrupts or exceptions before starting the next instruction (Module 25).

      The PC is a register with an incrementer and a load path, which is the counter of Module 15: it counts through sequential instructions and is loaded with a new value by branches, jumps, function calls and interrupts.

      From C to instructions

      A compiler maps each C statement onto this machinery. For a[i] = a[i] + 5; with a 32-bit int array whose base address is in register a0 and with i in a1, a RISC-V compiler produces:

      slli t0, a1, 2      # t0 = i * 4 (byte offset of a[i])
add  t0, a0, t0     # t0 = &a[i]
lw   t1, 0(t0)      # t1 = a[i]
addi t1, t1, 5      # t1 = a[i] + 5
sw   t1, 0(t0)      # a[i] = t1

      Array indexing becomes a shift and an add (the scaling by the element size is why pointer arithmetic in C is scaled), the variable lives in a register while it is used, and memory is touched only by the load and the store. A function call saves the return address in a register (the link register), passes arguments in registers, and uses the stack in memory for anything that does not fit, according to a calling convention that is part of the platform's ABI.

      Summary

      • A computer is processor + memory + I/O on buses; memory-mapped I/O makes device registers look like memory locations.
      • The ISA is the hardware-software contract. Load-store (RISC) ISAs compute only in registers; registers cut memory traffic.
      • Instructions are fields; decoding is slicing plus a combinational decoder for the opcode.
      • Register file: write port = decoder + enables; read port = wide mux (m copies of an n-to-1 mux).
      • Single-cycle datapath: PC, instruction memory, register file, ALU with ALUSrc mux, data memory, MemtoReg mux; control signals come from a decoder of the opcode.
      • Instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute, memory, write back, check interrupts.

      Practice problems

      In the 16-bit format (4-bit opcode, dst, src1, src2) with opcodes 0 = ADD, 1 = SUB, 2 = AND, 3 = OR, decode 0x3254 and encode "SUB R7, R1, R3" (R7 ← R1 − R3).

      Solution

      0x3254 → opcode 3 (OR), dst 2, src1 5, src2 4: R2 ← R5 OR R4. SUB R7, R1, R3 → 1, 7, 1, 3 → 0x1713.

      What is memory-mapped I/O? Give an example of what a store instruction to a device address can do.

      Solution

      Device registers are given addresses in the processor's address space and accessed with ordinary loads and stores. A store to a GPIO output register such as PORTB changes pin voltages (turning an LED on); a store to a UART data register starts transmitting a byte; a load from a status register reports whether a device is ready.

      Count the data-memory accesses needed to compute F = (X + Y)·(X − Y), with X, Y and F in memory, on a memory-to-memory machine and on a load-store machine.

      Solution

      Memory-to-memory: three operations (add, subtract, multiply), each reading two operands and writing one result: 9 accesses. Load-store: load X, load Y, three register operations, store F: 3 accesses.

      A register file has 32 registers of 64 bits, two read ports and one write port. What decoder does the write port need, and how many 32-to-1 multiplexers do the read ports need in total?

      Solution

      Write port: a 5-to-32 decoder (ANDed with RegWrite). Read ports: each 64-bit port is 64 32-to-1 muxes; two ports need 128.

      Give the control signal values for sw and explain why MemtoReg is a don't care for it.

      Solution

      RegWrite 0, ALUSrc 1 (immediate offset), ALU add, MemRead 0, MemWrite 1, Branch 0, MemtoReg x. MemtoReg only chooses what would be written to the register file, and a store writes no register (RegWrite = 0), so its value cannot matter.

      Encode the RISC-V instruction add x5, x6, x7 in hexadecimal. (R-type: funct7 = 0000000, rs2, rs1, funct3 = 000, rd, opcode = 0110011.)

      Solution

      Fields: 0000000 | 00111 | 00110 | 000 | 00101 | 0110011. Grouped in fours: 0000 0000 0111 0011 0000 0010 1011 0011 = 0x007302B3.

      Which datapath elements does each of add, lw, sw and beq use? Which instruction determines the single-cycle clock period, and why?

      Solution

      All use instruction memory, the register file read ports and the ALU. add: plus register write. lw: plus data memory read and register write. sw: plus data memory write (no register write). beq: plus the branch/next-PC logic (no memory, no register write). lw sets the period because its path is longest: instruction fetch, register read, ALU, data memory read, register write setup.

      Why must a single-cycle processor have separate instruction and data memories, while a multi-cycle processor can share one?

      Solution

      In the single-cycle design a load or store reads its instruction and accesses data in the same cycle, so it needs two memory accesses at once: a structural conflict unless there are two memories (or a dual-ported one). A multi-cycle design fetches in one cycle and accesses data in a later one, so one memory, shared over time, suffices.

      Write RISC-V-style instructions for x = y + z * 8; with y in a1, z in a2 and x to be left in a0, using only add, addi and slli. How would the compiler handle * 10?

      Solution

      slli t0, a2, 3 (t0 = z·8), add a0, a1, t0. Multiplying by 10 = 8 + 2: slli t0, a2, 3; slli t1, a2, 1; add t0, t0, t1; add a0, a1, t0, or a single mul if the ISA has one. Compilers replace multiplication by constants with shifts and adds when that is cheaper.

      In C on an AVR, *(volatile uint8_t *)0x25 = 0x20; has the same effect as PORTB = 0x20;. Explain what the cast does and why volatile is needed.

      Solution

      The integer 0x25 is converted to a pointer to an 8-bit unsigned value, and the assignment stores through it: a store instruction to data address 0x25, where PORTB is mapped. volatile tells the compiler that accesses to that location have side effects it cannot see, so it must perform every read and write exactly as written, rather than removing "redundant" stores or caching values in registers (Module 25).

      A single-cycle processor's clock is set by lw at 800 ps. A multi-cycle version uses a 200 ps clock; lw takes 5 cycles, R-type and sw 4, beq 3. For a mix of 25% lw, 45% R-type, 10% sw and 20% beq, compare the average time per instruction.

      Solution

      Single-cycle: 800 ps for every instruction. Multi-cycle CPI = 0.25·5 + 0.45·4 + 0.10·4 + 0.20·3 = 1.25 + 1.8 + 0.4 + 0.6 = 4.05 → 4.05 × 200 = 810 ps. About the same here: the multi-cycle design's benefit is mostly hardware reuse; the large speedup comes from pipelining, which keeps the short cycle and approaches CPI = 1.

      The five supported opcodes have bits op[6:4] = 011 (R-type), 001 (addi), 000 (lw), 010 (sw) and 110 (beq); all other codes never occur. Derive minimal equations for RegWrite, ALUSrc, MemWrite and Branch from op[6:4].

      Solution

      Use the three unused codes (100, 101, 111) as don't cares and minimize each signal over op6 op5 op4:

      • Branch = op6: only beq has op6 = 1.
      • RegWrite = op5′ + op4: 1 for 000, 001 and 011; the don't cares absorb op6.
      • ALUSrc = op5′ + op6′·op4′: 1 for 000, 001 and 010.
      • MemWrite = op6′·op5·op4′: only 010; op6′ is required because beq (110) also has op5 = 1 and op4 = 0.

      Choosing opcode bit patterns so that control signals are single bits or small functions is a deliberate part of ISA design.

      Module19of 28

      Part V: Computer organization and architecture

      Performance and pipelining

      How performance is measured and improved: latency and throughput, the processor performance equation, Amdahl's law, pipelining and its limits, data and control hazards with forwarding and branch prediction, and how superscalar out-of-order processors go further.

      Builds onProcessor datapath, TimingToolsAmdahl's law, Pipeline hazard visualizerPractice13 problems

      Making hardware faster means either finishing each task sooner or finishing more tasks per unit time. The two are different, they are improved by different techniques, and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes in performance reasoning. This module builds the quantitative tools first and then applies them to the most important performance technique in hardware: pipelining.

      Latency and throughput

      Latency

      The time from the start of one task to its completion, for example the time to execute one instruction or to fetch one cache line.

      Throughput

      The number of tasks completed per unit time, for example instructions per second or bytes per second.

      A fighter jet carries one person at 2,400 km/h; a large airliner carries 400 people at 900 km/h. The jet has lower latency for a single traveler; the airliner moves 360,000 person-kilometers per hour against the jet's 2,400, so it has 150 times the throughput. Caches primarily reduce latency (Module 20); pipelining and parallelism primarily raise throughput, and can even increase the latency of each individual task.

      The processor performance equation

      The time a program takes on a processor factors into three terms:

      execution time = instruction count × CPI × clock period = IC × CPI / f

      CPI is the average number of clock cycles per instruction. Each factor is controlled by different decisions: the instruction count by the ISA and compiler, CPI by the microarchitecture (pipelining, caches, branch prediction) and the instruction mix, and the clock period by the circuit design and process technology (Module 17). The factors interact, which is why a single number such as clock frequency, or instructions per second without regard to what the instructions do, is a poor measure of performance. A deeper pipeline raises f but usually raises CPI too; a richer ISA lowers the instruction count but may lengthen the cycle.

      Speedup compares two systems running the same work: speedup = timeold/timenew.

      Amdahl's law

      If an improvement speeds up only part of a task, the rest limits the overall gain. If a fraction p of the original time is accelerated by a factor s and the remaining 1 − p is unchanged:

      speedup = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/s) ≤ 1/(1 − p) as s → ∞

      A program that is 90% parallelizable can never run more than 10 times faster on any number of processors; on 16 processors it reaches 1/(0.1 + 0.9/16) = 6.4. Amdahl's law tells you where to spend design effort: on the part that dominates the remaining time.

      Gustafson's law describes the opposite situation, where the problem grows with the machine: if the parallel part scales with N processors while the serial part stays fixed, the scaled speedup is (1 − p) + p·N. Amdahl's law describes strong scaling (fixed problem size), Gustafson's weak scaling (fixed time per processor), and both are needed to reason about GPUs and clusters (Module 22).

      Pipelining

      Suppose a block of combinational logic takes 10 ns, and we must process a stream of 100 inputs, for example computing C[i] = (A[i] + B[i])/4. Without pipelining, each input must pass all the way through before the next can enter: 100 × 10 ns = 1000 ns. Inserting a register halfway through the logic splits it into two stages of 5 ns each. Now a new input can enter every 5 ns, while the previous input is in the second stage.

      With k equal stages of delay Ts, the first result appears after k·Ts (the pipeline fills) and then one result emerges every Ts, so N inputs take (k + N − 1)·Ts:

      StagesStage timeTime for 100 inputsSpeedup
      110 ns1000 ns1.0
      25 ns(2 + 99) × 5 = 505 ns1.98
      42.5 ns(4 + 99) × 2.5 = 257.5 ns3.88

      For long streams the speedup approaches k. The latency of each individual input did not improve: it still spends 10 ns in the logic. Three effects limit how far pipelining can go:

      • Register overhead. Each stage pays tclk→Q + tsetup (plus skew margin). If the logic takes T and the overhead is treg, the stage time is T/k + treg, so throughput can never exceed 1/treg and returns diminish as k grows.
      • Balance. The clock is set by the slowest stage, so an unbalanced split wastes time in every other stage.
      • Dependencies. Pipelining helps only if inputs are independent. When one input needs the result of the previous one, it must wait, as the next sections show.

      The registers are essential, not incidental: without them, fast signals for the next input would catch up with slow signals for the current one somewhere inside the logic, mixing two computations (this is exactly the race of Module 14).

      The instruction pipeline

      A processor applies the same idea to the instruction cycle. The classic RISC pipeline has five stages, matching the steps of Module 18: instruction fetch (IF), decode and register read (ID), execute (EX), memory access (MEM) and write back (WB). Each stage takes one cycle, and a new instruction can start every cycle, so the ideal CPI is 1 even though each instruction takes five cycles.

      The ideal is broken by hazards, situations in which the next instruction cannot proceed in the next cycle:

      • Structural hazards: two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle, for example one memory for both instruction fetch and data access. Separate instruction and data caches remove the most common case.
      • Data hazards: an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not yet written back.
      • Control hazards: the processor does not know which instruction to fetch next until a branch is resolved.

      Data hazards and forwarding

      In add x1, x2, x3 followed by sub x4, x1, x5, the sub reads x1 in ID one cycle after the add was there, but the add writes x1 only in WB, three cycles later. Stalling until the write completes would cost several cycles per dependency. But the add's result already exists at the end of its EX stage, sitting in the EX/MEM pipeline register. Forwarding (bypassing) adds multiplexers at the ALU inputs that select a value from the EX/MEM or MEM/WB register instead of the register file whenever a hazard-detection unit sees that an older instruction in flight writes the register being read. With forwarding, back-to-back dependent ALU instructions run without stalls.

      A load is different: its value is not available until the end of MEM, too late to forward to an instruction in EX in the very next cycle. A dependent instruction immediately after a load must stall one cycle (a load-use hazard): the hazard unit holds the PC and the IF/ID register and injects a bubble (a no-op) into EX. Compilers reduce these stalls by scheduling an independent instruction between the load and its use.

      Control hazards and branch prediction

      A conditional branch is resolved (taken or not, and where to) in EX in the simple pipeline, two cycles after it was fetched. Meanwhile the processor has already fetched the next two instructions. If it simply guesses "not taken" and continues sequentially, it wins whenever the branch falls through and must flush the two wrong-path instructions otherwise: a 2-cycle penalty per taken branch. Because about one instruction in five is a branch, and modern pipelines resolve branches 10 to 20 cycles after fetch, this cost would be enormous without branch prediction.

      • Static prediction uses a fixed rule, such as predicting backward branches (loops) taken and forward branches not taken.
      • Dynamic prediction learns from history. The basic element is a 2-bit saturating counter per branch (indexed by bits of the branch's address): it predicts taken in its two upper states, and it takes two consecutive mispredictions to change the prediction, so a loop's single exit does not flip the guess for the next run of the loop.
      • A branch target buffer caches the target addresses of taken branches so that fetch can redirect in the very next cycle. Modern predictors combine global and local history and achieve accuracies well above 95%.

      Stalls simply add to the CPI: CPI = 1 + (stall cycles per instruction), summed over every hazard type. For example, if 25% of instructions are loads and 40% of them are followed immediately by a dependent instruction (1 stall), and 15% are branches mispredicted 30% of the time with a 2-cycle penalty, CPI = 1 + 0.25 × 0.4 × 1 + 0.15 × 0.3 × 2 = 1.19.

      Beyond the simple pipeline

      High-performance processors extract more instruction-level parallelism (ILP) with several techniques built on the same foundations:

      • Superscalar issue fetches, decodes and executes several instructions per cycle (4 to 8 in current designs), with multiple ALUs and more register file ports, so CPI can fall below 1 (often quoted as IPC, instructions per cycle, above 1).
      • Out-of-order execution lets later independent instructions run while an earlier one waits for a cache miss. Instructions wait in a scheduling window until their operands are ready. Register renaming maps the architectural registers onto a larger pool of physical registers, eliminating false dependencies (write-after-read and write-after-write) that come only from reusing register names. A reorder buffer retires instructions in program order, so exceptions remain precise and the program cannot observe the reordering.
      • Speculation executes past predicted branches and discards the results if the prediction was wrong.
      • Simultaneous multithreading (SMT) lets two or more threads share one core's execution units to fill slots that a single thread leaves idle.

      These techniques cost large amounts of area and power for diminishing gains, because real programs have limited ILP. Combined with the end of voltage scaling (Module 12), this pushed the industry toward many simpler cores and massively parallel processors such as GPUs (Module 22).

      Summary

      • Latency is time per task; throughput is tasks per time. Pipelines raise throughput, not latency.
      • Time = IC × CPI × T. Speedup = old time/new time.
      • Amdahl: speedup = 1/((1 − p) + p/s) ≤ 1/(1 − p). Gustafson (scaled): (1 − p) + pN.
      • k-stage pipeline: N items take (k + N − 1)Ts; stage time T/k + treg; balance matters.
      • Hazards: structural, data (forwarding removes most; load-use costs a stall), control (prediction; 2-bit counters, BTB).
      • CPI = 1 + Σ(frequency × penalty) over stall sources. Superscalar, out-of-order execution, renaming and speculation go beyond CPI = 1 at a high cost in power.

      Practice problems

      A program executes 2 × 109 instructions with an average CPI of 1.5 on a 3 GHz processor. How long does it take?

      Solution

      2 × 109 × 1.5 / (3 × 109) = 1.0 s.

      80% of a program's time is spent in a function you make 4 times faster. What is the overall speedup? What is the maximum possible speedup from optimizing that function?

      Solution

      1/(0.2 + 0.8/4) = 1/0.4 = 2.5. Maximum (function takes no time): 1/0.2 = 5.

      A 10 ns block is split into a 5-stage pipeline of 2 ns stages (ignore register overhead). How long do 1000 inputs take, unpipelined and pipelined?

      Solution

      Unpipelined: 1000 × 10 = 10,000 ns. Pipelined: (5 + 999) × 2 = 2008 ns, a speedup of 4.98.

      A program has 25% serial work. What speedup does it get on 8 cores, and what is the limit with unlimited cores?

      Solution

      1/(0.25 + 0.75/8) = 1/0.34375 = 2.91. Limit: 1/0.25 = 4.

      Processor A runs at 4 GHz with CPI 2.0; processor B runs at 3 GHz with CPI 1.2 on the same program (same instruction count). Which is faster, and by how much?

      Solution

      Time per instruction: A = 2.0/4 = 0.5 ns, B = 1.2/3 = 0.4 ns. B is 1.25 times faster despite its lower clock frequency.

      Logic of 8 ns is pipelined with a register overhead of 0.5 ns per stage. Compute the clock period and throughput speedup (relative to one stage) for 1, 4, 8 and 16 stages.

      Solution

      T = 8/k + 0.5. k = 1: 8.5 ns (1.0). k = 4: 2.5 ns (3.4×). k = 8: 1.5 ns (5.7×). k = 16: 1.0 ns (8.5×). Doubling the stages from 8 to 16 gives only 1.5× more, and no number of stages can beat 1/0.5 ns = 2 GHz.

      In a 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding and a one-cycle load-use stall, how many stall cycles does this sequence incur?

      lw   x1, 0(x2)
add  x3, x1, x4
sub  x5, x3, x6
lw   x7, 4(x2)
and  x8, x5, x9
or   x10, x7, x8
      Solution

      add uses x1 right after the load: 1 stall. sub uses x3 from add: forwarded, no stall. and uses x5 from sub (two instructions back): forwarded, no stall; it does not use x7. or uses x7 from the second load, which is two instructions back: by then the load has finished MEM, so it is forwarded from MEM/WB, no stall. Total: 1 stall cycle. (Swapping the second lw above sub would not remove the first stall; moving it between the first lw and add would.)

      Compute the CPI for a pipeline with base CPI 1 where 30% of instructions are loads, half of which have a dependent instruction immediately after (1 stall), and 20% are branches, predicted with 90% accuracy and a 3-cycle misprediction penalty.

      Solution

      CPI = 1 + 0.30 × 0.5 × 1 + 0.20 × 0.10 × 3 = 1 + 0.15 + 0.06 = 1.21.

      A loop branch is taken 9 times and then not taken once, and the loop runs many times. What is the steady-state accuracy of a 1-bit predictor (predict the last outcome) and of a 2-bit saturating counter?

      Solution

      1-bit: it mispredicts the exit (predicting taken) and then the first iteration of the next run (predicting not taken, the last outcome): 2 misses per 10, 80%. 2-bit: the exit moves the counter from strongly to weakly taken, so the next run's first iteration is still predicted taken: 1 miss per 10, 90%.

      Using Gustafson's law, what scaled speedup does a workload with a 5% serial fraction achieve on 64 processors? Compare with Amdahl's prediction for the same fraction.

      Solution

      Gustafson: 0.05 + 0.95 × 64 = 60.85. Amdahl (fixed problem size): 1/(0.05 + 0.95/64) ≈ 15.4. The difference is the assumption: Gustafson grows the problem so that the parallel part dominates.

      Design A is a 5-stage pipeline at 1 GHz with a 2-cycle branch misprediction penalty. Design B is a 10-stage pipeline at 1.8 GHz with a 5-cycle penalty. With 20% branches and a 10% misprediction rate (and no other stalls), which is faster and by how much?

      Solution

      A: CPI = 1 + 0.2 × 0.1 × 2 = 1.04 → 1.04 ns per instruction. B: CPI = 1 + 0.2 × 0.1 × 5 = 1.10 → 1.10/1.8 = 0.611 ns. B is 1.70 times faster. With a worse predictor (say 30% mispredictions) B's CPI would be 1.30 → 0.72 ns, still faster but by less: deeper pipelines need better prediction.

      Identify every true (read-after-write), anti (write-after-read) and output (write-after-write) dependence in this code, and say which ones register renaming removes.

      div  x1, x2, x3
add  x4, x1, x5
sub  x1, x6, x7
mul  x8, x1, x4
      Solution

      RAW: add reads x1 from div; mul reads x1 from sub and x4 from add. WAR: sub writes x1, which add reads (sub must not overwrite x1 before add has read it). WAW: div and sub both write x1. Renaming gives sub's x1 a new physical register, which removes the WAR and WAW dependences, so sub can execute immediately instead of waiting behind the slow div and add. The RAW dependences are real data flow and remain.

      Why does pipelining increase the latency of an individual operation slightly, and why do designers accept that?

      Solution

      Each stage adds register overhead (tclk→Q + tsetup), and the clock is set by the slowest stage, so an operation spends k × Tstage ≥ Tlogic + k·treg in the pipeline. Designers accept it because the goal is throughput over long streams of independent operations (instructions, pixels, packets), where the rate of one result per cycle dominates. When an operation's result is needed immediately by the next (dependencies), latency matters again, which is why forwarding and short critical loops (ALU to ALU, load to use) get so much attention.
