      Part V: Computer organization and architecture

      Caches and virtual memory

      Why memory is the bottleneck and how caches hide it: locality, the memory hierarchy, tags, indices and offsets, associativity, replacement and write policies, miss types and average access time, writing cache-friendly code, and virtual memory with TLBs.

      Builds onPerformance and pipeliningToolsCache simulatorPractice14 problems

      A modern core can execute several instructions per nanosecond, but a read from DRAM takes 60 to 100 nanoseconds: hundreds of cycles. If every load went to main memory, the processor would spend almost all its time waiting. Caches, small fast memories that keep copies of recently used data close to the processor, close most of that gap, and their behavior largely determines the performance of real programs.

      The memory hierarchy

      Fast memory is small and expensive; large memory is slow and cheap. No single technology offers both, so systems stack several levels, each a copy of part of the level below it.

      The hierarchy works because programs exhibit locality:

      • Temporal locality: data used recently is likely to be used again soon (loop counters, a function's local variables, the instructions of a loop body).
      • Spatial locality: data near recently used data is likely to be used soon (the next array element, the next instruction).

      A cache exploits temporal locality by keeping what was recently accessed, and spatial locality by moving data in blocks (also called lines), typically 64 bytes: a miss on one byte brings in its whole neighborhood. Caches are managed entirely by hardware and are invisible to the program's correctness, unlike registers, which the compiler manages explicitly.

      Finding data in a cache: tag, index and offset

      A cache must answer, for every address, "is this block here, and where?" in about a nanosecond. The address is split into three fields:

      • The offset selects a byte within the block: log2(block size) bits.
      • The index selects which set of the cache the block can live in: log2(number of sets) bits.
      • The tag is the rest of the address. It is stored alongside the block and compared on every access to confirm that the block in that set is the one requested.

      Each line also has a valid bit (does it hold anything?) and, in write-back caches, a dirty bit (has it been modified?).

      Worked example

      Splitting an address

      For the cache above, the address 0x12345678 has offset = the low 6 bits = 0x38 (byte 56 of the block), index = bits 13 to 6 = 0x59 (line 89), and tag = bits 31 to 14 = 0x48D1. An access hits if line 89 is valid and holds tag 0x48D1. Every address whose bits 13 to 6 are 0x59 competes for that one line.

      Associativity

      In a direct-mapped cache each block has exactly one possible location. That makes lookup fast and simple (one tag comparison), but two frequently used blocks that share an index evict each other repeatedly, even if the rest of the cache is empty.

      An N-way set-associative cache groups lines into sets of N; a block can go in any of the N ways of its set. A lookup reads all N tags of the set in parallel and compares them simultaneously, using N comparators and an N-to-1 multiplexer for the data. A fully associative cache is a single set: any block can go anywhere, at the cost of comparing against every tag. For a cache of capacity C, block size B and associativity N, the number of sets is C/(B·N). Typical L1 caches are 8- to 12-way, and larger caches 16-way or more.

      When a set is full, a replacement policy picks the victim. Least recently used (LRU) works well but is costly to track exactly beyond a few ways, so hardware uses approximations (pseudo-LRU trees) or even random replacement for large caches.

      Writes

      • Write-through: every write updates both the cache and the next level. Simple and always consistent, but it generates a lot of traffic, so it is paired with a write buffer that absorbs bursts.
      • Write-back: writes update only the cache and set the line's dirty bit; the block is written to the next level only when it is evicted. Much less traffic when data is written repeatedly; this is what most caches above main memory use.
      • On a write miss, write-allocate brings the block into the cache and then writes it (natural with write-back); no-write-allocate writes straight to the next level.

      Why misses happen

      • Compulsory (cold) misses: the first access to a block. Larger blocks and prefetching reduce them.
      • Capacity misses: the program's working set is larger than the cache. Only a larger cache, or a program that reuses data in smaller pieces, helps.
      • Conflict misses: too many active blocks map to the same set. More associativity reduces them.
      • In multiprocessors, coherence misses occur when another core's write invalidates a cached copy (Module 22).

      Average memory access time

      Cache performance is summarized by the average memory access time:

      AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty

      With several levels, the miss penalty of one level is the AMAT of the next: AMAT = tL1 + mL1·(tL2 + mL2·tmem), where mL2 is the local miss rate of L2 (misses per access that reaches L2). With tL1 = 1 ns, mL1 = 10%, tL2 = 5 ns, mL2 = 20% and tmem = 100 ns, AMAT = 1 + 0.1 × (5 + 0.2 × 100) = 3.5 ns. Without L2 it would be 1 + 0.1 × 100 = 11 ns.

      In processor terms, misses add stall cycles: CPI = CPIbase + (memory accesses per instruction) × (miss rate) × (miss penalty in cycles). A miss penalty of 200 cycles with a 1% miss rate on 0.3 data accesses per instruction adds 0.6 to the CPI, which is why out-of-order processors try so hard to keep working while misses are outstanding (Module 19).

      Writing cache-friendly code

      The same algorithm can run several times faster or slower depending on its memory access pattern. C stores two-dimensional arrays in row-major order: a[r][0], a[r][1], … are consecutive in memory.

      // Good: the inner loop walks consecutive addresses (stride 1)
for (int r = 0; r < N; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < N; c++)
        sum += a[r][c];

// Bad for large N: the inner loop jumps N * sizeof(int) bytes per access
for (int c = 0; c < N; c++)
    for (int r = 0; r < N; r++)
        sum += a[r][c];

      With 4-byte ints and 64-byte lines, the first loop misses once per 16 elements. In the second, if N is large enough that a column's worth of lines does not fit in the cache, every access misses: 16 times more misses for identical arithmetic. Other standard techniques:

      • Loop interchange reorders nested loops so the innermost loop has stride 1.
      • Blocking (tiling) splits a large computation, such as matrix multiplication, into sub-blocks small enough to stay in the cache while they are reused, turning capacity misses into hits. GPU programs do the same with on-chip shared memory (Module 22).
      • Structure of arrays instead of array of structures, when a loop uses only one field: the loop then streams through one dense array instead of skipping over the unused fields.
      • Keep hot data compact and aligned, and avoid pointer-chasing structures (linked lists) in performance-critical loops: each node may be a separate miss.

      Virtual memory

      Programs do not use physical addresses directly. Each process sees its own virtual address space, which the hardware translates to physical addresses using tables maintained by the operating system. This isolates processes from each other, lets each program be linked as if it owned the whole address space, enforces permissions (read, write, execute, kernel-only), and lets the OS keep only the actively used parts of a program in DRAM.

      Translation works in units of pages, typically 4 KB. The low 12 bits of an address (the page offset) are unchanged; the upper bits, the virtual page number, are mapped through a page table to a physical page number. Because a flat table for a 48-bit address space would be enormous, page tables are trees of several levels, and walking them takes several memory accesses. To avoid that on every access, the processor caches recent translations in a translation lookaside buffer (TLB), a small, highly associative cache of page table entries.

      Translation and caching interact. Many L1 caches are virtually indexed, physically tagged: the index bits are taken from the page offset, which needs no translation, so the cache lookup starts in parallel with the TLB lookup. That works only if the cache's size divided by its associativity is at most the page size, one reason L1 caches are typically 32 to 48 KB with 8 to 12 ways.

      Summary

      • Locality (temporal and spatial) lets small fast caches serve most accesses; data moves in 64-byte blocks.
      • Address = tag | index | offset. Offset bits = log2 B; sets = C/(B·N); index bits = log2 sets.
      • Direct-mapped is fast but suffers conflict misses; N-way set-associative compares N tags in parallel; replacement is LRU or an approximation.
      • Write-back + write-allocate is the norm; write-through needs a write buffer.
      • Misses: compulsory, capacity, conflict (+ coherence). AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, applied level by level.
      • Stride-1 access, loop interchange, blocking and compact layouts make code cache-friendly.
      • Virtual memory translates pages through page tables; the TLB caches translations.

      Practice problems

      A 32 KB direct-mapped cache has 64-byte blocks and 32-bit addresses. How many offset, index and tag bits are there?

      Solution

      Offset: log2 64 = 6. Lines: 32 KB/64 B = 512 → index 9. Tag: 32 − 9 − 6 = 17.

      A cache has a 1 ns hit time, a 5% miss rate and an 80 ns miss penalty. What is the AMAT?

      Solution

      1 + 0.05 × 80 = 5 ns.

      Repeat the address split for a 32 KB, 4-way set-associative cache with 64-byte blocks and 32-bit addresses.

      Solution

      Sets = 32 KB/(64 × 4) = 128 → index 7 bits; offset 6; tag 32 − 13 = 19. Higher associativity means fewer sets, so fewer index bits and more tag bits.

      Classify each miss as compulsory, capacity or conflict: (a) the first time a program touches an array; (b) a loop over a 1 MB array, repeated, with a 256 KB cache; (c) two small arrays whose addresses differ by exactly the cache size, accessed alternately in a direct-mapped cache.

      Solution

      (a) compulsory; (b) capacity: the working set does not fit no matter how it is placed; (c) conflict: they map to the same lines and evict each other although the cache is mostly empty.

      Why do caches transfer 64-byte blocks instead of just the bytes requested?

      Solution

      To exploit spatial locality: neighboring data is likely to be needed soon, and DRAM delivers a burst of consecutive bytes for little more than the cost of the first one. Larger blocks reduce compulsory misses and amortize the per-access overhead, but blocks that are too large waste bandwidth and cache space on unused bytes and increase conflict misses.

      A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines of 4 bytes. Trace the byte addresses 0x00, 0x04, 0x10, 0x00, 0x14, 0x04, 0x10, giving hit or miss for each. Then repeat with a 2-way set-associative cache of the same total size (2 sets, LRU).

      Solution

      Direct-mapped, index = (address >> 2) mod 4: 0x00 → line 0 miss; 0x04 → line 1 miss; 0x10 → line 0 miss (evicts 0x00); 0x00 → miss (evicts 0x10); 0x14 → line 1 miss (evicts 0x04); 0x04 → miss; 0x10 → miss. 7 misses.

      2-way, set = (address >> 2) mod 2: 0x00 → set 0 miss; 0x04 → set 1 miss; 0x10 → set 0 miss (both fit); 0x00 → hit; 0x14 → set 1 miss; 0x04 → hit; 0x10 → hit. 4 misses, 3 hits: the extra way removed the conflict misses.

      L1: 1 ns hit, 8% miss rate. L2: 6 ns hit, 25% local miss rate. Memory: 90 ns. Compute the AMAT with and without the L2, and the global L2 miss rate.

      Solution

      With L2: 1 + 0.08 × (6 + 0.25 × 90) = 1 + 0.08 × 28.5 = 3.28 ns. Without: 1 + 0.08 × 90 = 8.2 ns. Global L2 miss rate (fraction of all accesses that go to memory): 0.08 × 0.25 = 2%.

      A processor has a base CPI of 1.0. Each instruction makes one instruction fetch and, on average, 0.3 data accesses. The instruction cache misses 2% of fetches and the data cache 5% of accesses; each miss costs 100 cycles. What is the effective CPI?

      Solution

      CPI = 1 + 1 × 0.02 × 100 + 0.3 × 0.05 × 100 = 1 + 2 + 1.5 = 4.5. Memory stalls make this processor four and a half times slower than its ideal, which is why miss rates of a few percent matter so much.

      A 1024 × 1024 array of 4-byte ints is summed with a cache of 32 KB and 64-byte lines. Estimate the number of cache misses for row-order and for column-order traversal.

      Solution

      Row order: one miss per 16 ints: 220/16 = 65,536 misses. Column order: walking down one column touches 1024 different lines (one per row), 64 KB of lines, more than the 32 KB cache, so the lines are evicted before the next column could reuse them: essentially every access misses, about 1,048,576 misses, 16 times more.

      A loop writes 1000 times to the same 4-byte variable. How much traffic reaches the next memory level with a write-through cache and with a write-back cache?

      Solution

      Write-through: every write is forwarded: 1000 writes (4 KB of traffic, possibly merged by a write buffer). Write-back: the line is marked dirty and written back once, when it is eventually evicted: one 64-byte block write.

      A system has 32-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages, with 4-byte page table entries. How large is a single-level page table for one process? Why do real systems use multi-level tables?

      Solution

      The VPN has 32 − 12 = 20 bits: 220 entries × 4 B = 4 MB per process, mostly describing unused address space. A two-level table allocates second-level tables only for regions in use, so a small process needs a few kilobytes. For 48-bit addresses the flat table would be 512 GB, so four or five levels are used.

      For blocked (tiled) multiplication of double-precision matrices, three B × B tiles (one each of A, B and C) should fit in a 32 KB L1 cache. What is the largest power-of-two tile size B? Why does tiling reduce misses?

      Solution

      3 × 8 bytes × B2 ≤ 32,768 → B2 ≤ 1365 → B ≤ 36, so B = 32 (24 KB, leaving room for other data). Without tiling, each element of B is loaded once per row of A, and for large matrices it has been evicted by the time it is needed again (capacity misses). With tiles that stay resident, each loaded element is reused B times before eviction, cutting memory traffic by roughly a factor of B.

      An L1 cache is virtually indexed and physically tagged with 4 KB pages. Why must cache size/associativity be at most 4 KB? Give two cache configurations that satisfy this for a 48 KB cache and a 32 KB cache.

      Solution

      The index and offset bits must lie within the 12-bit page offset, which is the same in virtual and physical addresses, so the set can be selected before translation finishes. Bytes per way = size/associativity must be ≤ 4 KB (212 bytes). 48 KB → 12-way (4 KB per way); 32 KB → 8-way. This is why L1 associativity grows when L1 capacity grows.

      A TLB has 64 entries. What is its reach (the memory it can map without misses) with 4 KB pages and with 2 MB pages? Why do large-memory applications such as databases and GPU drivers use huge pages?

      Solution

      4 KB pages: 64 × 4 KB = 256 KB. 2 MB pages: 64 × 2 MB = 128 MB. A program touching gigabytes of data with 4 KB pages takes TLB misses constantly, each costing a page table walk of several memory accesses; huge pages extend the reach by 512 times and also shorten the walks.

      Module21of 28

      Part V: Computer organization and architecture

      Memories, programmable logic and FPGAs

      How memories are built and used: ROM, flash, SRAM and DRAM cells, array organization and control signals, building larger memories, DRAM timing and bandwidth, memory as logic, FPGAs from lookup tables, ASIC versus FPGA, and byte order and alignment.

      Builds onLatches and flip-flops, CachesPractice14 problems

      Memories are the largest structures on most chips and in most systems, and they come in several technologies with very different trade-offs. This module looks at how each kind stores a bit, how bits are organized into arrays that can be addressed, and how a memory can implement arbitrary logic, which is the idea behind the FPGA.

      Kinds of memory

      Memories are classified first by whether they keep their contents without power (non-volatile) and by how they are written.

      TypeStorage mechanismVolatileWriteTypical use
      Mask ROMconnections fixed at manufacturenoneverboot code in high-volume chips
      EEPROMcharge on a floating gatenobyte by byte, slow, limited cyclessmall configuration data
      Flash (NOR, NAND)charge on a floating gatenoerase large blocks, then program pages; ~103–105 cyclesfirmware (NOR), SSDs and SD cards (NAND)
      SRAMcross-coupled inverters (6 transistors)yesfast, unlimitedcaches, register files, FPGA configuration
      DRAMcharge on a capacitor (1 transistor + 1 capacitor)yes, and must be refreshedfast, unlimitedmain memory

      Flash's asymmetry, writes that can only clear bits after a slow erase of a whole block, and its limited endurance, are why SSDs contain a controller with a flash translation layer that remaps writes and spreads them evenly across blocks (wear leveling).

      The SRAM cell

      An SRAM bit is the bistable pair of inverters from Module 14, plus two access transistors that connect its two nodes to a pair of bit lines when the word line is high.

      SRAM is fast (a cache array can be read in under a nanosecond) and needs no refresh, but six transistors per bit make it about an order of magnitude less dense than DRAM. On-chip caches, register files and FPGA configuration memory are SRAM.

      The DRAM cell

      A DRAM bit is a tiny capacitor (a few femtofarads) behind a single access transistor. This is about as small as a memory cell can be, which is why gigabytes of DRAM fit on a module.

      The price is complexity. Reading shares the cell's charge with a bit line whose capacitance is far larger, so the signal is a few tens of millivolts and the read destroys the stored value; sense amplifiers amplify the difference and write the value back. Charge leaks away in milliseconds, so every row is periodically refreshed (read and rewritten), typically within every 64 ms.

      DRAM is organized in banks of rows and columns. An access first activates a row, copying the whole row (several kilobytes) into the bank's sense amplifiers, the row buffer; then reads or writes columns from it; then precharges the bank before a different row can be opened. Accesses to an already open row are fast; accesses to a different row pay the precharge and activate delays. These are the familiar timings tRP (precharge), tRCD (activate to column access) and CL (column access latency). Memory controllers reorder requests to maximize row-buffer hits.

      Bandwidth comes from wide, fast interfaces. DDR (double data rate) memory transfers data on both edges of its clock: a DDR4-3200 channel performs 3200 million transfers per second on a 64-bit (8-byte) bus, 25.6 GB/s. GPUs use GDDR, which runs narrower buses much faster, or HBM (high-bandwidth memory), which stacks DRAM dies on the processor package and uses a 1024-bit interface per stack to reach hundreds of gigabytes per second per stack at lower energy per bit.

      Organizing an array

      A memory with 2n words of m bits each is described as 2n × m and needs n address bits. Internally the cells form a two-dimensional array that is roughly square, because a long thin array has long, slow word lines or bit lines and a huge decoder. The upper address bits select a row through the row decoder (Module 8); all cells of that row drive their bit lines; sense amplifiers detect the small bit-line signals; and a column multiplexer driven by the lower address bits selects the requested word from the row.

      A discrete memory chip exposes the array through a few control signals, usually active-low:

      • CS′ (chip select) enables the chip; when it is high the chip ignores everything and its data pins float (high impedance).
      • WE′ (write enable) low means write: the chip stores the value on the data pins at the given address.
      • OE′ (output enable) low during a read lets the chip drive the data pins with the addressed word.

      A write therefore consists of placing the address and data on the buses, asserting CS′ and pulsing WE′ low while respecting the datasheet's setup and hold times; a read asserts CS′ and OE′ and samples the data after the access time.

      Building larger memories

      Memory chips combine in two directions:

      • Width expansion: chips side by side share the address and control lines, and each supplies part of the data word. Two 1K × 8 chips make a 1K × 16 memory.
      • Depth expansion: chips share address and data lines, and a decoder on the extra upper address bits drives their chip selects, so exactly one chip responds to each address.

      To build an A × B memory from a × b chips, use (A/a) × (B/b) chips: A/a rows of chips selected by a log2(A/a)-to-(A/a) decoder, each row containing B/b chips side by side.

      Memory as logic

      A memory with n address bits and m data bits can implement any function of n inputs and m outputs: connect the inputs to the address lines and store the function's truth table as the contents. Each output column of the truth table becomes a column of stored bits. From outside, nothing distinguishes it from a gate-level implementation.

      For example, a 3-bit squarer needs an 8 × 6 memory (the largest result, 49, needs 6 bits), and row 5 holds 011001 = 25. A 4-bit by 4-bit multiplier needs 8 address bits and 8 output bits, a 256 × 8 memory, in which row 0010 0111 (39) holds 2 × 7 = 0000 1110. The catch is scaling: the memory doubles with every additional input, so a 32-bit adder (64 inputs) is impossible this way. Small memories used this way are called lookup tables (LUTs), and they are the logic elements of FPGAs.

      FPGAs

      A field-programmable gate array is a chip whose logic and wiring are defined by configuration data loaded after manufacture. Its basic logic cell contains:

      • a small LUT, typically 4 to 6 inputs, that implements any function of its inputs;
      • a flip-flop that can register the LUT's output;
      • a multiplexer, set by configuration, that chooses the combinational or registered output.

      Cells are arranged in a grid embedded in routing channels. Programmable switch boxes, multiplexers controlled by configuration bits, connect wire segments to each other and to cell inputs and outputs.

      Mapping logic onto an FPGA means covering the design with functions of at most k inputs. The water-pump controller of Module 16 (inputs L and H, one state bit Q, D = Q′·L′ + Q·H′) fits in a single 3-input LUT plus the cell's flip-flop. Adding a third input such as a KILL switch still fits in a 4-input LUT, but a function with more inputs than one LUT has must be split across cells, adding a routing delay. Routing in fact dominates FPGA delay and area: a large fraction of an FPGA's silicon is switches and wires.

      Because most FPGAs store their configuration in SRAM, they load it from external flash every time they power up. Modern devices also contain hard blocks that would be inefficient to build from LUTs: block RAMs, DSP slices (multiply-accumulate units), clock managers, high-speed serial transceivers, PCIe controllers and even processor cores.

      ASIC versus FPGA versus software

      The same function can be run as software on a processor, configured into an FPGA, or built as a custom chip (an ASIC). The trade-offs:

      PropertySoftware on a CPUFPGAASIC
      Up-front costlowestlow (buy chips, write HDL)highest: masks and engineering cost millions of dollars (NRE)
      Per-unit costlow (commodity CPU)highlowest at high volume
      Performance and energybaselineoften 10–100× better than software for parallel, regular worktypically 3–10× faster and lower power than the same design on an FPGA
      Flexibilitychange anytimereconfigure in the fieldfixed after manufacture
      Time to marketfastestfastslowest (months of verification and fabrication)

      FPGAs are used for low- and medium-volume products, for hardware that must change after deployment (networking, telecom, test equipment), and to prototype ASICs before tape-out (Module 28). ASICs win when volume is high enough to amortize the up-front cost or when the last factor in performance and power matters, as in phones, GPUs and AI accelerators.

      Byte order and alignment

      Almost all memories are byte-addressable: each address names one byte, and a 32-bit value occupies four consecutive addresses. The order of those bytes is the machine's endianness. A little-endian machine (x86, most ARM and RISC-V systems) stores the least significant byte at the lowest address; a big-endian machine stores the most significant byte first, which is also the standard "network byte order" of internet protocols. The value 0x12345678 at address 0x100 is stored as 78 56 34 12 on a little-endian machine and 12 34 56 78 on a big-endian one.

      uint32_t x = 0x12345678;
uint8_t *p = (uint8_t *)&x;      // look at x one byte at a time
bool little_endian = (p[0] == 0x78);

      Processors also prefer, and some require, that an n-byte value be stored at an address that is a multiple of n (alignment), so that it never straddles two cache lines or memory words. C compilers therefore insert padding in structures: on a typical 64-bit platform, struct { char a; int b; char c; } occupies 12 bytes (3 bytes of padding after a, 3 after c), while reordering the fields to { int b; char a; char c; } needs only 8. Endianness and padding matter whenever bytes cross a boundary: binary file formats, network packets, memory-mapped device registers, and data shared between a CPU and a GPU or FPGA.

      Summary

      • Non-volatile: ROM, EEPROM, flash (block erase, limited endurance). Volatile: SRAM (6T, fast, caches) and DRAM (1T1C, dense, refreshed, destructive reads).
      • DRAM: banks, rows, row buffer; activate, column access, precharge. DDR transfers on both clock edges; HBM goes wide.
      • Arrays: row decoder, word lines, bit lines, sense amplifiers, column mux. Chips: CS′, WE′, OE′.
      • Width expansion shares addresses; depth expansion decodes upper address bits into chip selects.
      • A 2n × m memory implements any n-input, m-output function; FPGAs are built from small LUTs, flip-flops and programmable routing.
      • Software, FPGA and ASIC trade flexibility and up-front cost against performance, power and unit cost.
      • Little-endian stores the low byte first; alignment rules add padding to C structures.

      Practice problems

      How many address lines does a 64K × 8 memory need, and how many bits does it store?

      Solution

      64K = 216 words: 16 address lines. 216 × 8 = 524,288 bits (512 Kbit, 64 KB).

      Why are caches built from SRAM and main memory from DRAM?

      Solution

      SRAM is fast and needs no refresh but uses six transistors per bit; DRAM uses one transistor and a capacitor per bit, so it is roughly ten times denser and cheaper per bit, but slower, refreshed and destructively read. Small, fast levels use SRAM; the large, capacity-driven level uses DRAM.

      How many 1K × 8 chips are needed to build a 4K × 16 memory? How are they arranged and how many decoder outputs are needed?

      Solution

      (4K/1K) × (16/8) = 8 chips: four rows (depth) of two chips side by side (width). A 2-to-4 decoder on A11–A10 drives the four chip-select rows; within a row both chips share the select and supply the low and high bytes.

      What memory size implements a function with 4 inputs and 3 outputs? With 10 inputs and 8 outputs?

      Solution

      24 × 3 = 16 × 3 (48 bits). 210 × 8 = 1K × 8 (8 Kbit).

      The 32-bit value 0x12345678 is stored at address 0x100. List the bytes at addresses 0x100 to 0x103 on a little-endian and on a big-endian machine.

      Solution

      Little-endian: 78 56 34 12. Big-endian: 12 34 56 78.

      What is the peak bandwidth of one DDR4-3200 channel with a 64-bit bus? Of a dual-channel system?

      Solution

      3200 × 106 transfers/s × 8 bytes = 25.6 GB/s per channel; dual channel 51.2 GB/s.

      Give the contents of an 8 × 6 memory implementing a 3-bit squarer, and the row and contents that compute 2 × 7 in a 256 × 8 memory implementing a 4-bit × 4-bit multiplier (multiplicand in the upper address bits).

      Solution

      Squarer rows 0–7: 000000, 000001, 000100, 001001, 010000, 011001, 100100, 110001 (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49). Multiplier: address 0010 0111 = row 39, contents 0000 1110 = 14.

      Give sizeof for each structure on a typical 64-bit platform (int 4 bytes, double 8, natural alignment): (a) struct { char a; int b; char c; } (b) struct { int b; char a; char c; } (c) struct { char a; double d; int i; }.

      Solution

      (a) a at 0, pad to 4, b at 4–7, c at 8, pad to a multiple of 4: 12. (b) b 0–3, a 4, c 5, pad to 8: 8. (c) a at 0, pad to 8, d at 8–15, i at 16–19, pad to a multiple of 8: 24. Ordering fields from largest to smallest minimizes padding.

      A DRAM has 8192 rows per bank that must each be refreshed every 64 ms, and each refresh operation occupies the bank for 350 ns. How often must a refresh be issued, and what fraction of time does refresh consume?

      Solution

      64 ms/8192 = 7.8 μs between refreshes. 350 ns/7.8 μs ≈ 4.5% of the time the bank is unavailable. Refresh overhead grows with density, which is why newer DRAM generations refresh per bank and in finer steps.

      A DRAM is clocked at 1600 MHz (0.625 ns per cycle) with CL = tRCD = tRP = 16 cycles. What is the latency to the first data for (a) a row-buffer hit, (b) an access to a bank with no open row, (c) an access to a bank with a different row open?

      Solution

      (a) CL: 16 × 0.625 = 10 ns. (b) tRCD + CL: 20 ns. (c) tRP + tRCD + CL: 30 ns. The controller's scheduling of row hits versus conflicts can change effective latency by a factor of three.

      An FPGA has 6-input LUTs. How many LUTs does an 8-input AND need? A 6-input XOR? An arbitrary 7-input function?

      Solution

      8-input AND: one LUT computes the AND of six inputs, a second ANDs that result with the other two: 2 LUTs (2 levels). 6-input XOR: 1 LUT, since any 6-input function fits. Arbitrary 7-input function: two LUTs compute it for the 7th input = 0 and = 1 (Shannon expansion), and a 2-to-1 mux selects: 2 LUTs + a mux, which FPGA cells provide as a dedicated wide-function multiplexer.

      Design a 64 × 8 memory from 16 × 4 chips: how many chips, what does each address bit connect to, and what selects each chip?

      Solution

      (64/16) × (8/4) = 8 chips in four rows of two. A3–A0 go to every chip's address pins. A5–A4 drive a 2-to-4 decoder whose outputs are the chip selects of the four rows. In each row, one chip supplies D7–D4 and the other D3–D0; all rows share the 8-bit data bus through tristate outputs.

      Map the water-pump controller (D = Q′·L′ + Q·H′, output pump = Q) into one FPGA logic cell with a 3-input LUT. Give the 8 LUT contents in the order of the address Q L H = 000 to 111, and say which output the cell's mux selects.

      Solution

      D as a function of Q L H: 000 → 1, 001 → 1, 010 → 0, 011 → 0, 100 → 1, 101 → 0, 110 → 1, 111 → 0. LUT contents: 1 1 0 0 1 0 1 0. The LUT output drives the flip-flop's D; the flip-flop's Q is both the pump output and the feedback into the LUT's Q input, so the mux selects the registered output.

      A company needs 2,000 units of a video-processing board. An FPGA costs $400 per unit; an ASIC would cost $150 per unit after $3 million of design and mask (NRE) costs and take 12 extra months. Compare the costs and name two non-cost factors in the decision.

      Solution

      FPGA: 2000 × 400 = $0.8 M. ASIC: 3 M + 2000 × 150 = $3.3 M. The FPGA wins until volume exceeds 3 M/(400 − 150) = 12,000 units. Non-cost factors: time to market (12 months), the ability to fix bugs or update algorithms in the field (FPGA), and power, performance or size requirements that an FPGA might not meet (ASIC).

      Module22of 28

      Part V: Computer organization and architecture

      Parallel processors and GPUs

      Why computing went parallel, multicore cache coherence and synchronization with atomics, SIMD, and how GPUs run tens of thousands of threads: warps and SIMT execution, the CUDA programming model, shared memory, coalescing, occupancy, and the roofline model.

      Builds onPerformance and pipelining, CachesPractice17 problems

      For thirty years single-thread performance improved by roughly 50% per year, from faster clocks and smarter pipelines. Around 2005 that curve flattened: supply voltage stopped scaling, so higher clock frequencies meant unmanageable power density (Module 12), and programs ran out of instruction-level parallelism to exploit (Module 19). Transistor counts kept growing, so the extra transistors went into parallel hardware: more cores per chip, wider vector units, and massively parallel processors such as GPUs. This module covers how that hardware works and what it asks of the programmer.

      Forms of parallelism

      • Instruction-level: overlapping independent instructions inside one core (pipelining, superscalar and out-of-order execution).
      • Data-level: applying the same operation to many data elements at once (SIMD vector units, GPUs).
      • Thread- or task-level: running independent instruction streams on separate cores (multicore processors, clusters).

      Flynn's classic taxonomy names machines by their instruction and data streams: SISD (a simple uniprocessor), SIMD (one instruction applied to a vector of data), MIMD (independent cores, each with its own program counter) and the rarely used MISD. GPUs follow a hybrid that NVIDIA calls SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads): programs are written as independent threads, but the hardware executes them in groups that share one instruction stream.

      Shared-memory multiprocessors and coherence

      A multicore processor has several cores, each with private L1 and usually L2 caches, sharing a last-level cache and main memory. Because each private cache can hold its own copy of a line, a write by one core could leave stale copies in others. A cache coherence protocol prevents that by guaranteeing that all cores see a single, consistent order of writes to each location. The widely used MESI protocol tracks each line in each cache in one of four states:

      StateMeaningLocal readLocal writeAnother core readsAnother core writes
      M (Modified)only valid copy, differs from memoryhithitsupply the data, write back, go to Ssupply or write back, go to I
      E (Exclusive)only copy, cleanhithit, go to M with no bus trafficgo to Sgo to I
      S (Shared)clean; other caches may also hold ithitinvalidate other copies, go to Mstay Sgo to I
      I (Invalid)not presentmiss; go to E if no other cache has it, else Smiss; read for ownership, go to M——

      Small systems implement coherence by snooping: every cache watches a shared bus or ring for other cores' requests. Large systems use a directory that records which caches hold each line, so invalidations go only where needed.

      Coherence works on whole lines, which creates a performance trap. If two cores repeatedly write two different variables that happen to share a cache line, every write invalidates the other core's copy, and the line bounces between them at the cost of a coherence miss each time. This is false sharing.

      struct alignas(64) PaddedCounter {   // each counter gets its own 64-byte line
    std::atomic<long> value{0};
};
PaddedCounter per_thread[8];

      Synchronization and atomic operations

      When threads share data, ordinary loads and stores are not enough. The statement counter++ is a load, an add and a store; if two threads interleave them, one increment can be lost. If two threads each increment a shared counter 1000 times without synchronization, the final value can be anything from 2 to 2000. Such a data race is a bug, and in C and C++ it is formally undefined behavior.

      Hardware provides atomic read-modify-write instructions that perform a load and a store as one indivisible operation, with the coherence protocol holding the line exclusively in between: fetch-and-add, exchange, and compare-and-swap (CAS: write a new value only if the location still holds an expected value), or the load-linked/store-conditional pair on RISC architectures. Locks, semaphores and lock-free data structures are all built from these.

      A second issue is ordering. Compilers and processors reorder independent memory operations for speed, so another core may observe one thread's writes in a different order than they were written. Languages expose this through a memory model. In C++, std::atomic operations are sequentially consistent by default, and the weaker release/acquire pair is enough for the most common pattern, handing data from one thread to another:

      #include <atomic>
#include <cassert>

int payload;                                      // ordinary data
std::atomic<bool> ready{false};

void producer() {
    payload = 42;                                 // 1. write the data
    ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release); // 2. publish: earlier writes become visible first
}

void consumer() {
    while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) { }  // 3. wait for the flag
    assert(payload == 42);                        // 4. guaranteed to see the data
}

std::atomic<int> counter{0};
void work() { for (int k = 0; k < 1000; ++k) counter.fetch_add(1); }  // no lost updates

      Common mistake

      volatile is not a synchronization mechanism between threads in C or C++: it prevents the compiler from removing or caching accesses, but it does not make them atomic and does not order them with respect to other memory operations or other cores. It is the right tool for memory-mapped device registers and for variables shared with interrupt handlers on a single-core microcontroller (Module 25); between threads, use atomics or locks.

      SIMD vector units

      A SIMD instruction operates on a short vector held in a wide register: with 256-bit AVX registers, one instruction adds eight pairs of 32-bit floats. Compilers vectorize simple loops automatically when iterations are independent and data is contiguous; intrinsics or annotations handle harder cases. SIMD exploits data parallelism within one core at low cost, since the control logic (fetch, decode, scheduling) is shared across all lanes.

      GPUs: designed for throughput

      A CPU core is built to make a single thread fast: large caches, branch prediction and out-of-order execution all reduce the latency of one instruction stream. A GPU makes the opposite trade. It spends its transistors on arithmetic units, thousands of them, and tolerates latency instead of avoiding it: each processor holds many threads at once, and when one group of threads waits for memory, the scheduler simply issues instructions from another group in the next cycle. With enough threads in flight, the arithmetic units stay busy even though each individual memory access takes hundreds of cycles.

      A GPU consists of many streaming multiprocessors (SMs). Each SM has warp schedulers, a large register file (so that thousands of threads can keep their state on-chip and switching between them costs nothing), integer and floating-point lanes, specialized matrix units (tensor cores), load/store units, and an on-chip memory that serves as L1 cache and programmer-managed shared memory.

      Threads are executed in warps of 32. All threads of a warp execute the same instruction at the same time, each on its own data and registers. When threads of one warp take different sides of a branch, the warp executes both paths one after the other, disabling the lanes that did not take each path. This branch divergence wastes lanes; code whose branches are uniform across each warp (for example, conditions that depend on the warp index rather than on individual thread data) avoids it.

      The CUDA programming model

      A CUDA program runs on a host CPU and launches kernels, functions executed by many GPU threads in parallel. A launch creates a grid of thread blocks; each block contains up to 1024 threads that run on the same SM, can share that SM's shared memory, and can synchronize with each other. Blocks are independent: the hardware runs them in any order, on any SM, which is what lets the same program scale across GPUs of different sizes.

      __global__ void vadd(const float *a, const float *b, float *c, int n)
{
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;   // this thread's element
    if (i < n)                                       // the last block may be partly empty
        c[i] = a[i] + b[i];
}

// host side: one thread per element, 256 threads per block
int threads = 256;
int blocks  = (n + threads - 1) / threads;           // round up
vadd<<<blocks, threads>>>(d_a, d_b, d_c, n);

      The arrays d_a, d_b and d_c live in the GPU's own DRAM (global memory), allocated with cudaMalloc and filled with cudaMemcpy across the PCIe or NVLink connection, or managed automatically with unified memory. Transfers between host and device are slow compared with GPU memory bandwidth, so efficient programs keep data on the GPU across many kernels.

      Shared memory is fast on-chip storage visible to all threads of a block. The standard pattern is to load a tile of data from global memory into shared memory, synchronize, and then let every thread reuse it many times. A parallel sum (reduction) shows both shared memory and synchronization:

      __global__ void block_sum(const float *in, float *out, int n)
{
    __shared__ float s[256];                         // one slot per thread of the block
    int tid = threadIdx.x;
    int i   = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + tid;
    s[tid] = (i < n) ? in[i] : 0.0f;
    __syncthreads();                                 // all loads done before anyone reads s[]
    for (int stride = blockDim.x / 2; stride > 0; stride /= 2) {
        if (tid < stride)
            s[tid] += s[tid + stride];               // halve the number of partial sums
        __syncthreads();
    }
    if (tid == 0)
        out[blockIdx.x] = s[0];                      // one result per block
}

      Each step halves the number of active threads, so a block of 256 sums its values in log2 256 = 8 steps rather than 255 sequential additions; a second kernel (or atomics) combines the per-block results.

      Feeding the GPU: coalescing and occupancy

      GPU memory performance depends on access patterns at the level of a warp. When the 32 threads of a warp access consecutive addresses, the hardware coalesces them into a few wide transactions; scattered or strided accesses need many transactions for the same amount of useful data.

      This is why GPU code favors structure-of-arrays layouts (separate arrays of x, y and z) over arrays of structures when a kernel reads one field, the same advice as for CPU caches (Module 20) but with a larger penalty.

      Occupancy is the number of warps resident on an SM relative to its maximum. More resident warps give the scheduler more chances to hide latency. Occupancy is limited by whichever per-SM resource runs out first: registers (a kernel using many registers per thread allows fewer threads), shared memory per block, or the maximum number of blocks and threads per SM. Maximum occupancy is not always necessary, but too little leaves the SM idle while waiting for memory.

      How much parallelism is enough? Little's law, a result from queueing theory, answers this. In any steady-state system, the average number of items inside equals the rate at which they arrive multiplied by the average time each one spends inside. Applied to a memory system, the amount of data that must be in flight (requested but not yet returned) to sustain a bandwidth B when each request takes latency L is the product of the two:

      data in flight = bandwidth × latency

      A GPU with 2 TB/s of bandwidth and a loaded memory latency of 500 ns needs 2 × 1012 B/s × 500 × 10−9 s = 1 MB of requests outstanding at every moment. Spread over 100 SMs, that is 10 KB per SM, or 2500 four-byte loads. An SM holding its maximum of 2048 threads cannot reach that if each thread issues one 4-byte load and waits for it before issuing the next. Fast kernels therefore give each thread several independent loads in flight, by unrolling loops so that loads are issued before earlier results are used, or by using 8- and 16-byte vector loads (float2, float4). Occupancy is one way to supply concurrency, and instruction-level parallelism within each thread is the other. The same law limits CPUs: a core can track only a fixed number of outstanding cache misses, which caps the bandwidth a single thread can draw no matter how fast the memory is.

      Shared memory has its own access rule. It is divided into 32 banks, each 4 bytes wide, with successive 4-byte words in successive banks: word w lives in bank w mod 32. Each bank delivers one word per cycle, so a warp's access completes in one pass only if its 32 threads touch 32 different banks, or read the same word, which is broadcast to all of them. When k threads access different words in the same bank, the hardware replays the access k times: a k-way bank conflict. Stride-1 access, s[tid], is conflict free. s[2*tid] places two threads in each even-numbered bank, a 2-way conflict. Reading down a column of a 32 × 32 tile, s[tid][c], places all 32 threads in bank c, a 32-way conflict, because every row is 32 words long and starts in bank 0. The standard fix is padding: declared as s[32][33], element (r, c) is word 33r + c, in bank (r + c) mod 32, so the 32 elements of any column fall in 32 different banks at the cost of 32 unused words.

      Matrix engines and precision

      Dense linear algebra, the core of neural-network training and inference, maps well onto GPUs because matrix multiplication performs many operations per byte loaded. Modern GPUs add tensor cores that compute small matrix products (for example a 4 × 4 × 4 multiply-accumulate) in one instruction, in reduced precisions such as FP16, BF16 or FP8 with FP32 accumulation. The formats of Module 4 matter here: BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range with fewer mantissa bits, which suits training, while narrower formats double throughput again at the cost of precision.

      The roofline model

      Whether a kernel is limited by computation or by memory traffic depends on its arithmetic intensity: floating-point operations performed per byte moved to or from DRAM. Attainable performance is the lower of the processor's peak compute rate and its memory bandwidth multiplied by the intensity.

      attainable FLOP/s = min( peak FLOP/s, memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity )

      Vector addition performs one addition per 12 bytes (two 4-byte loads and one 4-byte store), an intensity of 1/12: at 2 TB/s it can reach only about 0.17 TFLOP/s, under 0.3% of peak, no matter how it is written. A large matrix multiplication with good tiling reuses each loaded element many times, reaches high intensity, and runs near the compute peak. The roofline tells an engineer which optimization matters: for a memory-bound kernel, reduce or reuse data movement (tiling into shared memory, fusing kernels, smaller data types); for a compute-bound one, use better instructions (tensor cores) or fewer operations.

      Summary

      • Power and ILP limits turned extra transistors into parallel hardware: multicore, SIMD and GPUs.
      • Coherence (MESI: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) keeps private caches consistent per line; false sharing makes unrelated writes conflict.
      • Data races lose updates; use atomic read-modify-write operations or locks, and release/acquire ordering to publish data. volatile is not thread synchronization.
      • GPUs hide latency with massive multithreading; warps of 32 threads execute in lockstep (SIMT), and divergent branches serialize.
      • CUDA: kernels launch grids of blocks of threads; i = blockIdx.x·blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; shared memory and __syncthreads() enable cooperation within a block.
      • Coalesced, stride-1 access and adequate occupancy keep the memory system and the SMs busy.
      • Little's law: data in flight = bandwidth × latency. Hiding latency needs enough independent requests outstanding, from many warps, several loads per thread, or wider loads.
      • Shared memory has 32 four-byte banks; threads of a warp accessing different words in one bank serialize. Pad 2-D tiles (for example [32][33]) to make column access conflict free.
      • Roofline: performance = min(peak, bandwidth × intensity). Low-intensity kernels are memory bound.

      Practice problems

      A CUDA kernel is launched with 256 threads per block. Which global element does thread 17 of block 3 handle?

      Solution

      i = 3 × 256 + 17 = 785.

      Classify in Flynn's taxonomy: (a) an 8-core CPU running different programs on each core; (b) an AVX instruction adding eight floats; (c) a GPU warp.

      Solution

      (a) MIMD; (b) SIMD; (c) SIMT, a form of SIMD in which each lane is programmed as an independent thread with its own registers.

      How many blocks of 256 threads are needed for n = 1,000,000 elements? Why does the kernel need the test if (i < n)?

      Solution

      ⌈1,000,000/256⌉ = 3907 blocks, which launch 1,000,192 threads. The last 192 threads have no element; without the bounds check they would read and write past the end of the arrays.

      Core 0 reads a line that no cache holds, then writes it; then core 1 reads the same line. Give the MESI state of the line in each cache after each step.

      Solution

      Core 0 read: core 0 E. Core 0 write: core 0 M, with no bus traffic, because no other copy exists. Core 1 read: core 0 supplies the data and writes it back; both caches hold it in S.

      What is the arithmetic intensity of single-precision vector addition c[i] = a[i] + b[i], and what performance can it reach on a GPU with 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth?

      Solution

      1 FLOP per 12 bytes: 1/12 FLOP/B. 2 × 1012 B/s × 1/12 ≈ 167 GFLOP/s, a tiny fraction of the compute peak: the kernel is memory bound.

      Two threads each execute counter++ 1000 times on a shared int with no synchronization. Explain how updates are lost, and show that the final value can be as low as 2. Give two correct fixes.

      Solution

      Each increment is load, add, store. If thread A loads the value, thread B performs several complete increments, and A then stores its stale value + 1, B's increments vanish. A worst case: A loads 0; B runs 999 increments (counter = 999); A stores 1; B loads 1; A runs its remaining 999 increments (counter = 1000); B stores 2. Final value 2. Fixes: std::atomic<int> with fetch_add, or protect the increment with a mutex (or give each thread its own counter and sum at the end, which is also fastest).

      In a warp, threads with even threadIdx.x take the if path (cost 100 cycles) and odd ones take the else path (cost 60 cycles). How long does the warp take? What if the condition were (threadIdx.x / 32) % 2 == 0 instead?

      Solution

      Every warp contains both even and odd threads, so each warp executes both paths: 160 cycles, with half the lanes idle each time. With the warp-level condition, all threads in a warp agree: each warp takes 100 or 60 cycles, and no lanes are wasted.

      An SM has 65,536 registers and supports at most 64 resident warps. A kernel uses 64 registers per thread. What is the maximum occupancy? What if it used 32 registers?

      Solution

      65,536/64 = 1024 threads = 32 warps → 50% occupancy. With 32 registers: 2048 threads = 64 warps → 100% (if no other limit applies). Reducing register use, for example by recomputing values, can raise occupancy, at the risk of spilling to slower memory.

      On the GPU of the roofline figure (60 TFLOP/s, 2 TB/s), what performance does a kernel with intensity 8 FLOP/B reach, and what intensity is needed to become compute bound?

      Solution

      min(60, 2 × 8) = 16 TFLOP/s: memory bound. The ridge point is 60/2 = 30 FLOP/B; above it the kernel is limited by compute.

      Multiplying two N × N single-precision matrices performs 2N3 operations and, with perfect reuse, moves 3N2 values. What is its best-case arithmetic intensity, and is N = 4096 compute bound on the example GPU?

      Solution

      2N3/(3N2 × 4 bytes) = N/6 FLOP/B. For N = 4096: about 683 FLOP/B, far above the ridge at 30, so a well-tiled implementation is compute bound. Without tiling, data is reloaded many times and the effective intensity, and performance, collapse.

      A kernel reads only the x field of an array of struct { float x, y, z, w; }. Compared with a separate array of x values, how many times more memory traffic does each warp generate?

      Solution

      Consecutive threads read addresses 16 bytes apart, so the 32 x values of a warp are spread over 512 bytes instead of 128: about 4 times the traffic (and transactions), three quarters of it unused. Converting to a structure of arrays restores fully coalesced access.

      A GPU has 3 TB/s of memory bandwidth, a loaded memory latency of 600 ns, and 132 SMs, each holding up to 2048 threads. How many bytes must each SM keep in flight to use the full bandwidth? How many independent 4-byte loads must each thread have outstanding at full occupancy?

      Solution

      Little's law: 3 × 1012 B/s × 600 × 10−9 s = 1.8 MB in flight across the chip, or 1.8 MB/132 ≈ 13.6 KB per SM. Divided among 2048 threads that is about 6.7 bytes per thread, so each thread needs at least two independent 4-byte loads outstanding (or one 8-byte vector load). With fewer resident threads, each thread needs proportionally more.

      A CPU core can track 12 outstanding cache misses, each for a 64-byte line, and memory latency is 80 ns. What is the most memory bandwidth one core can draw? Why can a single thread not saturate a memory system rated at 100 GB/s?

      Solution

      Bandwidth = data in flight/latency = 12 × 64 B/80 ns = 9.6 GB/s. The core runs out of miss-tracking entries (often called line fill buffers) long before the memory runs out of bandwidth; reaching 100 GB/s takes about ten cores' worth of outstanding misses. Hardware prefetchers help a single thread only by keeping those entries busy.

      A transpose kernel loads a 32 × 32 tile into __shared__ float t[32][32] by rows and then reads it by columns: thread i of a warp reads t[i][c]. What bank conflict does the column read cause? Show that declaring t[32][33] removes it.

      Solution

      Element (i, c) of the unpadded tile is word 32i + c, in bank (32i + c) mod 32 = c for every i: all 32 threads hit one bank, a 32-way conflict, so the read takes 32 passes. With rows of 33 words, element (i, c) is word 33i + c, in bank (i + c) mod 32, which is different for each i = 0 … 31: no conflict. The row-wise load stays conflict free as well, since consecutive threads still access consecutive words.

      In the producer/consumer example, suppose both atomic operations used memory_order_relaxed. What could go wrong, and why do release and acquire prevent it?

      Solution

      Relaxed atomics guarantee only that the flag itself is updated atomically; they impose no ordering on other memory operations. The compiler or hardware could make the store to ready visible before the store to payload, or the consumer could read payload before its read of ready completes, so the consumer may see ready == true and still read the old payload. A release store guarantees that all earlier writes by the producer become visible before the flag; an acquire load guarantees that later reads by the consumer happen after it. Together they create a happens-before relationship from the write of payload to its read.

      A memory-bound kernel runs on a CPU with 100 GB/s of memory bandwidth and on a GPU with 2 TB/s. The GPU also has 30 times the CPU's peak FLOP rate. Estimate the speedup, and explain why the FLOP ratio is irrelevant here.

      Solution

      For a memory-bound kernel, time ≈ bytes moved/bandwidth, so the speedup is the bandwidth ratio: 2000/100 = about 20× (ignoring the cost of copying data to the GPU, which can erase the gain for a single short kernel). The FLOP ratio would matter only for compute-bound kernels to the right of both machines' ridge points.

      The block_sum reduction uses if (tid < stride) with stride halving from 128. Why is this ordering better than the "interleaved" version that uses if (tid % (2*stride) == 0) with stride doubling from 1? Consider both divergence and shared-memory access.

      Solution

      With tid < stride, the active threads are always a contiguous range starting at 0, so whole warps are either fully active or fully idle: there is no divergence until fewer than 32 threads remain, and idle warps retire early. Consecutive threads also access consecutive shared-memory words, avoiding bank conflicts. The interleaved version leaves scattered threads active in every warp (divergence at every step) and accesses words with growing strides, which causes bank conflicts.

      Part VI: Embedded systems

      Microcontrollers, GPIO and bit manipulation in C

      Programming hardware directly: what is inside a microcontroller, C integer types on an 8-bit machine, the DDR, PORT and PIN registers, the bit-manipulation idioms and the mistakes that break them, copying bit fields, and reading buttons with debouncing.

      Builds onProcessor datapath, Interfacing, Number systemsToolsRegister bit-fiddling playgroundPractice15 problems

      A microcontroller puts a processor, memory and peripherals on one chip, and a program controls the hardware by reading and writing the peripherals' registers. Embedded C is mostly ordinary C, plus one essential skill: changing exactly the bits you mean to change in a register, and nothing else. This module uses the ATmega328P, the 8-bit AVR microcontroller on the Arduino Uno, programmed directly through its registers rather than through the Arduino library.

      What is in a microcontroller

      The ATmega328P has an 8-bit AVR core running at 16 MHz on the Uno, 32 KB of flash for the program, 2 KB of SRAM for data, and 1 KB of EEPROM for settings that must survive power-off. Program and data memories are separate (a Harvard architecture), so constant data placed in flash needs special access functions. There is usually no operating system: the program starts at reset and runs forever. It is compiled with avr-gcc into a binary image that a bootloader or programmer writes into flash.

      C integer types on an 8-bit machine

      C's built-in integer sizes depend on the platform. On AVR, int is only 16 bits (−32,768 to 32,767), so code that assumes 32-bit ints silently overflows. Embedded code therefore uses the fixed-width types from <stdint.h>:

      TypeBitsRange
      uint8_t80 to 255
      int8_t8−128 to 127
      uint16_t160 to 65,535
      int16_t16−32,768 to 32,767
      uint32_t320 to 4,294,967,295
      int32_t32−2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647

      Two rules of C arithmetic cause most surprises:

      • Integer promotion: operands smaller than int are converted to int before arithmetic. With uint8_t a = 200, b = 100; the expression a + b is the int 300; only assigning it back to a uint8_t truncates it to 300 − 256 = 44.
      • Constants are int by default: on AVR, 1 << 15 overflows a 16-bit signed int and 1 << 20 is undefined. Write 1UL << 20 (unsigned long, 32 bits) when the result must be wider than 16 bits.

      Use char for text and uint8_t/int8_t for small numbers. A character is stored as its ASCII code: '0' is 0x30, so '0' + 7 is the character '7', while sending the number 7 to a display shows an unprintable control character (Module 2).

      GPIO: the DDR, PORT and PIN registers

      The ATmega328P's general-purpose I/O pins are grouped into 8-bit ports B, C and D. Each port has three registers, and bit n of each register controls pin n of that port:

      RegisterMeaning of bit n
      DDRx (data direction)1 = pin is an output, 0 = input. All bits are 0 after reset, so every pin starts as an input.
      PORTxIf output: the value driven (1 = high, 0 = low). If input: 1 enables the internal pull-up resistor.
      PINxRead: the current logic level on the pin, whether input or output. Writing 1 to a PIN bit toggles the corresponding PORT bit.

      Changing one bit without disturbing the others

      A register holds eight independent controls, so assigning a whole value (PORTB = 0x20;) changes all eight pins. To change one bit, read the register, modify the bit with a mask, and write it back. A mask is a constant with 1s in the bit positions of interest, written in hexadecimal (0x20) or built with a shift (1 << 5, which the AVR headers let you write as 1 << PB5).

      The reasoning behind each operation is the identity table of each operator: x | 1 = 1 and x | 0 = x; x & 0 = 0 and x & 1 = x; x ^ 1 = x′ and x ^ 0 = x. The mask's 1 bits select which positions are affected; its 0 bits leave the rest alone. The six recipes cover nearly all GPIO code:

      DDRB  |=  (1 << PB4);          // make PB4 an output
DDRB  &= ~(1 << PB4);          // make PB4 an input
PORTB |=  (1 << PB4);          // drive PB4 high (or enable its pull-up if input)
PORTB &= ~(1 << PB4);          // drive PB4 low (or disable its pull-up)
if ((PINB & (1 << PB4)) != 0)  // PB4 reads 1
if ((PINB & (1 << PB4)) == 0)  // PB4 reads 0
PORTB ^=  (1 << PB4);          // toggle PB4

      Several bits are handled at once by ORing shifted ones: PORTD |= (1 << 7) | (1 << 2); sets bits 7 and 2. For I/O registers in the low part of the address space, the compiler turns single-bit set and clear operations into the AVR's one-instruction sbi and cbi, which cannot be interrupted halfway (Module 25).

      Bitwise versus logical operators, and precedence

      C has two families of operators that look alike and behave very differently:

      • Bitwise & | ^ ~ operate on each bit position independently and produce a number.
      • Logical && || ! treat any nonzero value as true and produce 0 or 1.

      So 1 && 2 is 1 but 1 & 2 is 0; !0x10 is 0 but ~0x10 is 0xEF (and, after promotion to int, nonzero, so if (~x) is true even for x = 1).

      Operator precedence is the other trap. From highest to lowest, the relevant groups are: ~ ! (unary), then * / %, + −, shifts << >>, comparisons < > <= >=, equality == !=, then &, ^, |, then &&, ||, and finally assignment. Because == binds more tightly than &, a missing pair of parentheses changes the meaning completely.

      Common mistake

      The classic GPIO bugs:

      • PORTB &= (1 << 3); keeps bit 3 and clears every other bit. To clear bit 3, the mask must be complemented: &= ~(1 << 3).
      • PORTB |= (0 << 3); does nothing: 0 shifted anywhere is 0. ORing cannot clear bits, and ANDing cannot set them.
      • if (PIND & (1 << 3) == 0) parses as PIND & ((1 << 3) == 0), which is PIND & 0: always false. Parenthesize the AND.
      • if ((PIND & (1 << 3)) == 1) is never true: the masked value is 0 or 8, not 0 or 1. Compare with 0 (!= 0 or == 0).
      • PORTB = (1 << 5); when you meant |= turns off every other output on the port.

      Copying a group of bits

      A common task is to copy a multi-bit field from one place to another, for example to put a 4-bit value onto four output pins without changing the other four. Because OR can only make 1s and AND can only make 0s, the destination field must be cleared first and then ORed with the new value, after the new value has been shifted into position and masked to that field.

      PORTB &= ~0x38;                    // clear PB5..PB3
PORTB |= (PORTC >> 2) & 0x38;      // bring in C7..C5 at positions 5..3

// The general pattern, for a field of width w starting at bit s:
//   mask = ((1 << w) - 1) << s;
//   dest = (dest & ~mask) | ((value << s) & mask);

      Doing it in two statements briefly exposes an intermediate value on the pins (the field cleared to 0). When that matters, compute the new value in a variable and write the register once.

      Reading a button

      A push button is normally wired between the pin and ground with the internal pull-up enabled, so it reads 1 when released and 0 when pressed (Module 13). Mechanical contacts do not close cleanly: they bounce, making and breaking contact several times over a few milliseconds.

      The simplest software debouncer waits a few milliseconds after a change and checks again, then waits for the release, so that one press is handled exactly once:

      #include <avr/io.h>
#include <util/delay.h>

int main(void)
{
    DDRB  |= (1 << PB5);                     // LED on PB5 (Uno D13): output
    DDRD  &= ~(1 << PD2);                    // button on PD2: input
    PORTD |= (1 << PD2);                     // with pull-up: reads 0 when pressed

    while (1) {
        if ((PIND & (1 << PD2)) == 0) {      // looks pressed
            _delay_ms(5);                    // let the bounce settle
            if ((PIND & (1 << PD2)) == 0) {  // still pressed: a real press
                PORTB ^= (1 << PB5);         // toggle the LED once
                while ((PIND & (1 << PD2)) == 0) { }   // wait for release
                _delay_ms(5);                // ignore release bounce
            }
        }
    }
}

      This works but blocks: while it waits for the release, the program can do nothing else. Module 24 restructures the same logic as a state machine that never blocks, and Module 25 replaces busy-wait delays with timers.

      Summary

      • On AVR, int is 16 bits; use uint8_t, int16_t, uint32_t and suffixes such as 1UL. Small types are promoted to int before arithmetic.
      • DDRx sets direction (1 = output), PORTx sets the output value or the pull-up, PINx reads the pins.
      • Set: |= mask. Clear: &= ~mask. Toggle: ^= mask. Test: (reg & mask) != 0.
      • Bitwise and logical operators differ; == binds tighter than &, so parenthesize masks.
      • Copy a field: clear the destination field, then OR in the shifted, masked source.
      • Buttons bounce; debounce with a short delay and confirmation, and act once per press.

      Practice problems

      Write statements that make PD7–PD4 outputs driving 0 and PD3–PD0 inputs with pull-ups, assuming nothing else uses port D.

      Solution

      DDRD = 0xF0; (upper nibble output) and PORTD = 0x0F; (outputs low, pull-ups on the lower nibble). If other code shares the port, use |= and &= with the same masks instead of plain assignment.

      What is the value of each expression for x = 0x5A? (a) x | 0x0F (b) x & 0x0F (c) x ^ 0xFF (d) x >> 4 (e) x && 0x0F

      Solution

      (a) 0x5F (b) 0x0A (c) 0xA5 (d) 0x05 (e) 1 (both operands nonzero).

      True or false: PORTD &= (3 << 5); clears bits 5 and 6 of PORTD.

      Solution

      False. 3 << 5 = 0x60, so the AND keeps bits 5 and 6 and clears the other six. Clearing bits 5 and 6 needs PORTD &= ~(3 << 5);.

      Why is if ((PINC & (1 << 4)) == 1) wrong, and what are two correct ways to write the test?

      Solution

      The masked value is 0 or 16 (0x10), never 1, so the condition is never true. Correct: if ((PINC & (1 << 4)) != 0) or if (PINC & (1 << 4)).

      Write one statement that toggles PB0 and PB1 together and one that sets PC2 and clears PC5 in a single write to PORTC.

      Solution

      PORTB ^= (1 << PB0) | (1 << PB1); and PORTC = (PORTC & ~(1 << PC5)) | (1 << PC2);.

      After uint8_t x = 200; x = x + 100;, what is x? What type and value does the expression x + 100 have before it is assigned?

      Solution

      x is promoted to int, so x + 100 is an int with value 300. Storing it in a uint8_t keeps the low 8 bits: x = 300 − 256 = 44.

      Extract bits 6–4 of PIND as a number from 0 to 7.

      Solution

      (PIND >> 4) & 0x07: shift the field down to bit 0, then mask off the bits above it.

      What does the condition if (PIND & 1 << 3 == 0) actually test? Rewrite it to test whether PD3 is 0.

      Solution

      Shift binds tighter than ==, which binds tighter than &: it is PIND & ((1 << 3) == 0) = PIND & 0 = 0, always false. Correct: if ((PIND & (1 << 3)) == 0).

      On AVR, what is wrong with uint32_t mask = 1 << 20; and how is it fixed? Why does the same line work on a desktop PC?

      Solution

      The constant 1 is a 16-bit int on AVR, and shifting it by 20 exceeds its width: undefined behavior, typically giving 0. Write 1UL << 20 (or (uint32_t)1 << 20). On a PC, int is 32 bits, so 1 << 20 fits; the bug only appears when the code is ported.

      Put the 4-bit value v (0–15) onto PD7–PD4 without disturbing PD3–PD0, in a single write to PORTD.

      Solution

      PORTD = (PORTD & 0x0F) | ((v << 4) & 0xF0);. The AND keeps the low nibble and clears the high one; the shifted, masked value supplies the new high nibble.

      Write an expression that is true when exactly one bit of the unsigned value x is 1, and explain why it works.

      Solution

      x != 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0. Subtracting 1 clears the lowest set bit and sets all bits below it; ANDing with x therefore clears the lowest set bit. If x had only one set bit, the result is 0. (This is the power-of-two test.)

      Count the 1 bits in a byte with a loop that runs once per set bit.

      Solution
      uint8_t popcount8(uint8_t x)
{
    uint8_t n = 0;
    while (x) {
        x &= x - 1;   // clear the lowest set bit
        n++;
    }
    return n;
}

      It iterates once per 1 bit (Kernighan's method), so 0x81 takes two iterations.

      Using the debouncing program in the text, what happens if the button is held down for 3 seconds? How many times does the LED toggle?

      Solution

      It toggles once: after confirming the press it waits in the release loop for the whole 3 seconds, then debounces the release. The cost is that nothing else runs during those 3 seconds.

      Show that x ^= y; y ^= x; x ^= y; swaps two variables without a temporary. When does it fail?

      Solution

      Let the originals be a and b. After the first line x = a ⊕ b. Then y = b ⊕ (a ⊕ b) = a. Then x = (a ⊕ b) ⊕ a = b. It fails if x and y are the same object (for example swapping a[i] with a[j] when i = j): the first line sets it to a ⊕ a = 0 and it stays 0. It is also no faster than using a temporary on modern compilers.

      Write a macro or inline function that writes a w-bit value into bits s to s + w − 1 of a register, and use it to set bits 5–3 of PORTB to the value 6.

      Solution
      static inline uint8_t set_field(uint8_t reg, uint8_t s, uint8_t w, uint8_t value)
{
    uint8_t mask = ((1u << w) - 1u) << s;
    return (uint8_t)((reg & ~mask) | ((value << s) & mask));
}

PORTB = set_field(PORTB, 3, 3, 6);   // bits 5..3 become 110

      The mask for s = 3, w = 3 is 0x38; 6 << 3 = 0x30, so bits 5 and 4 become 1 and bit 3 becomes 0.
