      Part VI: Embedded systems

      State machines in software

      Structuring embedded programs as state machines: the read-decide-act loop, enums and switch statements, non-blocking debouncing, time-based transitions, running several tasks at different rates without an operating system, and string-matching automata.

      Builds onMicrocontrollers and GPIO, State machinesPractice13 problems

      The button program in Module 23 works, but it cannot do anything else while it waits for the button to be released. Real embedded programs juggle several activities at once: blinking an indicator, scanning a keypad, updating a display, watching a sensor. Without an operating system, the standard way to do that is to write each activity as a state machine that does a small amount of work and returns, and to step all of them from one loop. The state machine model is exactly the one from Module 16; only the implementation changes from flip-flops to variables.

      State in software

      The state of a program is whatever it must remember to interpret its next inputs. A play/pause button needs one bit (playing or paused) to know what a press means. In hardware that bit lives in a flip-flop; in software it lives in a variable. A state diagram is drawn the same way in both cases, with Moore outputs inside states and Mealy outputs on transitions, written as condition / action.

      Every time step of a state machine, in hardware or software, does the same three things: read the inputs, use the current state and the inputs to determine the outputs and the next state, and move to the next state.

      The structure of the program

      • Keep the state in a variable, and name the states with an enum.
      • Run a while (1) loop with exactly one delay per iteration (or, better, wait for a timer tick; see Module 25). That makes every iteration one time step of known length.
      • Read each input once per iteration into a local variable, so that every decision in the iteration sees the same value.
      • Use a switch (or if-else chain) on the current state; inside each case, check the inputs, set the next state and perform the transition actions.
      • Never wait inside a case. A state that needs to wait simply stays in the same state on the next iteration.

      Example: debouncing without blocking

      Debouncing is a natural state machine: the program must remember whether the button is up or down and whether it has been stable long enough. Sampling once per millisecond and requiring five consecutive identical samples gives a 5 ms debounce that never blocks.

      enum state { RELEASED, MAYBE_DOWN, PRESSED, MAYBE_UP };

int main(void)
{
    enum state s = RELEASED;
    uint8_t count = 0;
    DDRB |= (1 << PB5);                            // LED output
    PORTD |= (1 << PD2);                           // button input with pull-up

    while (1) {
        uint8_t down = (PIND & (1 << PD2)) == 0;   // read the input once

        switch (s) {
        case RELEASED:
            if (down) { s = MAYBE_DOWN; count = 0; }
            break;
        case MAYBE_DOWN:
            if (!down)
                s = RELEASED;                      // it was a bounce
            else if (++count == 5) {
                s = PRESSED;
                PORTB ^= (1 << PB5);               // Mealy action: once per press
            }
            break;
        case PRESSED:
            if (!down) { s = MAYBE_UP; count = 0; }
            break;
        case MAYBE_UP:
            if (down)
                s = PRESSED;
            else if (++count == 5)
                s = RELEASED;
            break;
        }
        /* other tasks go here, each taking a short step */
        _delay_ms(1);                              // one time step
    }
}

      The distinction between Moore and Mealy outputs matters in software too. Code placed in a state's case runs on every iteration spent in that state (a Moore output, like keeping a motor on); code placed on a transition runs once (a Mealy action, like counting a press). Toggling the LED inside case PRESSED would toggle it every millisecond while the button is held.

      Time-based transitions

      With a fixed time step, time is measured by counting iterations. A traffic light with a 1-second loop that must stay green for 30 s, yellow for 5 s and red for 35 s keeps a counter, resets it on every transition, and leaves each state when the counter reaches that state's duration. Transitions that always happen when time runs out are drawn with the label "1" (unconditional) or with the timer condition.

      enum light { GREEN, YELLOW, RED };
enum light s = GREEN;
uint8_t t = 0;                       // seconds spent in the current state

while (1) {
    t++;
    switch (s) {
    case GREEN:  if (t == 30) { s = YELLOW; t = 0; } break;
    case YELLOW: if (t == 5)  { s = RED;    t = 0; } break;
    case RED:    if (t == 35) { s = GREEN;  t = 0; } break;
    }
    set_lamps(s);                    // Moore outputs: a function of the state only
    _delay_ms(1000);
}

      Several tasks at different rates

      A program that must blink an LED every 250 ms and also scan buttons every 100 ms cannot simply delay 250 ms or 100 ms. Instead, choose a base tick that divides every task's period, the greatest common divisor: GCD(250, 100) = 50 ms. Each task keeps its own counter and runs every k ticks.

      uint8_t blink_ticks = 0, scan_ticks = 0;
while (1) {
    if (++blink_ticks == 5) { blink_ticks = 0; PORTD ^= (1 << PD7); }   // every 250 ms
    if (++scan_ticks == 2)  { scan_ticks = 0;  scan_buttons(); }        // every 100 ms
    _delay_ms(50);                                                      // the base tick
}

      Key idea

      This structure, often called a superloop with cooperative multitasking, is how a great deal of firmware is written. Its rule is that no task may block: each one does a little work and returns, so that every task is serviced every tick. A task that needs to wait for something keeps a state that says so and checks again next tick. Getting stuck in a long loop or a long delay inside one task (tunnel vision) starves all the others.

      The delay-based tick has a weakness: each iteration takes the delay plus however long the tasks ran, so the timing drifts as the program grows. Driving the loop from a hardware timer interrupt fixes that (Module 25).

      State machines for recognizing strings

      Searching a stream of characters for a pattern is another state machine problem, the software twin of the hardware sequence detectors in Module 16. A naive search compares the pattern at every starting position, re-reading characters, which costs O(N·T) for text length N and pattern length T. A finite automaton whose state is "how many characters of the pattern currently match" reads each character exactly once, O(N), using the same longest-suffix-that-is-a-prefix rule to decide where to go on a mismatch (this is the Knuth–Morris–Pratt algorithm). The Aho–Corasick algorithm extends the idea to many patterns at once, as needed for searching text for a set of keywords.

      Summary

      • State is what must be remembered; in software it is a variable, usually an enum.
      • Loop structure: read inputs once, switch on the state to choose outputs and the next state, then wait one tick.
      • Code in a state runs every tick (Moore); code on a transition runs once (Mealy).
      • Count ticks for time-based transitions; reset the count on every transition.
      • Multiple rates: base tick = GCD of the periods, one counter per task; never block.
      • Pattern matching with an automaton reads each input once: O(N) instead of O(N·T).

      Practice problems

      How many states does the controller of a single play/pause button need, and what is the output in each?

      Solution

      Two: PAUSED (output: stopped) and PLAYING (output: playing). Each debounced press moves to the other state.

      Tasks must run every 250 ms and every 100 ms. What base tick should the loop use, and after how many ticks does the combined pattern repeat?

      Solution

      GCD(250, 100) = 50 ms. The pattern repeats after LCM(250, 100) = 500 ms = 10 ticks.

      Why should a software state machine read each input once per iteration into a variable instead of reading the port register in every if?

      Solution

      The pin can change between two reads, so different tests in the same iteration could see different values: for example, one branch sees "pressed" and moves to a new state while another sees "released" and performs a release action. Reading once makes the iteration a consistent snapshot, exactly as a clocked hardware machine samples its inputs at one edge.

      An LED must blink at 2 Hz (one full on-off cycle every 500 ms). How often must the program toggle it, and what statement does the toggle?

      Solution

      Toggle every 250 ms. For an LED on PD7: PORTD ^= (1 << PD7);.

      The traffic light loop runs once per second. How many iterations long is one complete cycle, and what happens if each iteration's task code takes 20 ms in addition to the 1-second delay?

      Solution

      30 + 5 + 35 = 70 iterations. With 20 ms of work per iteration each cycle takes 70 × 1.02 = 71.4 s instead of 70 s: the timing drifts by 2% and keeps drifting. A timer-driven tick removes the error.

      Write the software state machine for a detector whose output is 1 after two or more consecutive 1s on an input sampled once per tick (states S0, S1, S2 as in Module 16).

      Solution
      enum st { S0, S1, S2 };
enum st s = S0;
while (1) {
    uint8_t x = read_input();
    switch (s) {
    case S0: s = x ? S1 : S0; break;
    case S1: s = x ? S2 : S0; break;
    case S2: s = x ? S2 : S0; break;
    }
    write_output(s == S2);      // Moore output
    wait_tick();
}

      Equivalently the state can be a saturating count of consecutive 1s: count = x ? min(count + 1, 2) : 0; with output count == 2; the count variable is the state.

      Tasks must run every 30 ms and every 45 ms. Give the base tick, the tick counts for each task, and the length of the repeating schedule.

      Solution

      GCD(30, 45) = 15 ms. Task A every 2 ticks, task B every 3 ticks. LCM(30, 45) = 90 ms = 6 ticks.

      The debouncer samples once per millisecond. The input (1 = down) reads 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 after starting in RELEASED. On which sample is the press recognized?

      Solution

      Sample 1 (down): → MAYBE_DOWN, count 0. Sample 2 (up): → RELEASED (a bounce). Sample 3 (down): → MAYBE_DOWN, count 0. Samples 4–8 (down) increment count to 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; at sample 8 count reaches 5 and the machine enters PRESSED, toggling the LED once.

      In the washing machine, the rinse counter N is decremented "on the transition from DRAIN to FILL". What goes wrong if a programmer instead writes N-- inside case DRAIN:?

      Solution

      Code inside a state runs on every iteration spent in that state. Draining takes many ticks, so N would be decremented once per tick rather than once per cycle, running out (or wrapping around, if N is unsigned) almost immediately. Actions that must happen once belong on transitions.

      What is wrong with this task in a superloop, and how would you restructure it?

      void beep_task(void) {
    if (alarm) {
        for (int k = 0; k < 500; k++) { PORTB ^= (1 << PB1); _delay_us(500); }
    }
}
      Solution

      The loop blocks for 500 × 0.5 ms = 250 ms, during which no other task runs (buttons are missed, displays freeze). Restructure as a state machine: keep a counter of remaining half-periods; on each tick (or in a timer interrupt at 2 kHz) toggle the pin once and decrement, and stop when the count reaches 0. Better still, generate the tone with a hardware timer in PWM or CTC toggle mode (Module 25).

      Design a thermostat state machine with states OFF, HEAT and COOL, a temperature input T and a setpoint S. Heating starts below S − 1 and stops at S; cooling starts above S + 1 and stops at S. Give the transitions and explain the role of the 1-degree band.

      Solution

      OFF → HEAT when T < S − 1; OFF → COOL when T > S + 1; otherwise stay OFF. HEAT → OFF when T ≥ S; else stay. COOL → OFF when T ≤ S; else stay. The gap between the start and stop thresholds is hysteresis: without it, measurement noise around S would switch the heater on and off rapidly, wearing out relays and wasting energy. The state remembers which way the system was heading, which a function of T alone cannot do.

      Build the string-matching automaton for the pattern "abab" over the alphabet {a, b}: states 0–4 (characters matched), with state 4 meaning a match. Give the transitions, assuming overlapping matches are reported.

      Solution

      0: a → 1, b → 0. 1 ("a"): a → 1, b → 2. 2 ("ab"): a → 3, b → 0. 3 ("aba"): a → 1, b → 4 (match). 4 ("abab"): a → 3 (the text ends in "aba"), b → 0. Each character causes exactly one transition, so a text of N characters is scanned in O(N), whereas checking every starting position separately can take O(N·T).

      A program uses the 50 ms superloop. A new display task takes 70 ms to redraw the screen. What happens to the other tasks, and how can the display task be made to fit?

      Solution

      Every iteration in which the display runs takes over 120 ms instead of 50, so the 250 ms and 100 ms tasks run late and timing becomes irregular. Split the redraw into pieces that each fit comfortably in a tick (for example, one line of the display per tick, keeping the next line number as the task's state), or move it to a lower-priority background slot that runs only with leftover time. Measuring each task's worst-case execution time is part of designing such a system.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Part VI: Embedded systems

      Interrupts and timers

      Responding to events without polling: how an interrupt is taken, vectors and enables on the AVR, pin-change interrupts, hardware timers in CTC and PWM modes, the flag idiom, why shared variables must be volatile, and how to avoid races with critical sections.

      Builds onSoftware state machinesToolsAVR timer calculatorPractice13 problems

      So far the processor has found out about events by checking for them: reading a button pin every loop iteration, or spinning in a delay loop to measure time. Checking is called polling, and it has two costs: the processor spends time checking things that have not happened, and anything that happens between checks waits. I/O events occur on a scale of milliseconds while instructions take tens of nanoseconds, so a processor that polls spends almost all its time asking "anything yet?". Interrupts reverse the responsibility: the device signals the processor when something happens, and the processor stops what it is doing just long enough to deal with it.

      What happens when an interrupt occurs

      An interrupt is one kind of exception: an event that diverts the processor from the normal flow of the program. Exceptions include hardware interrupts from devices (a pin changed, a timer expired, a byte arrived), error conditions detected by the processor itself (an illegal instruction, an invalid address, division by zero on processors that trap it), and deliberate traps such as system calls into an operating system. Hardware detects the event; software, in an interrupt service routine (ISR), handles it.

      1. The device sets an interrupt flag in one of its registers.
      2. After finishing the current instruction (the fourth step of the instruction cycle in Module 18), the processor checks for enabled, pending interrupts.
      3. If one is pending, it saves the return address on the stack, disables further interrupts by clearing the global interrupt-enable bit, and jumps to the address stored for that interrupt in the vector table.
      4. The ISR runs. Its reti (return from interrupt) instruction restores the program counter and re-enables interrupts, and the interrupted program continues exactly where it left off.

      An ISR looks like a function but is not called by the program. It runs asynchronously, between any two instructions of the main code; it takes no arguments and returns no value. It communicates with the rest of the program only through global variables and hardware registers.

      Interrupts on the AVR

      The ATmega328P has over twenty interrupt sources, each with its own vector: external interrupts INT0 and INT1; pin-change interrupts for each port (PCINT0 for port B, PCINT1 for C, PCINT2 for D); timer compare-match and overflow interrupts; USART receive-complete and transmit interrupts; SPI and TWI transfer complete; ADC conversion complete; and others. In avr-gcc an ISR is written with the ISR() macro and the vector's name, such as ISR(TIMER1_COMPA_vect) or ISR(PCINT2_vect).

      An interrupt is taken only when three things are true:

      • its local enable bit is set in the peripheral's interrupt mask register (for example OCIE1A in TIMSK1);
      • the global interrupt enable (the I bit in the status register) is set, with sei(); cli() clears it;
      • the event has occurred and set the interrupt flag (for example OCF1A in TIFR1). The flag is cleared automatically when the ISR starts.

      Common mistake

      Enabling an interrupt without defining its ISR sends the processor to a default handler, which on the AVR jumps to the reset vector: the program appears to restart at random. Every enabled interrupt needs an ISR.

      A pin-change interrupt fires when any enabled pin of its port changes in either direction. It does not say which pin changed or which way, so the ISR reads the PIN register and compares it with the previous value:

      #include <avr/io.h>
#include <avr/interrupt.h>

volatile uint8_t button_changed = 0;

ISR(PCINT2_vect)                    // any enabled pin on port D changed
{
    button_changed = 1;             // just record the event; keep the ISR short
}

int main(void)
{
    PORTD  |= (1 << PD2);           // button input with pull-up
    PCMSK2 |= (1 << PCINT18);       // PD2 is pin-change source PCINT18
    PCICR  |= (1 << PCIE2);         // enable pin-change interrupts for port D
    sei();                          // global enable

    while (1) {
        if (button_changed) {
            button_changed = 0;
            /* read PIND, debounce, act */
        }
    }
}

      Hardware timers

      A timer is a counter (TCNT) clocked by the system clock divided by a prescaler N (1, 8, 64, 256 or 1024 on the AVR). It counts at a precisely known rate, independent of what the program is doing, which makes it far more accurate than counting loop iterations: a delay-based loop runs late by however long its other work took, while a timer does not drift.

      In CTC (clear timer on compare) mode, the counter is compared with an output-compare register (OCR) on every count; on a match it sets the compare flag, optionally requests an interrupt, and resets to zero. The result is a periodic event with

      period = (OCR + 1) × N / fclk ⇒ OCR = fclk × period / N − 1

      Worked example

      A quarter-second tick

      With fclk = 16 MHz and prescaler N = 256, the timer counts at 62.5 kHz (16 μs per count). A 0.25 s period needs 0.25 × 62,500 = 15,625 counts, so OCR1A = 15,624. (Many examples use 15,625, which gives 0.250016 s, an error of 0.006%.) The 16-bit Timer1 is needed because the count exceeds 255.

      void timer1_init(void)
{
    TCCR1B |= (1 << WGM12);         // CTC mode, TOP = OCR1A
    OCR1A   = 15624;                // 0.25 s at 16 MHz / 256
    TIMSK1 |= (1 << OCIE1A);        // enable the compare-match A interrupt
    TCCR1B |= (1 << CS12);          // prescaler 256: this starts the timer
}

volatile uint8_t tick = 0;
ISR(TIMER1_COMPA_vect) { tick = 1; }

      The prescaler is chosen as the smallest one for which OCR fits in the timer's width, which gives the finest resolution.

      Driving the superloop of Module 24 from a timer replaces _delay_ms() with "wait until the tick flag is set, then clear it". Each iteration then starts exactly one period after the previous one, however long the tasks took, as long as they finish within the period.

      PWM with timers

      Timers also generate waveforms directly on output pins with no software involvement. In fast PWM mode the counter ramps from 0 to TOP and wraps; the output pin is set at the start of each period and cleared when the counter passes the compare value, so the duty cycle is set by the compare register:

      • 8-bit fast PWM: fPWM = fclk/(N × 256), duty = (OCR + 1)/256. With 16 MHz and N = 64, fPWM ≈ 977 Hz.
      • Phase-correct PWM counts up and then down, halving the frequency (fclk/(N × 510)) but producing pulses centered in each period, which motor drivers prefer.
      • A hobby servo wants a 50 Hz frame with a 1 to 2 ms pulse. Timer1 with TOP set by ICR1 provides it: with N = 8 the timer counts at 2 MHz, so TOP = 2 MHz/50 − 1 = 39,999 and a 1.5 ms pulse needs OCR1A = 2999.

      PWM controls LED brightness, motor speed and heater power, and with a low-pass filter becomes a simple DAC (Module 11).

      Writing correct ISRs

      Interrupts introduce concurrency: the main program and the ISR share variables and hardware, and the ISR can run between any two instructions. Three rules prevent most bugs.

      Keep ISRs short. While an AVR ISR runs, other interrupts are disabled and wait. Long ISRs delay other events and can lose them (a second event of the same kind only sets a flag that is already set). The usual idiom is for the ISR to do only what must happen immediately, set a flag or store a value, and let the main loop do the rest. Never write to a slow display or wait inside an ISR.

      Declare shared variables volatile. Within one function, the compiler may keep a variable in a register and assume it cannot change behind its back. In

      uint8_t flag = 0;            // missing volatile
ISR(TIMER1_COMPA_vect) { flag = 1; }
...
while (flag == 0) { }        //! may compile to an infinite loop

      the compiler can load flag once, see that nothing in the loop changes it, and loop forever. volatile forces a fresh memory access every time the variable is read or written. It is required for every global shared between an ISR and other code (and for memory-mapped registers, which the AVR headers already declare volatile).

      Protect multi-step accesses. An operation that takes several instructions can be interrupted in the middle. On an 8-bit processor, even reading a 16-bit variable takes two instructions. If an ISR increments a 16-bit counter from 0x00FF to 0x0100 between the main program's two byte reads, the main program can read the low byte 0xFF and then the new high byte 0x01, getting 0x01FF, a value the counter never held. Read-modify-write sequences such as x++ or PORTB |= 0x01 (load, OR, store) have the same problem when the ISR modifies the same variable or register. The fix is a critical section that disables interrupts for the few instructions involved:

      #include <util/atomic.h>

volatile uint16_t ticks;            // incremented by a timer ISR

uint16_t read_ticks(void)
{
    uint16_t copy;
    ATOMIC_BLOCK(ATOMIC_RESTORESTATE) {   // disables interrupts, restores the previous state afterwards
        copy = ticks;
    }
    return copy;
}

      ATOMIC_RESTORESTATE restores the interrupt-enable bit to what it was, rather than blindly re-enabling interrupts, so the block is safe even if called from code that already had interrupts disabled. Critical sections must be short, because they add to the latency of every interrupt.

      Latency, priority and the watchdog

      Interrupt latency, the time from the event to the first instruction of the ISR, is a few cycles plus the remainder of the current instruction plus any time interrupts are disabled, by another ISR or a critical section. When several interrupts are pending, the AVR serves them in a fixed priority order given by the vector table and does not nest ISRs unless the programmer re-enables interrupts inside one. Larger microcontrollers have interrupt controllers with programmable priorities and nesting, so an urgent interrupt can preempt a less urgent ISR.

      A watchdog timer is a timer that resets the microcontroller if it ever expires. The program restarts it periodically ("kicks the dog") from its main loop; if a bug or a glitch hangs the program, the kicks stop and the watchdog forces a reset instead of leaving the system stuck.

      Summary

      • Polling checks repeatedly; interrupts let the device notify the processor. ISRs run asynchronously, between any two instructions.
      • Taking an interrupt: finish the instruction, save the PC, disable interrupts, jump through the vector table; reti returns and re-enables.
      • AVR: local enable + global I bit (sei/cli) + flag. Every enabled interrupt needs an ISR.
      • Timers count prescaled clock cycles. CTC: period = (OCR + 1)·N/fclk. Fast PWM: f = fclk/(N·256), duty from OCR.
      • Keep ISRs short (set a flag); declare shared globals volatile; protect multi-byte and read-modify-write accesses with critical sections.

      Practice problems

      List the three conditions that must all hold for the Timer1 compare-match A interrupt to be taken.

      Solution

      The local enable OCIE1A in TIMSK1 is set; the global enable (I bit) is set with sei(); and the compare match has occurred, setting the flag OCF1A.

      With a 16 MHz clock and a prescaler of 64, how fast does a timer count, and how long is one count?

      Solution

      16 MHz/64 = 250 kHz, so one count is 4 μs.

      What OCR value gives a 1 ms CTC period at 16 MHz with prescaler 64? Does it fit in an 8-bit timer?

      Solution

      OCR = 16 × 106 × 0.001/64 − 1 = 250 − 1 = 249, which fits in 8 bits (≤ 255), so Timer0 or Timer2 can generate it.

      What is the longest CTC period Timer1 (16 bits) can produce at 16 MHz, and with which prescaler?

      Solution

      Prescaler 1024 and OCR = 65,535: 65,536 × 1024/16 × 106 = 4.19 s. Longer intervals need a software counter of timer ticks.

      Why does a delay-based superloop drift over time while a timer-driven one does not?

      Solution

      A delay loop's iteration time is the delay plus the time the tasks take, and that varies; the errors accumulate. A timer counts the clock continuously in hardware, and the ISR marks each period's start independently of how long the software took (provided the tasks finish within the period).

      Explain why the loop while (flag == 0) { } can hang forever if flag is set by an ISR but not declared volatile, and why volatile fixes it.

      Solution

      The compiler sees no assignment to flag inside the loop or the function, so it may load it into a register once and test that register forever, or even replace the loop with an infinite loop. The ISR's write to memory is never re-read. volatile tells the compiler the value can change outside the visible code, so every read in the loop is a real memory load.

      A timer ISR increments volatile uint16_t ticks. The main program reads it with a simple assignment while the value changes from 0x00FF to 0x0100. Which wrong value can it see, and how do you prevent it?

      Solution

      The 8-bit AVR reads the low byte and the high byte with separate instructions. If it reads the low byte (0xFF), then the ISR increments the counter, then it reads the high byte (0x01), the result is 0x01FF = 511, although the counter went from 255 to 256. Read it inside ATOMIC_BLOCK(ATOMIC_RESTORESTATE) (or between cli() and the previous state's restoration) so the ISR cannot run between the two byte reads.

      Configure 8-bit fast PWM at 16 MHz with prescaler 8. What is the PWM frequency, and what OCR value gives a 25% duty cycle?

      Solution

      f = 16 × 106/(8 × 256) = 7812.5 Hz. Duty = (OCR + 1)/256 = 0.25 → OCR = 63.

      Set up Timer1 for a hobby servo: a 50 Hz frame with prescaler 8 at 16 MHz. What TOP value goes in ICR1, and what OCR1A values give 1.0 ms, 1.5 ms and 2.0 ms pulses?

      Solution

      The timer counts at 2 MHz (0.5 μs). TOP = 2 × 106/50 − 1 = 39,999. Pulses: 1.0 ms = 2000 counts → OCR1A = 1999; 1.5 ms → 2999; 2.0 ms → 3999.

      A pin-change interrupt is enabled for PD2 and PD3. Inside the ISR, how can the program determine which pin changed and in which direction?

      Solution

      Keep the previous value of PIND in a static (or global) variable. In the ISR: uint8_t now = PIND; uint8_t changed = now ^ prev; prev = now;. A 1 in bit 2 or 3 of changed marks a pin that changed; that bit of now gives its new level (1 = rose, 0 = fell).

      The main program executes PORTB |= 0x01; (compiled as load, OR, store) while a timer ISR toggles bit 7 of PORTB. Describe the race, and give two fixes.

      Solution

      If the ISR runs after the main program loads PORTB but before it stores the result, the ISR's change to bit 7 is overwritten by the stale copy: the toggle is lost. Fixes: wrap the main program's read-modify-write in a critical section (disable interrupts briefly); or use operations that are atomic in hardware, such as single-bit sbi/cbi on low I/O registers or writing 1 to the PIN register to toggle one bit; or arrange for only one context to write that register.

      A UART at 115,200 baud receives 10-bit frames back to back. How much time is there between received bytes, how many 16 MHz clock cycles is that, and what does it imply for the receive ISR and for critical sections elsewhere?

      Solution

      115,200/10 = 11,520 bytes/s → 86.8 μs per byte = about 1389 cycles. The hardware receive buffer holds very little, so the ISR must read each byte before the next one arrives; the ISR itself should take tens of cycles, and no other ISR or critical section may block interrupts for anything close to 1389 cycles, or bytes are lost (an overrun).

      Why should an ISR not write to an LCD, and how should the program be structured instead?

      Solution

      Writing to the display takes tens of microseconds to milliseconds per character, and on the AVR other interrupts are blocked while the ISR runs, so timer ticks, received bytes and button events would be delayed or lost. The display code may also be interrupted halfway through a command by the main program's own display code, corrupting the protocol. The ISR should store the new value and set a flag; the main loop checks the flag and updates the display.

      Part VI: Embedded systems

      Talking to devices: displays and serial buses

      How a microcontroller exchanges data with other chips: reading a datasheet, driving a character LCD over a 4-bit parallel interface with correct strobe timing, and the three standard serial buses (UART, SPI and I2C), with framing, timing, addressing and trade-offs.

      Builds onInterrupts and timers, InterfacingPractice13 problems

      A microcontroller is useful only through the devices around it: displays, sensors, memories, radios and other processors. Each device defines a protocol, a precise description of which signals change, in what order and with what timing. This module works through a parallel interface in detail and then the three serial buses that connect most chips on a board.

      Reading a datasheet

      Every interfacing task starts with the device's datasheet. For each signal, it answers five questions: what voltage levels are valid (Module 13); how much current the pin needs or can supply; which polarity is active (a bar or a trailing # or N in a signal name, as in CS′, means active-low); what timing is required (minimum pulse widths, setup and hold times relative to a clock or strobe, delays before the next operation); and what sequence of operations the device expects, including its power-up initialization. Code that works on the bench but ignores a timing requirement tends to fail when the compiler, the clock speed or the temperature changes.

      A character LCD on a parallel interface

      The common 16 × 2 character LCD module contains a controller (HD44780 or compatible) with an internal command register and data register. It can be connected with an 8-bit or a 4-bit data bus; the 4-bit mode saves pins by sending each byte as two nibbles.

      • RS (register select) chooses the destination: 0 for a command (clear the screen, move the cursor), 1 for character data to display.
      • E (enable) is a strobe: the controller latches the data lines when E goes from 1 back to 0. A strobe is needed because the controller cannot tell a new value from the old one by watching the data lines. Sending the byte 0x77 in 4-bit mode puts the nibble 0111 on the bus twice in a row; without a strobe, the second nibble would be indistinguishable from no transfer at all.
      • Each byte goes as the upper nibble first, then the lower nibble, each latched by its own E pulse, followed by a delay while the controller executes the command (tens of microseconds, or about 1.5 ms for clear-screen).

      Commands are single bytes. 0x01 clears the display; 0x02 returns the cursor home; 0x0C turns the display on (0x0F also shows a blinking cursor); and 0x80 + address moves the cursor. Row 0 starts at address 0x00 and row 1 at 0x40, so position (row, column) is reached with the command 0x80 + column for row 0 and 0xC0 + column for row 1. The addresses between the rows are unused because the controller supports wider displays, and nothing wraps automatically: text written past column 15 goes to addresses that are not visible.

      The software is naturally layered:

      // Lowest layer: put the upper 4 bits of x on PD7..PD4 and pulse E (PB1)
static void lcd_writenibble(uint8_t x)
{
    PORTD = (PORTD & 0x0F) | (x & 0xF0);  // copy the nibble, keep PD3..PD0
    PORTB |= (1 << PB1);                  // E = 1
    PORTB |= (1 << PB1);                  // repeated to stretch the pulse (see below)
    PORTB &= ~(1 << PB1);                 // E = 0: the LCD latches the nibble
}

static void lcd_writebyte(uint8_t b, uint8_t rs)
{
    if (rs) PORTB |= (1 << PB0); else PORTB &= ~(1 << PB0);
    lcd_writenibble(b);                   // upper nibble
    lcd_writenibble(b << 4);              // lower nibble
    _delay_us(40);                        // most commands finish within about 40 us
}

void lcd_writecommand(uint8_t c) { lcd_writebyte(c, 0); }
void lcd_writedata(char ch)      { lcd_writebyte((uint8_t)ch, 1); }
void lcd_moveto(uint8_t row, uint8_t col) { lcd_writecommand((row ? 0xC0 : 0x80) + col); }
void lcd_stringout(const char *s) { while (*s) lcd_writedata(*s++); }

      Worked example

      When the code is too fast

      The controller's datasheet requires E to stay high for at least 230 ns. At 16 MHz one clock cycle is 62.5 ns, and the set-bit and clear-bit instructions the compiler generates for PORTB |= … and PORTB &= ~… take 2 cycles each. Setting E and immediately clearing it gives a pulse of only 2 × 62.5 = 125 ns, too short, so the display ignores some nibbles. Repeating the set instruction stretches the pulse to 250 ns; inserting two nop instructions (62.5 ns each) works too; _delay_us(1) also works but wastes time. The general lesson: when software generates a signal for hardware, its timing is set by instruction counts and must be checked against the datasheet.

      Serial communication

      Parallel buses need one wire per bit, which is impractical between boards and expensive in pins. Serial interfaces send one bit at a time over very few wires. They fall into two families. Synchronous interfaces send a clock along with the data, so the receiver knows exactly when to sample (SPI, I2C). Asynchronous interfaces send no clock; both sides agree on a bit rate in advance and the receiver synchronizes on each frame (the UART). High-speed links such as USB and PCIe embed the clock in the data stream and recover it at the receiver.

      UART: asynchronous serial

      A UART (universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter) sends each byte as a frame on a line that idles high: a start bit (0), the data bits least significant first, an optional parity bit, and one or two stop bits (1). The common "8N1" format has 8 data bits, no parity and 1 stop bit, 10 bits per byte.

      The receiver detects the start bit's falling edge and then samples each bit near its middle, typically using a clock 16 times the bit rate to locate the middles precisely. Because there is no shared clock, the two sides' bit rates must match closely: the timing error accumulates across the frame, and by the stop bit it must still be under half a bit. That allows roughly 4 to 5% of total mismatch in theory and about 2% per side in practice.

      The AVR USART derives its bit rate from the system clock: UBRR = fclk/(16 × baud) − 1. At 16 MHz and 9600 baud, UBRR = 103.2, rounded to 103, which gives 9615 baud, an error of 0.16%. Each side needs TX, RX and a common ground; RS-232 ports use inverted ±12 V levels and need a level converter, while USB-to-serial adapters present a UART at logic levels.

      SPI: a fast synchronous bus

      The Serial Peripheral Interface connects one controller to one or more peripherals with four signals: SCK (clock from the controller), MOSI (data from controller to peripheral), MISO (data from peripheral to controller) and one active-low select (SS′ or CS′) per peripheral.

      Both sides contain a shift register. On each clock cycle the controller shifts one bit out on MOSI while the peripheral shifts one bit out on MISO, so after 8 clocks the two registers have exchanged their contents: SPI is inherently full duplex, and to read a byte the controller must send one (often a dummy). The clock polarity (CPOL) and phase (CPHA) settings, four "modes" in all, define which clock edge launches data and which samples it, and both sides must agree.

      SPI has no addressing, acknowledgment or flow control, which keeps it simple and fast (tens of MHz): it is the usual choice for flash memories, displays, SD cards and fast ADCs and DACs.

      I2C: a two-wire addressed bus

      I2C (inter-integrated circuit, also called TWI on AVR) needs only two wires, SDA (data) and SCL (clock), shared by all devices. Both are open-drain lines with pull-up resistors (Module 13), so any device can pull a line low and none ever drives it high, which makes sharing safe.

      • A transfer begins with a START condition (SDA falls while SCL is high) and ends with a STOP (SDA rises while SCL is high). Otherwise SDA changes only while SCL is low and is sampled while SCL is high.
      • The first byte after START is a 7-bit address plus a read/write bit. The addressed device acknowledges by pulling SDA low during a ninth clock (ACK); if nobody responds the line stays high (NACK).
      • Data bytes follow, each acknowledged by the receiver. Speeds are 100 kHz (standard), 400 kHz (fast) and 1 MHz (fast-plus).
      • A slow device can hold SCL low to pause the controller (clock stretching), and several controllers can share the bus, because a controller that tries to send a 1 but sees a 0 knows it has lost arbitration.

      The rising edges are slow, set by the pull-up resistors and the bus capacitance, which is what limits I2C's speed and the number of devices on a bus.

      Choosing an interface

      PropertyUARTSPII2C
      Wires (besides ground)2 (TX, RX)3 + one select per device2 (SDA, SCL)
      Clocknone: agreed bit ratefrom the controllerfrom the controller
      Typical speed9.6 kbit/s to a few Mbit/s1 to 50+ Mbit/s0.1, 0.4 or 1 Mbit/s
      Devicespoint to pointone controller, several selected peripheralsup to ~112 addressed devices
      Acknowledgmentno (optional parity)noyes, per byte
      Typical usesconsoles, GPS, Bluetooth modules, debuggingflash, SD cards, displays, fast converterssensors, EEPROMs, configuration registers

      Summary

      • Datasheets specify voltage, current, polarity, timing and sequence; check generated timing against them.
      • LCD 4-bit interface: RS selects command or data; each nibble is latched by an E strobe; row 0 at 0x80 + column, row 1 at 0xC0 + column.
      • UART: start bit, data LSB first, stop bit; 8N1 is 10 bits per byte; UBRR = f/(16·baud) − 1; rates must match within a few percent.
      • SPI: SCK, MOSI, MISO, SS′; full-duplex shift-register exchange; four clock modes; fast and simple.
      • I2C: open-drain SDA and SCL with pull-ups; START, address + R/W, ACK, data, STOP; slower but only two wires for many devices.

      Practice problems

      Which LCD command moves the cursor to row 1, column 5? To row 0, column 0?

      Solution

      Row 1: 0xC0 + 5 = 0xC5. Row 0, column 0: 0x80.

      How many signal wires (not counting ground) does each bus need to connect a microcontroller to three peripherals: UART, SPI, I2C?

      Solution

      UART is point to point, so three separate links of 2 wires each (or more UARTs). SPI: SCK, MOSI, MISO plus three selects: 6. I2C: 2, shared by all three.

      At 9600 baud in 8N1 format, how long does one byte take, and how many bytes per second can be sent?

      Solution

      10 bits/9600 bit/s = 1.04 ms per byte; 960 bytes/s.

      List the bits on the TX line, in time order, when a UART sends the character 'K' (0x4B) in 8N1 format.

      Solution

      0x4B = 0100 1011. Start 0, then data LSB first 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, then stop 1.

      Compute UBRR for 115,200 baud with a 16 MHz clock (normal speed mode), the actual baud rate, and the error.

      Solution

      UBRR = 16 × 106/(16 × 115,200) − 1 = 7.68 → 8. Actual: 16 × 106/(16 × 9) = 111,111 baud, an error of −3.5%, too large to be reliable. AVR's double-speed mode (divisor 8) gives UBRR = 16 and 117,647 baud (+2.1%), and many designs use a 14.7456 MHz crystal so that standard baud rates divide exactly.

      Why does the LCD need an E strobe at all, instead of latching whenever the data lines change? Use the byte 0x77 in 4-bit mode as the example.

      Solution

      In 4-bit mode 0x77 is sent as the nibble 0111 twice. The second nibble leaves the data lines unchanged, so a device watching for changes would see only one nibble and lose synchronization. The same happens whenever the next value equals the current one. A separate strobe marks each transfer explicitly, independent of the data.

      The E pulse must be at least 230 ns. Each set or clear instruction takes 2 cycles at 16 MHz. How long is the pulse produced by set-then-clear, and how many nop instructions (1 cycle each) must be inserted?

      Solution

      Set-then-clear: 125 ns. Missing: 230 − 125 = 105 ns, which needs 2 cycles of 62.5 ns: 2 nops, giving 250 ns. Repeating the 2-cycle set instruction once achieves the same.

      An SPI controller sends 0xA5 to a peripheral whose shift register holds 0x3C. After 8 clock cycles, what does each side hold?

      Solution

      The two 8-bit shift registers form a ring and have exchanged contents: the controller holds 0x3C and the peripheral holds 0xA5.

      An I2C temperature sensor has 7-bit address 0x48. What is the first byte after START for a write, and for a read? Who drives SDA during the ACK bit of that byte?

      Solution

      The address is shifted left one place and the R/W bit appended: write 0x90, read 0x91. The sensor (the receiver of the address byte) pulls SDA low during the ninth clock to acknowledge.

      Estimate the maximum payload throughput of I2C at 400 kHz and of SPI at 10 MHz, ignoring software overhead.

      Solution

      I2C sends 9 clocks per byte (8 data + ACK): at most 400,000/9 ≈ 44 KB/s, less after START, address and STOP. SPI sends 8 clocks per byte: 10 × 106/8 = 1.25 MB/s.

      A UART receiver resynchronizes on the start bit's falling edge and samples each bit at its middle. Estimate the largest total baud-rate mismatch between transmitter and receiver that still samples the stop bit correctly in an 8N1 frame.

      Solution

      The stop bit's middle is 9.5 bit periods after the start edge. The accumulated timing error there must stay below half a bit: 9.5 × e < 0.5 → e < 5.3% total mismatch. Edge detection uncertainty and the need for margin for slow edges and noise reduce the practical budget to about 2% per side.

      An NTC thermistor (10 kΩ at 25 °C) is the lower resistor of a divider with a fixed 10 kΩ resistor to 5 V, read by a 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference. Give the reading at 25 °C and the formula for the thermistor resistance from a reading A. What does a reading of 682 mean?

      Solution

      At 25 °C the divider gives 2.5 V: A ≈ 512. In general V = 5·Rt/(Rt + 10k) and A = 1024·V/5, so Rt = 10 kΩ × A/(1024 − A). For A = 682: 10k × 682/342 ≈ 19.9 kΩ, about twice the 25 °C value, meaning the sensor is cold: NTC resistance rises as temperature falls, and for a typical part (β ≈ 3950 K) this is about 10 °C. A table or the β equation converts resistance to temperature.

      Choose an interface for each: (a) eight temperature sensors read once per second; (b) an ADC delivering 16-bit samples at 1 MS/s; (c) a debug console to a PC. Justify each choice.

      Solution

      (a) I2C: two wires for all eight addressed sensors, and the data rate is tiny. (b) SPI: it needs at least 16 Mbit/s of payload, so SPI at 20 MHz or more (or a parallel or LVDS interface) is required; I2C is far too slow. (c) UART: universally supported by USB-to-serial adapters and terminal programs, point to point, and speed is not critical.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Part VII: Implementation

      Describing hardware in Verilog

      Hardware description at the register-transfer level: modules, vectors and operators, combinational logic without accidental latches, clocked logic with nonblocking assignments, state machines, hierarchy and generate, self-checking testbenches, and how code becomes gates.

      Builds onState machines, TimingPractice13 problems

      Real digital designs are not drawn as schematics; they are written in a hardware description language (HDL). Verilog, its extension SystemVerilog, and VHDL let a designer describe circuits at the register-transfer level (RTL): registers, and the combinational logic that computes their next values. A simulator executes the description to check its behavior, and a synthesis tool turns it into gates. The essential mindset is that HDL code describes hardware that all exists and operates at once; it is not a sequential program, even when it looks like one.

      Modules, signals and values

      The unit of design is the module, a block with named ports. Signals are single bits or vectors; [7:0] declares eight bits with bit 7 the most significant. Literals give a width, a base and a value: 8'hA5, 4'b1010, 6'd42. Each bit can be 0, 1, x (unknown, as at power-up in simulation) or z (high impedance).

      module mux2 #(parameter W = 8) (
    input  wire [W-1:0] a,
    input  wire [W-1:0] b,
    input  wire         sel,
    output wire [W-1:0] y
);
    assign y = sel ? b : a;      // continuous assignment: always equal to this expression
endmodule

      A wire is a connection driven continuously by an assign or a module output. A reg is a variable assigned inside an always block; despite the name, it becomes a register only if the block describes one. (SystemVerilog replaces both with logic for most uses.) parameter makes a module generic, here in its width.

      OperatorMeaningExample (a = 4'b1100, b = 4'b1010)
      & | ^ ~bitwise AND, OR, XOR, NOTa & b = 4'b1000
      &a, |a, ^areduction: AND, OR, XOR of all bits of one vector^a = 0 (even number of 1s)
      && || !logical, result 1 bita && b = 1
      {a, b}concatenation8'b1100_1010
      {3{2'b10}}replication6'b101010
      << >> >>>shifts (>>> is arithmetic on signed values)a >> 2 = 4'b0011
      ? :conditional (a multiplexer)sel ? b : a
      + − * == != < >arithmetic and comparisona + b = 4'b0110 in 4 bits

      Expression width follows the widest operand and the destination: 8'd200 + 8'd100 assigned to an 8-bit signal gives 44, but assigned to a 9-bit signal gives 300, because the addition is then carried out at 9 bits.

      Combinational logic

      Combinational logic is written either with assign statements or with an always @* block (SystemVerilog: always_comb), which re-evaluates whenever any input it reads changes. Inside it, use blocking assignments (=), which take effect immediately, like ordinary variable assignments.

      module dec2to4 (
    input  wire [1:0] a,
    input  wire       en,
    output reg  [3:0] y
);
    always @* begin
        y = 4'b0000;          // default first: every path through the block assigns y
        if (en)
            y[a] = 1'b1;      // one-hot output selected by a
    end
endmodule

// A priority encoder: the first matching pattern wins
always @* begin
    casez (req)               // ? matches either value
        4'b1???: grant = 2'd3;
        4'b01??: grant = 2'd2;
        4'b001?: grant = 2'd1;
        default: grant = 2'd0;
    endcase
end

      Common mistake

      If some path through a combinational block does not assign an output, the output must keep its old value on that path, and the only hardware that can do that is a latch. Synthesis infers one, usually unintentionally:

      always @* begin
    if (en)
        q = d;                //! no else: q holds when en = 0, so a latch is inferred
end

      Avoid inferred latches by assigning a default value at the top of the block, covering every branch of every if and case (with a default), or by using always_comb, whose tools warn about them.

      The structure of the code shapes the hardware. A chain of if / else if becomes a priority chain of multiplexers, with the first condition closest to the output; a case on one selector whose items are mutually exclusive becomes a single parallel multiplexer. Both are correct; they differ in delay and size.

      Sequential logic

      Registers are written as blocks triggered by a clock edge, using nonblocking assignments (<=). A nonblocking assignment evaluates its right-hand side immediately but updates the left-hand side only after every block triggered by the same edge has evaluated, which is exactly how a set of flip-flops behaves: all sample their inputs at the edge, then all outputs change together.

      module counter #(parameter W = 4) (
    input  wire         clk,
    input  wire         rst,      // synchronous, active high
    input  wire         en,
    output reg  [W-1:0] count
);
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (rst)
            count <= {W{1'b0}};
        else if (en)
            count <= count + 1'b1;
    end
endmodule

// Asynchronous, active-low reset: the reset appears in the sensitivity list
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) q <= 1'b0;
    else        q <= d;

      Blocking versus nonblocking

      The two assignment types give different hardware in a clocked block:

      always @(posedge clk) begin   // two-stage shift register, as intended
    b <= a;
    c <= b;                   // uses the old b
end

always @(posedge clk) begin   // not a shift register
    b = a;
    c = b;                    //! uses the new b, which is already a
end

      Key idea

      Three rules avoid nearly all simulation-synthesis mismatches: use nonblocking (<=) in clocked blocks; use blocking (=) in combinational blocks; and assign each signal from only one always block. Two blocks driving the same signal describe two circuits fighting over one wire, which synthesis rejects and simulation resolves arbitrarily.

      State machines in Verilog

      The FSM template of Module 16 maps directly onto code: a clocked block for the state register, a combinational block for the next-state logic, and assignments for the outputs.

      module det101 (                         // Moore detector for 101, overlapping
    input  wire clk,
    input  wire rst,
    input  wire x,
    output wire found
);
    localparam S0 = 2'd0, S1 = 2'd1, S2 = 2'd2, S3 = 2'd3;
    reg [1:0] state, next;

    always @(posedge clk)                // state register
        if (rst) state <= S0;
        else     state <= next;

    always @* begin                      // next-state logic
        case (state)
            S0:      next = x ? S1 : S0;
            S1:      next = x ? S1 : S2;
            S2:      next = x ? S3 : S0;
            S3:      next = x ? S1 : S2;
            default: next = S0;
        endcase
    end

    assign found = (state == S3);        // Moore output: a function of the state
endmodule

      The state encoding is chosen by the localparam values here; synthesis tools can also re-encode FSMs automatically (often to one-hot on FPGAs). SystemVerilog's typedef enum gives states readable names in simulation waveforms.

      Hierarchy and generate

      Larger designs instantiate modules inside other modules, connecting ports by name. A generate loop instantiates repeated structure, such as a ripple-carry adder built from full adders:

      module full_adder (input wire a, b, cin, output wire s, cout);
    assign s    = a ^ b ^ cin;
    assign cout = (a & b) | (cin & (a ^ b));
endmodule

module ripple4 (
    input  wire [3:0] a, b,
    input  wire       cin,
    output wire [3:0] s,
    output wire       cout
);
    wire [4:0] c;
    assign c[0] = cin;
    genvar i;
    generate
        for (i = 0; i < 4; i = i + 1) begin : stage
            full_adder fa (.a(a[i]), .b(b[i]), .cin(c[i]), .s(s[i]), .cout(c[i+1]));
        end
    endgenerate
    assign cout = c[4];
endmodule

      In practice one would write assign {cout, s} = a + b + cin; and let synthesis choose an adder architecture (ripple, carry-lookahead, prefix) that meets the timing constraint, which is one of the main benefits of RTL design.

      Testbenches

      A testbench is a module with no ports that instantiates the design under test (DUT), generates its clock and inputs, and checks its outputs. Testbenches may use constructs that have no hardware meaning: initial blocks, delays (#5), random numbers, $display. A good testbench is self-checking: it computes the expected result with a simple reference model and reports mismatches, instead of relying on someone to read waveforms.

      `timescale 1ns/1ps
module tb_counter;
    reg        clk = 1'b0, rst = 1'b1, en = 1'b0;
    wire [3:0] count;
    reg  [3:0] expected;
    integer    errors = 0, k;

    counter #(.W(4)) dut (.clk(clk), .rst(rst), .en(en), .count(count));

    always #5 clk = ~clk;                       // 10 ns period

    initial begin
        expected = 4'd0;
        @(negedge clk);                         // change inputs away from the active edge
        @(negedge clk) rst = 1'b0;
        for (k = 0; k < 40; k = k + 1) begin
            en = $random;                       // random 0 or 1
            @(posedge clk);                     // the DUT updates at this edge
            if (en) expected = expected + 1'b1; // reference model
            #1;
            if (count !== expected) begin
                errors = errors + 1;
                $display("t=%0t count=%0d expected=%0d", $time, count, expected);
            end
            @(negedge clk);
        end
        $display("%0d errors", errors);
        $finish;
    end
endmodule

      Driving inputs on the falling edge (or with nonblocking assignments) avoids a classic race in which the testbench and the DUT both react to the same rising edge and the result depends on the simulator's arbitrary ordering. Industrial verification adds constrained-random stimulus, functional coverage, assertions (SystemVerilog Assertions) and methodologies such as UVM, and verification typically takes more engineering effort than design.

      From code to gates

      A synthesis tool reads RTL plus constraints (clock periods, input and output delays) and a library of standard cells, infers registers from clocked blocks and logic from everything else, optimizes, and produces a gate-level netlist that meets timing (Module 17). Not everything that simulates can be synthesized: delays are ignored, initial blocks are ignored in ASIC flows (FPGA tools can use them for power-up values), loops must have constant bounds and are unrolled into hardware, and system tasks such as $display exist only in simulation. Writing code whose simulated behavior matches the synthesized hardware is the core skill of RTL design.

      Summary

      • Modules with ports; wires for continuous assignments, regs for always-block variables; vectors, sized literals, reduction, concatenation and replication operators.
      • Combinational: assign or always @* with blocking assignments; assign every output on every path to avoid latches.
      • Sequential: always @(posedge clk) with nonblocking assignments; resets synchronous (inside the block) or asynchronous (in the sensitivity list).
      • One driver per signal; <= in clocked blocks, = in combinational blocks.
      • FSM = state register block + next-state block + output assignments.
      • Self-checking testbenches compare the DUT with a reference model; drive inputs away from the active clock edge.

      Practice problems

      With a = 4'b1010 and b = 2'b11, what are {a, b}, {2{b}}, &a and ^a?

      Solution

      {a, b} = 6'b101011; {2{b}} = 4'b1111; &a = 0 (not all ones); ^a = 0 (two ones, even parity).

      Which assignment operator belongs in a clocked always block, and which in a combinational one?

      Solution

      Clocked: nonblocking (<=). Combinational: blocking (=).

      Write a 4-to-1 multiplexer for 8-bit inputs d0–d3 and a 2-bit select using an always @* block and a case statement.

      Solution
      module mux4 (
    input  wire [7:0] d0, d1, d2, d3,
    input  wire [1:0] sel,
    output reg  [7:0] y
);
    always @* begin
        case (sel)
            2'd0:    y = d0;
            2'd1:    y = d1;
            2'd2:    y = d2;
            default: y = d3;
        endcase
    end
endmodule

      The default covers every remaining selector value, so y is assigned on every path and no latch is inferred.

      Does this block infer a latch? Fix it.

      always @* begin
    case (op)
        2'b00: y = a + b;
        2'b01: y = a - b;
        2'b10: y = a & b;
    endcase
end
      Solution

      Yes: for op = 2'b11, y is not assigned and must hold its old value, so a latch is inferred. Add default: y = a | b; (or whatever op 11 should do), or put y = 0; before the case.

      What value does each produce? (a) wire [7:0] s = 8'd200 + 8'd100; (b) wire [8:0] t = 8'd200 + 8'd100;

      Solution

      (a) The expression is evaluated at 8 bits: 300 − 256 = 44. (b) The destination is 9 bits, so the addition is carried out at 9 bits: 300.

      Write a parameterized register with load enable and an asynchronous active-low reset.

      Solution
      module regen #(parameter W = 8) (
    input  wire         clk,
    input  wire         rst_n,
    input  wire         en,
    input  wire [W-1:0] d,
    output reg  [W-1:0] q
);
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)  q <= {W{1'b0}};
        else if (en) q <= d;          // no else: holding is what a register does
    end
endmodule

      Omitting the else in a clocked block is fine: the flip-flops simply keep their value, implemented with an enable or a feedback mux. Only in combinational blocks does a missing assignment create a latch.

      Write a module that outputs a one-cycle pulse when a synchronous input x rises.

      Solution
      module rise_detect (
    input  wire clk,
    input  wire rst,
    input  wire x,
    output wire pulse
);
    reg x_d;                          // x delayed by one cycle
    always @(posedge clk)
        if (rst) x_d <= 1'b0;
        else     x_d <= x;
    assign pulse = x & ~x_d;          // now 1, previously 0
endmodule

      If x is asynchronous, pass it through a two-flip-flop synchronizer first and detect edges on the synchronized signal.

      Write a two-flip-flop synchronizer module, and explain why it must be written with nonblocking assignments.

      Solution
      module sync2 (
    input  wire clk,
    input  wire async_in,
    output reg  sync_out
);
    reg meta;
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        meta     <= async_in;
        sync_out <= meta;             // the old value of meta
    end
endmodule

      With blocking assignments, sync_out = meta would read the value just assigned, collapsing the two stages into one and removing the resolution time the second flip-flop provides.

      A designer writes two always blocks: one sets busy <= 1 on start, the other clears busy <= 0 on done. What is wrong, and how should it be written?

      Solution

      Two blocks drive the same register: in hardware that is two flip-flops (or drivers) fighting over one signal. Synthesis reports multiple drivers, and simulation produces whichever block ran last. Write one block that decides: always @(posedge clk) if (rst) busy <= 0; else if (start) busy <= 1; else if (done) busy <= 0;, with the priority stated explicitly.

      Describe the hardware produced by each, and when each is preferable:

      // version A
always @* if (s[0]) y = a; else if (s[1]) y = b; else if (s[2]) y = c; else y = d;
// version B
always @* case (s) 3'b001: y = a; 3'b010: y = b; 3'b100: y = c; default: y = d; endcase
      Solution

      A is a priority chain of three 2-to-1 muxes: s[0] wins over s[1], which wins over s[2]; the delay grows with the chain length, and it behaves sensibly even if several bits of s are 1. B is a parallel one-hot select (a 4-to-1 mux with decoded selects), shallower and faster, but it only matches its intent when s is guaranteed one-hot (other values fall to d). Use A when priority is part of the specification, B when the selects are mutually exclusive.

      Write a synchronous FIFO with parameterized width and a depth of 8, with push, pop, full and empty. Explain how the pointers distinguish full from empty.

      Solution
      module fifo8 #(parameter W = 8) (
    input  wire         clk, rst,
    input  wire         push, pop,
    input  wire [W-1:0] din,
    output wire [W-1:0] dout,
    output wire         full, empty
);
    reg [W-1:0] mem [0:7];
    reg [3:0]   wp, rp;                       // one extra bit beyond the 3 address bits

    assign empty = (wp == rp);
    assign full  = (wp[2:0] == rp[2:0]) && (wp[3] != rp[3]);
    assign dout  = mem[rp[2:0]];

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (rst) begin
            wp <= 4'd0;
            rp <= 4'd0;
        end else begin
            if (push && !full) begin
                mem[wp[2:0]] <= din;
                wp <= wp + 1'b1;
            end
            if (pop && !empty)
                rp <= rp + 1'b1;
        end
    end
endmodule

      With 3-bit pointers, equal pointers would mean both empty and full. The fourth bit counts laps: equal including the lap bit means empty; equal addresses with different lap bits means the writer is exactly one lap ahead, so the FIFO is full. (This version presents the head entry combinationally on dout; pushing and popping in the same cycle works when the FIFO is neither empty nor full.)

      Write a binary counter that also outputs its value in Gray code, and say why the Gray output should come from a register if it crosses clock domains.

      Solution
      module gray_counter #(parameter W = 4) (
    input  wire         clk, rst, en,
    output reg  [W-1:0] bin,
    output reg  [W-1:0] gray
);
    wire [W-1:0] bin_next = bin + (en ? 1'b1 : 1'b0);
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (rst) begin
            bin  <= {W{1'b0}};
            gray <= {W{1'b0}};
        end else begin
            bin  <= bin_next;
            gray <= bin_next ^ (bin_next >> 1);   // registered Gray code
        end
    end
endmodule

      A Gray code computed combinationally from bin can glitch while the XOR gates settle (several bits of bin change at once), and a synchronizer in another domain could sample a glitch. Registering it guarantees that each change is a single clean bit transition at a clock edge.

      In a testbench, the stimulus is applied with @(posedge clk) en = 1; while the DUT samples en in always @(posedge clk). Why can the DUT see either the old or the new value, and how is this fixed?

      Solution

      Both the testbench process and the DUT's always block wake up at the same rising edge, and the simulator may run either first. If the testbench's blocking assignment runs first, the DUT sees the new en at that edge; otherwise it sees the old one. This is a race. Fix it by changing stimulus away from the active edge (at the falling edge or after a small delay), or by using nonblocking assignments for stimulus (en <= 1;), so the update happens after all blocks triggered by the edge have sampled their inputs.
