      Part VII: Implementation

      From design to silicon: fabrication, test, power and heat

      How a design becomes working chips: the ASIC flow from specification through synthesis and physical design to signoff, fabrication and yield economics, chiplets and packaging, manufacturing test with scan, and the power delivery, thermal and reliability limits every chip must respect.

      Builds onVerilog, CMOSPractice13 problems

      Integrated circuits range from a 74HCT00, four NAND gates built from 16 transistors, to processors with tens of billions of transistors, such as NVIDIA's GA100 GPU (54 billion, 128 multiprocessors) and Apple's M4 (28 billion). Designing at that scale is possible only because of a disciplined flow of tools and checks that turns RTL code into a manufacturable layout, and because manufacturing, test and packaging are engineered as carefully as the logic. This module follows a design from specification to a tested part and covers the physical limits, power and heat, that shape every modern chip.

      The ASIC design flow

      • Specification and architecture. Requirements are set as targets for power, performance and area (PPA), plus cost and schedule. Architects partition the design into blocks, define interfaces, and budget each block's timing, area and power. Decisions here (how many cores, cache sizes, which accelerators) matter far more than any later optimization.
      • RTL design in Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL (Module 27).
      • Verification establishes that the RTL does what the specification says: simulation with self-checking, constrained-random testbenches; coverage measurement; formal verification, which proves properties for all inputs; and emulation or FPGA prototyping to run real software before silicon exists. Verification usually consumes more effort than design.
      • Logic synthesis maps RTL onto a standard-cell library: hundreds of pre-designed gates, flip-flops and complex cells, each characterized for delay, power and area at every combination of process, voltage and temperature (PVT corner). Timing constraints (clock periods, I/O delays) steer the optimization.
      • Design for test (DFT) inserts scan chains and built-in self-test so that manufactured chips can be tested (below).
      • Physical design: floorplanning places large blocks, I/O and the power grid; placement positions millions of cells; clock tree synthesis builds a balanced clock network to control skew (Module 17); routing connects everything on 10 to 15 or more metal layers, thin ones near the transistors for local wires and thick ones on top for power and long global wires.
      • Signoff confirms the final layout: static timing analysis at every PVT corner, power and voltage-drop analysis, electromigration checks, design-rule checks (DRC: spacing, width and density rules of the process), and layout-versus-schematic (LVS: the layout implements exactly the netlist).
      • Tapeout sends the layout database to the foundry. Fabrication takes about three months; then wafers are tested, diced, packaged and tested again.

      Fabrication

      Chips are made on silicon wafers, today 300 mm in diameter, in hundreds of process steps. Each layer is patterned by photolithography: a light-sensitive resist is exposed through a mask, developed, and the pattern is transferred by etching, deposition or ion implantation; chemical-mechanical polishing flattens the surface for the next layer. Leading-edge processes use extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) light at 13.5 nm for the finest layers. The front end of line builds the transistors; the back end of line builds the metal interconnect above them. A leading-edge design needs dozens of masks, and a full mask set costs on the order of tens of millions of dollars, which is the main reason ASICs require high volumes (Module 21).

      Yield and the cost of a die

      Manufacturing defects (particles, pattern failures) land randomly on the wafer. A die that contains a killer defect does not work. If defects have density D per unit area and the die area is A, a simple Poisson model gives the fraction of good dies:

      yield ≈ e−D·A

      Larger dies therefore cost more than proportionally. The number of dies per wafer is roughly the wafer area divided by the die area, minus partial dies around the edge (about π·d/√(2A) for wafer diameter d), and the cost of each good die is the wafer cost divided by the number of good dies.

      Worked example

      Small die versus large die

      A 300 mm wafer costs $17,000 and the process has D = 0.1 defects/cm2.

      A 100 mm2 die: about 707 − 67 ≈ 640 dies per wafer; yield e−0.1 = 90.5%; 579 good dies; about $29 each.

      A 600 mm2 die: about 118 − 27 ≈ 90 dies per wafer; yield e−0.6 = 54.9%; 49 good dies; about $347 each: twelve times the cost for six times the area.

      This is the economic case for chiplets: building a large system from several smaller dies, each tested before assembly (known-good die), and connecting them inside one package. Memory, I/O and compute can also be made in different processes, each suited to its job. Large chips that remain monolithic recover yield with redundancy, such as spare cache rows or extra cores that can be disabled, which is why products often ship with some units fused off.

      Packaging

      The package connects the die to the board, spreads its heat and protects it. Older packages connect pads on the die's edge with wire bonds; high-performance chips are mounted face-down (flip chip) on an array of solder bumps covering the whole die, giving thousands of power and signal connections with low inductance. In 2.5D packaging several dies sit side by side on a silicon interposer with very dense wiring, the way GPUs connect to stacks of high-bandwidth memory (Module 21). In 3D stacking, dies are bonded on top of each other and connected by through-silicon vias or direct hybrid bonding. Standard die-to-die interfaces such as UCIe let chiplets from different sources interoperate.

      Manufacturing test

      Verification asks whether the design is correct; manufacturing test asks whether a particular manufactured chip matches the design. Every die is tested, so tests must be fast and must detect defects with high probability. Defects are modeled as faults, most simply as stuck-at faults, in which a wire behaves as if permanently tied to 0 or 1. A test pattern detects a fault if the faulty circuit's output differs from the correct one: a stuck-at-0 fault on an AND gate's output is detected only by the input 11, the one pattern for which the good output is 1.

      The difficulty is reaching deep internal logic from the pins. Scan design solves it: every flip-flop gets a multiplexer in front of its D input, and in test mode the flip-flops are chained into long shift registers. The tester shifts a pattern into all flip-flops, applies one functional clock to capture the logic's response, and shifts the result out while shifting the next pattern in. Automatic test-pattern generation (ATPG) computes compact pattern sets that reach well over 99% fault coverage.

      Memories are tested by built-in self-test (BIST) engines that run march algorithms writing and reading patterns through every cell. JTAG boundary scan, a standard serial test port, lets boards test the connections between chips. Parts are also speed-binned: tested at several frequencies and voltages and sold as different products according to how fast they run.

      Power delivery

      A large processor can draw hundreds of amperes at under one volt, and that current changes by tens of amperes within nanoseconds as activity changes. Voltage regulators on the board (and increasingly inside the package) convert higher supply voltages down; a dense mesh of wide upper-metal wires distributes power across the die. Two effects reduce the voltage the transistors actually see: resistive IR drop in the grid (100 A through 0.5 mΩ is 50 mV, over 6% of a 0.8 V supply) and inductive droop from L·di/dt when current steps (Module 10). Decoupling capacitance at every level, from the board to on-die capacitors, supplies fast current transients, and the timing analysis must assume the lowest voltage the grid can reach. Power gating and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling manage the power drawn in the first place (Module 12).

      Heat

      Nearly all electrical power consumed by a chip becomes heat, which must flow from the transistors (the junction) through the package and heatsink to the air or coolant. Each part of that path has a thermal resistance θ in °C/W, and temperature differences follow the thermal equivalent of Ohm's law, ΔT = P·θ:

      A processor dissipating 250 W through θJC = 0.1, θCS = 0.05 and θSA = 0.15 °C/W with 25 °C air reaches TJ = 25 + 250 × 0.3 = 100 °C. Typical maximum junction temperatures are around 95 to 110 °C. When the limit is approached, the chip throttles, lowering its frequency and voltage. Temperature also feeds back into power: leakage current rises steeply with temperature, so a hotter chip leaks more and gets hotter still; designs must ensure this loop settles rather than running away. The maximum sustained power a cooling system is designed to remove is the thermal design power (TDP), and the inability to power and cool every transistor at once is why parts of large chips are idle at any moment ("dark silicon").

      Reliability

      • Electromigration: high current density gradually moves metal atoms in wires, eventually opening or shorting them. Signoff limits current density in every wire.
      • Aging: transistors slowly shift their threshold voltages under stress (bias temperature instability, hot carriers), so circuits slow down over years; designs include timing margin for end-of-life conditions.
      • Soft errors: alpha particles from packaging materials and neutrons from cosmic rays can flip bits in SRAM, DRAM and flip-flops without permanent damage. Memories are protected with error-correcting codes.

      The standard code is a Hamming code extended with an overall parity bit, SECDED (single-error correcting, double-error detecting). In a Hamming code, check bits sit at the power-of-two positions 1, 2, 4, 8, …, and check bit 2ᵏ is the parity of every position whose index has bit k set; when a single bit flips, recomputing the checks gives a syndrome equal to the position of the flipped bit. Protecting 64 data bits takes 7 Hamming check bits plus 1 overall parity bit: the common (72, 64) code with 12.5% overhead.

      Summary

      • ASIC flow: specification and architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis, DFT, physical design (floorplan, place, clock tree, route), signoff (STA, power, DRC, LVS), tapeout, fabrication, test and packaging.
      • Yield ≈ e−DA; cost per good die grows faster than area, motivating chiplets and redundancy.
      • Packaging ranges from wire bond to flip chip, 2.5D interposers with HBM and 3D stacking.
      • Manufacturing test uses fault models, scan chains and ATPG; memories use BIST; boards use JTAG.
      • Power delivery fights IR drop and L·di/dt droop; heat flows through series thermal resistances, TJ = TA + P·Σθ.
      • Reliability threats include electromigration, aging and soft errors; SECDED ECC protects memories.

      Practice problems

      Put these steps in order: routing, RTL design, tapeout, logic synthesis, placement, specification, signoff, verification.

      Solution

      Specification → RTL design → verification → logic synthesis → placement → routing → signoff → tapeout. (Verification continues alongside later steps, and failures loop back.)

      A chip dissipates 100 W with a total junction-to-ambient thermal resistance of 0.5 °C/W in 25 °C air. What is its junction temperature?

      Solution

      TJ = 25 + 100 × 0.5 = 75 °C.

      With a defect density of 0.2 defects/cm2, what fraction of 2 cm2 dies are good? Of 0.5 cm2 dies?

      Solution

      e−0.4 ≈ 67%; e−0.1 ≈ 90%.

      Which input pattern(s) detect a stuck-at-0 fault on the output of a 2-input AND gate? A stuck-at-1 fault on input A?

      Solution

      Output stuck-at-0: only A B = 11 (the good output is 1, the faulty one 0). Input A stuck-at-1: the pattern must set A = 0 and make A matter, so B = 1: A B = 01 (good output 0, faulty output 1).

      How does manufacturing test differ from functional verification?

      Solution

      Verification checks that the design meets its specification, before fabrication, and needs to be done once. Manufacturing test checks that each fabricated chip matches the verified design, on every unit, quickly and cheaply, using fault models and structures such as scan to reach internal nodes.

      Estimate dies per wafer, yield, good dies and cost per good die for a 200 mm2 die on a 300 mm wafer costing $17,000 with D = 0.1/cm2. Use dies ≈ πr2/A − πd/√(2A).

      Solution

      πr2/A = π × 1502/200 ≈ 353.4; edge loss π × 300/√400 = 47.1; about 306 dies. Yield e−0.2 = 81.9% → about 250 good dies → $68 each.

      A 250 W processor has θJC = 0.1 and θCS = 0.05 °C/W. In 35 °C air, what heatsink thermal resistance θSA keeps the junction at or below 95 °C?

      Solution

      Allowed rise 95 − 35 = 60 °C → total θ ≤ 60/250 = 0.24 °C/W → θSA ≤ 0.24 − 0.15 = 0.09 °C/W, which requires a large heatsink with strong airflow or liquid cooling.

      Encode the 4-bit value 1011 (d1 d2 d3 d4) with a Hamming (7,4) code, positions 1–7 = p1 p2 d1 p4 d2 d3 d4, using even parity: p1 covers positions 1, 3, 5, 7; p2 covers 2, 3, 6, 7; p4 covers 4, 5, 6, 7. Then show how an error in position 6 is located.

      Solution

      d1 = 1 (pos 3), d2 = 0 (pos 5), d3 = 1 (pos 6), d4 = 1 (pos 7). p1 = d1 ⊕ d2 ⊕ d4 = 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 0; p2 = d1 ⊕ d3 ⊕ d4 = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 1 = 1; p4 = d2 ⊕ d3 ⊕ d4 = 0 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. Codeword (positions 1–7): 0 1 1 0 0 1 1. If position 6 flips (0 1 1 0 0 0 1), recomputing: check 1 (positions 1, 3, 5, 7) = 0 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 0; check 2 (2, 3, 6, 7) = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 1; check 4 (4, 5, 6, 7) = 0 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. Syndrome (c4 c2 c1) = 110 = 6: flip position 6 back.

      A chip has 10,000 scan flip-flops arranged in 10 chains of 1000. Testing needs 5,000 patterns with a 50 MHz scan clock. Roughly how long does the scan test take? How would you cut the time?

      Solution

      Each pattern needs about 1000 shift cycles (loading the next pattern while unloading the previous result) plus a capture cycle: ≈ 5000 × 1001 ≈ 5 × 106 cycles at 20 ns = about 0.1 s. Use more, shorter chains (more test pins), a faster scan clock, or on-chip test compression that expands a few tester channels into many internal chains.

      A chip draws 100 A at 0.8 V and its power grid has an effective resistance of 0.5 mΩ from the regulator to the transistors. What is the IR drop, as a fraction of the supply? Why does it matter for timing?

      Solution

      100 A × 0.5 mΩ = 50 mV, 6.25% of 0.8 V. Gate delay rises as the supply voltage falls (less gate overdrive), so timing must be verified at the lowest voltage the transistors actually see; otherwise paths that pass at the nominal voltage fail in operation.

      Compare silicon cost per good product for a 600 mm2 monolithic die and for four 150 mm2 chiplets with D = 0.1/cm2, assuming chiplets are tested before assembly and ignoring edge loss and packaging costs.

      Solution

      Monolithic: yield e−0.6 = 0.549, so each good product consumes 600/0.549 ≈ 1093 mm2 of processed silicon. Chiplets: yield e−0.15 = 0.861 each, and only good chiplets are assembled, so 4 × 150/0.861 ≈ 697 mm2, about 36% less. The savings are offset by the interconnect area on each chiplet, the advanced package, and die-to-die communication power, which is why the trade-off favors chiplets mainly for very large designs.

      Explain thermal runaway in terms of leakage, and why a cooling system that is adequate at 25 °C ambient might fail at 45 °C.

      Solution

      Leakage current grows roughly exponentially with temperature. Higher temperature increases leakage power, which raises temperature further through P·θ. At low temperature the loop converges: the extra heat raises temperature only slightly. Above some point the leakage increase per degree exceeds what the cooling removes per degree, and temperature runs away until throttling or damage. A higher ambient starts the chip closer to that point, so the same heatsink that settles comfortably at 25 °C may not reach equilibrium at 45 °C. Throttling (DVFS) and thermal sensors guard against it.

      Why does a (72, 64) SECDED code use 8 check bits? How many check bits would a single-error-correcting code need for 32 data bits?

      Solution

      A Hamming code with r check bits can identify 2ʳ − 1 single-bit error positions, so it needs 2ʳ ≥ m + r + 1 for m data bits. For m = 64: r = 7 (128 ≥ 72). One more overall parity bit distinguishes single errors (correctable) from double errors (detectable): 8. For 32 data bits: r = 6 (64 ≥ 39), so 6 for SEC, 7 with double-error detection (a (39, 32) code).

      Numbers and codes

      Powers of two (Module 2). Memory capacities use binary prefixes (1 KiB = 210 bytes, 1 MiB = 220, 1 GiB = 230, often written KB, MB and GB); data rates and frequencies use decimal ones (1 GB/s = 109 bytes per second; 1 GHz is a period of 1 ns). Since 210 ≈ 103, 230 ≈ 109 and 240 ≈ 1012.

      Integer ranges (Module 3):

      WidthUnsignedTwo's complementC types
      8 bits0 to 255−128 to 127uint8_t, int8_t
      16 bits0 to 65,535−32,768 to 32,767uint16_t, int16_t (int on the AVR)

      • Negation in two's complement: invert every bit and add 1, so −x = x′ + 1. The most negative value has no positive counterpart.
      • Subtraction: A − B = A + B′ + 1, an adder with inverted B and a carry in of 1.
      • Overflow: unsigned addition overflows when the carry out of the top bit is 1. Signed addition overflows when both operands have the same sign and the result has the other; equivalently V = (carry into the top bit) ⊕ (carry out of it).
      • Extension: sign-extend two's complement values by copying the sign bit into the new high bits; zero-extend unsigned values.
      • Shifts: a left shift by k multiplies by 2ᵏ; a logical right shift divides an unsigned value by 2ᵏ, rounding down; an arithmetic right shift divides a signed value by 2ᵏ, rounding toward −∞.
      • Other codes (Module 2): BCD stores each decimal digit in 4 bits; excess-B stores u to represent u − B; Gray code g = b ⊕ (b ≫ 1) changes one bit per step; one-hot uses n bits for n values.

      Floating-point formats (Module 4). Normal values are (−1)ˢ × 1.f × 2e − bias. An exponent field of all zeros encodes ±0 (f = 0) and subnormals (−1)ˢ × 0.f × 21 − bias; all ones encodes ±∞ (f = 0) and NaN (f ≠ 0). Every integer up to 2p is exact, where p is the number of fraction bits plus one: 224 for FP32, 253 for FP64.

      Boolean algebra

      Each identity has a dual, obtained by swapping AND with OR and 0 with 1 (Module 5).

      NameOR formAND form
      IdentityX + 0 = XX · 1 = X
      Null elementX + 1 = 1X · 0 = 0
      IdempotencyX + X = XX · X = X
      ComplementX + X′ = 1X · X′ = 0
      Involution(X′)′ = X
      DistributivityX + Y·Z = (X + Y)·(X + Z)X·(Y + Z) = X·Y + X·Z
      CoveringX + X·Y = XX·(X + Y) = X
      CombiningX·Y + X·Y′ = X(X + Y)·(X + Y′) = X
      SimplificationX + X′·Y = X + YX·(X′ + Y) = X·Y
      ConsensusX·Y + X′·Z + Y·Z = X·Y + X′·Z(X + Y)(X′ + Z)(Y + Z) = (X + Y)(X′ + Z)
      De Morgan(X + Y)′ = X′·Y′(X·Y)′ = X′ + Y′
      • XOR: X ⊕ Y = X·Y′ + X′·Y; X ⊕ 0 = X; X ⊕ 1 = X′; X ⊕ X = 0; (X ⊕ Y)′ = X ⊕ Y′ (XNOR). XOR is commutative and associative, and an n-input XOR is 1 when an odd number of its inputs are 1.
      • Shannon expansion: F = X′·F(X = 0) + X·F(X = 1), the basis of building any function from multiplexers (Module 8).
      • Complete sets: {NAND}, {NOR}, {AND, NOT}, {OR, NOT}, and the 2-to-1 multiplexer. There are 2^(2n) distinct functions of n variables.
      • Canonical forms (Module 6): F = Σm(minterms where F = 1) = ΠM(maxterms where F = 0). AND-OR logic equals NAND-NAND; OR-AND equals NOR-NOR.
      • K-maps (Module 7): rows and columns in Gray-code order (00, 01, 11, 10); a group of 2ᵏ adjacent 1s eliminates k variables; cover every 1 with the fewest, largest groups, starting with essential prime implicants.

      Registers and bits used in the embedded modules (Module 23, Module 25, Module 26). Bits are set with REG |= (1 << BIT) and cleared with REG &= ~(1 << BIT).

      Verilog at a glance

      ConstructExampleNotes
      Module and portsmodule m (input wire a, b, output reg y);Module 27
      Sized literals8'hFF, 4'b10x1, 16'd100width'base value; x = unknown, z = high impedance
      Continuous assignmentassign y = s ? b : a;combinational; drives a wire
      Combinational blockalways @* begin ... endblocking (=); assign every output on every path, or a latch is inferred
      Clocked blockalways @(posedge clk) q <= d;nonblocking (<=) for every register
      Asynchronous resetalways @(posedge clk or posedge rst) if (rst) q <= 0; else q <= d;release it through a reset synchronizer
      Casecase (s) 2'b00: y = a; ... default: y = 0; endcasethe default prevents latches
      Concatenation, replication{a, b}, {4{1'b0}}, {{8{x[7]}}, x}the last sign-extends 8 bits to 16
      Reduction&v, |v, ^vAND, OR or XOR of all bits; ^v is the parity
      Shifts<<, >>, >>>>>> is arithmetic for signed operands
      Equality==, ===== gives x when an operand has x or z bits; === compares exactly (simulation only)
      Parametersmodule c #(parameter W = 8) (...); c #(.W(16)) u1 (...);override per instance
      Generate loopfor (i = 0; i < N; i = i + 1) begin : g ... endinside generate, with genvar i; replicates hardware
      Testbench clockalways #5 clk = ~clk;a 10-time-unit period

      Rules that prevent most RTL bugs: blocking assignments in combinational blocks and nonblocking in clocked ones; never assign one variable from two always blocks; give every combinational output a value on every path; pass every asynchronous input through a synchronizer; keep delays, initial blocks and $display out of synthesizable code.

      Clear bit nx &= ~(1u << n)
      Toggle bit nx ^= 1u << n

      Insert v into that fieldx = (x & ~(m << p)) | ((v & m) << p)with m = (1u << w) − 1

      Round up to a multiple of 2ᵏ(x + (1u << k) - 1) & ~((1u << k) - 1)alignment

      Count set bits__builtin_popcount(x), std::popcount(x)GCC and Clang; C++20 header <bit>
      Sign-extend a b-bit field(int32_t)(x ^ m) - (int32_t)mm = 1u << (b − 1); x holds the field in its low b bits
      Binary to Grayg = b ^ (b >> 1)
      Swap without a temporarya ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;fails if a and b are the same object

      Rules to remember (Module 23, Module 25): shifting by the width of the type or more, and signed overflow, are undefined behavior; unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2n; operands narrower than int are promoted to int before arithmetic; hardware registers and variables shared with interrupt handlers must be volatile, and multi-byte shared variables must be read with interrupts disabled.

      Glossary

      Every definition from the guide, plus other key terms, in alphabetical order. Each term links to the place where it is explained.

      121 terms

      Amdahl's law
      The overall speedup from making a fraction p of a task s times faster: 1/((1 − p) + p/s), which can never exceed 1/(1 − p) however large s becomes. Module 19
      Analog signal
      A signal whose information is carried by its exact value. Every voltage in the allowed range has a distinct meaning, so any disturbance of the voltage changes the information it carries. Module 1
      Arithmetic intensity
      The number of arithmetic operations a program performs per byte it moves to or from main memory. Through the roofline model it decides whether the program is limited by memory bandwidth or by compute. Module 22
      Arithmetic logic unit (ALU)
      A combinational block that performs the arithmetic or logical operation selected by its control inputs and reports status flags such as zero, negative, carry and overflow. Module 9
      Asynchronous FIFO
      A queue whose write side and read side run on different clocks. Gray-coded pointers cross between the domains through synchronizers so the full and empty flags can be computed safely. Module 17
      Average memory access time (AMAT)
      Hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, applied level by level through a memory hierarchy. Module 20
      Bank conflict
      Two or more threads of a warp accessing different words in the same shared-memory bank in one instruction, which forces the hardware to serialize the accesses. Module 22
      Binary-coded decimal (BCD)
      A code that stores each decimal digit separately in 4 bits, using the patterns 0000 to 1001. Module 2
      Branch prediction
      Guessing the outcome of a branch so that a pipeline can keep fetching instructions; a wrong guess flushes the instructions fetched after it and costs a penalty of several cycles. Module 19
      Cache coherence
      The guarantee that all cores see one consistent order of values for each memory location even though each has a private cache; maintained by protocols such as MESI. Module 22
      Cache line
      The unit of data that a cache stores and transfers, typically 64 bytes, with one tag for the whole line. Also called a block. Module 20
      Capacitor
      Two conductors separated by an insulator. It stores charge Q = C·V on its plates; capacitance C is measured in farads. Because current is the rate of change of charge, i = C·dv/dt: a capacitor's voltage cannot change instantly, and it passes no DC current once charged. Module 10
      Carry flag (C)
      The carry out of the most significant column of an addition. For unsigned addition, C = 1 means the result overflowed. For subtraction computed as A + B′ + 1, C = 0 means a borrow occurred (A < B as unsigned numbers), so the unsigned result is wrong. Module 3
      Carry-lookahead adder
      An adder that computes its carries from generate (g = a·b) and propagate (p = a ⊕ b) signals in a tree, so its delay grows with the logarithm of the width instead of linearly. Module 9
      Clock domain crossing (CDC)
      A signal passing between logic clocked by unrelated clocks. It needs a synchronizer, a handshake or an asynchronous FIFO, depending on what is being passed. Module 17
      Clock gating
      Stopping the clock of idle registers to save dynamic power, using an integrated clock-gating cell (a latch and an AND gate) so that no glitches reach the clock. Module 15
      Clock skew
      The difference between the arrival times of the same clock edge at two flip-flops. It adds to the margin of one of the setup and hold checks and subtracts from the other. Module 17
      CMOS
      Complementary MOS logic: each gate has a PMOS pull-up network and a dual NMOS pull-down network, so that in steady state one of them is off and almost no current flows. Module 12
      Coalescing
      Combining the memory accesses of the 32 threads of a warp into as few wide transactions as possible, which happens when consecutive threads access consecutive addresses. Module 22
      Combinational logic
      Logic whose outputs depend only on the present values of its inputs. Given the same inputs it always produces the same outputs, after a short delay. Module 1
      Control unit
      The logic, a decoder or a state machine, that generates the signals steering a datapath through each instruction. Module 18
      Critical path
      The slowest register-to-register path in a design; it sets the minimum clock period. Module 17
      Current
      The rate at which charge flows past a point, I = dQ/dt, measured in amperes (1 A = 1 coulomb per second). By convention current flows from higher to lower potential through a load, opposite to the direction electrons actually move. Module 10
      Data race
      Two threads accessing the same memory location concurrently without synchronization, at least one of them writing. It is undefined behavior in C and C++. Module 22
      Datapath
      The part of a processor that holds and transforms data: registers, the ALU, multiplexers and the connections between them, steered by control signals. Module 18
      De Morgan's theorems
      (X·Y)′ = X′ + Y′ and (X + Y)′ = X′·Y′: the complement of an AND is the OR of the complements, and the complement of an OR is the AND of the complements. Module 5
      Debouncing
      Filtering the rapid transitions a mechanical switch produces when it opens or closes, by accepting a new level only after the input has been stable for several milliseconds. Module 24
      Decoder
      A block with n inputs and 2n outputs that asserts exactly one output: the one whose index equals the binary value of the input. Equivalently, output Yi is the minterm mi of the inputs. The output pattern is one-hot. Module 8
      Digital signal
      A signal whose range is divided into a small number of bands, each mapped to one symbol. A binary digital signal has two bands, read as 0 and 1, separated by a band of voltages that no valid signal may occupy. Small disturbances that keep the voltage inside its band do not change the information. Module 1
      Diode
      A two-terminal device, usually a p-n junction, that conducts current easily in one direction (anode to cathode, forward bias) and blocks it in the other (reverse bias). The symbol's bar marks the cathode. Module 11
      Don't-care
      An input combination whose output value does not matter, because it never occurs or its output is ignored. It may be treated as 0 or 1, whichever gives the simpler circuit. Module 7
      DRAM
      Dynamic RAM: one transistor and one capacitor per bit. It is dense and cheap, but reading is destructive and every cell must be refreshed periodically. Module 21
      Duty cycle
      The fraction of each period that a periodic signal spends high. A PWM signal with duty cycle D averages to D × Vhigh. Module 25
      Dynamic power
      The power spent charging and discharging capacitance as signals switch, α·C·V2·f. Module 12
      Edge-triggered
      Sampling an input only at a clock transition, as a flip-flop does, rather than throughout a clock level, as a latch does. Module 14
      Essential prime implicant
      A prime implicant that is the only prime covering some 1 of the function. Every minimal SOP must contain all of the essential prime implicants. Module 7
      Excess-B (biased) code
      A representation in which the stored unsigned value u stands for u − B. IEEE 754 uses it for exponents. Module 3
      Fan-out
      The number of inputs a gate output drives, limited by the current the output can supply and by the capacitance it must charge. Module 13
      Finite state machine
      A model of sequential behavior consisting of a finite set of states, an initial state, a set of inputs and outputs, a next-state function that maps (current state, input) to the next state, and an output function. In a Moore machine the outputs depend only on the current state; in a Mealy… Module 16
      Fixed-point number
      A fraction represented as an integer with an implied binary point at an agreed position, such as Q8.8; its arithmetic is integer arithmetic plus scaling. Module 4
      Flip-flop
      An edge-triggered storage element: it captures its D input at the active clock edge and holds it until the next one. Module 14
      Forwarding
      Routing a result from a later pipeline stage straight to the ALU inputs of a following instruction, so that it need not wait for the register write. Also called bypassing. Module 19
      FPGA
      Field-programmable gate array: a chip of lookup tables, flip-flops, memory blocks and arithmetic units joined by programmable routing, configured after manufacture to implement a digital design. Module 21
      Full adder
      A circuit that adds three bits A, B and Cin, producing S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin and Cout = A·B + Cin·(A ⊕ B). Module 9
      Gray code
      An ordering of binary codes in which consecutive values differ in exactly one bit; g = b ⊕ (b ≫ 1). Module 2
      Hamming code
      An error-correcting code that adds parity bits over overlapping subsets of the data bits, so the pattern of failed checks locates any single-bit error. Module 2
      Hazard (static)
      A momentary glitch at a combinational output that should stay constant, caused by unequal path delays when one input changes. Adding the consensus term removes it. Module 7
      Hold time
      The minimum time a flip-flop's input must stay stable after the active clock edge. Module 17
      IEEE 754
      The standard floating-point formats and arithmetic rules: sign, biased exponent and fraction with a hidden leading 1, plus zeros, subnormals, infinities and NaNs, with correctly rounded operations. Module 4
      Implicant
      A product term that is 1 only where the function is 1 (or don't care). On a K-map, any valid group that covers only 1s and Xs. Module 7
      Instruction set architecture
      The contract between hardware and software: the registers a program can see, the instructions and their binary encodings, the data types, how memory is addressed, and how exceptions behave. Any processor implementing the ISA runs the same programs; ARM, x86-64 and RISC-V are ISAs. Module 18
      Interrupt service routine (ISR)
      A function the processor runs automatically when an enabled interrupt occurs. It should be short, and variables it shares with the main program must be volatile and accessed atomically. Module 25
      I2C
      Inter-integrated circuit: a two-wire (SDA, SCL), open-drain bus on which a controller addresses devices by 7-bit address and every byte is acknowledged. Module 26
      Karnaugh map (K-map)
      A truth table laid out in Gray-code order so that minterms differing in one variable are adjacent, which makes the largest groupings, and the minimal expression, visible. Module 7
      Latch
      A level-sensitive storage element: transparent, with the output following the input, while its enable is active, and holding its value while the enable is inactive. Module 14
      Latency
      The time from the start of one task to its completion, for example the time to execute one instruction or to fetch one cache line. Module 19
      Linear-feedback shift register (LFSR)
      A shift register whose input is the XOR of selected bits. With the right taps it cycles through all 2n − 1 nonzero states, producing pseudo-random sequences. Module 15
      Little's law
      In a steady-state system, the average number of items inside equals the throughput multiplied by the time each spends inside. For memory: data in flight = bandwidth × latency. Module 22
      Load-use hazard
      An instruction that needs the value loaded by the instruction just before it. The value arrives too late for forwarding, which costs one stall cycle in the classic five-stage pipeline. Module 19
      Lookup table (LUT)
      A small memory addressed by a function's inputs that holds the function's truth table; the basic logic element of an FPGA. Module 21
      Maxterm
      A sum term that contains every variable exactly once. A maxterm equals 0 for exactly one row: variables that are 1 in that row appear complemented, and variables that are 0 appear uncomplemented. The maxterm for row i is written Mi, and Mi = mi′. Module 6
      Mealy machine
      A state machine whose outputs depend on the current state and the current inputs. Module 16
      Metastability
      A flip-flop state between 0 and 1 that can last for an unbounded time when the input changes inside the setup-and-hold window. The probability that it persists decays exponentially with the time allowed. Module 17
      Minterm
      A product term that contains every variable of the function exactly once, complemented or not. A minterm equals 1 for exactly one row of the truth table: the row in which each uncomplemented variable is 1 and each complemented variable is 0. The minterm for row i is written mi. Module 6
      Moore machine
      A state machine whose outputs depend only on the current state. Module 16
      MOSFET
      Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor. A voltage on the gate, insulated from the silicon by a thin oxide, creates or removes a conducting channel between the source and drain. The gate draws no DC current: it controls the channel through the electric field across the oxide, like the… Module 12
      Multiplexer (mux)
      A block with 2n data inputs, n select inputs and one output, which passes the data input whose index equals the select value. A 2-to-1 mux computes Y = S′·I0 + S·I1. Module 8
      Noise margin
      The noise voltage a logic signal can tolerate before it may be misread: NMH = VOH − VIH and NML = VIL − VOL. Module 13
      Nonblocking assignment
      The Verilog <= assignment: all right-hand sides in a time step are evaluated before any left-hand side changes, which models flip-flops that all sample at the same edge. Module 27
      Nyquist rate
      Twice the highest frequency present in a signal. Sampling more slowly causes aliasing, in which high frequencies appear as false low ones. Module 11
      Occupancy
      The number of warps resident on a GPU multiprocessor as a fraction of the maximum, limited by registers, shared memory and block limits. Module 22
      One-hot code
      A code of n bits for n values with exactly one bit set; used for state encodings and select signals because decoding it is trivial. Module 2
      Open-drain output
      An output that can only pull low or let go. A pull-up resistor supplies the high level, so several outputs can share one wire without conflict. Module 13
      Operational amplifier
      A differential amplifier with very high voltage gain (typically 105 or more), very high input impedance and low output impedance. Its output is A·(V+ − V−), limited to the range between its supply rails. Module 11
      Out-of-order execution
      Executing instructions as soon as their operands are ready rather than in program order, while a reorder buffer commits the results in order to keep exceptions precise. Module 19
      Overflow flag (V)
      Signed (two's complement) overflow. It occurs exactly when two operands with the same sign produce a result with the opposite sign. In hardware, V = (carry into the MSB) ⊕ (carry out of the MSB). Module 3
      Parity bit
      An extra bit chosen so that the total number of 1s is even (or odd), so that any single-bit error is detected. Module 2
      Pipelining
      Dividing an operation into stages separated by registers so that several operations are in progress at once, which raises throughput at a cost in latency and hazards. Module 19
      Prime implicant
      An implicant that cannot be enlarged: removing any literal from it would make it cover a 0. On a map, a group that is not contained in any larger valid group. Module 7
      Priority encoder
      A circuit that outputs the index of its highest-priority active input, together with a flag saying whether any input is active. Module 8
      Propagation delay
      tpd: the maximum time from an input change to the moment the output has settled at its new valid value. Its companion, the contamination delay tcd, is the minimum time from an input change until the output first starts to change. Module 1
      Pull-up resistor
      A resistor to the supply that sets the level of a line when nothing drives it, used with buttons, open-drain buses and unused inputs. Module 13
      Pulse-width modulation (PWM)
      Controlling an average voltage or power by switching fully on and fully off at a fixed frequency and varying the duty cycle. Module 25
      Register file
      The array of a processor's general-purpose registers, with typically two read ports and one write port. Module 18
      Ripple-carry adder
      An n-bit adder made of n full adders in a chain, each passing its carry to the next. It is simple, but its delay grows linearly with n. Module 9
      Roofline model
      A bound on performance: attainable FLOP/s = min(peak FLOP/s, memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity). Module 22
      Scan chain
      A test structure in which a multiplexer at each flip-flop's input links the flip-flops into one long shift register in test mode, giving direct control and observation of the internal state. Module 28
      Schmitt trigger
      A comparator with two thresholds (hysteresis), so a slowly changing or noisy input produces one clean transition instead of several. Module 11
      Sequential circuit
      A circuit whose outputs depend on the history of its inputs as well as their present values. The history is summarized by the circuit's state, stored in memory elements (latches or flip-flops) and fed back into its logic. Module 14
      Sequential logic
      Logic whose outputs depend on its present inputs and on stored state, which summarizes past inputs. It contains memory elements such as latches and flip-flops. Module 1
      Setup time
      The minimum time a flip-flop's input must be stable before the active clock edge. Module 17
      Shannon expansion
      F = X′·F(X = 0) + X·F(X = 1): any function can be split on one variable into two smaller functions, which is how multiplexers implement arbitrary logic. Module 8
      Shift register
      A chain of flip-flops, each feeding the next, that moves data one position per clock; used for serial-to-parallel conversion, delays and LFSRs. Module 15
      Sign extension
      Widening a two's complement number by copying its sign bit into the new high-order bits, which preserves its value. Module 3
      SIMT
      Single instruction, multiple threads: the GPU execution model in which a warp executes one instruction stream in lockstep, each thread with its own registers and data. Module 22
      Slack
      The margin by which a timing path meets its requirement: required time minus arrival time. Negative slack is a violation. Module 17
      SPI
      Serial Peripheral Interface: a synchronous, full-duplex bus with a clock, two data lines and one select line per peripheral. Module 26
      SRAM
      Static RAM: each bit is a pair of cross-coupled inverters with two access transistors, six transistors in all. It is fast and needs no refresh; caches and register files use it. Module 21
      Static timing analysis (STA)
      Checking every register-to-register path against the setup and hold requirements by adding up worst-case and best-case delays, without simulating any inputs. Module 17
      Successive-approximation ADC
      An analog-to-digital converter that finds its output code by binary search, one bit per step, using an internal DAC and a comparator. Module 11
      Sum of products (SOP)
      A Boolean expression written as an OR of AND terms, which maps directly onto two-level AND-OR or NAND-NAND logic. Module 6
      Synchronizer
      Two or more flip-flops in series in the receiving clock domain, which give a possibly metastable sample time to resolve before the rest of the logic uses it. Module 17
      Synthesis
      The automatic translation of RTL code and timing constraints into a netlist of gates from a standard-cell library. Module 27
      Testbench
      Simulation-only code that drives a design under test and checks its outputs, ideally against a reference model. Module 27
      Throughput
      The number of tasks completed per unit time, for example instructions per second or bytes per second. Module 19
      Thévenin equivalent
      Seen from two terminals, any linear network behaves as one voltage source in series with one resistor: VTh is the open-circuit voltage and RTh the resistance seen with the sources turned off. Module 10
      Time constant
      τ = RC for a resistor-capacitor circuit: the time a step response takes to cover 63% of its remaining change. Module 10
      Translation lookaside buffer (TLB)
      A small cache of recent virtual-to-physical page translations, which lets most memory accesses skip the page-table walk. Module 20
      Transmission gate
      An NMOS and a PMOS transistor in parallel, driven by complementary signals, forming a switch that passes both 0 and 1 at full strength. Module 12
      Tristate output
      An output with a third, high-impedance state in which it drives neither high nor low, so that several outputs can take turns driving a shared bus wire. Module 12
      Two's complement
      A signed binary representation in which the MSB has weight −2n−1 instead of +2n−1, and all other bits keep their usual positive weights. An n-bit two's complement number ranges from −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1 and has exactly one zero. Module 3
      UART
      Universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter: sends bytes as frames of a start bit, data bits and a stop bit at an agreed bit rate, with no shared clock. Module 26
      Unit in the last place (ulp)
      The gap between a floating-point number and the next larger representable number. For a normal FP32 value with true exponent E, one ulp is 2E − 23. The ulp of 1.0 is the machine epsilon: 2−23 ≈ 1.19 × 10−7 for FP32 and 2−52 ≈ 2.2 × 10−16 for FP64. Module 4
      Virtual memory
      Translating each program's virtual addresses to physical addresses page by page through page tables, which isolates programs and lets memory be allocated in pages. Module 20
      volatile
      A C and C++ qualifier telling the compiler that an object may change, or that accessing it has effects, outside the code it can see, so every access written in the source must actually be performed. Module 25
      Voltage
      The potential difference between two points: the energy per unit charge gained or lost moving between them, measured in volts (1 V = 1 joule per coulomb). A voltage is always between two nodes; "the voltage at a node" means relative to a chosen reference node called ground. Module 10
      Warp
      A group of 32 GPU threads that are scheduled together and execute the same instruction at the same time. Module 22
      Warp divergence
      Threads of one warp taking different paths through a branch, which the warp executes one after the other with the inactive threads disabled. Module 22
      Watchdog timer
      A hardware timer that resets the processor unless software restarts it periodically, so that a hung program is recovered automatically. Module 25
      Write-back cache
      A cache that updates only its own copy on a store and writes a modified (dirty) line to the next level when the line is evicted. Module 20
      Yield
      The fraction of manufactured dies that work. In the Poisson model it is e−D·A for defect density D and die area A. Module 28

      No glossary entries match. Try a shorter word.

      InterviewQ121 problems

      Part VIII: Reference and practice

      Interview problem set

      Problems in the style of online assessments and technical interviews for hardware, silicon and embedded roles, grouped by topic. Each solution explains the reasoning an interviewer listens for, and links back to the module that teaches it.

      Practice121 problems

      The problems below are typical of the questions asked in screening tests and technical interviews for digital design, verification, architecture, GPU and embedded positions. They mix quick checks of fundamentals, short design tasks and longer questions with a trap in them. Interviewers usually care less about the final number than about the reasoning: say what you are assuming, name the principle you are applying, and check your answer against a simple case. Each section links to the modules that teach its material.

      Use the level filter in the toolbar to start with the easier questions, and the Random problem button for mixed review. When you miss one, reread the linked module and work its medium and hard problems before coming back.

      Numbers and arithmetic

      Convert 6158 to hexadecimal.

      Solution

      Through binary: 6 1 5 → 110 001 101 → regroup in fours from the right: 1 1000 1101 → 0x18D (= 397). (Module 2)

      What is the minimum number of bits needed to give 384 different items distinct codes?

      Solution

      28 = 256 < 384 ≤ 512 = 29: 9 bits.

      What is the range of an 8-bit two's complement number? What is the result of negating −128 in 8 bits, and why?

      Solution

      Range −128 to +127. Negating −128 (1000 0000) by inverting and adding 1 gives 0111 1111 + 1 = 1000 0000 = −128 again: +128 is not representable, so the negation overflows. (Module 3)

      Interpret the byte 1001 0011 as an unsigned number, a sign-magnitude number and a two's complement number.

      Solution

      Unsigned: 128 + 16 + 2 + 1 = 147. Sign-magnitude: sign 1, magnitude 001 0011 = 19 → −19. Two's complement: 147 − 256 = −109.

      Write a C expression that detects signed overflow in s = a + b for 32-bit ints, computing the sum without undefined behavior.

      Solution

      Compute in unsigned arithmetic, which wraps legally: uint32_t s = (uint32_t)a + (uint32_t)b;. Overflow occurred if a and b have the same sign and s has a different one: ((a ^ s) & (b ^ s)) >> 31 (as unsigned), i.e. the sign bit of (a ⊕ s) AND (b ⊕ s). This is the software form of the hardware rule V = Cn−1 ⊕ Cn. GCC and Clang also offer __builtin_add_overflow.

      Multiply an integer x by 7 using only shifts and one addition or subtraction. By 10?

      Solution

      7x = (x << 3) − x. 10x = (x << 3) + (x << 1). Compilers do this automatically when it is cheaper than a multiply.

      Encode −0.75 in IEEE 754 single precision (hex).

      Solution

      0.75 = 1.12 × 2−1. Sign 1; exponent −1 + 127 = 126 = 0111 1110; fraction 1000…0. Bits: 1 01111110 1000 0000 0000 0000 0000 000 = 0xBF400000. (Module 4)

      Why does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluate to false in C with doubles? How should floating-point values be compared?

      Solution

      None of the three values is exactly representable in binary (each is a repeating binary fraction), so each is rounded, and the rounded sum of the first two differs from the rounded 0.3 in the last bit (the sum is stored as 0.3000000000000000444…, while 0.3 is stored as 0.2999999999999999888…). Compare with a tolerance appropriate to the magnitudes involved, for example fabs(x − y) <= 1e-12 * fmax(fabs(x), fabs(y)), or restructure the computation to avoid needing equality.

      What is the smallest positive integer that cannot be represented exactly in FP32? Why?

      Solution

      FP32 has 24 bits of significand (23 stored plus the hidden 1), so every integer up to 224 = 16,777,216 is exact. Above that, consecutive representable values are 2 apart, so 16,777,217 is the first that cannot be represented (it rounds to 16,777,216). A float counter incremented by 1 stops growing there.

      A 12-bit two's complement value arrives in the low bits of an unsigned 32-bit variable x (upper bits zero). Sign-extend it to a 32-bit signed value without branches.

      Solution

      int32_t v = (int32_t)(x ^ 0x800u) - 0x800;. If bit 11 is 0, the XOR adds 2048 and the subtraction removes it again. If bit 11 is 1, the XOR removes 2048 and subtracting another 2048 yields x − 4096, the correct negative value. The XOR result is between 0 and 4095, so the conversion to int32_t and the signed subtraction are always well defined. The common alternative ((int32_t)(x << 20)) >> 20 relies on implementation-defined behavior: converting an out-of-range unsigned value to a signed type, and right-shifting a negative number.

      Write a branchless saturating addition of two uint8_t values (results above 255 clamp to 255).

      Solution
      uint8_t sat_add_u8(uint8_t a, uint8_t b)
{
    uint16_t r = (uint16_t)a + b;      // 0..510, the carry lands in bit 8
    r |= -(r >> 8);                    // if bit 8 is set, OR in all ones
    return (uint8_t)r;
}

      If the sum is below 256, r >> 8 is 0 and nothing changes. Otherwise it is 1, its negation is all ones, and the low byte becomes 0xFF. Hardware does the same with the carry-out driving a mux. DSP and GPU instruction sets have saturating arithmetic built in.

      What is the Gray code of 13, and how is it computed in general?

      Solution

      G = B ⊕ (B >> 1): 1101 ⊕ 0110 = 1011. Consecutive Gray codes differ in exactly one bit, which is why Gray-coded counters are safe to pass between clock domains. (Module 2)

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Combinational logic

      Using only 2-to-1 multiplexers (and the constants 0 and 1), build NOT, AND and OR.

      Solution

      A mux computes S′·I0 + S·I1. NOT A: S = A, I0 = 1, I1 = 0. A AND B: S = A, I0 = 0, I1 = B. A OR B: S = A, I0 = B, I1 = 1. Since NOT and AND form a complete set, a 2-to-1 mux is universal. (Module 8)

      What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to build XOR? Sketch the structure.

      Solution

      Four. N1 = (AB)′; N2 = (A·N1)′; N3 = (B·N1)′; Y = (N2·N3)′ = A ⊕ B. The shared first gate is the trick. (Module 5)

      Build a 4-to-1 mux from 2-to-1 muxes. Then build an 8-to-1 mux from 4-to-1 and 2-to-1 muxes.

      Solution

      4-to-1: two 2-to-1 muxes on S0 select between (I0, I1) and (I2, I3); a third, on S1, selects between their outputs: 3 muxes. 8-to-1: two 4-to-1 muxes on S1S0 handle I0–I3 and I4–I7; a 2-to-1 mux on S2 picks one: 2 + 1.

      Implement an arbitrary 3-input function F(A, B, C) with a single 4-to-1 mux and at most one inverter.

      Solution

      Use A and B as the selects. For each of the four (A, B) combinations, F restricted to that combination is a function of C alone, which can only be 0, 1, C or C′; connect that to the corresponding data input (one inverter supplies C′). This is Shannon expansion: F = A′B′·F(0,0,C) + A′B·F(0,1,C) + AB′·F(1,0,C) + AB·F(1,1,C). An FPGA LUT is the same idea taken to all inputs.

      Minimize F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15).

      Solution

      The 1s are all cells with B = D = 0 (the four corners) and all cells with B = D = 1 (the center square): F = B′D′ + BD = (B ⊕ D)′, an XNOR of B and D; A and C are irrelevant. (Module 7)

      Derive a minimal SOP for A > B, where A = A1A0 and B = B1B0 are 2-bit unsigned numbers.

      Solution

      A > B = A1·B1′ + A1·A0·B0′ + A0·B1′·B0′. The first term is "the high bits decide" (A1 = 1, B1 = 0). The other two cover "the high bits are equal and A0 > B0": A1·A0·B0′ handles A1 = B1 = 1, and A0·B1′·B0′ handles A1 = B1 = 0. Each has dropped one literal by merging with cells the first term already covers, which is why the K-map gives three-literal terms rather than four-literal ones.

      Write the equations of a 4-input priority encoder (I3 has the highest priority) with outputs Y1 Y0 and a valid flag V.

      Solution

      Y1 = I3 + I2, Y0 = I3 + I2′·I1, V = I3 + I2 + I1 + I0. Y0 is 1 for index 3 or for index 1, and index 1 wins only if I2 is not active (I3 is already covered by the first term).

      F = A·B′ + B·C has a static-1 hazard. When does it glitch, and how is it removed?

      Solution

      With A = C = 1, F should stay 1 when B changes, but as B falls, the B·C term can turn off before the A·B′ term turns on (B′ is delayed by the inverter), giving a brief 0. Adding the consensus term A·C covers the transition and removes the hazard; it is logically redundant. (Module 7)

      Is {XOR, AND} functionally complete? What if the constant 1 is also available?

      Solution

      Without constants, no: both gates output 0 when all inputs are 0, so every circuit built from them maps all-zeros to 0 and can never produce NOT. With the constant 1, yes: NOT x = x ⊕ 1, and {AND, NOT} is complete. (This basis is the algebraic normal form used in cryptography.)

      How many distinct Boolean functions of n inputs exist? Give the number for n = 2 and n = 4.

      Solution

      A truth table has 2n rows, each 0 or 1: 2^(2n) functions. n = 2: 16. n = 4: 65,536.

      Design a circuit whose output is 1 when the 4-bit unsigned input ABCD is a multiple of 3. A K-map gives no simplification at all; find a better structure.

      Hint

      Work modulo 3: what is 2 equal to, mod 3?

      Solution

      The multiples (0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15) are pairwise non-adjacent, so the minimal SOP is six 4-literal minterms. But 2 ≡ −1 (mod 3), so 8A + 4B + 2C + D ≡ −A + B − C + D. With each bit 0 or 1 this sum lies between −2 and 2, so it is a multiple of 3 exactly when it is 0: the number of 1s among B and D equals the number among A and C. That compares two 2-bit counts, a few gates; for wider numbers the same alternating-sum idea extends (and an FSM handles serial input; see the sequential section).

      How many select lines does a 32-to-1 multiplexer need? How many 2-to-1 muxes would build it as a tree?

      Solution

      5 select lines. A tree of 2-to-1 muxes needs 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 31.

      Build a 3-to-8 decoder from two 2-to-4 decoders with active-high enables and one inverter.

      Solution

      Connect A1 A0 to both decoders' inputs. Enable the first (outputs 0–3) with A2′ (through the inverter) and the second (outputs 4–7) with A2. If the 3-to-8 decoder needs its own enable E, use E·A2′ and E·A2 instead. (Module 8)

      Estimate, in gate delays, the worst-case delay of a 32-bit ripple-carry adder and of a carry-lookahead adder built as a tree of 4-bit lookahead units.

      Solution

      Ripple: the carry passes through an AND-OR (2 gate delays) per bit, roughly 64 gate delays. Lookahead: a tree of 4-bit units needs ⌈log4 32⌉ = 3 levels, and each AND-OR step costs 2 gate delays. The bit generate and propagate signals take 1; group signals rise through the first two levels (4); the top level computes its carries (2); the carries descend two levels (4); the sum XOR adds 1. Total 1 + 4 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 12. The delay grows with the logarithm of the width instead of linearly, at the cost of area and fan-in. (Module 9)

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Sequential logic and state machines

      What is the difference between a latch and a flip-flop? Where is each used?

      Solution

      A latch is level-sensitive: transparent (output follows input) while its enable is active, holding otherwise. A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it samples its input only at a clock edge. Flip-flops are the default in synchronous design because data cannot race through them; latches appear inside flip-flops, in clock-gating cells, and in some high-performance designs that use time borrowing. (Module 14)

      Convert a D flip-flop into a T flip-flop and into a JK flip-flop.

      Solution

      T: D = T ⊕ Q. JK: D = J·Q′ + K′·Q.

      Bits of a binary number arrive serially, most significant bit first. Design an FSM whose output says whether the number received so far is divisible by 3.

      Solution

      The state is the remainder r ∈ {0, 1, 2}. Appending bit b turns the value v into 2v + b, so r* = (2r + b) mod 3. Transitions: r0: b = 0 → r0, b = 1 → r1; r1: 0 → r2, 1 → r0; r2: 0 → r1, 1 → r2. Output 1 in r0 (Moore). Three states, two flip-flops. (Module 16)

      How many states does a Mealy machine need to detect the pattern 1101 with overlapping matches? List the transitions.

      Solution

      Four (S0 nothing, S1 "1", S2 "11", S3 "110"). S0: 1 → S1, 0 → S0. S1: 1 → S2, 0 → S0. S2: 1 → S2, 0 → S3. S3: 1 → S1 with output 1 (pattern complete; the trailing 1 is a new prefix), 0 → S0. All other transitions output 0. The Moore version needs a fifth state for "found".

      How many flip-flops does a counter need to divide a clock by 1000? How many states does a 5-flip-flop Johnson counter have?

      Solution

      A modulo-1000 counter needs ⌈log2 1000⌉ = 10 flip-flops. A Johnson counter with n flip-flops has 2n = 10 states. (Module 15)

      Design a divide-by-4 clock with a 50% duty cycle, and a divide-by-3 clock with a 50% duty cycle.

      Solution

      Divide by 4: a 2-bit counter's MSB, or two toggle flip-flops in series (each halves the frequency). Divide by 3 at 50%: a mod-3 counter on rising edges produces a signal high for 1 of 3 cycles; a falling-edge flip-flop delays it by half a cycle; ORing the two gives a signal high for 1.5 of 3 cycles. Odd divisors with 50% duty always need both clock edges.

      Design a circuit that produces a one-clock-cycle pulse on each rising edge of a synchronous signal x. What changes if x is asynchronous?

      Solution

      Delay x by one flip-flop (x_d) and output x·x_d′. If x is asynchronous, first pass it through a two-flip-flop synchronizer and apply the detector to the synchronized signal, otherwise the AND can see a metastable or inconsistent value.

      What is the longest sequence a 3-bit LFSR can produce, and why can it never produce all 8 states?

      Solution

      7 states (23 − 1). The all-zeros state feeds back XOR(0, 0) = 0 and maps to itself, so a maximal LFSR cycles through all nonzero states and must never enter zero.

      Design a serial odd-parity checker: its output is 1 when an odd number of 1s has been received so far.

      Solution

      One flip-flop holding the parity: P* = P ⊕ x, output P, reset to 0. It is a T flip-flop with T = x.

      Why is assign clk_out = sel ? clk_b : clk_a; a dangerous way to switch between two clocks, and how does a glitch-free clock multiplexer work?

      Solution

      If sel changes while either clock is high, the output can produce a runt pulse (part of a high phase from one clock followed immediately by the other), which may clock some flip-flops and not others. A glitch-free mux gives each clock an enable flip-flop clocked on that clock's falling edge; each enable can turn on only after the other has turned off (they are cross-coupled through synchronizers), and each clock is ANDed with its enable before the two are ORed. Switching therefore happens only while both clocks are low, and there is a short gap with no clock rather than a glitch.

      Compare synchronous and asynchronous resets: one advantage and one risk of each.

      Solution

      Synchronous: reset is ordinary data, so it is timed by STA and filtered of glitches; but it needs a running clock to take effect and adds logic to the D path. Asynchronous: works without a clock and costs no data-path logic; but its release is asynchronous and can cause metastability or flip-flops leaving reset in different cycles, so it must be deasserted through a reset synchronizer. (Module 17)

      A producer writes bursts of 120 words, one per cycle at 200 MHz, and then stays idle long enough for the FIFO to drain. The consumer reads one word per cycle at 150 MHz continuously. What is the minimum FIFO depth?

      Solution

      A burst lasts 120/200 MHz = 600 ns. In that time the consumer removes 600 ns × 150 MHz = 90 words. The FIFO must absorb the difference: 120 − 90 = 30 words. Real designs add margin for the latency of synchronizing pointers across clock domains (a few entries) and for any consumer stalls.

      A vending machine accepts nickels (N) and dimes (D) and dispenses an item at 15 cents without giving change; extra money carries over. How many states, and what are the transitions?

      Solution

      States by credit: 0, 5, 10 cents (three, since 15 or more immediately dispenses). From 0: N → 5, D → 10. From 5: N → 10, D → 0 with dispense (15). From 10: N → 0 with dispense, D → 5 with dispense (20 − 15 = 5 carried). Dispense is a Mealy output on those transitions; a Moore version adds states for "dispensing".

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Timing, clocking and clock domains

      tclk→Q = 70 ps, logic delay 520 ps, tsetup = 40 ps. What is the maximum clock frequency?

      Solution

      Tmin = 70 + 520 + 40 = 630 ps → fmax ≈ 1.59 GHz. (Module 17)

      A path has tclk→Q,min = 30 ps, a minimum logic delay of 10 ps, and the capture flip-flop's hold time is 55 ps. Is there a problem? Does slowing the clock fix it?

      Solution

      30 + 10 = 40 < 55: a 15 ps hold violation. Slowing the clock does not help, since the period does not appear in the hold check. Insert delay (buffers) on that path or reduce clock skew.

      The capture clock arrives 50 ps after the launch clock. How does this skew affect the setup and hold checks?

      Solution

      Setup: the data has 50 ps more time (T + 50 ≥ tcq + tpd + tsu), which helps. Hold: the capture flop holds its sampling window open 50 ps later, so the new data must arrive at least 50 ps later than before (tcq + tcd ≥ th + 50), which hurts. Skew moves margin from one check to the other.

      A ring oscillator has 5 inverters, each with a 20 ps delay. What is its frequency? Why must the number of inverters be odd?

      Solution

      A transition must travel around the ring twice per period (once to flip every node, once to flip it back): f = 1/(2·N·tpd) = 1/(2 × 5 × 20 ps) = 5 GHz. With an even number of inversions the ring has a stable state (it is a latch, like cross-coupled inverters) and does not oscillate.

      What is metastability, and how much does adding a third flip-flop to a two-flip-flop synchronizer improve its MTBF?

      Solution

      When a flip-flop samples an input that changes within its setup/hold window, its internal loop can balance near the midpoint and take an unbounded time to resolve. The probability of still being unresolved after time t decays as e−t/τ. A third stage adds roughly one more clock period of resolution time, multiplying the MTBF by about eT/τ, an enormous factor (for T = 1 ns and τ = 20 ps, e50). The cost is one more cycle of latency.

      Why can't an 8-bit counter value be passed to another clock domain by putting a two-flip-flop synchronizer on each bit? Give two correct methods.

      Solution

      Bits that change at the same time may be sampled in different cycles, producing values the counter never held (for example 0111 1111 → 1000 0000 could be read as 1111 1111). Correct methods: convert to Gray code (one bit changes per increment) before synchronizing; or hold the value stable and pass a single handshake signal (request/acknowledge) through synchronizers; or use an asynchronous FIFO for streams of data.

      A block of logic takes 1.8 ns, but the design runs at 1 GHz, and its result is only needed every other cycle. How can the design be made to work without pipelining the logic?

      Solution

      Treat it as a multicycle path: make the source registers hold their values for two cycles and the destination register load only every second cycle (with an enable driven by a toggle flip-flop), then tell the timing tool that the path has two cycles for setup (and adjust the hold check accordingly). The logic then has 2 ns, enough for 1.8 ns plus register overheads.

      Why do designs use integrated clock-gating cells instead of an AND gate between the clock and an enable?

      Solution

      If the enable changes while the clock is high, an AND gate produces a truncated pulse (a glitch) that may clock some registers and not others. An ICG cell latches the enable while the clock is low, so the AND's enable input is stable whenever the clock is high and only whole pulses pass. Clock gating is still worth doing because it removes the dynamic power of idle registers and their clock wiring. (Module 15)

      A design fails at high temperature but passes at room temperature, and lowering the clock frequency fixes it. A second design fails at all frequencies but only on some chips. What kind of timing problem does each likely have?

      Solution

      The first is a setup problem: delays grow at high temperature (and low voltage), the critical path no longer fits in the period, and a slower clock gives it the time it needs. The second points to a hold problem (or a clock-domain-crossing bug): hold violations do not depend on frequency, and process variation makes some chips' short paths fast enough, relative to their clock skew, to fail.

      What is clock jitter, and how does it enter the setup equation?

      Solution

      Jitter is the variation of each clock edge from its ideal time, from noise in the PLL and clock network. In the worst case two edges arrive closer together than the nominal period, so the setup check uses the shortened period: T − tjitter ≥ tcq + tpd + tsu.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Verilog and RTL design

      After a rising edge, with a = 1, b = 0, c = 0 beforehand, what are b and c in each block?

      always @(posedge clk) begin b <= a; c <= b; end   // block 1
always @(posedge clk) begin b = a;  c = b;  end   // block 2
      Solution

      Block 1 (nonblocking): b = 1, c = 0 (c receives the old b): a shift register. Block 2 (blocking): b = 1, c = 1: c receives the new b. (Module 27)

      Write a parameterized modulo-N counter that outputs a one-cycle tick when it wraps.

      Solution
      module modn #(parameter N = 10, parameter W = $clog2(N)) (
    input  wire         clk, rst,
    output reg  [W-1:0] count,
    output wire         tick
);
    assign tick = (count == N - 1);
    always @(posedge clk)
        if (rst || tick) count <= 0;
        else             count <= count + 1'b1;
endmodule

      Using the tick as an enable for slower logic keeps everything on one clock.

      What is wrong with always @(a or b) y = a & b & c;?

      Solution

      The sensitivity list omits c, so in simulation y does not update when only c changes, while synthesis ignores the list and builds a 3-input AND: the simulated and synthesized designs disagree. Use always @* (or always_comb), or an assign.

      Write a 4-bit register that can load a parallel value, shift left with a serial input, or hold, selected by a 2-bit mode.

      Solution
      module shreg4 (
    input  wire       clk, rst, sin,
    input  wire [1:0] mode,          // 00 hold, 01 load, 10 shift left
    input  wire [3:0] d,
    output reg  [3:0] q
);
    always @(posedge clk)
        if (rst) q <= 4'b0000;
        else case (mode)
            2'b01:   q <= d;
            2'b10:   q <= {q[2:0], sin};
            default: q <= q;
        endcase
endmodule

      Explain the difference between == and === in Verilog, and why it matters in testbenches.

      Solution

      == is logical equality: if either operand has x or z bits, the result is x (unknown), which an if treats as false. === is case equality: it compares x and z literally and always returns 0 or 1. A testbench that checks if (out == expected) silently passes or fails wrongly when out is x (for example an uninitialized register); !==/=== catch it. Case equality is simulation-only and not synthesizable.

      What hardware does this produce?

      always @* begin
    count = 0;
    for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1)
        count = count + d[i];
end
      Solution

      The loop is unrolled at synthesis time into a chain (which the tool usually rebalances into a tree) of adders that sums the 8 bits of d: a population counter with a 4-bit result. Loops in synthesizable code describe replicated hardware, not repeated execution over time.

      Describe how to implement a 4-requester round-robin arbiter in hardware.

      Solution

      Keep a register with the index of the last granted requester. Mask the request vector so that only requesters after that index remain, and feed it to a priority encoder; if the masked vector is empty, use a second priority encoder on the unmasked requests (wrapping around). Grant the chosen requester (one-hot) and update the pointer. This gives every requester a turn within four grants, unlike a fixed-priority arbiter, which can starve low-priority requesters.

      Why do many designers write state machines with a separate clocked block for the state register and a combinational block for the next state, instead of one clocked block?

      Solution

      The two-block style mirrors the hardware (register + next-state logic), makes Mealy outputs and next-state values available combinationally, keeps blocking and nonblocking assignments in their proper places, and makes it easy to see that every state assigns every next-state value (with a default). A single clocked block is fine for Moore machines with registered outputs, but it registers everything assigned inside it, which can add an unintended cycle of latency to outputs.

      Find the clock-domain-crossing bug:

      // in clock domain B
always @(posedge clk_b) begin
    s1 <= a_valid & a_ready;   // a_valid, a_ready come from domain A
    s2 <= s1;
end
      Solution

      The synchronizer input is combinational logic of two signals from the other domain. The AND can glitch when its inputs change at different times, and the two inputs may be sampled inconsistently, so domain B can see a pulse that never existed in domain A. Compute the AND in domain A, register it there, and synchronize that single registered signal.

      Write a module that outputs a pulse one clock cycle wide every N cycles, without using a second clock.

      Solution

      Use a modulo-N counter and output its terminal count, as in the mod-N counter above: assign pulse = (count == N - 1);. Downstream logic uses pulse as a clock enable; generating a divided clock would create a new clock domain with skew and timing complications.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Computer architecture

      A program runs 5 × 109 instructions with a CPI of 0.8 on a 4 GHz processor. How long does it take?

      Solution

      5 × 109 × 0.8/(4 × 109) = 1.0 s. (Module 19)

      A 64 KB, 4-way set-associative cache with 64-byte lines serves 48-bit addresses. How many offset, index and tag bits?

      Solution

      Offset log2 64 = 6. Sets = 64 KB/(64 × 4) = 256 → index 8. Tag = 48 − 14 = 34. (Module 20)

      L1 hit time 1 ns, miss rate 5%; L2 hit time 8 ns, local miss rate 30%; DRAM 100 ns. Compute the AMAT.

      Solution

      1 + 0.05 × (8 + 0.3 × 100) = 1 + 0.05 × 38 = 2.9 ns.

      Why can summing a large 2-D C array column by column be many times slower than row by row?

      Solution

      C arrays are row-major. Row-by-row access is stride 1: every byte of each 64-byte line fetched is used. Column-by-column access jumps a whole row per element, so each access touches a different line, and for large arrays those lines are evicted before the next column could reuse them: up to one miss per element instead of one per 16 ints. Swap the loops (loop interchange) or tile.

      Compare write-through and write-back caches. Which is used for L1 data caches in most CPUs, and why?

      Solution

      Write-through sends every store to the next level (simple, the next level is always current, but heavy traffic); write-back updates only the cache and writes a dirty line back on eviction (much less traffic, needs dirty bits and more complex coherence). Most CPU L1 data caches are write-back (with write-allocate), because repeated stores to the same lines are common and bandwidth to L2 is limited.

      In a 5-stage pipeline with forwarding, which data hazard still causes a stall, and why? How does the compiler help?

      Solution

      The load-use hazard: a loaded value exists only at the end of MEM, too late to forward to an instruction that wants it in EX in the next cycle, so one bubble is inserted. Compilers schedule an independent instruction into the slot after the load. (Module 19)

      Base CPI 1. 20% of instructions are loads, half followed immediately by a dependent instruction (1 stall). 15% are branches, mispredicted 8% of the time with a 12-cycle penalty. What is the CPI?

      Solution

      1 + 0.2 × 0.5 × 1 + 0.15 × 0.08 × 12 = 1 + 0.1 + 0.144 = 1.244. Even an accurate predictor matters when the penalty is long.

      Why does a 2-bit saturating counter predict loop branches better than a 1-bit predictor?

      Solution

      A 1-bit predictor flips its prediction after the loop's single exit, so it mispredicts both the exit and the first iteration of the next execution of the loop. A 2-bit counter needs two consecutive mispredictions to change its prediction, so the exit only weakens it and the next run starts with a correct prediction: one miss per loop execution instead of two.

      A workload is 70% parallelizable. What speedup do 4 and 16 cores give, and what is the limit?

      Solution

      4 cores: 1/(0.3 + 0.7/4) = 2.11. 16 cores: 1/(0.3 + 0.7/16) = 2.91. Limit: 1/0.3 = 3.33. The serial 30% dominates quickly.

      x86-64 uses 48-bit virtual addresses, 4 KB pages and 8-byte page-table entries, with each page-table level occupying exactly one page. How many levels are needed, and how many bits does each level translate?

      Solution

      The page offset is 12 bits, leaving 36 bits of virtual page number. A 4 KB table holds 4096/8 = 512 entries = 9 bits per level. 36/9 = 4 levels of 9 bits. (Five-level paging extends this to 57-bit addresses.)

      What is a TLB, and what happens on a TLB miss?

      Solution

      The translation lookaside buffer is a small, highly associative cache of recent virtual-to-physical page translations, so that most memory accesses need no page-table walk. On a miss, hardware (or, on some architectures, software) walks the multi-level page table in memory to find the entry, fills the TLB and retries; if the page is not present in memory, a page fault transfers control to the operating system.

      Why does an out-of-order processor need a reorder buffer, if instructions are allowed to execute out of order anyway?

      Solution

      Execution may be out of order, but the architectural state must change in program order, so that an exception or a mispredicted branch leaves the machine exactly as if every earlier instruction completed and no later one did (precise exceptions and recoverable speculation). The reorder buffer holds completed results until all older instructions have completed, then commits them in order, and discards everything younger than a mispredicted branch or a faulting instruction.

      How can a C program determine whether the machine is little-endian?

      Solution

      Store a known multi-byte value and inspect its first byte: uint32_t x = 1; bool little = *(uint8_t *)&x == 1;. On a little-endian machine the least significant byte is at the lowest address. (Reading through a uint8_t or unsigned char pointer is allowed by the aliasing rules.) (Module 21)

      Two threads on different cores each increment their own counter in a loop, but the program runs far slower with two threads than with one. The counters are adjacent elements of an array. What is happening and how is it fixed?

      Solution

      False sharing: both counters share one 64-byte cache line, so each increment needs exclusive ownership of the line, which the coherence protocol takes away from the other core: the line ping-pongs between the cores' caches. Fix by placing each counter in its own line (padding or alignas(64)), or by accumulating in local variables and combining once at the end. (Module 22)

      No problems here match the current filter.

      GPUs and parallel computing

      A kernel is launched with 128 threads per block. Which global index does thread 5 of block 10 handle? How many blocks cover 10,000 elements?

      Solution

      10 × 128 + 5 = 1285. ⌈10,000/128⌉ = 79 blocks (with a bounds check for the last 112 threads). (Module 22)
