      Within a warp, half the threads take an if branch costing 200 cycles and half take the else branch costing 100 cycles. How long does the warp take? How could the code be restructured?

      Solution

      The warp executes both paths serially: 300 cycles, with half the lanes idle in each. Reorganize the data or the thread-to-work mapping so that the condition is uniform within each warp (for example, sort or partition the work so whole warps take the same branch), or replace the branch with arithmetic when both paths are short.

      Shared memory has 32 banks of 4-byte words. Which accesses by the 32 threads of a warp cause bank conflicts: s[tid], s[2*tid], s[32*tid], s[0]?

      Solution

      s[tid]: each thread a different bank, no conflict. s[2*tid]: banks 0, 2, …, 30, each used twice: 2-way conflict (two passes). s[32*tid]: all in bank 0: 32-way conflict. s[0]: all threads read the same word, which is broadcast without conflict.

      Why do GPUs devote relatively little area to caches and out-of-order logic, and how do they tolerate memory latency instead?

      Solution

      GPUs optimize throughput rather than single-thread latency. Each SM keeps many warps resident with all their registers on chip, and when one warp waits for memory the scheduler issues instructions from another in the next cycle at no cost. With enough warps in flight, the arithmetic units stay busy despite hundreds of cycles of memory latency, so area goes to ALUs and register files instead of large caches and speculation.

      A GPU has 40 TFLOP/s of compute and 1.6 TB/s of memory bandwidth. A kernel performs 4 FLOP per byte loaded. What performance can it reach, and what is the bottleneck?

      Solution

      min(40, 1.6 × 4) = 6.4 TFLOP/s: memory bound. The ridge point is 40/1.6 = 25 FLOP/byte; reaching peak would require improving data reuse (tiling in shared memory, fusing kernels) to raise the intensity.

      An SM has 64K 32-bit registers and supports up to 2048 resident threads. A kernel needs 40 registers per thread. How many threads can be resident, and what is the occupancy?

      Solution

      65,536/40 = 1638 threads, rounded down to whole warps (and allocation granularity): about 1632 threads (51 warps) → occupancy ≈ 51/64 ≈ 80%. Reducing to 32 registers per thread would allow 2048 threads (100%).

      Explain how tiling matrix multiplication into shared memory reduces global-memory traffic, and by roughly what factor for T × T tiles.

      Solution

      In a naive kernel each thread computing one output element reads a full row of A and column of B from global memory, so every input element is fetched N times. With tiling, a block loads a T × T tile of A and of B into shared memory once, synchronizes, and every thread in the block reuses those values T times. Each global element is therefore loaded N/T times instead of N times: traffic falls by a factor of about T (16 or 32 in practice), raising arithmetic intensity by the same factor.

      Many threads atomically increment bins of a 256-bin histogram in global memory, and the kernel is slow. Why, and what is the standard fix?

      Solution

      Atomics to the same address serialize, and popular bins see heavy contention in global memory. Privatize: each block accumulates a histogram in shared memory (fast atomics, contention only within the block), then adds its 256 bins to the global histogram once at the end.

      Implement an atomic increment using only compare_exchange_weak in C++, and explain why the loop is needed.

      Solution
      #include <atomic>

void increment(std::atomic<int>& x)
{
    int old = x.load();
    while (!x.compare_exchange_weak(old, old + 1)) {
        // on failure, old has been updated to the current value; try again
    }
}

      Another thread may change x between the load and the compare-and-swap; the CAS then fails (and reloads old), and the loop retries with the fresh value. The weak form may also fail spuriously on some architectures, which the loop handles. This read-modify-write retry pattern is the basis of lock-free algorithms.

      What is the difference between a data race and a race condition? Is volatile enough to prevent data races between threads in C++?

      Solution

      A data race is two threads accessing the same memory location concurrently, at least one writing, without synchronization: undefined behavior in C and C++. A race condition is any bug where correctness depends on timing, which can occur even with atomics (for example check-then-act). volatile is not enough: it neither makes operations atomic nor orders them between threads. Use std::atomic, mutexes, or other synchronization.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Circuits, CMOS and analog

      A 12 V source feeds a divider of 8 kΩ (top) and 4 kΩ (bottom). What is the output unloaded, and with a 4 kΩ load?

      Solution

      Unloaded: 12 × 4/12 = 4 V. Loaded: 4 kΩ ∥ 4 kΩ = 2 kΩ → 12 × 2/10 = 2.4 V. (Module 10)

      R = 2 kΩ, C = 10 nF. What are the time constant, the 10–90% rise time and the −3 dB frequency of the RC low-pass?

      Solution

      τ = 20 μs; rise time 2.2τ = 44 μs; fc = 1/(2π × 20 μs) ≈ 7.96 kHz.

      A chip has 50 nF of switched capacitance with an activity factor of 0.15, runs at 1.5 GHz and 0.9 V. Estimate its dynamic power, and the power if voltage drops to 0.75 V and frequency to 1.2 GHz.

      Solution

      P = αCV2f = 0.15 × 50 × 10−9 × 0.81 × 1.5 × 109 ≈ 9.1 W. Scaled: × (0.75/0.9)2 × (1.2/1.5) = × 0.694 × 0.8 = × 0.556 → about 5.1 W. (Module 12)

      Draw (in words) the static CMOS implementation of F = (A + B·C)′. How many transistors?

      Solution

      Pull-down (NMOS, implements A + BC): A in parallel with the series pair B–C. Pull-up (PMOS, the dual): A in series with the parallel pair B ∥ C. 6 transistors.

      Why are NAND gates generally preferred over NOR gates in CMOS?

      Solution

      A NOR has its PMOS transistors in series. PMOS carriers (holes) are 2 to 3 times slower than electrons, so series PMOS stacks must be made very wide to match drive strength, giving more area and input capacitance (logical effort 5/3 for NOR2 versus 4/3 for NAND2). A NAND puts the series stack in the faster NMOS. High fan-in NORs are especially slow.

      A driver has VOH = 2.4 V and VOL = 0.4 V; a receiver has VIH = 2.0 V and VIL = 0.8 V. What are the noise margins? Would a receiver with VIH = 3.5 V work?

      Solution

      NMH = 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 V; NML = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 V. With VIH = 3.5 V, NMH = −1.1 V: no, a high output can fall in the receiver's undefined region; a level shifter is needed. (Module 13)

      Choose a resistor for a green LED (VF = 2.2 V) at 8 mA from 3.3 V.

      Solution

      R = (3.3 − 2.2)/0.008 ≈ 137 Ω; use 150 Ω (7.3 mA). The small headroom (1.1 V) makes the current sensitive to VF variation.

      Design a non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 11, and an inverting amplifier with a gain of −5 and an input resistance of 10 kΩ.

      Solution

      Non-inverting: 1 + Rf/Rg = 11 → e.g. Rf = 100 kΩ, Rg = 10 kΩ. Inverting: Rin = 10 kΩ, Rf = 50 kΩ (−Rf/Rin = −5). (Module 11)

      A minimum inverter must drive a load equal to 256 times its own input capacitance. How many inverter stages minimize the delay, and roughly how much faster is that than driving the load directly?

      Solution

      Delay is minimized with a stage effort near 4: log4 256 = 4 stages, each 4 times larger than the previous. Using the model delay = effort + 1 per stage: direct = 256 + 1 = 257 units; chain = 4 × (4 + 1) = 20 units, about 13 times faster.

      An open-drain interrupt line at 3.3 V has 150 pF of capacitance and must rise from 0 to 2.0 V within 500 ns. Drivers can sink 4 mA at VOL = 0.4 V. What range of pull-up resistance works?

      Solution

      Rise: 3.3(1 − e−t/RC) = 2.0 → t = RC·ln(3.3/1.3) = 0.93RC ≤ 500 ns → R ≤ 500 ns/(0.93 × 150 pF) ≈ 3.6 kΩ. Sink limit: R ≥ (3.3 − 0.4)/4 mA ≈ 725 Ω. Choose, for example, 2.2 kΩ.

      A 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference: what is one LSB, and what is the ideal SQNR?

      Solution

      3.3/4096 ≈ 0.81 mV. SQNR ≈ 6.02 × 12 + 1.76 ≈ 74 dB.

      A 1 kHz sampling system sees a 940 Hz interference tone. At what frequency does it appear, and what should have been done?

      Solution

      |940 − 1000| = 60 Hz, inside the band of interest and indistinguishable from a real 60 Hz signal. An analog anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the ADC must attenuate everything above 500 Hz; aliasing cannot be undone digitally after sampling.

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Embedded C and bit manipulation

      Write macros to set, clear, toggle and test bit n of a register r.

      Solution
      #define BIT_SET(r, n)    ((r) |=  (1u << (n)))
#define BIT_CLR(r, n)    ((r) &= ~(1u << (n)))
#define BIT_TGL(r, n)    ((r) ^=  (1u << (n)))
#define BIT_TST(r, n)    (((r) >> (n)) & 1u)

      The parentheses around every argument and the whole expression protect against operator-precedence surprises when the macros are used with expressions. (Module 23)

      Write an expression that is true exactly when an unsigned x is a power of two.

      Solution

      x != 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0. Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and every bit below it, so the AND clears the lowest set bit; the result is 0 only if there was just one.

      Isolate the lowest set bit of x, and clear it.

      Solution

      Isolate: x & -x (for unsigned x, −x = ~x + 1, which keeps only the lowest 1). Clear: x & (x - 1). For x = 0b10110: x & −x = 0b00010; x & (x − 1) = 0b10100.

      Reverse the bits of a byte without a loop.

      Solution
      uint8_t rev8(uint8_t x)
{
    x = (uint8_t)(((x & 0xF0) >> 4) | ((x & 0x0F) << 4));   // swap nibbles
    x = (uint8_t)(((x & 0xCC) >> 2) | ((x & 0x33) << 2));   // swap pairs
    x = (uint8_t)(((x & 0xAA) >> 1) | ((x & 0x55) << 1));   // swap neighbors
    return x;
}

      Each step swaps groups of half the previous size: log2 8 = 3 steps. A 256-entry lookup table is the other common answer.

      What does the volatile qualifier do, and give two situations in embedded code that require it.

      Solution

      It tells the compiler that the object can change, or that accessing it has effects, outside the code it can see, so every read and write in the source must actually be performed, in order, and not cached in registers or removed. Required for memory-mapped hardware registers and for variables shared between an ISR and the main program. It does not make accesses atomic. (Module 25)

      Give three different meanings of the keyword static in C.

      Solution

      (1) A local variable declared static keeps its value between calls (static storage duration, initialized once). (2) A global variable or function declared static has internal linkage: visible only within its source file. (3) In an array parameter, int a[static 10] promises at least 10 elements (C99). (In C++ it additionally marks class members shared by all instances.)

      On a typical 64-bit platform, what is sizeof(struct { char c; double d; short s; }), and how can it be made smaller?

      Solution

      c at 0, 7 bytes of padding, d at 8–15, s at 16–17, padding to a multiple of 8: 24 bytes. Reordering to { double d; short s; char c; } gives 8 + 2 + 1 + 5 padding = 16 bytes. (Module 21)

      Which of these have undefined behavior in C for a 32-bit int x? (a) x << 32 (b) INT_MAX + 1 (c) (unsigned)UINT_MAX + 1u (d) -1 >> 1 (e) 1 << 31

      Solution

      (a) UB: shifting by the width or more. (b) UB: signed overflow. (c) defined: unsigned arithmetic wraps to 0. (d) implementation-defined (not UB; arithmetic shift giving −1 on common compilers). (e) UB in C (the result is not representable as an int), though common compilers produce INT_MIN; write 1u << 31.

      A circular buffer has N = 64 entries. Write the index update without a division or a branch, and explain why N should be a power of two.

      Solution

      head = (head + 1) & (N - 1);. For N = 2ᵏ, masking with N − 1 keeps the low k bits, which equals (head + 1) mod N. For other sizes the mask does not compute the modulus, and a % (a division) or a compare-and-reset is needed.

      Swap the two nibbles of a byte, and extract bits 5–2 of a byte as a number.

      Solution

      Swap: (uint8_t)((x << 4) | (x >> 4)). Extract bits 5–2: (x >> 2) & 0x0F.

      On an 8-bit microcontroller, a timer ISR increments a 32-bit tick counter. Write a function that safely returns the counter in the main program, and explain the failure it prevents.

      Solution
      #include <util/atomic.h>
volatile uint32_t ticks;

uint32_t get_ticks(void)
{
    uint32_t t;
    ATOMIC_BLOCK(ATOMIC_RESTORESTATE) {
        t = ticks;                 // four byte reads with interrupts disabled
    }
    return t;
}

      Reading 32 bits takes four separate byte loads. If the ISR increments the counter between them (for example from 0x0000FFFF to 0x00010000), the main program can assemble a torn value such as 0x0001FFFF that never existed. Disabling interrupts for the four loads makes the read atomic; restoring the previous interrupt state makes the function safe to call from code that already disabled interrupts. (Module 25)

      Every element of an array appears twice except one. Find it in O(n) time and O(1) memory.

      Solution

      XOR all elements: pairs cancel (a ⊕ a = 0) and XOR is associative and commutative, so the result is the unpaired element. The same identity underlies parity and RAID-5 reconstruction.

      With uint8_t a = 200, b = 100;, what are a + b > 255 and (uint8_t)(a + b) > 255? Why?

      Solution

      a + b is computed as an int after promotion, 300, so the first comparison is true. Casting to uint8_t gives 44 before the comparison, so the second is false. Integer promotion means small types never overflow inside an expression; truncation happens only when the result is stored or cast.

      Design a hardware debouncer for a push button sampled by a 1 MHz clock, accepting a new level only after it has been stable for 5 ms.

      Solution

      Synchronize the button with two flip-flops. Keep the current debounced output in a register and a 13-bit counter (5 ms × 1 MHz = 5000 < 213). Each clock: if the synchronized input equals the debounced output, clear the counter; otherwise increment it, and when it reaches 4999, copy the input to the output and clear the counter. Any bounce resets the count, so the output changes only after 5 ms of a stable new level. An edge detector on the output gives a one-cycle "pressed" pulse. (Module 24)

      No problems here match the current filter.

      Verification, implementation and silicon

      A synchronous FIFO has 8 entries, addressed by a write pointer and a read pointer. When both pointers are equal the FIFO could be empty or full. How do designers tell the two apart without a separate counter?

      Solution

      Make each pointer one bit wider than the address: 4 bits for 8 entries. The low 3 bits address the memory; the extra bit flips every time a pointer wraps around. Empty: all 4 bits equal (the reader has caught up with the writer on the same lap). Full: the low 3 bits equal and the top bits different (the writer is exactly one lap ahead, so write − read = 8). In an asynchronous FIFO the pointers are Gray-coded before crossing clock domains, and the full test becomes: the top two bits differ and the rest are equal. (Module 17)

      How would you verify a FIFO design? List the checking mechanisms and the scenarios you would make sure to cover.

      Solution

      Checking: a reference model (a simple queue in the testbench) and a scoreboard that compares every word read with the model's next word; assertions that a write when full and a read when empty are refused (or flagged), that the occupancy never exceeds the depth, and that the flags agree with the model. Stimulus: directed tests for reset, filling to full, draining to empty and the error cases, then constrained-random tests with random write and read patterns over long runs. Coverage, to know when to stop: full and empty both reached, simultaneous read and write while empty, full and in between, every pointer wrapping around, back-to-back full/empty transitions. For an asynchronous FIFO, add many clock-frequency ratios and phase relationships and a CDC analysis tool, because simulation alone does not model metastability. (Module 27)

      What is the difference between code coverage and functional coverage? Is 100% code coverage enough?

      Solution

      Code coverage is measured automatically from the RTL: which lines, branches, expressions, signal toggles and FSM states and transitions were exercised. Functional coverage is written by the verification engineer from the specification: which features, scenarios and combinations of conditions occurred (for example, "a burst write while the FIFO is one entry from full"). 100% code coverage is not enough: it cannot reveal functionality that is missing from the code, and it does not show that important combinations of conditions occurred together, or that the outputs were checked.

      Every request must be granted within 1 to 4 cycles. Write this as a SystemVerilog assertion and explain each part.

      Solution
      assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst)
                 req |-> ##[1:4] gnt)
    else $error("req not granted within 4 cycles");

      @(posedge clk) samples the signals at each rising edge. disable iff (rst) turns the check off during reset. req |-> is an implication: the property is checked starting at every edge where req is 1, and passes trivially elsewhere. ##[1:4] gnt requires gnt to be 1 at some edge 1 to 4 cycles later. The same property can be simulated as a checker or proved for all possible inputs by a formal tool.

      What does the stuck-at fault model assume, and what must a test pattern do to detect a stuck-at-0 fault on an internal node? How does scan help?

      Solution

      It models a manufacturing defect as one node permanently fixed at 0 or 1. To detect stuck-at-0 on node n, a pattern must excite the fault (set the inputs so that a good circuit drives n to 1) and propagate the difference to an observable output (set the other gates along a path so that the output depends on n). Deep inside sequential logic both are hard, because the inputs and outputs of internal logic are flip-flops. Scan chains let the tester load every flip-flop directly and read every flip-flop back, so each block of combinational logic between flip-flops can be tested as if its inputs and outputs were pins; ATPG tools then generate patterns covering typically more than 99% of stuck-at faults. (Module 28)

      A die of 6 cm2 is made in a process with 0.1 defects per cm2. Using the Poisson model, what fraction of dies are free of defects? Why do very large GPUs ship with some of their SMs disabled?

      Solution

      Y = e−D·A = e−0.6 ≈ 55%. Almost half the dies contain at least one defect, and most defects land in the large replicated arrays of SMs and cache. Designing the product with fewer active units than the die contains (for example 132 of 144 SMs) lets a die with defects in a few SMs be sold after those SMs are fused off, which raises the effective yield far above 55%. Dies are also binned by how many units work and how fast they run, into different products. (Module 28)

      A processor dissipates 300 W. The thermal resistance from junction to ambient is 0.2 °C/W and the air is at 35 °C. What is the junction temperature? What is the maximum power if the junction must stay below 105 °C?

      Solution

      TJ = 35 + 300 × 0.2 = 95 °C. Pmax = (105 − 35)/0.2 = 350 W.

      A chip draws 200 W at 0.8 V. What current flows, and what total resistance can the power-delivery network have if the IR drop must stay below 2% of the supply?

      Solution

      I = 200/0.8 = 250 A. 2% of 0.8 V is 16 mV, so R ≤ 16 mV/250 A = 64 μΩ, the reason a large chip uses thousands of power and ground bumps in parallel, thick upper metal layers, and voltage regulators placed close to the package. Fast changes in current add an L·di/dt droop on top of this, which on-die and package decoupling capacitors supply. (Module 28)

      Why does lowering the supply voltage together with the clock frequency (DVFS) save much more energy than lowering the frequency alone?

      Solution

      Dynamic power is αCV2f, and the energy per operation is αCV2, independent of frequency. Lowering only f lowers the power, but the task takes proportionally longer, so the energy to finish it stays about the same (and leakage energy grows, because the chip is on longer). Lowering V reduces the energy per operation quadratically. Voltage cannot drop alone, because gates slow down at lower voltage, so the frequency must drop with it: DVFS pairs each frequency with the lowest voltage that still meets timing. (Module 12)

      A design that reaches 2 GHz as an ASIC runs at only 300–500 MHz on an FPGA. Why? Why are FPGAs still used in chip development?

      Solution

      In an FPGA, logic is built from lookup tables and connected through programmable routing, chains of multiplexers and switches whose resistance and capacitance add delay at every hop; routing typically dominates the delay, and a function that is one optimized cell in an ASIC becomes one or more LUTs plus routing. FPGAs are still used because they can be reprogrammed in minutes: whole chips are prototyped or emulated on large FPGA systems before tapeout to run real software and find bugs months before silicon exists, and FPGAs ship in products whose volume does not justify an ASIC. (Module 21)

      What does clock-tree synthesis do, and why does the clock network matter so much for power?

      Solution

      It builds a network of buffers and wires (trees, H-trees or meshes) that distributes the clock from its source to every flip-flop with nearly equal arrival times (low skew) and sharp transitions, within the timing budget. The clock is the only signal that switches twice every cycle (activity factor 1) and it drives the clock pins of every flip-flop, so the clock network can account for a third or more of a chip's dynamic power, which is why clock gating is used so widely. (Module 17)

      A chip passes all its tests, but in the system it fails occasionally, only when a neighboring high-power block switches from idle to full activity. What are the likely causes, and how would you investigate?

      Solution

      The symptom points to supply noise: the sudden current step causes a voltage droop (IR drop plus L·di/dt) that slows the gates of the failing block until a critical path misses setup. Crosstalk from switching neighbors and temperature gradients are other candidates. To investigate: reproduce with controlled workloads; check whether the failure disappears at a lower frequency or a higher supply voltage (a strong sign of a timing margin problem); measure the supply with on-die droop detectors or monitors; and compare with power-integrity simulation of that scenario. Fixes include more decoupling capacitance, slowing down the ramp of the aggressor block (staggered wake-up), adaptive clocking that stretches the clock during droops, or more timing margin on the affected paths.

      No problems here match the current filter.
